# Fast, Cheap, Harmful: The Hidden Cost of Ultra-Processed Foods

Reliance on ultra-processed foods can reshape hormones and metabolism, with effects on fertility, pregnancy, and long-term health.

Fellow   [Aidan Stotz](https://publichealthpost.org/authors/aidan-stotz/)

 ![portrait of a young Black man looking at beverage products while grocery shopping](https://publichealthpost.org/wp-content/webp-express/webp-images/uploads/2025/11/DB_AS_Male-Repro-Health-Diet.png.webp)

Read Time: 3 minutes

Published:

 

[Ultra-processed foods](https://www.usnews.com/news/health-news/articles/2025-11-12/why-ultra-processed-foods-dominate-the-grocery-store-and-what-it-means-for-your-health) now stretch from the frozen aisle to the drive-thru, [showing up](https://publichealthpost.org/health-equity/home-cooking-crisis-processed-foods-dominate-american-diets/) at breakfast, lunch, and in late-night snacks. Instant noodles, sugary breakfast cereals, and—a college favorite—Hot Pockets, offer speed and low cost, but new research links this convenience to serious harm for men’s metabolic and reproductive health.

A recent [nutritional intake study led by Jessica M. Preston](https://www.cell.com/cell-metabolism/fulltext/S1550-4131(25)00360-2) examined how ultra-processed foods affect health in men aged 20-35. Over the course of three weeks, a group of 43 men rotated between ultra-processed and unprocessed diets. During the ultra-processed weeks, approximately 77% of calories came from industrially prepared foods in the highest [NOVA category](https://publichealthpost.org/health-equity/the-fdas-blind-spot-on-upfs/), including packaged ready meals, refined breads and cereals, processed meats, and sweetened drinks and desserts. During the unprocessed weeks, about two-thirds of calories came from whole or minimally processed foods like vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, eggs, and plain yogurt, with almost no ultra-processed products.

Even when the meals were matched for calories, men gained about one kilogram more fat on the ultra-processed diet, and markers like LDL cholesterol and blood pressure shifted in an unhealthy direction. The figure below zooms in on follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, which helps the testes make sperm. Each dot shows a man’s hormone levels before and after each diet.

On the ultra-processed plan (in yellow), most lines tilt downward, meaning FSH levels declined. The drop was strongest in the group given an extra 500 calories a day (on the right), a surplus that drives faster fat gain and puts added strain on the heart and blood vessels. In lab tests, sperm quality also began to slip, with total motility, or how well sperm move, trending downward. Together, higher fat mass, lower FSH, and less active sperm point toward poorer fertility and may signal higher risks for future heart disease.

The study also picked up changes in thyroid and appetite hormones, which help regulate energy use, hunger, and mood. These shifts line up with global concern about sperm counts falling by [more than half in the past 50 years](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/search/research-news/17742/) and growing rates of metabolic diseases, such as diabetes. Global diet changes, as well as the levels of phthalates, a chemical often used in [food packaging](https://publichealthpost.org/environment/cooking-up-contamination/), interact to [interfere with hormone signaling.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7559247/)

Heavy reliance on ultra-processed foods in young adulthood can quietly reshape hormones and metabolism, with ripple effects on fertility, pregnancy, and long-term heart and brain health. Small shifts toward beans, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables can improve markers like blood pressure and cholesterol, but no one shopper can fix a food system built around ultra-processed options. Policies such as front-of-package warning labels, [soda taxes](https://publichealthpost.org/health-equity/a-spoonful-of-sugar-a-spoonful-of-artificial-sweetener/), and stronger school meal standards can help make healthier foods the easier choice.

## Abstract

### Introduction

Fiscal policies can shift relative food prices to encourage the purchase and consumption of minimally processed foods while discouraging the purchase and consumption of unhealthy ultraprocessed foods, high in calories and nutrients of concern (sodium, sugar, and saturated fats), especially for low-income households.

### Methods

The 2017–2018 packaged food purchase data among U.S. households were used to derive household income- and composition-specific demand elasticities across 22 food and beverage categories. Policy simulations, conducted in 2022–2023, assessed the impact of national taxes on unhealthy ultraprocessed food and beverage purchases, both separately and alongside subsidies for minimally processed foods and beverages targeted to low-income households. Resultant nutritional implications are reported on the basis of changes in purchased calories and nutrients of concern. In addition, financial implications for both households and the federal government are projected.

### Results

A sugar-based tax on sugar-sweetened beverages would lower both volume and calories purchased with the largest impact on low-income households without children. Meanwhile, targeted subsidies would increase fruit, vegetable, and healthier drink purchases without substantially increasing calories. Under tax simulations, low-income households would make larger reductions in their absolute volume and calorie purchases of taxed foods and beverages than their higher-income counterparts, suggesting that these policies, if implemented, could help narrow nutritional disparities.

### Conclusions

Levying national taxes on unhealthy ultraprocessed foods/beverages and offering targeted subsidies for minimally processed foods/beverages could promote healthier food choices among low-income households. Such policies have the potential to benefit low-income households financially and at a relatively low cost for the federal government annually.

For each household and category, weekly purchase data were aggregated to a quarterly level. The analysis sample included 386,736 household-quarter observations from 11,152 low-income households and 47,518 higher-income households (Appendix Table 4, available online).

Appendix Figure 2 (available online) displays the sample's average per-capita household spending (dollars/quarter), purchase volume (oz/quarter), and energy content (kcal/day) by category. Assuming no food waste and a 2,000 kcal/day reference diet, these 22 categories provide approximately 47% of daily energy requirements. The largest sources of purchased calories are unhealthy ultraprocessed desserts/sweets, snacks, unhealthy ultraprocessed dairy products, and high-sugar SSBs. These categories also contribute significantly to purchased sugar, sodium, and saturated fats (Appendix Figure 3, available online).

Concerning unit prices, unhealthy versions of UPFs were often more expensive than their BFY counterparts for many categories but not all (Appendix Figure 4, available online). Within each subpopulation based on household income and composition, similar patterns in spending, energy, and nutrient content across categories can be seen; however, households without children generally spent more per capita on each category than households with children (Appendix Figures 5–8, available online).

args.summary:
This is a research article published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine (Volume 67, Issue 1, July 2024, pp. 3-14) titled "Promoting Healthier Purchases: Ultraprocessed Food Taxes and Minimally Processed Foods Subsidies for the Low Income" by Pourya Valizadeh, PhD (Texas A&M University) and Shu Wen Ng, PhD (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill).

**Purpose:** To predict the impact of nationwide taxes on unhealthy ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) and subsidies for minimally processed foods (MPFs) for low-income households, assessing changes in purchased calories, nutrients of concern, and financial implications.

**Methods:** The study used 2017–2018 Nielsen Homescan Panel data (packaged food purchases from 11,152 low-income and 47,518 higher-income U.S. households). Products were classified into 22 categories using WIC nutritional standards and Chile's 2012 Food & Marketing Law thresholds. A demand system model estimated household income- and composition-specific price elasticities. Policy simulations were conducted in 2022–2023.

**Key Findings:**
- A sugar-based tax on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) would lower both volume and calories purchased, with the largest impact on low-income households without children.
- Targeted subsidies would increase fruit, vegetable, and healthier drink purchases without substantially increasing calories.
- Under tax simulations, low-income households would make larger reductions in absolute volume and calorie purchases of taxed foods/beverages than higher-income households, suggesting the policies could help narrow nutritional disparities.
- The policies could benefit low-income households financially at a relatively low cost for the federal government annually.

**Conclusion:** Levying national taxes on unhealthy UPFs/beverages and offering targeted subsidies for MPFs/beverages could promote healthier food choices among low-income households.

# Food Prices for Nutrition DataHub: global statistics on the Cost and Affordability of Healthy Diets

![Image](/content/dam/wbr/stayconnected/icons-linkin32x32.svg "LinkedIn")

![fpn banner](/content/dam/photos/480x125/2022/jun/banner-FPN-header-480-x-125.jpg)

![fpn banner](/content/dam/photos/480x125/2022/jun/banner-FPN-header-480-x-125.jpg)
![A world map showing the number of people unable to afford a healthy diet by size of bubble for each country, and the percentage of each country's population affected, shown by shade of color.](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sWCuw/full.png)

The**Food Prices for Nutrition DataHub**provides access to global statistics of a healthy diet and related indicators. These [data](https://databank.worldbank.org/source/food-prices-for-nutrition) use food item availability and prices from the [International Comparison Program](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/icp) (ICP), combined with food composition data and nutritional requirements from a wide range of sources including [the Healthy Diet Basket](https://www.fao.org/agrifood-economics/publications/detail/en/c/1601210/) based on national dietary guidelines.

The 51 indicators and their metadata cover:

#### ***Diet cost***

#### ***Diet affordability***

For further information on definitions and methods please refer to [Methodology](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/icp/brief/foodpricesfornutrition#3).

[ [Back to page top](#D_top) ]

**DATA HIGHLIGHTS**

[ [Back to page top](#D_top) ]

## Cost of a healthy diet and the population unable to afford the diet in countries

The cost per person per day of a healthy diet in each economy with data for the years 2017 to 2025 is plotted against the prevalence of unaffordability or the share of population who cannot afford the diet. Data on the number of people affected are also provided.

![scatter visualization](https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/29708713/thumbnail)

[ [Back to page top](/en/programs/icp/brief/foodpricesfornutrition?cq_ck=1646845586643#D_top) ]

**Food Prices for Nutrition** was established to provide governments and development agencies with accurate and updated metrics to inform agricultural, food systems, social protection, and health and nutrition interventions.

Food Prices for Nutrition's outputs – indicators of the cost and affordability of diets and food groups and data for over 170 countries - use observed consumer prices and household expenditures to provide an operational measure of people’s access to locally available foods in the proportions needed for health.

The cost and affordability (CoAHD) indicators developed by Food Prices for Nutrition underlie the estimates published in United Nations' 2020 report [The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World](https://www.fao.org/publications/sofi) (SOFI) that over 3 billion – or two in five people on the planet - could not afford a healthy diet in 2017. These data were used to frame the [2021 UN Food System Summit summary and statement of action](https://www.un.org/en/food-systems-summit/news/making-food-systems-work-people-planet-and-prosperity). Ongoing global food inflation and supply shocks further underscore the need for timely data on the cost and affordability of healthy diets and nutritious food items and groups. The [Food Prices for Nutrition Datahub](https://databank.worldbank.org/source/food-prices-for-nutrition), as the authoritative source for internationally standardized statistics, indicators, and granular data, meets this need for a global cohort of policy makers, development analysts, and other users.

Since 2022, in close collaboration with Food Prices for Nutrition global partners, the World Bank and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) have led the methodological improvement for these indicators, and systematically monitor and disseminate the data series. The latest data and estimates reported in the [SOFI 2025 report](https://www.fao.org/publications/fao-flagship-publications/the-state-of-food-security-and-nutrition-in-the-world/en) show that the total number of people unable to afford a healthy diet in 2024 was around about 2.6 billion, about one third of the global population. This is a reduction in the global prevalence of unnaffordability following the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, the recovery has been uneven, with a worsening trend in low-income countries and the sub-Saharan African region.

Food Prices for Nutrition supports efforts within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture by 2030 ([SDG 2](https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/hunger/)). It can also support the monitoring of progress towards the World Bank’s objective of [building food systems that can feed everyone, everywhere, every day](https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/agriculture/brief/food-security-update) by promoting “nutrition-sensitive agriculture” and improving food safety.

[ [Back to page top](#Overview_top) ]

 The **Food Prices for Nutrition DataHub**'s diet cost and affordability indicators use the least cost combination of locally available foods to meet the needs of a representative adult requiring 2,330 kcal per day at three levels of diet quality: a healthy diet; a nutrient adequate diet; and an energy sufficient diet.   ![ladder of unaffordability showing three diet standards and a woman and ladder](https://worldbank.scene7.com/is/image/worldbankprod/new-ladder-July-13?wid=780&hei=439&qlt=85,0&resMode=sharp)

![ladder of unaffordability showing three diet standards and a woman and ladder](https://worldbank.scene7.com/is/image/worldbankprod/new-ladder-July-13?wid=780&hei=439&qlt=85,0&resMode=sharp)

[ [Back to page top](#M_top) ]

![chart visualization](https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/24462231/thumbnail)

**COST INDICATORS**

For each of the diets listed above, costs per day are based on requirements for a median adult woman aged 19-30 in a healthy population as defined by the World Health Organization. For the Cost of a Nutrient Adequate Diet and the Cost an Energy Sufficient Diet, please refer to the Food Policy article [“Cost and affordability of nutritious diets at retail prices: Evidence from 177 countries”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306919220301871) (Bai et al. 2021).  Information on the variation in the cost of nutrient adequacy by age, sex and reproductive status can be found in the Lancet article "[Global variation in the cost of a nutrient-adequate diet by population group: an observational study](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanplh/article/PIIS2542-5196(21)00285-0/fulltext)" (Bai, Herforth and Masters 2022).

[ [Back to page top](#M_top) ]

**AFFORDABILITY INDICATORS**

The affordability of each diet is measured by comparing diet costs to available income and four affordability metrics for each level of diet quality are calculated. According to an[updated method applied in 2024](https://files-faostat.fao.org/production/CAHD/Methods_Brief_FAOSTAT_CoAHD_indicators.pdf), the first three indicators rely on the food expenditure share and basic non-food expenditure share of low-income consumers by countries’ income group classification, based on [recent household survey data](https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/opendata/pandemic-prices-and-poverty) compiled by the World Bank. This updated method was also used for [The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World](https://doi.org/10.4060/cd1254en)(SOFI) 2024 report. The fourth metric uses actual food expenditure. The metrics available are:

args.key_excerpts: The cost and affordability (CoAHD) indicators developed by Food Prices for Nutrition underlie the estimates published in United Nations' 2020 report The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI) that over 3 billion – or two in five people on the planet - could not afford a healthy diet in 2017., The latest data and estimates reported in the SOFI 2025 report show that the total number of people unable to afford a healthy diet in 2024 was around about 2.6 billion, about one third of the global population., Food Prices for Nutrition's outputs – indicators of the cost and affordability of diets and food groups and data for over 170 countries - use observed consumer prices and household expenditures to provide an operational measure of people's access to locally available foods in the proportions needed for health., The Food Prices for Nutrition DataHub's diet cost and affordability indicators use the least cost combination of locally available foods to meet the needs of a representative adult requiring 2,330 kcal per day at three levels of diet quality: a healthy diet; a nutrient adequate diet; and an energy sufficient diet., According to an updated method applied in 2024, the first three indicators rely on the food expenditure share and basic non-food expenditure share of low-income consumers by countries' income group classification.
args.summary: The Food Prices for Nutrition DataHub is a World Bank-hosted platform providing global statistics on the cost and affordability of healthy diets across over 170 countries. It uses data from the International Comparison Program (ICP), food composition data, and nutritional requirements based on the Healthy Diet Basket approach. The platform tracks 51 indicators covering diet cost (cost per day for a healthy, nutrient adequate, and energy sufficient diet) and diet affordability (comparing diet costs to available income). Key findings from the SOFI 2025 report indicate that approximately 2.6 billion people (about one-third of the global population) could not afford a healthy diet in 2024, representing a reduction from the COVID-19 pandemic peak in 2020, though recovery has been uneven with worsening trends in low-income countries and sub-Saharan Africa. The initiative supports SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and the World Bank's food security objectives. The indicators use the least-cost combination of locally available foods to meet the needs of a representative adult requiring 2,330 kcal per day at three diet quality levels. The platform provides access to data via DataBank, Data Catalog, and Data360, and includes reports, papers, blogs, and media coverage on related topics.

# The latest

# How inflation is hurting the diets of low-income Americans

Michael Howerton

![A man in background reaches into a microwave to grab a TV dinner in foreground.](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/f8dfdd95-874d-4c9c-92db-aeea2e0e6e19/Drupal/NEWS_Man-reaching-for-microwave-dinner-Monkey-Business-Images-Shutterstock.jpg) 

Photo credit: Monkey Business Images // Shutterstock

 

## Eating healthy is costly in America; rising prices are making Americans reach for sugary, processed foods

 

Rising inflation at the supermarket has changed the way Americans buy food, altering family menus and daily diets as shoppers stretch their dollars to feed their families. Higher food prices [hurt those with lower incomes](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/what-are-social-determinants-of-health "Addressing the social determinants of health") the most, limiting access to healthy food and impacting long-term health.

In particular, the price of healthy foods has surged. One study from the University of Warwick found that Americans pay 40% more for fruits and vegetables due to enormous fixed costs in supplying them to markets, resulting in less consumption of these healthier foods. A 2022 national survey found that the perceived high cost of healthy food was the biggest barrier to a healthier diet, with nearly half (46%) of respondents saying so.

The result is that Americans are compensating by eating too many sugary and ultra-processed foods — which tend to be cheaper and more durable — and not enough fruits, vegetables, and other nutrient-rich whole foods. Despite government programs encouraging and subsidizing healthy foods, the problem is only growing.

"There's evidence that inflation continues to shape food choices, particularly for low-income Americans who prioritize price over healthfulness," [Constance Brown-Riggs, MSEd, RDN, CDCES, CDN](https://www.diversityindiabetes.org/care-directory/new-york/constance-brown-riggs/404d0ebf-000f-4b6b-a193-b4db18c918b3#:~:text=Constance%20is%20the%20past%20chair,the%20Long%20Island%20Dietetic%20Association. "About Constance Brown-Riggs"), a registered nurse and nutritionist specializing in [diabetes care](https://www.northwell.edu/endocrinology-diabetes-metabolism/treatments/nutritional-counseling-and-diabetes "About nutritional counseling for diabetes at Northwell"), told Stacker.

According to the International Food Information Council's 2024 Food & Health Survey, at least 3 in 4 American consumers cited price as a key driver of food purchases; however, just over half (55%) of low-income households ranked healthfulness as a top factor. In contrast, the healthfulness of food purchases only became more important than the price for those households earning $100,000 or more.

![A woman with a full shopping cart stops to examine a bottle of milk.](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/e09e85fd-bf5f-4317-84cd-8ca3cd720728/Drupal/NEWS_Stacker-story-9-Stokkete-Shutterstock.jpg)   

### [How US dietary recommendations have changed over the last 50 years](https://www.northwell.edu/news/the-latest/us-dietary-recommendations-changes-last-50-years)

   Guidelines are updated every 5 years. Learn what's changed in every installment — and what hasn't.    [Read more](https://www.northwell.edu/news/the-latest/us-dietary-recommendations-changes-last-50-years)

 

"These results highlight the disparity in how income influences food priorities," Brown-Riggs said, adding that higher food prices often increase [food insecurity](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/food-insecurity-growing-wellness-on-wheels "Food insecurity: growing Wellness on Wheels"). "These shifts increase the risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and [obesity](https://www.northwell.edu/endocrinology-diabetes-metabolism/conditions/obesity "Obesity: what it is, how it's treated")."

The United States Department of Agriculture's [Healthy Eating Index](https://www.fns.usda.gov/cnpp/hei-scores-americans "USDA: HEI scores for Americans") reflects this need for better-quality American diets. The most recent index found that Americans (older than 2) scored an average of 58 out of 100, which is hardly encouraging.

"It has become increasingly clear that diet-related chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular disease, [type 2 diabetes](https://www.northwell.edu/endocrinology-diabetes-metabolism/conditions/diabetes0 "Type 2 diabetes: what it is, how it's treated"), obesity, [liver disease](https://www.northwell.edu/doctors-offices/northwell-health-center-for-liver-disease-and-transplantation "About the Center for Liver Disease and Transplantation at Northwell"), some types of cancer and [cavities](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/sugar-rotten-teeth-causes-remedies "How sugar causes rotten teeth") pose a major public health problem for Americans," the [2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines for Americans](https://www.dietaryguidelines.gov/sites/default/files/2021-03/Dietary_Guidelines_for_Americans-2020-2025.pdf "2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines for Americans report") report found. Adults over 60 did a bit better, averaging a score of 61.

Northwell Health partnered with Stacker to examine how rising prices for healthy foods impact low-income families, using data from the USDA's Healthy Eating Index.

![A graph showing Americans' consumption of various food groups, set against Department of Agriculture recommendations.](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/9d8df0cf-5494-49d7-8ddf-f4e54dcb2f01/thumbnail/webimage-US-eating-habits-stray-from-dietary-guidelines)

 

## Americans aren't eating enough whole foods

 

While several factors contribute to the quality of American diets, rising prices are a meaningful component. With the cost of goods rising across the economy, consumers must make difficult choices regarding necessities like food.

The USDA [estimates](https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/food-nutrition-assistance/food-security-in-the-us/key-statistics-graphics "USDA: Food insecurity in U.S. households") that 18 million households experienced food insecurity in 2023, an increase of 1 million households since 2022. About 3.2 million families with children under 18 had to reduce or skip their meals altogether. With increasing costs at the cash register, everyday healthy foods may be too expensive for millions of Americans. As a result, many are skimping to fill their shopping carts, but more affordable foods can sometimes come at a higher cost to their long-term health.

When cost is a factor, more people opt for these processed foods, which tend to be cheaper, have longer shelf lives, and produce a short-term feeling of being full due to containing higher carbohydrates, said Aimee Aristotelous, nutritionist and bestselling author of "Almost Keto" and "The Whole Food Pregnancy Plan."

"These items are convenient, calorie-dense, widely accessible, and marketed aggressively," she said. Cheap and easily available items like this include breakfast cereals, pasta, deli meats, ultra-processed snack foods, sugary beverages, shelf-stable and frozen meals, and packaged desserts.

"The health implications of these processed foods are dire, as most consist of empty calories that offer little nutrition," Aristotelous added. In other words, she said, the average American diet, when cost-conscious, lacks sufficient whole foods.

![A woman with short gray hair and eye glasses points to a banner that reads ](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/9f8a94c3-a139-434d-8a42-98e236982413/Drupal/NEWS_wellness-on-wheels-anastasia-schepers.jpg)       ![A woman with short gray hair and eye glasses points to a banner that reads ](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/9f8a94c3-a139-434d-8a42-98e236982413/Drupal/NEWS_wellness-on-wheels-anastasia-schepers.jpg)

 

### [Food insecurity: Growing Wellness on Wheels](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/food-insecurity-growing-wellness-on-wheels)

   Northwell’s mobile nutrition education program, Wellness on Wheels, brings interactive learning directly to schools and is one way health systems can address child food insecurity.    [Read more](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/food-insecurity-growing-wellness-on-wheels)

![A man brings a bucket of fresh produce to a doorstep. A woman at left accepts the bucket.](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/f77b2057-324b-444c-bc67-1554abd19c32/thumbnail/webimage-NEWS_Produce-bucket-Andrey-Popov-Shutterstock)

 

## Local and state governments work to improve food access

 

Government-funded programs such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) are two primary food assistance programs that provide low-income Americans with resources to purchase healthy food. Many use these benefits to buy fruits, vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, dairy products, bread and cereals, eggs, and baby foods and formulas.

Many local programs also try to alleviate some of the burden of high prices at the cash register. For instance, the Local Initiatives Support Corporation invests in food outlets like groceries, food co-ops, and farmers markets in urban and rural communities nationwide to support healthy food distribution. Another example is New York City's Green Carts program, which works to increase access to fresh fruits and vegetables in its neighborhoods.

As much as these advocacy and subsidy programs help, the downward trend in healthy eating is pervasive. Inflation makes shopping for healthy food harder but not impossible. It's about habits as much as price tags.

"An effective way to allocate more money to healthy foods is to eliminate empty-calorie foods and beverages from the grocery list," Aristotelous said. "Soda, packaged desserts, and chips are actually quite expensive in comparison to other nutritious selections."

![An Asian child rides on a shopping cart at the supermarket. Ram Raju, MD, calls to eliminate food insecurities by partnering state and local agencies with health care.](https://dam.northwell.edu/asset/e99750f7-1f61-486a-969c-d8f1df032f8b/Drupal/NEWS_New-York-must-lead-the-fight-on-food-insecurity.jpg)   

### [New York must lead the fight on food insecurity](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/new-york-must-lead-the-fight-on-food-insecurity)

   Ram Raju, MD: Partnership between state and local authorities and health care is critical to addressing the social issues impacting health and wellbeing.    [Read more](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/new-york-must-lead-the-fight-on-food-insecurity)

For example, she said, $5 can buy a six-pack of Coca-Cola or a gallon of milk. It can purchase five pounds of bananas or a large bunch of broccoli, while a bag of chips could be the same price.

"Whole foods that are less expensive than many unhealthy processed foods include sweet potatoes, lettuces, cabbage, carrots, squash, beans, lentils, quinoa, oranges, frozen berries, apples, canned fish, ground beef, and poultry," Aristotelous said. "Not only does it cut significant expenses, but drinking water as one's primary beverage is also the most beneficial beverage option for wellness."

Brown-Riggs offered two main tips for budget-friendly healthy meal planning: Buy in bulk and choose plant-based proteins. Nonperishable items like whole grains, beans and frozen vegetables can be purchased in large quantities to save money over time. Plant-based protein sources, such as beans and lentils, as well as eggs and canned fish, are also available and are often more affordable than meat.

Beyond the prices on store shelves, healthy eating is a complex issue that requires attention — and not just on an individual level. As the [American Heart Association](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001031#d1e1305 "AHA Journals: 2021 dietary guidance to improve cardiovascular health") pointed out, structural racism and neighborhood segregation plays a role in what gets on people's plates. These systemic issues have created "food deserts" and environments that often burden Black and Hispanic communities.

 

The government defines a food desert as an area with a poverty rate of at least 20% and where at least 33% of the population live more than 1 mile (or 10 miles in rural areas) from a grocery store. In these communities, residents often need access to public transit or a car and gas to reach their nearest supermarket. This makes it even more expensive to find healthy foods as transportation is the second-highest household expense behind housing and has also undergone widespread inflationary increases. Research has found that fast-food restaurants and advertising for processed foods and beverages often proliferate in food deserts, making them an unhealthy but far more convenient and affordable choice.

Apart from individual financial support, efforts can also be made to mount larger initiatives, such as [installing gardens](https://www.northwell.edu/news/insights/podcast-breaking-the-cycle-of-poverty-through-urban-farming-education "Urban farming: the health benefits of Harlem Grown") at schools, incentivizing grocery stores to be set up in underserved neighborhoods, and education programs that inform people about the benefits of healthy eating.

"We need a huge effort from a lot of fronts," prominent nutrition scholar Penny Kris-Etherton told the American Heart Association. "It needs to be across the board from multiple domains, and it really has to be intertwined."

Rising food prices, particularly for healthy foods, are forcing many to choose cheaper, ultra-processed foods over nutritious options. # Prioritizing profit over public health, corporations target Black and Latino children with ‘junk food’ marketing

U.S. food apartheid enhances the effectiveness of advertising for highly processed, calorie-dense, and nutritionally deficient prepackaged foods

![](https://prismreports.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Jennifer-K.-Rumple-Photo-150x150.jpg?crop=1)  by [Jennifer K. Rumple](https://prismreports.org/author/jennifer-k-rumple/)

### Share this:

* [Share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://prismreports.org/2026/07/22/junk-food-advertising-children/?share=x&nb=1)

![](https://i0.wp.com/prismreports.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GettyImages-2282115300-scaled.jpg?fit=780%2C520&ssl=1) 

FIFA World Cup meal is seen at a McDonald’s, on June 20, 2026. Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images

 

*Real journalists wrote and edited this (not AI)—independent, community-driven journalism survives because you back it.*[*Donate*](https://prismreports.org/ways-to-give/)*to sustain Prism’s mission and the humans behind it.*

Jeanette Driskell said she “was born with a silver spoon” in her mouth. She grew up in San Francisco’s Presidio, one of the most affluent neighborhoods in the Bay Area.

Her upbringing was a stark contrast to her 20s, when she became a single mother living in subsidized housing in the inner city’s Filmore District, about four miles away from her coastal childhood home.

At that time, Driskell relied on public assistance while taking care of her young daughter, working, and going to school full time. She didn’t have a car, so she took the bus to attend college classes and walked five blocks to the closest full-service supermarket.

“There were liquor stores and fast-food chains on every corner. To go buy real food for me and my daughter was a chore. McDonald’s was my go-to place,” said Driskell, 57. “It was quick. It was easy. It was cheap. My daughter loved the chicken nuggets. She’d always say, ‘I want a kids meal!’ You know, with the toys and everything?”

Rooted in a capitalist system that prioritizes profit over public health, those seemingly harmless toys play a significant role in the multibillion-dollar fast-food industry that markets unhealthy food to children, particularly those who are Black and Latino. The broader food industry also profits from exploiting systemic inequalities to target vulnerable communities, who have little access to healthy foods due to limited income, redlined neighborhoods, or [food apartheid](https://prismreports.org/2026/06/03/childrens-health-food-apartheid/).

Food systems under capitalism have always targeted BIPOC communities and their children, according to the health- and food-focused nonprofit organization [Food Empowerment Project](https://foodispower.org) (F.E.P.).

“Advertising has always been used as a tool of colonization, teaching BIPOC and low-income communities to view certain products as necessary for health, even when those products may harm their bodies,” explained Tyra Willis, F.E.P.’s communications team member, in an email.

“Corporations have the power to raise or lower prices, they choose not to. Corporations have the power to supply every community with affordable, healthy food choices. They choose not to. Corporations have the power to make harmful foods seem normal or necessary,” Willis added. “Profit and control continue to be the driving priority, not community, nor our well being.”

#### Disparity by design

The lack of access to healthy food choices enhances the effectiveness of marketing for highly processed, calorie-dense, and nutritionally deficient prepackaged foods. These cheaper, unhealthy options—often referred to as “junk food”—are more accessible and often more appealing. Fast food and similar items high in sugar, fat, and salt can be addictive because they [trigger the brain’s pleasure centers](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4059590/). The food industry peddling these unhealthy options are overwhelmingly profit-driven. Corporations seek to maximize revenue by targeting the communities most vulnerable to exploitation and least protected by political power, including by tapping deeply into cultural identity and aspirations, experts told Prism.

Clay Venetis, a policy associate at the [Center for Science in the Public Interest](https://www.cspi.org), advocates for better rules and practices for companies marketing food to kids. He told Prism that the industry often uses consumer culture as bait.

“They will use Bad Bunny for doing the Super Bowl halftime show or the World Cup. … It’s about tapping into a cultural moment to drive consumption,” Venetis said. “That is manipulative because culturally significant moments are emotional, which makes you a prime target for being influenced into doing something like making an impulse buy of an unhealthy product.”

Those unhealthy products, such as highly processed foods, are enormously profitable. Corn syrup, refined flour, oils, salt, and chemical additives are inexpensive to manufacture and have long shelf lives. Companies can produce them cheaply and sell them at huge markups. In contrast, fresh produce is perishable, labor intensive, and often less profitable. To maximize profits, corporations selling unhealthy products [aggressively target](https://sph.cuny.edu/life-at-sph/news/2022/07/06/predatory-marketing/) lower-income households that frequently face time constraints, lack of money, or access to buy healthier foods.

Driskell, who now lives in Oakland, recalled her younger years living in an upscale, suburban neighborhood with a backyard garden full of produce. Her family also made weekly visits to the local butcher for freshly cut meats.

“I went from that to eating highly processed and fast foods with my young daughter on the regular,” she said. “It’s frustrating. Sometimes I feel angry because if I was living in a white neighborhood, it wouldn’t be like this. The quality of food is better in an upscale neighborhood than it is in the projects. And, you sure don’t see these fast-food advertisements everywhere you turn.”

In June 2021, the University of Connecticut’s [Rudd Center for Food Policy and Health](https://uconnruddcenter.org) published its most recent [study](https://media.ruddcenter.uconn.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/2909/2024/06/FACTS2021.pdf) about food advertising to children. Researchers found that fast-food companies spent around $5 billion on advertising in the U.S. in 2019—an increase of more than $400 million since 2012. Those spending dollars are not uniformly distributed. The study found that advertising for unhealthy food products targeted Black and Hispanic youth significantly more than their white counterparts.

“Companies often put their money behind their least healthy products and target those to Black and Latino young consumers. We have evidence that there are disproportionate effects of diet-related disease among those groups. It’s higher,” said the Rudd Center’s Director of Marketing Initiatives Frances Fleming-Milici. “So when you target those groups with your least healthy products, you are making the problem worse.”

“It’s helping the bottom line, but it’s not helping the individuals who are consuming it,” she added.

Fleming-Milici has spent the last 15 years researching and analyzing race and ethnicity differences in the rates of exposure to unhealthy food and beverage advertising, and the impact of these practices on youth. Her current focus is to determine the effects of this marketing on parents.

“It’s really hard to have your children want to consume healthier foods. … It really saddens me when I step into communities and see the food environment, how it’s worse,” Fleming-Milici told Prism. “I think about the barriers people have to obtaining food, in terms of being accessible, affordable, and having the time.”

“Some parents are holding down a couple of different jobs and maybe have to have their kids be alone more often than other families,” Fleming-Milici added. “It’s just way, way, way harder in these communities. It doesn’t seem fair at all, really.”

#### Cradle-to-grave marketing

The Rudd Center also notes that food, beverage, and restaurant companies [annually spend](https://uconnruddcenter.org/research/food-marketing/) nearly $14 billion on advertising in the U.S.—80% of which promotes fast food, sugary drinks, candy, and unhealthy snacks. Corporations use a [wide array](https://uconnruddcenter.org/research/food-marketing/packaging-promotions-claims/) [of tactics](https://uconnruddcenter.org/research/food-marketing/tv-digitalmedia/) to make unhealthy products irresistibly appealing to kids. Cartoons with colorful mascots, celebrity endorsements, and popular influencers all play a role.

Sports sponsorships link unhealthy products to excitement and team loyalty, while mobile gaming ads, social media campaigns, and YouTube influencers target kids online. The Coca-Cola Company, for instance, frequently promotes elite athletes by featuring them on limited-edition, collectible packaging such as cans and soccer ball-shaped bottles. These campaigns are often tied to global sponsorships for major events, such as the Olympics and Paralympic Games, NCAA Championships, and the FIFA World Cup. Another popular advertising tactic is to place QR codes on products so that fans can scan it to unlock digital content, interactive quizzes, and sweepstakes to win official merchandise or game tickets.

Venetis, of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, is also a dad. He said his young son, like many other kids, is “very into superheroes.” Coca-Cola has partnered with Marvel Entertainment, placing Marvel Universe heroes and villains on limited-edition bottles and cans that also feature QR codes to access augmented reality animations and sweepstakes.

“These are sugary drinks that have packaging that’s very attractive. … [My son] will see the superhero on the soda can and express a want in it. It becomes a whole conversation, a back-and-forth as a parent,” said Venetis. “It may be after work. You may be tired, and sometimes parents cave. It takes a lot out of you and feels very unfair because it’s purely driven by these companies wanting to profit and having no consideration for a parent’s attempts at raising a healthy kid.”

Coca-Cola does not publicly disclose its spending on advertising to children, but it does tout its “[responsible marketing policy](https://www.coca-colacompany.com/policies-and-practices/legal-and-practices/responsible-marketing-policy),” which claims not to market directly to children younger than 13. Community health advocates call the policy a [public relations smokescreen](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10261624/), arguing that Coca-Cola and other corporations’ [broad marketing tactics and sponsorships](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10261624/) still reach and influence young kids.

The Coca-Cola Company did not respond to Prism’s requests for comment. Neither did McDonald’s Corporation.

Brands also partner with schools, placing their products and advertising directly into classrooms and cafeterias by way of vending machines, sponsored events, and other efforts. The omnipresence of this multiple-channel marketing ensures that children in targeted communities are bombarded with unhealthy food messages, the effects of which can last a lifetime. This is known as “cradle-to-grave” marketing.

Fleming-Milici explained corporations’ thinking behind the strategy. “‘Get them when they’re young, and they may stay with us for 10 to 20 years.’ The most egregious example from what I’ve looked at and studied is going into schools as partners and giving scholarships and things under the guise of good will. It’s profit over people.”

She also gave an example of food corporations pushing unhealthy products in “cause-related campaigns” that are important to Black and Latino neighborhoods, including donating money to childhood education, hunger relief, and equity initiatives.

“The perception is the company cares about the community and the young people in it and that they’re doing good things,” added Fleming-Milici. “It creates a positive corporate image that could last a long time. But the thing I think could be really helpful is if they created and marketed healthier food.”

Food corporations increasingly use sophisticated data analytics to [micro-target children](https://uconnruddcenter.org/research/food-marketing/tv-digitalmedia/) based on their ZIP codes, ethnicity, online behaviors, and purchasing patterns. In the digital age, precision advertising taps into how consumers use social networks, streaming platforms, and mobile games.

Children of color often face disproportionate exposure to this highly tailored marketing, particularly through platforms such as TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, where influencer campaigns align junk food with cultural icons. This kind of algorithmic targeting amplifies disparities, creating a relentless presence of unhealthy food marketing in the daily lives of Black and Latino children in low-income communities.

“I think that we have a culture in this country that’s pretty accepting of advertising. There is potentially a lack of recognition or lack of caring of the biased intent of advertising—especially with online influencers who have branded content that’s embedded into what they’re doing,” said Venetis. “Many times kids have very strong parasocial relationships, not realizing they’re being paid to talk about these products or play video games in a certain way.”

Venetis added that better education to recognize this bias may help kids and their parents look at things more critically.

“These unhealthy food companies use cultural moments and important milestones or events in kids’ lives as Trojan horses to sneak in their advertising. The goal is to hit people at the exact moment they’re most likely to be moved emotionally,” said Venetis. “Right then, you get the person to consume more of your unhealthy product.”

> The goal is to hit people at the exact moment they’re most likely to be moved emotionally. Right then, you get the person to consume more of your unhealthy product.
>
> Clay Venetis, Center for Science in the Public Interest policy associate

Marion Nestle, a public health advocate and professor of nutrition and food studies at New York University, agreed.

“Of course it’s a Trojan horse. That’s the whole point of community support and funding community activities,” said Nestle. “If you get kids to like and want a product, they will pester their parents for it and consume it for life.”

#### Accountability gaps

Food and beverage giants [spend millions of dollars](https://www.opensecrets.org/federal-lobbying/industries/summary?id=N01) lobbying to block regulations that would curb advertising to children, including state efforts to implement a soda tax, food warning labels, or advertising bans. This political influence allows corporations to shape public policy to protect profits at the expense of public health.

Driskell is now raising her 17-year-old grandson and 15-year-old granddaughter, both of whom are African American and Filipino. When Prism asked Driskell what she’d like food industry giants to know about how their targeted marketing strategies impact her family, she responded with questions of her own.

“How would they feel if these were the only food choices they had—eating the way lower-class citizens eat? How would they feel if the shoe was put on the other foot? Would they want to be eating McDonald’s every night? Would they want a fast-food restaurant and liquor store on every corner in their neighborhood? Hell no, they would not,” Driskell said.

“I don’t think it would make a difference, but it would get them thinking in different terms or a different way,” she added. “It would definitely start raising some type of awareness within their thinking.”

Federal agencies such as the [Department of Health and Human Services](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7955455/) (HHS), the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/pcd/issues/2011/sep/10_0272.htm) (CDC), and the [Federal Trade Commission](https://www.ftc.gov/food-marketing-to-children-and-adolescents) (FTC) classify targeted food marketing as a significant public health concern. Data also confirms “[racialized marketing](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9014864/)” and the private sector’s profit-driven practices contribute directly to higher rates of [diet-related diseases](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4501500/) among Black and Hispanic youth, childhood obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease being the top three.

Such practices exemplify negative [commercial determinants of health](https://www.who.int/health-topics/commercial-determinants-of-health#tab=tab_1) (CDoH). In this case, “Big Food” influences public health through aggressive marketing, lobbying, and research manipulation. The term is widely recognized for how these profit-driven actions negatively impact public health and reinforce inequities.

HHS does not specifically mention CDoH in its [Healthy People 2030](https://odphp.health.gov/healthypeople) initiative  to “set data-driven, national objectives to improve health and well-being over the next decade.” Instead, its focus is on the [social determinants of health](https://odphp.health.gov/healthypeople/priority-areas/social-determinants-health) (SDoH), environmental conditions that impact peoples’ health and contribute to disparities and inequities. Access to nutritious foods is listed as an SDoH, giving the example that people without “access to grocery stores with healthy foods are less likely to have good nutrition.” HHS’ stated [plan of action](https://odphp.health.gov/healthypeople/about/healthy-people-2030-framework) not only includes setting data-driven objectives, but also providing tools for evidence-based interventions and tracking progress across local and national levels.

Food justice advocates argue that these measures don’t go far enough, pointing to [HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://prismreports.org/2026/04/06/rfk-jr-maha-movement/) and the agency focusing on personal behavioral changes and not adequately confronting the corporate practices and systemic racism that underpin these issues.

“Children are raised inside a system of misinformation from the start, making them easy targets for future consumers rather than supporting them as a whole human, worthy of health and the tools to thrive,” Willis of F.E.P. explained. “Parents and our youth are blamed for food choices that they were groomed to make through corporate manipulation, colonialism, and racism. Real collective change requires us to confront systems, corporations, and organizations that prioritize profit over the people.”

That’s why advocates are calling for more robust regulations, including stringent limits on child-targeted advertising, better support for food sovereignty, and policies directly addressing economic inequality.

Venetis said more federal intervention is necessary to hold food and beverage companies’ “feet to the fire” for using deceptive marketing practices to manipulate kids.

Nestle also believes it’s the government’s responsibility to ban the advertising and marketing of unhealthy foods to children, put warning labels on these foods, and prevent them from being offered or sold in schools or supplied to their sports teams, as well as to “put far greater resources into improving school breakfasts and lunches, where many children get most of their daily calories.”

A [recent survey](https://www.childnourishlab.org/_files/ugd/383bcd_0a42f43b97f84f26860a980a284e5d91.pdf) of 1,226 school districts across eight states found that the majority of schools regularly served convenience foods and/or quick preparation foods, which primarily consisted of processed and ultraprocessed foods.

Fleming-Milici said clear initiatives and plans are what’s needed for true change.

“Getting the food industry to change is really hard. … There’s discussion of the importance of it. But without putting the supports in place to make it happen, how is it going to happen?” she said. “The proof is where you put the money and where you put the policy. And, when you don’t put the money behind the marketing of your healthier products, having them really just appears to be a public relations stunt. … There needs to be government policies that go across the board.”

HHS and the CDC did not respond to Prism’s requests for comment. The FTC’s Office of Public Affairs declined to comment.

#### Reclaiming health and justice

Food justice activists say real progress requires coordinated action: stronger policies restricting child-directed marketing, investment in equitable food access, community-led solutions rooted in food justice, and an unwavering demand for corporate accountability.

“In addition to trying to get laws passed, it’s organizing. It’s coalition building. It’s pressuring,” explained Venetis. “It’s making sure these companies recognize that they have their own responsibility to do something here—to check and see whether they’re overleveraged on unhealthy products and how they can shift their growth strategy toward healthier products.”

To address some of these issues, the Center for Science in the Public Interest is rolling out a consumer advocacy campaign called “[Flatten Big Soda](https://www.cspi.org/FlattenBigSoda).” The effort combines public pressure and policy to end aggressive advertising and marketing for sugary, sweetened beverages—demanding that companies reduce their multibillion-dollar budgets for these drinks and instead focus on marketing unsweetened alternatives.

“It will change. I do stand by that. It will change with a change in demand,” Venetis said. “A corporation is obligated to increase shareholder value. If the demand drops, then they have to accommodate. They have to shift their strategy.”

F.E.P. is largely focused on leveraging education for change. The organization encourages BIPOC children and their communities to actively interrogate examples of targeted marketing and see it as “a local issue instead of something distant or out of sight, out of mind,” explained Willis.

“Our mission is to help consumers make healthy and compassionate choices—which is why it is essential to educate and empower youth,” she added. “Young people are directly affected by the food system and should absolutely have a seat at the table in shaping the future they will inherit.”

Key findings include:
- Fast-food companies spent approximately $5 billion on U.S. advertising in 2019, with disproportionate targeting of Black and Hispanic youth compared to white youth (per University of Connecticut's Rudd Center for Food Policy and Health).
- Food, beverage, and restaurant companies spend nearly $14 billion annually on advertising in the U.S., with 80% promoting fast food, sugary drinks, candy, and unhealthy snacks.
- Corporations use sophisticated tactics including celebrity endorsements (e.g., Bad Bunny), sports sponsorships (FIFA World Cup, Olympics), QR code promotions, school partnerships, social media influencers, and algorithmic micro-targeting based on ZIP codes, ethnicity, and online behavior.
- The concept of "cradle-to-grave" marketing aims to hook children young for lifelong consumption.
- Federal agencies (HHS, CDC, FTC) classify targeted food marketing as a significant public health concern, with "racialized marketing" linked to higher rates of diet-related diseases (obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease) among Black and Hispanic youth.
- Food companies spend millions lobbying to block regulations on child-targeted advertising, soda taxes, and warning labels.
- Food justice advocates (Food Empowerment Project, Center for Science in the Public Interest) call for stronger regulations, including banning unhealthy food ads to children, warning labels, and policies addressing economic inequality. The CSPI's "Flatten Big Soda" campaign is one initiative pushing for change.
- The article profiles Jeanette Driskell, a mother who experienced the contrast between affluent and food-apartheid neighborhoods, illustrating how limited access to healthy food makes junk food marketing more effective in low-income communities of color.

The piece concludes that real change requires coordinated action: stronger policies, investment in equitable food access, community-led solutions, corporate accountability, and shifting consumer demand.

Prevention: Marketing to children

# Unhealthy food marketing and children: exposure and impact

Last updated 23-04-2026

Marketing of foods that are highly processed and high in sugar, salts, and fat undermine efforts towards healthy diets across populations. Children of all ages are vulnerable to the effects of marketing of unhealthy foods. Research has shown that young children’s exposure to food marketing effects their preference, requests and consumption of unhealthy foods. Older children (who make their own purchasing decisions) are also influenced by unhealthy food marketing through positive brand attitudes, and increased purchase and consumption of unhealthy foods. Children and adolescents encounter unhealthy food marketing through their daily lives, including online, as they travel to school, on television, through sports sponsorships, on packaging for unhealthy food products, and through collectible toys.

## Key Evidence

The average Australian 5 to 8-year-old is exposed to at least 827 unhealthy food advertisements on television each year

Australian adolescents are exposed to almost 100 promotions per week from online sources

Children aged 4 to 6 years believe a product tastes better if it has a cartoon character on the pack

Australian children see and interact with a large number of promotions for unhealthy foods that come from a variety of sources. Australian children aged 5 to 8-years-old are exposed to at least 827 unhealthy food advertisements on television each year.[1](#cite561) Australian adolescents are exposed to almost 100 promotions each week coming from online sources.[2](#cite2023) The majority of food and drink advertisements near schools and on children’s journeys to schools feature unhealthy products.[3](#cite2024) A study from Perth showed that schools have an average of 36 food advertisements within 500 m of the grounds.[3](#cite2024)

There is also evidence that children who come from a more socioeconomically disadvantaged background may be exposed to high volumes of unhealthy food marketing. For example, a study quantifying the nature and extent of food marketing across train stations in Sydney found that the highest proportion of advertisements for unhealthy foods occurred in areas with the lowest socioeconomic status.[4](#cite2026) Another study in Perth found more food advertisements and a higher proportion of unhealthy food advertisements near schools in lower socioeconomic areas.[3](#cite2024)

Food marketing influences the diets of children of all ages by taking advantage of their vulnerabilities as they age. For example, children younger than about 5 years are unable to tell the difference between a program and an advertisement. Even older children who can identify advertising lack the cognitive skills and experience to critically interpret marketing messages.[5](#cite555) Adolescent brains are biased towards rewards and they are more likely to respond to cues in the environment, such as marketing.[6](#cite556) Adolescents also have their own purchasing power and are heavily influenced by their peers.[7](#cite557) The food industry takes advantage of this, particularly with social media, using highly targeted and personalised marketing messages to encourage the purchase and consumption of their products.

Studies have found that exposure to unhealthy food advertisements increases food intake among children.[8](#cite9810) For example, an Australian study showed that children aged 7 to 12 years increased food intake following exposure to unhealthy food marketing, and did not compensate for this by reducing food intake at a subsequent meal.[9](#cite981)

## Online marketing of unhealthy food

Digital marketing is an important tool to market unhealthy food to children and teenagers as they spend significant amounts of time online. On a typical weekday, Australian 15-year-olds spend about two hours online when they are not at school, and a quarter of them are online for more than four hours.[10](#cite569) Research by the Australian eSafety Commissioner found that teens spent an average of 14.4 hours per week online, most often researching things that interest them, and watching videos, movies or TV.[11](#cite2035) An analysis of online activities among Australian 14 to 17-year-olds found a growing trend towards streaming of video and audio content.[2](#cite2023) Other popular activities included social networking, uploading content such as photos and videos, and playing games online.

As they spend time online, Australian children see a lot of unhealthy food marketing. A 2021 Australian study found that for every hour children (aged 13 to 17 years) are online, they are exposed to 17 unhealthy food advertisements.[2](#cite2023)

Unhealthy food marketers can target children and teenagers using digital media in various ways. Data driven advertisements, targeted and personalised to the characteristics of the users, are seamlessly integrated within social media feeds and website content. Influencers are used to endorse products and brands, including the use of ‘kidfluencers’ to promote food and drink products and brands among younger audiences.[12](#cite9816) Food companies are also promoting their products and brands through user generated content. For example, unhealthy food companies have been found to use social media app TikTok to encourage users to create short videos featuring their products and brands, in the words of TikTok, turning users into “unofficial brand ambassadors”.[13](#cite9818) In-game marketing, such as the placement of food and beverage logos or brands in virtual worlds, use of “advergames” (an online game created with the primary intention to promote a product or brand) by food companies are also used to embed products and brands into games and sponsorship of popular gaming influencers or the incorporation of branded content in live stream gaming further amplify the reach of unhealthy food marketing to children. Marketing on social media encourages teenagers to like and share brand posts with their friends, thereby harnessing the influence of peer networks.[14](#cite1388)

Adolescents are especially vulnerable to unhealthy food marketing online due to the strong engagement with technology, including social media platforms, gaming, streaming services and e-sports. A recent study of Australian children aged 10 to 16 years found that watching food-branded video content on YouTube and seeing favourite food brands advertised online were significantly associated with higher consumption of unhealthy food and drinks.[15](#cite572) A UK study found an increased intake of unhealthy snacks among children who viewed images of social media influencers with unhealthy snacks on Instagram, compared to children who had viewed images of influencers with healthy snacks or non-food products.[16](#cite985)

A US study found that playing food-branded ‘advergames’ increased children’s consumption of unhealthy snack foods, compared to playing advergames featuring healthy foods and non-food advergames.[17](#cite984) Within advergames, the technique of ‘rewarded video advertising’ in which players are shown an ad before progressing to a new level was shown to be particularly effective. An Australian study of children aged 7 to 12 found that children exposed to rewarded video advertising within an advergame chose the promoted brand significantly more than children in other arms of the study, when offered a choice of snacks afterwards.[18](#cite1389) Children exposed to the rewarded video advertising were far more likely to choose the promoted brand even compared to children who played an advergame with the promoted brand included as high-value game pieces, highlighting the sophisticated nature of advertising techniques being used to market unhealthy food to children online.

Digital media gives marketers data that can be used to target children based on their online behaviours, social networks, browsing history, app usage and device location data. Online marketers are building extensive, detailed profiles of anyone using the internet to tailor their marketing messages in unprecedented ways.

The World Health Organization’s Regional Office for Europe explains:[19](#cite578)

*Advertising delivered to users on the Internet is tailored either to the content that a user is viewing on a site (contextual advertising) or to characteristics and preferences of each individual user (online behavioural advertising). To deliver contextual advertising, information on users is collected within the website, app or platform itself. To deliver online behavioural advertising, all participants in the advertising ecosystem collect and sell extensive information on users, drawn from dozens or more trackers on any one site or platform. Information on users is merged from multiple Internet locations and devices to create deep individual profiles that go far beyond basic demographics. User profiles include detailed data on online browsing activity, devices and networks used, geo-locations, personal preferences and “likes” and social activities in digital social networks.*[19](#cite578)

Online marketing also relies on inferred information, where advertisers make educated guesses about users based on patterns of behaviour. For example, if a user frequently visits fast-food websites or watches food related content, advertisers may infer a preference for certain types of foods, even if the user has never directly provided such information. Inferred data, combined with explicit information, allows for highly refined advertising strategies that anticipate users' food and beverage choices, encouraging them to engage with specific products or brands. Advertisers follow children “throughout the day, at moments of happiness, frustration, hunger and intent” to deliver advertising with maximum impact.[19](#cite578) Marketers aim to engage children in emotional, entertaining experiences and encourage them to share these with friends.

## Television advertising of unhealthy food

Commercial television viewing is independently associated with obesity in children (not just because it is a sedentary activity) and researchers conclude this link is likely due to advertising of unhealthy foods.[20](#cite559) The promotion of unhealthy products not only encourages brand switching within a product category but increases consumption of particular categories of foods including fast food and soft drinks.[21](#cite982) It attracts new customers[22](#cite558) and establishes societal norms around acceptable and desirable foods.[23](#cite2027)[24](#cite560)

Studies from many countries have shown that marketing of unhealthy foods on television frequently targets children. Internationally, unhealthy food advertisements are more frequent during children’s typical viewing times, during school holidays, on children’s channels and around children’s programming.[23](#cite2027) In Australia, unhealthy food and drink advertisements are more common during children’s peak viewing times, but less common during school holidays.[25](#cite2030)[26](#cite2031)[27](#cite2032) A wide range of creative strategies are used that are likely to appeal to young people. These include celebrity endorsements, animations and promotional characters. International studies of television and other media have shown that these creative strategies were more common in the marketing of food to children than to adults.[23](#cite2027)

Researchers have calculated that the average Australian 5 to 8-year-old, who watches around 80 minutes of television each day, is exposed to at least 827 advertisements or four hours of unhealthy food advertising on television each year.[1](#cite561) However, the amount of free-to-air television that Australian children watch is continuing to decline.[28](#cite9814)

An Australian study of children aged 10 to 16 years found exposure to television advertising – not just the amount of time spent watching television – was associated with increased consumption of unhealthy food and drinks.[29](#cite562) The study found that the link between television viewing and poor diet was strongest for children who watched the most commercial television and were exposed to advertisements at the time of broadcast or did not skip through advertisements.[29](#cite562) A study of English children aged 6 to 13 years found that children had a greater preference for high-fat and high-carbohydrate foods (both branded and unbranded) after being exposed to food advertisements, compared to when the same children were shown control advertisements on a separate occasion.[30](#cite983) The effect was greatest in children who had high regular levels of television viewing.

## Other marketing of unhealthy food

While television and online advertising of unhealthy food to children forms a large part of the evidence base for the impact of advertising on children, the effect of **other types of marketing** has also been studied.

**Product packaging** that includes the presence of cartoon characters has been found to influence taste perceptions in young children. A recent systematic review found that children had significantly higher taste preferences for unhealthy foods when they are packaged with cartoons or licensed characters.[31](#cite9823) In one US study of children aged 4 to 6 years they believed a product with a cartoon character tasted better than the same food in a package without the character.[32](#cite564) In another US study, children aged 3 to 5 years tasted identical pairs of food and drink but felt they tasted better if they were in McDonald’s branded packaging.[33](#cite565)

**Collectible toys** are another means of altering children’s food preferences, and research has shown they can be used to encourage healthy choices. A US study of children aged 3 to 5 years found children were more likely to choose a meal with a collectible toy regardless of whether the meal was healthy or unhealthy.[34](#cite566) A similar Australian study of 5 to 9-year-olds found children were significantly more likely to select a healthier meal that included a collectible toy over an unhealthy meal without a collectible toy.[35](#cite567)

**Sports sponsorship** also influences children’s preferences. An Australian study of 10 to 14-year-olds involved in local sport found high awareness of their clubs’ sponsors, particularly when they were food and beverage companies.[36](#cite568) A majority of children in the study thought their club’s food and beverage sponsors were 'cool', and liked to return the favour to these sponsors by buying their products. Many of the children had received a voucher from a food or beverage company to reward good sport performance (86%), or a sporting certificate displaying a food or beverage company logo (76%). Another more recent Australian study found that most parents are concerned with sponsorship of local sport by unhealthy local and large food companies.[37](#cite9825)

**Outdoor advertising** can expose children to unhealthy food marketing as they move through their daily lives. Studies of routes taken by Australian children as they travel to school have found that children can view up to 37 unhealthy food advertisements each way to school[38](#cite9830), and that most of the outdoor advertisements near schools are for unhealthy foods or alcohol.[3](#cite2024)

**Retail outlets** (in-store or online) also strategically place unhealthy foods in prominent locations such as at end-of-aisles, islands, entrances, and checkouts to capture attention and stimulate impulse purchases. A 2020 study examining more than 100 Australian supermarkets found that unhealthy foods were consistently more likely than healthy foods to be placed at prominent store locations, with this being higher in supermarkets located in disadvantaged areas.[39](#cite9832) Parents report that these placement based marketing strategies undermine their efforts to support healthy food habits with their children.[40](#cite9834) Retailers also promote the purchase of unhealthy foods through use of price promotions, such as price discounts and multi buy offers. Price promotions typically lead to higher purchase volumes and may increase consumption of promoted products, particularly for unhealthy foods.[41](#cite4628) For more information on the use and impact of price promotions, and policies to address them, please see the Obesity Evidence Hub page on [Unhealthy food price promotions](https://www.obesityevidencehub.org.au/collections/prevention/new-approaches-restrictions-on-price-promotions).

**Child directed marketing** is commonly used to market unhealthy food. Brands use "fun" to make unhealthy food more appealing to children. This includes playful names (e.g., "party mix" lollies, "fun-sized" chocolate bars), bright colours, cartoon characters, and creative shapes like Freddo Frogs. McDonald's pioneered this approach in 1979 with the Happy Meal – a toy-packed kids' meal in a colourful box that remains a global success.

This emphasis on fun shifts children's relationships with food, making eating about entertainment rather than the food itself.[42](#cite584) It also diverts attention from health concerns and can lead to overconsumption. As children grow, marketing strategies evolve – "fun" gives way to "cool," with brands using viral campaigns to encourage peer sharing.[43](#cite986) However, it is important to note that even when marketing doesn’t explicitly focus on fun or excitement, children are still influenced by repeated exposure to branding, product placements, and endorsements, which shape their food preferences and choices over time.[44](#cite2028)

*Content for this page was reviewed and updated by Rebecca Bennett and Kathryn Backholer at the Global Centre for Preventive Health and Nutrition at Deakin University. For more information about the approach to content on the site please see* [***About | Obesity Evidence Hub***](https://www.obesityevidencehub.org.au/about "https://www.obesityevidencehub.org.au/about")*.*

args.summary:
This webpage from the Obesity Evidence Hub, last updated 23-04-2026, examines the exposure and impact of unhealthy food marketing on children. It provides comprehensive evidence that marketing of highly processed foods high in sugar, salt, and fat undermines healthy diets, with children of all ages being vulnerable to these effects. Research shows exposure influences children's preferences, requests, and consumption of unhealthy foods.

**Key Evidence:**

- The average Australian 5 to 8-year-old is exposed to at least 827 unhealthy food TV ads per year
- Australian adolescents are exposed to almost 100 promotions per week from online sources
- Children aged 4-6 believe a product tastes better with a cartoon character on the pack
- Children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds face higher exposure to unhealthy food marketing

**Online Marketing:** Digital marketing is a key tool for targeting children. Australian 15-year-olds spend about 2 hours online daily on weekdays. For every hour online, children aged 13-17 are exposed to 17 unhealthy food ads. Techniques include data-driven targeted ads, influencer marketing (including "kidfluencers"), user-generated content campaigns on TikTok, advergames, and rewarded video advertising. The WHO notes that online advertisers build deep individual profiles using data from multiple sources to deliver highly targeted messages.

**Television Advertising:** Commercial TV viewing is independently associated with childhood obesity. The average Australian 5-8 year old watching 80 minutes of TV daily is exposed to 4 hours of unhealthy food advertising annually. Studies show exposure to TV advertising is associated with increased consumption of unhealthy foods, with children watching commercial television most affected.

**Other Marketing Channels:**
- **Product packaging:** Cartoon characters significantly influence taste preferences in young children
- **Collectible toys:** Can alter children's food preferences, including being used to encourage healthier choices
- **Sports sponsorship:** High awareness among children aged 10-14 of club sponsors; most parents concerned about unhealthy food sponsorship
- **Outdoor advertising:** Children can view up to 37 unhealthy food ads each way to school
- **Retail outlets:** Unhealthy foods placed in prominent locations, especially in disadvantaged areas
- **Child-directed marketing:** Uses "fun" to make unhealthy food appealing, shifting children's relationship with food toward entertainment

Food, beverage and restaurant companies spend almost [$14 billion](https://uconnruddcenter.org/research/food-marketing/) per year on advertising, more than 80% of which promotes fast food, sugary drinks, candy, and unhealthy snacks. In 2019,kids and teens saw an average of two [fast-food ads](https://media.ruddcenter.uconn.edu/PDFs/FACTS2021.pdf) per day on television alone.

Because the beverage industry spends millions of dollars every year marketing to communities of color, African American children and teens see more than [twice](https://www.cspinet.org/resource/facts-sugar-drink-marketing) as many ads for sugary drinks than their white peers. Targeted marketing practices also contribute to African American and Hispanic youth consuming more sugary drinks and having higher rates of diabetes and heart disease, on average, compared to their white peers.
