The detrimental effect of UPFs on the gut microbiome and on the gut barrier.

## 2. Ultra-Processed Foods (UPFs)

### 2.1. The NOVA Classification System

The NOVA classification system is recognized by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations as a reliable tool for nutrition and public health research and policy development to classify “all foods according to the nature, extent, and purposes of the industrial processes they undergo” [[6](#B6-nutrients-17-00859),[7](#B7-nutrients-17-00859)], helping consumers to differentiate foods based on their level of processing and the types of ingredients used. In this system, food is categorized into four groups:

* (i)

  NOVA1: Unprocessed or Minimally Processed Foods. These foods undergo minimal processing, such as removing inedible parts and using methods like drying, crushing, and pasteurization, without adding chemicals like sugar, salt, or oils. This category includes cereals such as wheat and rice, legumes, and dairy products like milk and yogurt without added sugars [[6](#B6-nutrients-17-00859)].
* (ii)

  NOVA2: Processed Culinary Ingredients. This group includes ingredients derived from NOVA1 foods or processed through methods like pressing, refining, and grinding. Examples include salt, sugar, honey, butter, and vegetable oils, which are rarely consumed alone. It also includes items made from two NOVA2 components, such as salted butter and iodized salt. These ingredients are essential for cooking and enhance the flavor and preparation of minimally processed foods [[6](#B6-nutrients-17-00859)].
* (iii)

  NOVA3: Processed Foods. These foods are created by adding sugar, oil, salt, or other NOVA2 substances to NOVA1 foods, typically featuring two or three ingredients. Preservation and cooking methods, including non-alcoholic fermentation for items like bread and cheese, are used to enhance the durability and sensory qualities of NOVA1 foods. This category includes canned vegetables, canned legumes, salted nuts, cured meats, cheeses, and freshly baked bread [[6](#B6-nutrients-17-00859)].
* (iv)

  NOVA4: UPFs. These foods are characterized by industrial formulations with five or more ingredients; these products often include additives not commonly found in culinary preparations, alongside sugars, oils, fats, salt, and preservatives. UPFs usually contain little to no NOVA1 components and aim to mimic or mask the sensory qualities of these foods. Examples include non-sugar sweeteners, hydrogenated oils, casein, whey, packaged snacks, sugary drinks, fast food, ready-to-eat meals, processed meats, sweetened breakfast cereals, flavored yogurt, store-bought baked goods, and condiments with additives [[6](#B6-nutrients-17-00859)].

Clinicians and epidemiologists are increasingly using the NOVA classification to investigate the potential associations between highly processed food consumption and various health issues such as metabolic disorders, CVD, and certain types of cancers [[8](#B8-nutrients-17-00859),[9](#B9-nutrients-17-00859),[10](#B10-nutrients-17-00859)]. Latin American countries have already integrated NOVA into their dietary guidelines [[11](#B11-nutrients-17-00859)], and France aims to reduce ultra-processed food consumption by 20% using the NOVA guidelines [[12](#B12-nutrients-17-00859)]. This trend suggests NOVA’s application will continue to expand. However, despite some earlier research [[13](#B13-nutrients-17-00859)], the system’s robustness and functionality are not well defined, leading to ambiguity and varying interpretations [[14](#B14-nutrients-17-00859)], and causing disagreements among experts [[15](#B15-nutrients-17-00859),[16](#B16-nutrients-17-00859)]. One source of uncertainty arises from the description of UPFs (NOVA4) as “industrial formulations, typically with five or more and usually many ingredients”. This may have caused some researchers to classify foods with extensive ingredient lists as NOVA4, even if they lacked typical NOVA4 ingredients, such as “substances not commonly used in culinary preparations” [[17](#B17-nutrients-17-00859)].

### 2.2. Common Characteristics of Ultra-Processed Foods

UPFs are known for their diverse nutrient content but are often high in added sugars, which increase calorie intake without offering essential nutrients. They also contain unhealthy fats like saturated, trans fats, and hydrogenated oils, which can harm heart health. Additionally, UPFs are typically high in sodium, used as a preservative and flavor enhancer, and contain refined carbohydrates such as white flour. These foods usually lack dietary fiber, crucial for digestive and microbiota health. UPFs contain minimal whole foods and are often heavily processed with artificial additives to enhance taste and sensory appeal [[13](#B13-nutrients-17-00859)]. Common additives in UPFs include preservatives, colorings, flavorings, and emulsifiers, which are rarely found in home-cooked meals. Recent studies have highlighted the negative impact of various artificial food additives on gut microbiota and their links to chronic diseases through gut microbial modulation [[18](#B18-nutrients-17-00859)].

### 2.3. Processing-Induced Changes

UPFs experience a multitude of industrial procedures to preserve food, as well as enhance taste, texture, and convenience. Understanding these alterations is essential in order to assess the nutritional value of the end product and identify potential health implications. One of the most common processing techniques is the Maillard reaction, which is used to develop sensory attributes like color, flavor, aroma, and texture. While Maillard-reaction products can act as antioxidants, bactericides, antiallergens, and antibrowning agents, they can also function as prooxidants and carcinogens [[19](#B19-nutrients-17-00859)]. High-temperature heating during this process can also reduce the nutritional value of proteins. Extrusion is another method, in which a mixture of ingredients is forced through a narrow opening at high temperatures and pressures [[20](#B20-nutrients-17-00859)]. This process can induce lipid oxidation, leading to the formation of free radicals and the degradation of unsaturated fatty acids [[21](#B21-nutrients-17-00859)]. It is commonly used to create the textures and shapes of snacks, cereals, and processed meats. Hydrogenation involves adding hydrogen molecules to liquid oils to convert them into semi-solid or solid fats [[22](#B22-nutrients-17-00859)]. This technique, often used when making margarine, spreads, and baked goods [[23](#B23-nutrients-17-00859)], produces trans fats, which are linked to negative health effects such as increased LDL cholesterol levels [[24](#B24-nutrients-17-00859)]. Emulsification is a process that uses emulsifiers to create stable mixtures of substances that do not naturally blend, like oil and water [[25](#B25-nutrients-17-00859)]. Deep-frying is also commonly used to make fried snacks, fast food, and processed meats. This technique increases the oil content in food, promoting lipid oxidation and potentially generating harmful chemicals like heterocyclic amines [[26](#B26-nutrients-17-00859)]. Cryopreservation methods, such as freezing and thawing, are widely used to maintain the quality and extend the shelf life of food, particularly frozen foods and pre-packaged meals [[27](#B27-nutrients-17-00859)].

### 2.4. Meal Patterns and Eating Behaviors

UPF consumption (ready-to-eat/heat meals) typically requires less time and effort than unprocessed or minimally processed food intake. Recent research highlights that UPFs could be associated with eating speed, timing, and circadian rhythm disruption. Indeed, a recent study found that late eaters are prone to consume more UPFs and fewer minimally processed foods than early eaters, contributing to increased knowledge of the mechanisms underpinning the association of late eating with adverse cardiometabolic outcomes [[28](#B28-nutrients-17-00859)]. A recent meta-analysis also demonstrated that a high intake of UPFs is associated with reduced sleep duration and quality, regardless of age [[29](#B29-nutrients-17-00859)]. UPF consumption and sleep showed significant inverse associations.

## 3. Overview of the Human Gut Microbiome and Gut Barrier

### 3.1. Composition and Diversity of Gut Microbiome

The human gut microbiome is a dynamic ecosystem of microbes that includes bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, and protozoa, which reside within the gut. This complex community of microorganisms plays a crucial role in the maintenance of health and the pathogenesis of various diseases [[30](#B30-nutrients-17-00859)]. Bacteria are the most ubiquitous and deeply studied component and are classified into five key phyla: Firmicutes, comprising genera such as *Lactobacillus*, *Clostridium*, *Enterococcus*, and *Ruminococcus*; Bacteroidetes, which include genera such as *Bacteroides* and *Prevotella*; Actinobacteria, primarily represented by *Bifidobacteria*; Proteobacteria, which are less prevalent in healthy individuals, however this phylum includes genera such as *Escherichia, Klebsiella*, and *Enterobacter;* and Verrucomicrobia, predominantly represented by *Akkermansia muciniphila* [[31](#B31-nutrients-17-00859)]. Under physiological conditions, a homeostatic balance is observed among potentially beneficial bacteria species [[31](#B31-nutrients-17-00859)], and Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes constitute the predominant phyla. The ratio between these phyla (F:B) is approximately 1:1, although this may fluctuate depending on various factors, including dietary habits, age, health or disease status, and lifestyle [[32](#B32-nutrients-17-00859)]. Conversely, dysbiosis refers to the disruption or loss of this beneficial homeostatic balance [[33](#B33-nutrients-17-00859)], although an established definition is still not available. Beyond these dominant phyla, other microorganisms, including methanogenic archaea (*Methanobrevibacter* spp.), various fungi (*Candida* spp., *Saccharomyces* spp.), and viruses (predominantly bacteriophages), contribute to the gut’s functional diversity. These components interact in a complex manner, regulating metabolic pathways, immunological responses, and the gut’s structural integrity [[34](#B34-nutrients-17-00859)]. Microbial ecology parameters, such as α-diversity and β-diversity, represent an easy way to assess the balance of the gut microbiome [[35](#B35-nutrients-17-00859)]: α-diversity is a taxonomic measure of species diversity within a community that can be expressed by metrics such as richness, which indicate the number of observed species in a community, and evenness, which measures the relative abundance distribution of species within a community. It is widely recognized as a hallmark of a balanced and healthy gut microbiome, as a diverse microbiome is more resilient to external perturbations such as infections, antibiotic use, or dietary changes [[36](#B36-nutrients-17-00859)]. For example, β-diversity is a measure of microbial composition between samples (different samples or samples at different timepoints). The intricate interplay between different microbial species in a diverse microbiome also contributes to the production of beneficial metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and the modulation of the host’s immune system. Moreover, a diverse and healthy microbiome may play a crucial role in preventing the overgrowth of opportunistic pathogens, thus maintaining a balanced and healthy gut environment. These functions collectively contribute to maintaining gut homeostasis and promoting overall health [[36](#B36-nutrients-17-00859)].

### 3.2. The Functions and Metabolites of the Human Gut Microbiome

The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including metabolic functions, immune modulation, and the regulation of gut–brain axis. The gut microbiota is primarily associated with the degradation and fermentation of indigestible dietary components, especially complex carbohydrates, producing key SCFAs such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate, which are essential for gut health and beyond [[37](#B37-nutrients-17-00859)]. Firmicutes play a key role in the fermentation of dietary fibers, but Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria also support gut health through carbohydrate metabolism and complex polysaccharide degradation. *Akkermansia muciniphila*, *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, *Clostridium butyricum*, *Prevotella copri*, and *Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron* are among the main SCFA-producing species [[38](#B38-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.1. SCFAs

SCFAs provide colonocytes with an energy source and maintain the integrity of the intestinal barrier, regulating key processes such as tight junction expression, mucin secretion by goblet cells, the production of antimicrobial compounds by Paneth cells, and also reducing intestinal pH, creating an unfavorable environment for pathogen persistence [[33](#B33-nutrients-17-00859),[37](#B37-nutrients-17-00859)].

SCFAs also modulate appetite and improve insulin sensitivity through the secretion of gut hormones such as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), peptide YY (PYY), and the binding G protein-coupled receptor (GPR41 and GPR43) [[39](#B39-nutrients-17-00859),[40](#B40-nutrients-17-00859)]. Through the same receptors on vascular endothelial cells, SCFAs (in particular, acetate and propionate) influence cardiovascular health, reducing blood pressure [[41](#B41-nutrients-17-00859)], lowering cholesterol levels, and modulating hepatic lipid metabolism [[42](#B42-nutrients-17-00859)]. Moreover, SCFAs act as crucial systemic mediators that influence metabolism, immune function, and overall homeostasis. SCFAs have profound effects on immune modulation: butyrate promotes anti-inflammatory effects primarily through the suppression of NFkB and the upregulation of PPAR γ by means of epigenetic mechanisms such as the inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs) [[43](#B43-nutrients-17-00859)] and also the stimulation of the differentiation of Tregs, as well as an increase in levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10, the suppressing of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and the maintenance of epithelial barrier integrity [[44](#B44-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.2. Immune System Modulation

The gut microbiota has a relevant impact on the shaping of the host immune system, significantly influencing both local and systemic immune responses [[45](#B45-nutrients-17-00859)]. The microbial ecosystem interacts with the host through different pathways, including direct interactions with immune cells and the production of metabolites that regulate immune function [[46](#B46-nutrients-17-00859)]. One critical route by which the microbiota shapes immunity is through the development and maturation of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) [[47](#B47-nutrients-17-00859)]. Commensal bacteria stimulate the production of antimicrobial peptides, promote the development of isolated lymphoid follicles, and induce the differentiation of T helper cells, particularly Th17 and regulatory T cells (Tregs) [[47](#B47-nutrients-17-00859)]. These processes are crucial for maintaining intestinal homeostasis and preventing excessive inflammation. Furthermore, the microbiota influences the development and function of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), which are essential for mucosal immunity and tissue repair [[45](#B45-nutrients-17-00859)]. Recent studies have also highlighted that certain commensal bacteria and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) enhance the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy by boosting the function of antigen-presenting cells and enhancing T cell responses [[48](#B48-nutrients-17-00859),[49](#B49-nutrients-17-00859),[50](#B50-nutrients-17-00859)]. Conversely, dysbiosis has been associated with various immune-mediated disorders, including inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune conditions, and allergies [[51](#B51-nutrients-17-00859),[52](#B52-nutrients-17-00859),[53](#B53-nutrients-17-00859),[54](#B54-nutrients-17-00859),[55](#B55-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.3. Bile Acids (BAs)

The gut microbiota plays a pivotal role in the biotransformation of primary bile acids through mechanisms such as deconjugation, dehydroxylation, and epimerization, leading to the production of secondary bile acids (BAs) [[56](#B56-nutrients-17-00859)]. BAs act as signaling molecules by activating nuclear receptors such as the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and G-protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5) and exhibit many biological activities, including anti-inflammatory properties. For instance, BAs shift neutrophil chemotaxis and macrophage polarization in favor of the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, which is required for tissue repair and inflammation resolution and a decrease in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as e IFNγ and IL-6 [[57](#B57-nutrients-17-00859)]. In addition, BAs shape the microbial community composition, creating a feedback loop owing to intrinsic bacteriostatic activities [[57](#B57-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.4. Trimethylamine (TMA) Production

Among the gut microbiota’s numerous metabolic activities, the transformation of compounds containing trimethylamine groups, such as choline, carnitine, and phosphatidylcholine found in animal-derived foods, into trimethylamine (TMA) is of particular interest for human health. TMA is thereafter oxidized in the liver by flavin monooxygenase enzymes (FMO3) to form trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), which has been associated with the pathogenesis of CVD and metabolic syndrome (MetS) [[58](#B58-nutrients-17-00859)]. The synthesis of TMA is primarily attributed to Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, two phyla frequently increased in pro-inflammatory conditions [[59](#B59-nutrients-17-00859)]. In particular, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Clostridium sporogenes*, *Escherichia fergusonii*, and *Desulfovibrio desulfuricans* are among the principal TMA-producing bacterial species [[60](#B60-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.5. Gut–Brain Axis

Accumulating evidence indicates that the gut microbiota exerts powerful influences over the central nervous system (CNS) via the gut–brain axis [[61](#B61-nutrients-17-00859)]. This bidirectional communication system of hormonal, neural, and immunological pathways connects the gastrointestinal tract with the brain [[62](#B62-nutrients-17-00859)]. One of the mechanisms through which microbial species can affect the host is by modulating the synthesis of neurotransmitters including serotonin (5-HT) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which play an essential role in mood regulation, cognitive function, and mental well-being. *Lactobacillus* and *Bifidobacterium* species are well known for their association with increased GABA production [[63](#B63-nutrients-17-00859)], while *Enterococcus* species are involved in 5-HT synthesis [[64](#B64-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.6. Microbiota–Gonad Axis

A bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the gonads, termed the “microbiota-gonad axis,” has been identified [[65](#B65-nutrients-17-00859)]. This interaction involves endocrine, immunological, and metabolic mechanisms that directly influence reproductive function [[65](#B65-nutrients-17-00859)]. The gut microbiota strongly impacts the metabolism of sex hormones, such as estrogens and testosterone, via direct enzymatic actions and the indirect modulation of host physiology [[66](#B66-nutrients-17-00859)]. This process involves β-glucuronidase activity, essential for the hydrolysis of conjugated estrogen metabolites [[67](#B67-nutrients-17-00859)]. The gut microbiota also significantly influences sperm quality parameters in males, including motility, concentration, and morphology. Beneficial metabolites produced by intestinal bacteria, such as SCFAs, have demonstrated a positive impact on sperm health. [[65](#B65-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.7. Gut Microbiota’s Role in Defense and Metabolic Health

The gut microbiota provides defense against pathogen colonization through various mechanisms, including competitive exclusion, wherein commensal microorganisms outcompete pathogens for nutrients and epithelial binding sites [[68](#B68-nutrients-17-00859)]. Additionally, it produces antimicrobial compounds such as bacteriocins and bile acids, while simultaneously supporting intestinal barrier integrity to prevent pathogen translocation into the circulatory system [[69](#B69-nutrients-17-00859)]. Furthermore, the microbiota serves a crucial function in synthesizing indispensable vitamins, notably vitamin K and specific B vitamins, including B12, B6, and folate, which are fundamental to numerous metabolic processes within the host organism, encompassing mechanisms such as blood clotting, DNA synthesis, and cellular energy production [[70](#B70-nutrients-17-00859),[71](#B71-nutrients-17-00859)]. The mutualistic association between the microbiota and the host organism underscores the significant role of microbial populations in sustaining metabolic equilibrium and overall physiological function [[72](#B72-nutrients-17-00859)].

#### 3.2.8. Determinants of Gut Microbiota Composition

The gut microbiota composition shows a considerable interpersonal variability, influenced by a multifaceted interplay of factors encompassing dietary habits, chronological age, genetic predisposition, pharmacological interventions (e.g., antibiotic administration), and environmental influences [[73](#B73-nutrients-17-00859)]. While the microbiota typically achieves a comparatively stable state during adulthood, it maintains a dynamic ability to respond to modifications in dietary intake and lifestyle choices. Of particular significance is the impact of ultra-processed food consumption, characterized by elevated levels of refined sugars, detrimental fats, synthetic additives, and insufficient fiber content [[4](#B4-nutrients-17-00859)]. Such dietary patterns can perturb the equilibrium of microbial communities, fostering the expansion of potentially harmful taxa while concurrently diminishing the prevalence of beneficial commensal organisms [[4](#B4-nutrients-17-00859)]. This microbial imbalance, or dysbiosis, is linked to unfavorable metabolic and inflammatory consequences, underscoring the pivotal role of dietary quality in preserving gut microbial homeostasis and, by extension, overall physiological well-being [[74](#B74-nutrients-17-00859),[75](#B75-nutrients-17-00859)].

### 3.3. Gut Barrier

The gut barrier is a complex, multi-layered structure that plays a crucial role for preserving intestinal health and overall well-being. This barrier is structurally composed of the gut microbiota, which competes with pathogens and influences immunity; a mucus layer with antimicrobial properties; epithelial cells that form both a physical and immune barrier; and GALT, which is responsible for monitoring immune activity [[76](#B76-nutrients-17-00859)]. Tight junctions between epithelial cells regulate paracellular permeability, ensuring the gut barrier’s integrity. When the gut barrier is compromised, it can lead to a wide range of gastrointestinal and systemic disorders, including type 1 diabetes, allergies, and neurological disorders [[76](#B76-nutrients-17-00859)]. Recent studies have elucidated the impact of the gut microbiome on barrier function. Beneficial bacteria contribute to the barrier’s integrity by releasing SCFAs and other metabolites that promote mucus synthesis and tight junction formation [[37](#B37-nutrients-17-00859),[77](#B77-nutrients-17-00859)]. Dysbiosis, otherwise, can result in increased intestinal permeability, referred to as “leaky gut”, which has been associated with several clinical conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, metabolic abnormalities, and neurological disorders [[78](#B78-nutrients-17-00859)]. UPFs, stress, and exposure to environmental toxins all have a negative impact on gut barrier function [[79](#B79-nutrients-17-00859),[80](#B80-nutrients-17-00859),[81](#B81-nutrients-17-00859),[82](#B82-nutrients-17-00859)]. Understanding the complex connections between these variables and the gut barrier is critical for developing targeted treatment approaches to promote intestinal health and prevent illnesses.

## 4. UPFs-Driven Alterations of Gut Microbiome

An increasing body of evidence shows that UPF consumption can induce significant alterations in the composition and function of the gut microbiome [[79](#B79-nutrients-17-00859),[82](#B82-nutrients-17-00859),[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. UPFs, characterized by a high content of additives, preservatives, emulsifiers, and artificial compounds, are associated with the disruption of the microbial ecosystem, characterized by the proliferation of pro-inflammatory strains and a reduction in microbial α-diversity [[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. At the functional level, the consumption of UPFs has been linked to the decreased production of SCFAs and other protective metabolites by the microbiota [[79](#B79-nutrients-17-00859)]. The observed changes in microbial composition and function might have far-reaching impacts on human health, resulting in low-grade, systemic inflammation and oxidative stress, which are crucial elements in the onset of several types of chronic diseases attributed to UPF dietary consumption [[84](#B84-nutrients-17-00859),[85](#B85-nutrients-17-00859)]. A Spanish study assessed the gut microbiome of adult subjects who regularly consumed < 3 servings of UPFs daily (96 participants) and of those who consumed >5 servings of UPFs daily (90 participants) [[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. There were no variations in α-diversity measures among women across UPF intake groups, while α-diversity decreased in men who consumed a higher quantity of UPFs, suggesting that UPFs may affect microbiota composition differently in women and men [[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. Individuals who consumed high levels of UPFs exhibited an elevated presence of potentially harmful bacterial groups compared to those with low UPF intake [[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. These bacteria included *Granulicatella*, which is linked to metabolic disorders, as well as *Blautia*, *Carnobacteriaceae, Bacteroidaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Bacteroidia*, and *Bacteroidetes* [[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. Conversely, the high UPF consumers showed decreased levels of *Lachnospira* and *Roseburia*, which are known producers of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [[83](#B83-nutrients-17-00859)]. Commonly utilized emulsifiers, including carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), polysorbate 80 (P80), carrageenan, and gums, are known to alter gut microbiota composition, thereby promoting a pro-inflammatory microbial environment that may contribute to the development of metabolic disorders such as obesity and T2DM [[86](#B86-nutrients-17-00859),[87](#B87-nutrients-17-00859)]. These emulsifiers diminish the prevalence of beneficial bacteria such as *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Akkermansia muciniphila*, which possess anti-inflammatory properties and adversely affect the intestinal mucus layer, resulting in increased permeability (“leaky gut”) and bacterial translocation into the bloodstream, potentially eliciting systemic inflammation [[88](#B88-nutrients-17-00859),[89](#B89-nutrients-17-00859)].

Animal studies further reveal that exposure to emulsifiers leads to a decrease in microbial diversity, promotes the growth of opportunistic pathogens (such as *Escherichia coli*), and shifts gut microbiota metabolism towards a pro-inflammatory state [[90](#B90-nutrients-17-00859),[91](#B91-nutrients-17-00859)]. P80 enhances the vulnerability of the small intestine of murine models by promoting dysbiosis, increasing Gammaproteobacteria abundance and decreasing α-diversity in the small intestine [[92](#B92-nutrients-17-00859)]. CMC and P80 impact gut microbiota gene expression, leading to the increased production of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and flagellin, both known as inflammatory molecules that can damage the gut barrier [[91](#B91-nutrients-17-00859)]. Prolonged exposure to these emulsifiers also results in a reduction in mucus layer thickness, thereby compromising its protective function against pathogens. [[91](#B91-nutrients-17-00859)]. An ex vivo and in vivo study investigated direct P80 and CMC using a mucosal simulator of the human intestinal microbial ecosystem (M-SHIME), and then emulsifier-treated microbiotas were transferred to germ-free mice to assess potential host effects [[82](#B82-nutrients-17-00859)]. Both CMC and P80 altered microbiota composition and increased the pro-inflammatory potential; the germ-free mice colonized with emulsifier-treated microbiotas exhibited low-grade inflammation, increased metabolic markers, higher fasting blood glucose levels and increased adiposity, indicative of MetS [[82](#B82-nutrients-17-00859)]. A randomized controlled study (RCT) conducted on human participants investigated the effects of CMC on the gut microbiome and metabolic processes [[79](#B79-nutrients-17-00859)]. Participants who consumed CMC exhibited changes in gut microbiota composition, including decreases in *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Ruminococcus* sp., and increases in *Roseburia* sp. and Lachnospiraceae in the fecal metabolome, particularly with reductions in SCFAs and free amino acids [[79](#B79-nutrients-17-00859)]. Another study in healthy volunteers showed that the consumption of sweeteners such as sucralose and aspartame at high concentrations can induce apoptosis in intestinal epithelial cells, while their consumption at low concentrations reduces the expression of claudin 3, increasing the permeability of the intestinal barrier [[18](#B18-nutrients-17-00859)]. These sweeteners also stimulate the expression of pro-inflammatory mediators such as LPS and the activation of the NF-κB pathway, which is crucial for the progression of intestinal inflammation [[18](#B18-nutrients-17-00859)].

Additionally, UPFs tend to be high in saturated fat. This is because, during the industrialization process, ingredients such as refined vegetable oils, butter or animal fats are added to increase their content. These ingredients are added to improve taste, texture, and shelf life, but the high saturated fat content can be detrimental to health, especially if consumed in excess, as it can increase the risk of CVD [[93](#B93-nutrients-17-00859)]. Diets high in fat also impact the regulation of gut bacteria populations, causing a decrease in *Bacteroides*, *Verrucomicrobia*, *Eubacterium rectale*, *Clostridium coccoides*, and *Bifidobacterium* groups, while simultaneously increasing the proportion of *Firmicutes* and *Proteobacteria* [[84](#B84-nutrients-17-00859)], and increase pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α) [[94](#B94-nutrients-17-00859)]. In addition, saturated fat increases the concentration of plasma endotoxin derived from Gram-negative bacteria and promotes hyperinsulinemia and excessive lipid accumulation in the liver and adipose tissue [[84](#B84-nutrients-17-00859)]. The regular consumption of UPFs negatively affects both the gut microbiota and metabolic profiles, with a significant reduction in advantageous species which play crucial roles in maintaining gut health by fermenting fibers and generating SCFAs [[95](#B95-nutrients-17-00859)].

## 5. Impact of UPF-Induced Dysbiosis on Human Health

As previously outlined, a diet rich in UPFs leads to gut microbiome imbalance, impaired intestinal barrier function, and enhanced gut permeability. This allows harmful bacterial products, such as LPS, to enter the bloodstream, triggering a status of systemic low-grade inflammation [[31](#B31-nutrients-17-00859)]. This process contributes to the rising incidence of noncommunicable chronic disorders (NCDs), which are complex conditions characterized by persistent, low-grade inflammation and disrupted gut microbiota balance. These disorders include cardiometabolic conditions like MetS, T2DM, and CVD. Chronic gastrointestinal conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), are also part of this group. Furthermore, neurological and psychiatric conditions are linked to these inflammatory processes [[75](#B75-nutrients-17-00859)].

### 5.1. Cardiometabolic Disorders

The metabolic syndrome is a pathophysiological condition of metabolism which fulfils at least three of the five criteria concerning the following aspects: central obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and low serum HDL. It is associated with an increased risk of T2DM and CVD [[95](#B95-nutrients-17-00859)]. A consolidated body of evidence has shown a link between obesity, metabolic syndrome and gut microbiome imbalance, characterized by reduced microbial diversity and an increased capacity to extract energy and produce harmful compounds, such as TMAO [[96](#B96-nutrients-17-00859),[97](#B97-nutrients-17-00859)]. UPF-induced microbiome alterations have been linked to increased cardiometabolic risk: T2DM appears to be influenced by an elevated ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, which is associated with a pro-inflammatory state [[75](#B75-nutrients-17-00859)]. Moreover, *Akkermansia muciniphila*, which is less abundant in individuals consuming diets rich in UPFs, improves insulin sensitivity, insulin levels, and weight control in obese, insulin-resistant subjects, and is associated with a lean body type in both animal and human studies [[98](#B98-nutrients-17-00859)]. The microbiome also produces harmful compounds that may increase cardiovascular risk: the gut microbiome plays a role in metabolizing several aminoacides, producing TMA, which is then converted to TMAO. TMA is primarily produced by Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, two bacterial groups often increased in gut dysbiosis [[59](#B59-nutrients-17-00859)]. Higher TMAO production is linked to an increased risk of cardiometabolic diseases [[99](#B99-nutrients-17-00859)]. For instance, a prospective study of patients undergoing elective coronary angiography showed that fasting TMAO levels were directly related to major adverse CVD events over a 3-year follow-up period [[100](#B100-nu
</webpage_content>

args.summary: This is a peer-reviewed scientific article (published February 28, 2025, in Nutrients) that comprehensively reviews the detrimental impact of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) on the human gut microbiome and gut barrier. The authors define UPFs using the NOVA classification system (Group 4) as industrially manufactured products with five or more ingredients, including additives, emulsifiers, hydrogenated oils, and artificial substances not found in home kitchens. The article examines how UPFs reduce gut microbial diversity, decrease beneficial bacteria like Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and increase pro-inflammatory microorganisms. Key mechanisms include: emulsifiers (CMC, P80, carrageenan) altering microbiota composition and promoting inflammation; artificial sweeteners inducing apoptosis in intestinal epithelial cells; high saturated fat content increasing Firmicutes/Proteobacteria while decreasing beneficial Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium; and reduced SCFA production. The resulting gut dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut") contribute to systemic low-grade inflammation and are linked to chronic disorders including metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and colorectal cancer. The article also discusses impacts on the gut-brain axis and cognitive function. The authors conclude that dietary modifications incorporating fiber, fermented foods, and probiotics can help mitigate UPF effects, and call for stricter regulations, well-defined food labels, and further studies to inform evidence-based dietary guidelines.

## Abstract

Translate Abstract using AI

keyboard_arrow_down

Maternal nutrition plays a fundamental role in shaping fetal development and long-term health outcomes, forming the basis of the developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) paradigm. This perspective aims to examine how maternal nutritional status—before and during pregnancy, as well as in early postnatal life—acts as a key biological signal that programs gene expression, organ development, and metabolic function in the offspring. This paper highlights major mechanisms underlying developmental programming, including epigenetic modifications, hormonal influences, placental function, and the maternal microbiome. It also explores the consequences of both undernutrition and overnutrition, emphasizing the concept of environmental mismatch, whereby discordance between prenatal and postnatal environments increases susceptibility to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. In addition, the role of essential micronutrients and the importance of early-life nutrition during the first 1000 days are discussed, alongside emerging evidence of transgenerational effects. In conclusion, optimizing maternal nutrition represents a critical and modifiable determinant of lifelong health, with significant clinical and public health implications, offering a powerful strategy for reducing the global burden of non-communicable diseases across generations.

**Keywords:**maternal nutrition; developmental programming; epigenetics; maternal microbiome; obesity; insulin resistance; micronutrients; transgenerational effects

## 1. Introduction

The developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) paradigm has fundamentally reshaped our understanding of how health trajectories are established, by demonstrating that early-life environmental exposures exert long-lasting effects on human health [[1](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B1-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. While traditional models emphasized genetic predisposition and adult lifestyle factors, it is now widely recognized that many chronic diseases have their origins in early development, particularly during fetal life. Genetic inheritance provides a structural blueprint, but environmental exposures—particularly nutrition—determine how this blueprint is expressed, modified, and maintained throughout life.

The first 1000 days of life, spanning preconception, pregnancy, and early infancy, represent a uniquely sensitive period of biological plasticity during which biological systems are established and calibrated. During this time, the developing organism undergoes extraordinarily rapid cellular proliferation, differentiation, and organogenesis. These processes are tightly regulated yet highly responsive to environmental signals, among which maternal nutrition is among the most influential, making them particularly vulnerable to nutritional perturbations.

Maternal nutrition functions not only as a source of energy and essential substrates but also as a complex biological signal that modulates gene expression, endocrine pathways, immune maturation, and metabolic programming [[2](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B2-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Nutrients interact with transcription factors, signaling cascades, enzymatic processes, and epigenetic regulators, thereby shaping how genetic information is expressed, and shaping the structure and function of developing organs.

Crucially, adaptations made during early development are context-dependent. When the fetus develops in an environment characterized by nutrient scarcity, it adopts metabolic strategies that promote survival, such as enhanced energy storage and reduced growth of non-essential tissues. However, if postnatal conditions are characterized by abundance, these same adaptations may predispose individuals to obesity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease [[3](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B3-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. This mismatch between prenatal and postnatal environments is a central concept in DOHaD and helps explain the global rise in non-communicable diseases.

Furthermore, maternal nutrition is shaped by broader determinants, including socioeconomic status, food systems, cultural practices, education, and healthcare access. Thus, addressing these upstream factors by improving maternal nutrition is essential for translating scientific insights into meaningful improvements in population health and requires not only biological understanding but also coordinated public health and policy interventions.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 2. Mechanisms of developmental programming

Developmental programming is mediated through a network of interactions of multiple biological systems that translate maternal environmental signals and nutritional status into lasting physiological changes (**[Figure 1](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#Acad.Nutri.-3-326083-f001)**).

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)![Image 1: media/image001.png](https://journals.academia-photos.com/12/8329/image001.png)
##### Figure 1

. 

### The figure illustrates how maternal nutritional status (poor vs. healthy diet) directs fetal programming through interconnected biological mechanisms. Inadequate or optimal maternal nutrition influences epigenetic regulation (DNA methylation and histone modification), alters maternal–fetal hormonal signals (e.g., insulin, cortisol, leptin), modulates placental function governing nutrient and oxygen transfer, and shapes the maternal gut microbiome. These mechanisms converge to affect the intrauterine environment and fetal development, resulting in differential susceptibility to adverse health outcomes in the child and later adults (represented by the 3 people in the figure with an arrow pointing below to the effects, including obesity and diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive impairments, with potential transmission of these effects across generations. The figure was generated using ChatGPT.

Epigenetic regulation is one of the most critical mechanisms underlying fetal programming. DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA activity collectively regulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence [[2](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B2-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. These processes are particularly active during early embryogenesis and fetal development, when epigenetic marks are established and stabilized, and are highly sensitive to maternal nutrition, particularly during early embryonic development [[4](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B4-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Persistent epigenetic changes have been demonstrated in human studies [[5](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B5-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)–[7](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B7-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

One-carbon metabolism plays a key role in epigenetic regulation [[8](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B8-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Nutrients such as folate, choline, methionine, and vitamin B12 are essential components of one-carbon metabolism for generating methyl groups necessary for DNA methylation. For example, altered methylation of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid storage, and appetite regulation has been associated with increased risk of obesity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease. Deficiencies or imbalances in these nutrients can disrupt normal epigenetic marking, leading to aberrant epigenetic patterns affecting genes involved in metabolism, growth, inflammation, and neurodevelopment and can disrupt normal epigenetic marking, leading to altered gene expression patterns. These epigenetic changes can influence neurodevelopment, potentially contributing to cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Recent advances in epigenomics have revealed that these modifications are dynamic and responsive to environmental inputs, suggesting potential reversibility under certain conditions. Epigenetic programming is now recognized as a central mechanism in DOHaD [[6](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B6-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083), [7](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B7-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. It should be known that these changes are not transient. Studies have shown that early-life epigenetic modifications caused by changes in the maternal diet can persist throughout life, influencing methylation patterns in genes related to insulin signaling, adipogenesis, and appetite regulation, affecting metabolic regulation, immune responses, and neurodevelopment [[5](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B5-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. However, many epigenetic changes established during early development remain stable, underscoring the importance of optimal maternal nutrition. In some cases, these epigenetic markers may even be transmitted to subsequent generations, providing a biological basis for transgenerational effects [[6](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B6-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)–[9](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B9-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

The intrauterine endocrine environment plays a crucial role in shaping fetal development. Maternal nutritional status influences circulating levels of hormones such as insulin, leptin, thyroid hormones, and glucocorticoids. Elevated maternal cortisol levels, and excess glucocorticoids, often associated with stress or undernutrition, can cross the placenta and can alter fetal hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis development, leading to long-term changes in stress responsiveness, metabolic regulation, blood pressure regulation, and metabolic function [[4](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B4-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)] (**[Table 1](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#Acad.Nutri.-3-326083-t001)**).

In gestational diabetes, maternal hyperglycemia results in fetal hyperinsulinemia, promoting adipose tissue accumulation and altering metabolic pathways [[5](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B5-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Insulin acts as a growth-promoting hormone in the fetus, increasing adiposity and altering metabolic pathways. Similarly, altered leptin exposure during development may influence appetite regulation and long-term energy balance. These endocrine disruptions contribute to the programming of obesity and metabolic syndrome.

The placenta is a highly dynamic organ that regulates nutrient transfer, gas exchange, and endocrine signaling between mother and fetus. It possesses nutrient-sensing mechanisms that adapt to maternal nutritional status by altering transporter expression, vascular development, and hormonal output. In maternal undernutrition, placental growth may be restricted, resulting in the placenta prioritizing nutrient delivery to essential organs such as the brain, often at the expense of overall growth of the fetus. Conversely, maternal overnutrition, causing an increased nutrient transfer, can lead to fetal overgrowth and metabolic dysregulation [[4](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B4-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Placental dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a central mechanism linking maternal nutrition to fetal outcomes and long-term disease risk. The placental epigenome plays a key regulatory role in fetal development [[10](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B10-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Alterations in placental gene expression, transporter activity, and endocrine function are key mechanisms linking maternal nutrition to fetal development. These changes may have lasting effects on organ structure and function.

The maternal microbiome represents an additional mechanism through which nutrition influences offspring health. Maternal diet influences the composition of the gut microbiome, which contributes to infant microbial colonization and immune system development [[11](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B11-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. During birth and early life, microbial colonization of the infant gut plays a crucial role in immune system maturation. Early microbiome composition is associated with long-term metabolic and immune outcomes. The maternal microbiome represents an emerging mechanism in developmental programming [[12](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B12-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Maternal diet influences gut microbial composition, which affects metabolic and immune pathways.

At birth, microbial colonization of the infant gut begins, establishing the foundation for immune system development. Breast milk contributes beneficial bacteria and prebiotic compounds that support microbial diversity. Disruptions in early microbiome development have been linked to increased risk of obesity, allergic diseases, and autoimmune conditions. Thus, maternal nutrition indirectly influences offspring health through microbiome-mediated pathways.

Maternal obesity and nutritional imbalance can lead to oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, affecting placental function and fetal development. Oxidative stress can impair placental function and reduce nutrient delivery, while inflammation—particularly in maternal obesity—can alter fetal metabolic pathways and immune function. These processes contribute to long-term disease susceptibility. The mismatch between prenatal and postnatal environments is a key determinant of disease risk. Adaptive responses to undernutrition may become maladaptive in nutrient-rich environments, contributing to metabolic disease.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 3. Micronutrients and developmental programming

Micronutrients play a critical role in fetal development, programming and long-term health [[13](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B13-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Unlike macronutrients, they function primarily as cofactors in biochemical reactions and regulators of gene expression. Deficiencies in essential vitamins and minerals can have profound effects on organ development and long-term health outcomes.

Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and methylation, and its deficiency is associated with neural tube defects and altered epigenetic regulation. Iron is critical for oxygen transport and brain development, with deficiency linked to impaired cognitive outcomes. Iodine is required for thyroid hormone production and is essential for neurodevelopment. Zinc supports cell division and immune function, while vitamin D plays a role in skeletal development and immune regulation.

Deficiencies in these micronutrients during pregnancy can result in structural abnormalities, impaired organ development, and increased disease risk later in life. Conversely, excessive caloric intake without adequate micronutrient balance can also disrupt developmental programming. For example, excessive caloric intake can lead to maternal obesity and metabolic disturbances that influence fetal development. Ensuring optimal micronutrient status before and during pregnancy is therefore essential for both immediate and long-term health outcomes.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 4. Environment mismatch and postnatal growth

The concept of environmental mismatch is central to developmental programming. When fetal adaptations are mismatched with postnatal conditions, disease risk increases. For instance, a fetus exposed to undernutrition may develop a metabolism optimized for energy conservation. If postnatal nutrition is abundant, this mismatch can lead to excessive weight gain and metabolic disease. Rapid catch-up growth in infancy is strongly associated with increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. This highlights the importance of continuity between prenatal and postnatal environments.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 5. Conception and the embryonic stage

Developmental programming begins even before conception. Maternal nutritional status influences oocyte quality, mitochondrial function, and early embryonic development. Poor maternal nutrition may impair fertilization, embryo implantation, and early cell division. During early embryogenesis, extensive epigenetic reprogramming occurs, making this stage highly sensitive to environmental influences and nutritional perturbations [[4](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B4-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Nutritional deficiencies during this period can lead to long-lasting alterations in gene expression and organ development. Micronutrients such as folate, iron, iodine, and zinc are critical during this phase. Folate supports DNA synthesis and methylation, iron is essential for oxygen transport, iodine is required for thyroid hormone production, and zinc plays a role in cell division and immune function.

Emerging research also highlights the importance of paternal factors that contribute to developmental programming during this stage. Sperm epigenetic markers can be influenced by paternal diet, obesity, lifestyle and environmental exposures, affecting embryonic development and offspring health [[14](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B14-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 6. Pregnancy: adaptive responses and long-term consequences

During pregnancy, the fetus adapts to the nutritional environment provided by the mother [[15](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B15-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

The thrifty phenotype hypothesis provides a framework for understanding how fetal adaptations to undernutrition can have long-term consequences. In conditions of nutrient scarcity, the fetus adopts a “thrifty” phenotype characterized by energy conservation and prioritization of essential organs like the brain. These adaptations include changes in insulin sensitivity, glucose metabolism, and energy storage. While beneficial for survival in utero, they increase susceptibility to metabolic disease in later life [[3](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B3-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

Maternal overnutrition, including obesity and gestational diabetes, exposes the fetus to excess nutrients, promoting adiposity and metabolic dysregulation [[4](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B4-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. This environment promotes fetal adiposity, alters appetite regulation, and affects energy balance. Offspring of mothers with obesity or diabetes are at increased risk of obesity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease. These changes can persist throughout life and contribute to intergenerational cycles of disease [[4](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B4-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

Maternal nutrition influences multiple organ systems, including the pancreas, kidneys, cardiovascular system, and brain, influencing lifelong health outcomes. Maternal nutrition critically influences fetal neurodevelopment [[15](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B15-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Reduced nephron number may increase hypertension risk, altered pancreatic development may impair insulin secretion, and changes in brain development may affect cognition and behavior. Cardiovascular changes include altered vascular structure and endothelial function.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 7. Postnatal period: continued programming

The postnatal period represents a continuation of developmental plasticity. Nutrition during infancy influences growth trajectories, metabolic regulation, immune development, and neurodevelopment.

Breast milk is a biologically active fluid containing nutrients, hormones, growth factors, immune cells, and bioactive compounds. It supports optimal growth, immune protection, and metabolic regulation. Breastfeeding has been associated with reduced risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, infections, and allergic diseases. These benefits are partly mediated through its effects on the microbiome and immune system [[16](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B16-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

The introduction of solid foods is a critical stage in development and shapes dietary preferences and metabolic outcomes. Early dietary exposure to diverse, nutrient-rich foods influences taste preferences and eating behaviors. Long-term dietary patterns promote healthier long-term habits. A balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats supports optimal development [[17](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B17-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)], whereas diets high in processed foods and sugars may predispose to metabolic disorders [[18](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B18-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

Rapid catch-up growth following intrauterine growth restriction is associated with increased risk of obesity and metabolic disease, highlighting the importance of balanced growth trajectories.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 8. Transgenerational effects

Emerging evidence suggests that developmental programming effects may extend across generations. Epigenetic modifications induced by environmental exposures can be transmitted through germ cells, influencing the health of offspring and subsequent generations. Both maternal and paternal factors contribute to this process, and grandparental exposures may also influence disease risk, emphasizing the long-term impact of early-life environments [[5](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B5-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)–[9](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B9-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)]. Paternal nutrition and lifestyle can alter sperm epigenetic marks, while grandparental exposures may influence disease risk in grandchildren. These findings emphasize the importance of considering long-term and multigenerational perspectives in addressing maternal and child health [[13](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329#B13-Acad.Nutri.-3-326083)].

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 9. Clinical implications

From a clinical perspective, optimizing maternal nutrition represents one of the most effective strategies for preventing chronic disease. Healthcare providers should emphasize preconception counseling, nutritional assessment, and targeted supplementation. Screening for nutritional deficiencies, obesity, and gestational diabetes is essential for early intervention. Integrating nutrition into routine maternal care can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes and long-term health of offspring.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 10. Public health implications

The implications of developmental programming extend to global health challenges. The increasing prevalence of non-communicable diseases is closely linked to early-life exposures. At the population level, maternal nutrition is a critical determinant of health. Interventions targeting maternal nutrition represent a powerful strategy for disease prevention. Public health strategies should focus on improving access to nutritious foods, providing education on maternal and infant nutrition, and supporting maternal health services. Policies that promote breastfeeding, regulate unhealthy food marketing, and address food insecurity are essential. Healthcare systems should prioritize preconception and prenatal care, recognizing the long-term impact of early-life nutrition. Investing in maternal nutrition is a cost-effective approach to reducing the burden of non-communicable diseases.

[](https://www.academia.edu/3067-1345/3/2/10.20935/AcadNutr8329)
## 11. Conclusions

Maternal nutrition is a fundamental determinant of lifelong health and plays a central role in shaping the biological foundation of human health. Addressing developmental programming provides a powerful opportunity to improve outcomes across generations. Through complex and interconnected biological mechanisms, early-life nutritional exposures shape gene expression, organ development, and disease risk. Prioritizing maternal and early-life nutrition offers a powerful opportunity to improve health outcomes for current and future generations.

args.summary:
This is a perspective article published in *Academia Nutrition and Dietetics* (Volume 3, Issue 2, Special Issue on "Maternal Nutrition and Early-Life Programming") by Yousef M. Abdulrazzaq (Department of Pediatrics, UAE University). Published May 27, 2026, the article examines how maternal nutritional status before, during, and after pregnancy programs lifelong health outcomes in offspring through the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) paradigm.

**Key mechanisms** of developmental programming include:
- **Epigenetic modifications** (DNA methylation, histone changes) influenced by one-carbon metabolism nutrients (folate, choline, methionine, vitamin B12)
- **Hormonal signaling** (cortisol, insulin, leptin) affecting fetal HPA axis, metabolic regulation, and appetite
- **Placental function** adapting nutrient transport to maternal nutritional status
- **Maternal microbiome** influencing infant microbial colonization and immune development
- **Catch-up growth** linked to obesity and diabetes risk

**Micronutrients** (folate, iron, iodine, zinc, vitamin D) are critical for fetal development. The **environmental mismatch** concept—where prenatal adaptations to scarcity become maladaptive in postnatal abundance—is central to disease risk. Developmental programming begins **pre-conception** (oocyte quality, paternal epigenetic contributions) and continues through **pregnancy** (thrifty phenotype hypothesis, maternal overnutrition effects) and the **postnatal period** (breastfeeding benefits, complementary feeding).

**Transgenerational effects** may occur through epigenetic modifications transmitted via germ cells. The article concludes that optimizing maternal nutrition is a critical modifiable determinant of lifelong health with significant clinical and public health implications for reducing non-communicable disease burden across generations.

# The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD)

### Salvatore Lacagnina, DO

Salvatore Lacagnina, DO, System Medical
Director of Wellness and Employee Health, Lee Health, Lee Memorial Hospital,
2780 Cleveland Avenue, Suite 802—Employee Health, Fort Myers, FL 33901; e-mail:
Salvatore.lacagnina@leehealth.org.

Collection date 2020 Jan-Feb.

## Abstract

For years many have believed that genetic heritage defined one’s destiny, if an
individual would grow to be healthy, or if he or she would suffer from chronic
illness or cancer. Recent scientific evidence and the field of epigenetics has
proven this to be untrue. Certainly, the DNA sequence and the genetic code are
fixed; but the field of epigenetics has shown how methylation and other chemical
modifications of the genome directly influence the production of proteins that
can alter the phenotype of an organism. This article will lay out the supporting
research, the details on how the internal and external environments influence
genetic function, and will allow the reader to develop an action plan necessary
to influence the genetic code, with the goal of then moving the individual
toward optimal health. These research details will enable health care
professionals in every field of medicine to work with patients on positively
influencing the genetic output in order to improve the quality of life and
longevity.

**Keywords:** epigenetics, DNA modification, heredity, genetic code

‘. . . the field of epigenetics relates to nutritional deficiencies,
biochemistry, and how the external as well as the internal environments
influence the cells down to the level of the DNA’

## Objectives

The aim of this study was to relate lifestyle influence from the external as well as
the internal environment to genetic modifications and phenotypic alterations
beginning with the following:

Stage 1: The future parents

Stage 2: The preconception period

Stage 3: The perinatal period

Stage 4: Postdelivery and the first year of life

Stage 5: Childhood

Stage 6: The adolescent period

Stage 7: Adulthood

The term *epigenetics* was first proposed by Conrad Waddington in the
1940s to describe the interaction of genes with their environment during
development. The word itself has developed from the narrative term to an immensely
studied field of science in the 21st century. The current meaning of the term
epigenetics encompasses conformational changes in DNA and/or chromatin without
alterations in the basic genetic code.

To a large degree, the field of epigenetics relates to nutritional deficiencies,
biochemistry, and how the external as well as the internal environments influence
the cells down to the level of the DNA. The science of epigenetics explains the sum
total effect of everything that influences genetic function and dysfunction;
research, including anecdotal stories, helps us understand that this influence
starts generations before phenotypic and biochemical changes become apparent. The
purpose of this article is to report on how both the research and anecdotal stories
can influence how health care providers approach patients, especially in relation to
lifestyle behaviors. The take home message for both health care providers and the
public is that the genes people are born with can be significantly influenced to
create either disease or wellness, and much of this influence relates to the
lifestyle choices we make every day.

The developmental origins of the health and disease hypothesis (DOHaD) propose a link
between periconceptual, fetal, and early infant phases of life and the long-term
development of metabolic disorders. Research shows how external factors influence
genetic function, resulting in altered longevity and the incidence of cancer and
age-related diseases.

According to the DOHaD hypothesis, epigenetic adaptations are made to the
fetal/neonatal DNA in response to environmental influences.[1](#bibr1-1559827619879694) The hypothesis further explains that the body responds to the environment and
makes genetic changes (predictive adaptations) in anticipation of a presumed future
environment. If the predictive adaptations are incorrect, then the metabolic state
of the individual is altered to a degree whereby the risk of chronic disease in
adulthood is increased; research also shows that the increased risk might be transgenerational.[2](#bibr2-1559827619879694)

Roth et al[3](#bibr3-1559827619879694) explained that the regulation of energy balance is established early in
development, and nutritional challenges during pregnancy and/or lactation predispose
the offspring to a range of metabolic disorders. Studies also show how developmental
plasticity influences the genotype, which then can influence and change the
bio-physiology and the phenotype of the organism.

Wattex et al[4](#bibr4-1559827619879694) discussed how altered early life nutrition connects epigenetic changes within
the hypothalamus and alters concentrations of key adipokines such as leptin and
adiponectin, both of which regulate energy balance. These alterations have been
shown to contribute to long-lasting dysregulation of energy balance and obesity
following early adverse life events.[5](#bibr5-1559827619879694)

## How Does Lifestyle Affect the Health of a Child From Birth Through Adolescent and Adult Years?

The well-established viewpoint that noncommunicable disease (cardiovascular disease,
diabetes mellitus) are the product of the gene-lifestyle interaction in adult life
has undergone considerable evolution since the 1990s. It is now recognized that a
life course approach to understanding health is more appropriate, and the risk of
disease at any stage of life is determined by the interaction of genetics and the
cumulative exposures to lifestyle and environmental factors throughout life.

The concept that early life exposures influence the long-term risk of disease is
referred to as *developmental programming*[6](#bibr6-1559827619879694); the environmental factors include maternal nutrition, smoking, infant
feeding methods, maternal stress, and infection.

## What Impact Does the Health of the Mother Have on the Health of the Child, in Utero and Thereafter?

Whitaker[7](#bibr7-1559827619879694) found that children of obese mothers were twice as likely to be obese at 2
years of age as compared with normal-weight mothers. Multiple studies[8](#bibr8-1559827619879694),[9](#bibr9-1559827619879694) have reported that infants born
to overweight and obese mothers tend to have a higher fat mass at birth and to be at
significantly increased risk of developing obesity as well as associated metabolic
disorders in childhood and adulthood.

## What About the Father?

Radford et al[10](#bibr10-1559827619879694) reported on how undernutrition during prenatal life is able to compromise the
male germline (affecting the health of the sperm), which over time contributes to a
higher than normal incidence of environmentally induced diseases. This is reported
as *paternal transgenerational epigenetic inheritance*.

Changes to the epigenome brought about by early-life events have been shown to
contribute to long-term disease risk. Studies show that intrauterine life is
significantly affected by all that influences the mother and the fetus. When birth
occurs, it is known that the type of delivery influences the long-term health of the offspring.[11](#bibr11-1559827619879694) Vaginal delivery confers added immunological benefits to the child, and
conversely, cesarean delivery negatively influences the development of immunity and
the normal microbiome in the child. The latter results in a higher risk for
development of asthma and allergies. Breast feeding for 6 to 9 months confers
positive benefits to the child’s immune system.[12](#bibr12-1559827619879694) Antibiotic use in the first year of life brings negative effects on the
immune system and the microbiome.[13](#bibr13-1559827619879694),[14](#bibr14-1559827619879694)

## How Do Early Lifestyle Behaviors and Nutrition Affect the Risk and Incidence of Diabetes, Obesity, Heart Disease, and Even Cancer?

A study in the town of Hertfordshire in the United Kingdom[15](#bibr15-1559827619879694) with men in the United Kingdom born in the 1920s who weighed <2.5 kg found
a strong association between low birth weight and the risk and incidence of coronary
death, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. There was a similar study of people
born in Scotland in the 1950s, with similar results.

The Dutch Hunger Winter study describes the German occupation of The Netherlands in
1944, which resulted in the population eating only 400 to 800 calories per
day.[16](#bibr16-1559827619879694),[17](#bibr17-1559827619879694) When this
famine affected pregnant women, early gestation food restriction resulted in
elevated rates of adult obesity, hyperlipidemia, and cardiovascular disease. Calorie
restriction during midgestation and late gestation resulted in reduced birth weight
of the offspring, who also suffered from lower adult weight and stature. Exposure to
famine during any stage of gestation was associated with glucose intolerance.[18](#bibr18-1559827619879694)

## What About the Effects of Certain Types of Protein?

Chavarro et al[19](#bibr19-1559827619879694) reported on the relative risk of infertility depending on the type of protein
consumed. They found that mothers who ate more animal protein had a 39% higher risk
of infertility as compared with those eating more vegetable protein, who had a 22%
less risk. Substituting just 5% of the total energy intake as vegetable protein
lowered the risk of infertility by 50%.

Goh et al[20](#bibr20-1559827619879694) found that micronutrients have a positive epigenetic effect on fertility,
conferring a 41% lower risk of infertility and resulting in fewer miscarriages,
fewer birth defects, less pediatric cancer and less autism.

## Environmental Toxins Also Appear to Play a Role in Epigenetics and the Development of Chronic Illness

The EARTH study (the Environment and Reproductive Health) enrolled 155 men and found
that those exposed to more pesticides (residue on fruits and vegetables) had a 49%
lower total sperm count and 32% more abnormal sperm overall.[21](#bibr21-1559827619879694)

## How Does Inheritance of Gene Mutations Influence the Developing Health and How Does Science Explain Transgenerational Inheritance?

The explanation of transgenerational inheritance is seen in mice surviving on a
very-low-calorie diet, who then had underweight offspring prone to diabetes. The
males in this litter fathered another generation of offspring who also developed
diabetes even though they consumed a normal diet.

## Does the Inheritance of Bad Genes Always Translate Into the Development of Disease and What Lifestyle Interventions Decrease the Risk and Incidence of Disease?

Research conducted by Ornish et al[22](#bibr22-1559827619879694) showed that intensive lifestyle intervention influences 500 genes in males
with early prostate cancer. Similar results were seen in individuals with heart
disease. Nutrition focusing on whole plant foods revealed that many nutritional
compounds in food influence enzymatic activity and modulate gene expression: for
example, epigallocatechin gallate (ECGC) in green tea, resveratrol in red grapes,
genistein in soya, curcumin or turmeric, and isothiocyanates in cruciferous
vegetables.

Paternal transgenerational epigenetic inheritance describes how epigenetics affects
the male DNA. Radford et al[10](#bibr10-1559827619879694) reported on how undernutrition during prenatal life is able to compromise the
male germline (affecting the health of the sperm), which over time contributes to a
higher than normal incidence of environmentally induced diseases. Jensen et al[23](#bibr23-1559827619879694) found that the male diet also affects fertility. He studied Danish recruits
who ate the most saturated fat and found that they had 38% lower sperm
concentrations and sperm counts that were decreased by 41%.

Factors that affect the genes include micro and macro nutrients, fasting/calorie
restriction, exercise, chronic stress, sleep deprivation, mental health, how
individuals respond to life experiences, toxins, medications, heavy metals,
pesticides, tobacco, hormones, radioactivity, antibiotics, viruses, bacteria, and
more. Substances are not the only source of epigenetic changes. It is known that
high-quality maternal care results in better health of the offspring. Scientists at
Duke University[24](#bibr24-1559827619879694) analyzed DNA first from 5-year-old children and then again when these
children were 10 years of age. The children who experience physical or emotional
abuse or other life stressors between 5 and 10 years of age had shorter telomeres,
showing that life experiences have a direct influence on the expression of
genes.

The study of epigenetics might be described as follows: what we thought we knew to be
correct and much of what we thought factual was actually in error. We know from
history that there have been numerous times in medicine where dogma turned out not
to be true or what was thought to be understood was incomplete, and as such,
epigenetics might be an example of the same. There are many examples of what the
medical establishment in the 16th and 17th centuries thought they knew but found out
that was not the case, possibly similar to what we in the 21st century believe to be
true about the function of the genes and the destiny of the DNA.[25](#bibr25-1559827619879694)

In summary, the science of epigenetics is quickly growing with the understanding that
the environment and individual lifestyle directly interact with the genome to
influence epigenetic changes. Human epidemiological studies have provided evidence
that prenatal and postnatal environmental factors influence the adult risk of
developing various chronic illnesses and behavioral disorders. This research is
making it apparent that epigenetic effects occur not only in the womb but over the
full course of a human life span and that epigenetic changes can be reversed by
controlling lifestyle choices and environmental exposures. Therefore, we see that
there is a lot that can be done to affect the health of the DNA, showing us that
genes are not always our destiny!

args.summary:
This article by Salvatore Lacagnina, DO, published in the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine (Jan-Feb 2020), explains the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis and the science of epigenetics. The core premise is that genetic heritage does not define one's destiny; rather, lifestyle choices and environmental factors influence gene expression through epigenetic modifications (methylation and other chemical changes) without altering the DNA sequence itself.

The article traces influences across seven life stages: future parents, preconception, perinatal, first year of life, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. Key findings include:

- **DOHaD hypothesis**: Epigenetic adaptations occur in fetal/neonatal DNA in response to environmental influences. If predictive adaptations are incorrect, the risk of chronic disease in adulthood increases, potentially across generations.
- **Maternal impact**: Children of obese mothers are twice as likely to be obese at age 2. Infants of overweight/obese mothers have higher fat mass at birth and increased risk of metabolic disorders.
- **Paternal impact**: Undernutrition during prenatal life compromises the male germline, contributing to environmentally induced diseases (paternal transgenerational epigenetic inheritance). Men eating high saturated fat had 38% lower sperm concentrations and 41% lower sperm counts.
- **Delivery & feeding**: Vaginal delivery confers immunological benefits; cesarean delivery negatively impacts immunity and microbiome. Breastfeeding for 6-9 months benefits the immune system.
- **Historical studies**: The Hertfordshire study (UK) found low birth weight (<2.5 kg) associated with coronary death, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. The Dutch Hunger Winter study showed that famine during pregnancy resulted in elevated rates of adult obesity, hyperlipidemia, and cardiovascular disease.
- **Protein type**: Mothers eating more animal protein had 39% higher infertility risk; those eating more vegetable protein had 22% less risk. Substituting 5% energy as vegetable protein lowered infertility risk by 50%.
- **Environmental toxins**: The EARTH study found men exposed to more pesticides had 49% lower total sperm count and 32% more abnormal sperm.
- **Lifestyle intervention**: Ornish et al showed intensive lifestyle intervention influences 500 genes in men with early prostate cancer. Compounds like EGCG (green tea), resveratrol (red grapes), genistein (soya), curcumin, and isothiocyanates (cruciferous vegetables) modulate gene expression.
- **Life experiences**: Children who experienced abuse or stress between ages 5-10 had shorter telomeres, showing life experiences directly influence gene expression.

The article concludes that epigenetic changes can be reversed by controlling lifestyle choices and environmental exposures, demonstrating that "genes are not always our destiny."
