The advertisements selected for this study varied in duration, with two ads lasting approximately 30 s and the other two approximately one minute. Importantly, ad length was kept consistent within each food category: both healthy food advertisements (one child-targeted and one non-child-targeted) were one minute long, and both unhealthy food advertisements (one child-targeted and one non-child-targeted) were 30 s long. This decision was made to maintain internal consistency when comparing children’s responses to ads within each nutritional category. The variation in ad length was due to the limited availability of suitable pre-existing advertisements that met all selection criteria: each ad had to represent one of four categories—child-targeted healthy, child-targeted unhealthy, non-child-targeted healthy, and non-child-targeted unhealthy—and feature brands not available in the Canadian market to reduce the influence of prior exposure or brand recognition. Given these requirements, it was not feasible to standardize ad length across all categories.

### Data analysis

First, one researcher (JSG) conducted the interviews, and another researcher (SS) transcribed the audio from all interviews. Second, coding was conducted by two other researchers (JSG and MP). Thematic analysis was used to code and analyze the data, which provides a systematic approach to interpreting the data by focusing on recurring ideas, meanings, and perceptions articulated by participants [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379#CR49), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379#CR50)]. A hybrid coding approach was used, combining both deductive and inductive strategies: deductive codes were initially informed by prior research and theoretical constructs relevant to food advertising—specifically, awareness, attitudes, purchase intent, and perceived target audience—as outlined in Kelly et al.‘s (2015) hierarchy of effects model [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379#CR16)]. Simultaneously, the analysis remained open to inductive insights that emerged organically from participants’ own language and interpretations. The researchers began by getting familiarized with the data. In the initial coding phase, the researchers systematically examined every line and segment of the transcripts. A quotation was considered “relevant” if it provided meaningful insight into one of the overarching concepts (e.g., awareness, attitudes, purchase intent, and perceived target audience). These were coded without immediate concern for thematic organization to preserve the openness of the analysis. After this, one researcher (JSG) conducted the focused coding and developed the themes. In the focused coding phase, the most salient and recurring initial codes were selected for further development into broader categories and themes. Codes were deemed “most useful” based on their frequency, relevance to the research questions, and conceptual depth. Finally, the researcher grouped related focused codes into themes based on conceptual similarity, their relationship to the research questions, and theoretical coherence. Themes were refined in consultation with co-researchers and were validated through iterative comparison across the data set to ensure consistency and depth. Microsoft 365© tools (Excel and Word versions 2412) were used in the coding and analysis process. Throughout the entirety of this study’s process, participants were identified using their unique participation codes, which consisted of the study year combined with their recruitment order (e.g., P2301, P2302, P2303, etc.).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379)Results

### Sociodemographic and screen habits

Overall, 17 participants (11 girls, 6 boys) aged 6–11 years old were interviewed (Table[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379#Tab2)). Most participants were between ages 9–11 years (64.7%), Latino (47.1%), and with parents who declared that it was difficult to make ends meet (41.2%). Most children used a tablet several times a day (29.4%); a cell phone or smartphone once a day (23.5%) or several times a week (23.5%); used a computer several times a day (29.4%); and watched television once a day (35.3%). Also, most children used a screen for leisure purposes for either 2–4 h per day (41.2%) or 4–6 h per day (41.2%); and used a screen for educational purposes for 0–2 h per day (47.1%).

args.summary:
This is a qualitative research article published in BMC Public Health (2025) examining how children aged 6–12 perceive child-targeted versus non-child-targeted food advertising. The study, conducted by researchers from the University of Ottawa, Université Laval, and University of Calgary, involved 17 children (11 girls, 6 boys) who participated in online interviews where they were shown four advertisements: child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads for both healthy (plain milk) and unhealthy (chocolate) products.

**Key Background:** The study notes that approximately 30% of Canadian children aged 5–17 have overweight or obesity, and ultra-processed foods account for 49.1% of caloric intake among children aged 2–5 and 54.2% among those aged 6–12. Children are exposed to nearly 2,000 unhealthy food ads annually on television and over 4,000 on digital platforms in Canada.

**Methods:** Open-ended interviews were conducted via Zoom, with thematic analysis using a hybrid deductive-inductive coding approach. The ads featured brands not readily available in Canada (Milka, Dove, Arla) to minimize prior brand familiarity.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Awareness:** Most children could identify the product being advertised but showed no brand awareness, as expected with unfamiliar brands.
2. **Attitudes:** Most children expressed positive perceptions of the ads, regardless of whether they were child-targeted or non-child-targeted. Reasons for liking included: (i) seeing people eating the product, (ii) positive emotional appeal, (iii) pre-existing affinity with the product, and (iv) visibility of the product. Notably, the child-targeted milk ad (featuring an animated cookie character) was less well-received, with some children finding it "creepy" or confusing.
3. **Purchase Intent:** Most children expressed "negative purchase intent" for all ads due to pre-existing aversion to the product. Even children who liked the product often expressed negative purchase intent because they preferred other brands or flavors.
4. **Perceived Target Audience:** Children considered the type of product over marketing techniques when determining who the ad was for. Themes included "product for everyone" and "product for people that like the product."

**Conclusions:** Children's perceptions, purchase intent, and perceived targeted audience did not differ significantly between child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads. The study underscores the critical role of the product itself (rather than marketing techniques) in influencing children's responses to ads. The authors recommend that public policies and advertising regulations focus on restricting promotions of unhealthy products rather than solely addressing marketing techniques or target audiences.

--- SOURCE 1: Ultra-Processed Foods, Gut Microbiota, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Critical Review of Emerging Evidence ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/16/2677

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Nutrients (2025, 17(16), 2677) titled "Ultra-Processed Foods, Gut Microbiota, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Critical Review of Emerging Evidence." The review examines the influence of ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption on gut microbiota composition and function and its potential link to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Key findings include: (1) UPFs account for up to 58% of daily caloric intake in high-income countries and are associated with intestinal dysbiosis, reduced microbial diversity, decreased short-chain fatty acid production, impaired barrier integrity, and mucus layer disruption. (2) Consuming 10% of calories from UPFs per day is associated with a 19% increased risk of developing Crohn's disease. (3) Food additives like emulsifiers (e.g., carboxymethyl cellulose, polysorbate 80) can promote proinflammatory changes in the gut microbiota, enhance LPS release, and impair the mucus layer. (4) The persistent low-grade inflammation driven by UPF consumption can lead to "leaky gut" and increased intestinal permeability. The review notes that serum LPS levels are reportedly six times higher in patients with active Crohn's disease compared to healthy controls. The article concludes that high UPF consumption is associated with intestinal dysbiosis characterized by overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria such as Clostridium and Enterococcus, triggering inflammatory responses in the host.
</summary>

URL: https://www.news-medical.net/health/The-Science-of-Ultra-Processed-Foods-and-Mental-Health.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from News-Medical (dated April 3, 2025) explores the growing evidence linking ultra-processed foods (UPFs) to mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, and cognitive decline. UPFs—defined by the NOVA classification system as industrially processed foods like packaged snacks, sugary drinks, instant noodles, and processed meats—now constitute a significant portion of daily caloric intake in many countries.

**Key Evidence:**
- A 2020 study of over 10,000 US adults found that those consuming the most UPFs had a 35% greater likelihood of depressive symptoms.
- Harvard Medical School research found higher UPF consumption was associated with a 50% increased risk of depression, particularly with artificially sweetened beverages and processed snacks.
- A large cohort study of over 25,000 individuals followed for more than five years linked increased UPF intake to higher rates of depressive episodes, independent of lifestyle factors.

**Proposed Mechanisms:**
1. **Gut-brain axis dysfunction** – UPFs lack dietary fiber, disrupting gut microbiota and impairing production of mood-regulating neurotransmitters like serotonin and GABA.
2. **Chronic inflammation** – Refined carbohydrates, unhealthy fats, and additives promote systemic inflammation, with elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) linked to depression.
3. **Blood sugar fluctuations** – High glycemic index foods cause glucose spikes and crashes, affecting mood stability and cognitive function.
4. **Artificial additives** – Sweeteners like aspartame may alter neurotransmitter activity; emulsifiers can disrupt gut microbiota and influence neuroinflammatory pathways.

**Global Trends & Industry Response:** The food industry continues expanding UPF production due to cost-effectiveness and convenience demand. Some companies are reformulating products, but health impacts remain uncertain. Public health initiatives promoting whole-food diets (e.g., Mediterranean, DASH) are increasingly advocated.

**Limitations:** Most studies are observational, making causality difficult to establish. Reverse causality (people with depression may consume more UPFs as a coping mechanism) is possible. Self-reported dietary data is subject to recall bias, and confounding factors like socioeconomic status and genetics may influence outcomes.

**Future Directions:** Research should focus on elucidating mechanisms using microbiome analysis, neuroimaging, and biomarker assessments. Longitudinal studies with diverse populations are needed to establish causality. Public health policies should aim to reduce UPF consumption and promote whole-food-based diets.
</summary>

<summary>
This scientific review article, published February 28, 2025, in Nutrients journal (PMCID: PMC11901572, PMID: 40077728), examines the detrimental impact of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) on the human gut microbiome and gut barrier. Authored by researchers from Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore and Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Gemelli IRCCS in Rome, Italy, the review covers the following key areas:

**NOVA Classification System:** UPFs (NOVA4) are defined as industrially manufactured products with 5+ ingredients, including additives not commonly found in kitchens (e.g., hydrogenated oils, emulsifiers, artificial colors). Examples include soft drinks, packaged snacks, processed meats, and ready-to-eat meals.

**Gut Microbiome Overview:** The healthy gut microbiome is dominated by Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes phyla. Key beneficial bacteria include Akkermansia muciniphila, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Bifidobacteria. The microbiome produces essential short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like acetate, propionate, and butyrate, which maintain gut barrier integrity, modulate immunity, and regulate metabolism.

**UPF-Driven Gut Alterations:** UPF consumption is associated with decreased microbial α-diversity, reduced beneficial bacteria (Akkermansia muciniphila, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Lachnospira, Roseburia), and increased pro-inflammatory microorganisms (Granulicatella, Blautia, Bacteroidaceae). Emulsifiers (carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate 80) alter microbiota composition, promote pro-inflammatory environments, and compromise the mucus layer, leading to increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut").

**Health Implications:** UPF-induced dysbiosis contributes to systemic low-grade inflammation and is linked to metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and colorectal cancer. UPFs may also alter the gut-brain axis, potentially affecting cognitive function and mental health.

**Mitigation Strategies:** Dietary modifications incorporating fiber, fermented foods, and probiotics can help mitigate UPF effects. The authors advocate for stricter regulations on UPFs and well-defined food labels. The review notes that Latin American countries have already integrated NOVA into dietary guidelines, and France aims to reduce UPF consumption by 20%.

--- SOURCE 4: How ultra-processed foods affect our gut microbiome ---
URL: https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20260220-how-ultra-processed-foods-influence-our-gut-microbiome

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This BBC article examines how additives in ultra-processed foods (UPFs), particularly emulsifiers, affect the gut microbiome — the trillions of microbes in our digestive system. A healthy, diverse microbiome is linked to better mood, metabolism, brain health, sleep, and longevity. 

Key findings include:
- Emulsifiers, which help mix oils/water and extend shelf life, are found in about half of UK supermarket products (6,640 products analyzed).
- Animal studies (led by Benoit Chassaing at Institut Pasteur) show emulsifiers cause gut bacteria to move closer to the gut wall, eroding the protective mucus layer and triggering inflammation.
- Human correlational studies link emulsifier exposure to increased risk of type 2 diabetes (over 100,000 adults, 2024 French study) and breast/prostate cancers (over 90,000 adults).
- A clinical trial on Crohn's disease patients found those on a restricted emulsifier diet were three times more likely to experience reduced symptoms.
- A randomized control trial (Melissa Lane, Deakin University) found that a high-UPF diet reduced gut microbe diversity and increased constipation compared to a low-UPF diet with similar nutrients, likely due to differences in fiber types and additive content.
- Emulsifiers are approved for safety (tested for toxicity and DNA damage) but have not been tested for their direct effects on the microbiome. The "cocktail effect" of multiple additives is difficult to study.

Experts recommend cooking from scratch with fresh ingredients, eating more fiber and polyphenols, and practicing moderation rather than completely avoiding UPFs. The article emphasizes that food processing methods matter for gut health beyond just nutrient content.
</summary>

"You can think of gut diversity as like a forest. The more microbes that you have and the different types of microbes in your forest, the greater resilience you have to any perturbations," says Melissa Lane, a nutritional epidemiologist at Deakin University., "They are only tested for the toxicity effect or for the ability to induce DNA damage. And for those two aspects, they are perfectly fine. But they were never tested in the past for the direct effect on the microbiome," says Benoit Chassaing., "The higher ultra-processed food diet had mixtures of additives and, very low amounts of minimally processed ingredients, whilst the low-UPF diet had many different types of fibre coming from whole foods, and far fewer additives," said Melissa Lane., "I wouldn't want to be saying to the general public, 'never eat anything that has a food additive in it', I certainly don't do that and I'm not recommending people do it," says Kevin Whelan, professor of dietetics at King's College London.

--- SOURCE 5: How do processed foods affect the gut-brain axis? - Quadram Institute ---
URL: https://quadram.ac.uk/blogs/how-do-processed-foods-affect-the-gut-brain-axis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Quadram Institute, published March 22, 2024, explores how processed foods affect the microbiota-gut-brain axis. The microbiota-gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication network between gut microorganisms, gut cells, and the brain, facilitated by nerves and hormones. A varied diet rich in fibers promotes beneficial gut microbes, while a diet high in refined sugars and low in fiber reduces microbial diversity.

Key research findings from Quadram Institute scientists include:

1. **Mucin Glycosylation & Brain Function**: Researchers found that alterations in mucin glycosylation (sugars decorating the gut lining) are associated with a leaky gut and changes in brain function and cognition (studies referenced: PMID 35579971, PMID 37634035).

--- SOURCE 1: How bad is ultra-processed food for the planet? ---
URL: https://www.soilassociation.org/blogs/2022/august/24/how-bad-is-ultra-processed-food-for-the-planet

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published August 24, 2022) by the Soil Association examines the environmental impacts of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), based on a paper published by researchers from CSIRO and Deakin University in Australia. The paper reviewed 52 studies on UPF environmental impacts.

Key findings include that UPFs account for 17-39% of total diet-related energy use, 36-45% of diet-related biodiversity loss, up to a third of diet-related greenhouse gas emissions/land use/food waste, and up to a quarter of diet-related water use in high-income countries. UPF production relies on commodity ingredients like palm oil, soya, wheat, maize, milk, eggs, and meat, which have driven ecosystem destruction (e.g., rainforest clearing for palm oil in Indonesia, Cerrado conversion for soya in Brazil). UPFs contribute significantly to climate change, plastic pollution, and food waste.

The authors conclude that UPFs are "potentially counterproductive" to sustainable food system objectives and call on policymakers to regulate UPF production, availability, and consumption. Countries including Brazil, Canada, Chile, Ecuador, France, Israel, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay already encourage limiting UPF intake through dietary guidance and labeling. The UK is one of the highest consumers of UPFs, with these products making up over half of average weekly shopping baskets. The article calls for UK government action including reduction targets, consumer guidance, UPF labeling, and support for transition to agroecology and organic farming.
</summary>

The webinar features three expert speakers: Dr. Josiemer Mattei (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health), Dr. Lauren O'Connor (Texas A&M AgriLife Research), and Professor Jerold Mande (Nourish Science/Harvard).

**Key Points from Dr. Josiemer Mattei (UPF Overview and Epidemiology):**
- Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are defined using the Nova framework, which classifies foods into four categories (unprocessed/minimally processed, culinary ingredients, processed foods, and ultra-processed foods) based on the extent and purpose of industrial processing rather than nutritional composition.

- Nutrition research faces unique challenges compared to drug trials, including confounding by energy intake, complexity of food matrices, and the impact of comparison foods on study conclusions.

--- SOURCE 6: Measuring Progress | Healthy Food Policy Project ---
URL: https://healthyfoodpolicyproject.org/towards-equitable-and-just-food-systems/measuring-progress

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the "Towards Equitable and Just Food Systems" resource from the Healthy Food Policy Project. It examines common terms used to measure progress in food systems—food security, food deserts, food swamps, and hunger—along with their definitions, uses in policy and research, and significant limitations.

**Food Security** is defined as consistent access to sufficient, safe, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food. The USDA measures it on a spectrum from high to very low food security. However, the term is limiting as an ultimate goal because it does not address nutritional quality or root causes of inequity. Related terms include nutrition security, community food security, food access (with five dimensions: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability, accommodation), and food system resilience.

**Food Desert** refers to areas with low access to grocery stores. The term is being phased out at the federal level in favor of "low-income and low-access areas." It is criticized for implying scarcity is natural, masking deliberate policy decisions (e.g., redlining, suburbanization), ignoring racial disparities, and not reflecting community vibrancy. Baltimore, Maryland has shifted to using "Healthy Food Priority Areas."

**Food Swamp** describes areas where unhealthy food outlets (fast food, convenience stores) outnumber healthy options. Research suggests food swamps predict obesity better than food deserts and disproportionately impact low-income and Black communities. Root causes include redlining, white flight, and zoning policies. Critiques note the term still does not adequately address root causes, with some advocating for "food apartheid" as a better descriptor.

**Hunger** is an individual-level physical sensation from insufficient food intake, often conflated with food insecurity in surveys. It is difficult to measure directly, so food insecurity is used as a proxy. The Committee on National Statistics has recommended USDA stop using "hunger" to describe food insecurity indicators.

The page includes policy examples for each term and discussion questions for reflection.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Food Swamps Predict Obesity Rates Better Than Food Deserts in the United States ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5708005

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2017), investigates the effect of food environments on adult obesity rates across U.S. counties, comparing "food swamps" (areas with high-density of fast food/junk food outlets relative to healthy options) with "food deserts" (areas with limited access to affordable, nutritious food). 

Key findings include:
- Food swamps are a stronger predictor of obesity rates than food deserts across U.S. counties.
- Even after controlling for food desert effects, food swamps had a positive, statistically significant effect on adult obesity rates.
- The study used three measures of food swamps (Traditional Retail Food Environment Index and two expanded versions), all showing positive associations with obesity.
- An instrumental variables (IV) approach using highway exits corrected for endogeneity (people self-selecting into neighborhoods) and revealed a stronger effect of food swamps than ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates would suggest.
- The food swamp effect was stronger in counties with greater income inequality (p<0.05) and where residents are less mobile (p<0.01).
- OLS estimates underestimated the food swamp effect; IV estimates suggested policies like zoning laws could lower obesity rates by about three percent.

1. **Availability** – Measured via the "container method" (counting food retailers per area) or distance-based approaches. Distance must account for travel routes, public transit, walking paths, safety, and daily mobility patterns. Different store types (supermarkets vs. convenience stores) offer different ratios of produce to EDNP foods.
3. **Affordability** – Noted as beyond the scope of the guide but relevant when fresh foods are available at a premium price, forcing trade-offs.

**Data Processing Tools:**
- **Geographic Information Systems (GIS):** Used for spatial analysis of access, distance, and centrality. Advanced metrics like the Aggregated Accessibility Index account for route quality and effort.
- **Nexus Analysis:** A qualitative method for analyzing social dimensions of food access using observational data, interviews, and focus groups.
- **Machine Learning Algorithms:** Can process large datasets to categorize foods and assess menu balance across many outlets, enabling frequent, low-cost surveillance.

3. **Food reinforcement:** A significant difference was observed for rs1800497, where homozygous A1A1 showed less reinforcement (p=0.01), particularly in males (p=0.03).

4. **Bilocus score distribution:** 11.7% "very low" dopaminergic signaling, 24.4% "under", 49.7% "intermediate", 12.7% "high", and 1.4% "very high".

<summary>
This article by Salvatore Lacagnina, DO, published in the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine (Jan-Feb 2020), explains the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis and the science of epigenetics. The core premise is that genetic heritage does not define one's destiny; rather, lifestyle choices and environmental factors influence gene expression through epigenetic modifications (methylation and other chemical changes) without altering the DNA sequence itself.

The article traces influences across seven life stages: future parents, preconception, perinatal, first year of life, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. Key findings include:

- **DOHaD hypothesis**: Epigenetic adaptations occur in fetal/neonatal DNA in response to environmental influences. If predictive adaptations are incorrect, the risk of chronic disease in adulthood increases, potentially across generations.
- **Maternal impact**: Children of obese mothers are twice as likely to be obese at age 2. Infants of overweight/obese mothers have higher fat mass at birth and increased risk of metabolic disorders.
- **Paternal impact**: Undernutrition during prenatal life compromises the male germline, contributing to environmentally induced diseases (paternal transgenerational epigenetic inheritance). Men eating high saturated fat had 38% lower sperm concentrations and 41% lower sperm counts.

The Dutch Hunger Winter study showed that famine during pregnancy resulted in elevated rates of adult obesity, hyperlipidemia, and cardiovascular disease.
- **Protein type**: Mothers eating more animal protein had 39% higher infertility risk; those eating more vegetable protein had 22% less risk. Substituting 5% energy as vegetable protein lowered infertility risk by 50%.
- **Environmental toxins**: The EARTH study found men exposed to more pesticides had 49% lower total sperm count and 32% more abnormal sperm.
- **Lifestyle intervention**: Ornish et al showed intensive lifestyle intervention influences 500 genes in men with early prostate cancer. Compounds like EGCG (green tea), resveratrol (red grapes), genistein (soya), curcumin, and isothiocyanates (cruciferous vegetables) modulate gene expression.
- **Life experiences**: Children who experienced abuse or stress between ages 5-10 had shorter telomeres, showing life experiences directly influence gene expression.

--- SOURCE 30: The power of product: how food advertising affects children’s perceptions of child and non-child targeted food advertising? ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a qualitative research article published in BMC Public Health (2025) examining how children aged 6–12 perceive child-targeted versus non-child-targeted food advertising. The study, conducted by researchers from the University of Ottawa, Université Laval, and University of Calgary, involved 17 children (11 girls, 6 boys) who participated in online interviews where they were shown four advertisements: child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads for both healthy (plain milk) and unhealthy (chocolate) products.

**Key Background:** The study notes that approximately 30% of Canadian children aged 5–17 have overweight or obesity, and ultra-processed foods account for 49.1% of caloric intake among children aged 2–5 and 54.2% among those aged 6–12. Children are exposed to nearly 2,000 unhealthy food ads annually on television and over 4,000 on digital platforms in Canada.

**Methods:** Open-ended interviews were conducted via Zoom, with thematic analysis using a hybrid deductive-inductive coding approach. The ads featured brands not readily available in Canada (Milka, Dove, Arla) to minimize prior brand familiarity.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Awareness:** Most children could identify the product being advertised but showed no brand awareness, as expected with unfamiliar brands.
2. **Attitudes:** Most children expressed positive perceptions of the ads, regardless of whether they were child-targeted or non-child-targeted. Reasons for liking included: (i) seeing people eating the product, (ii) positive emotional appeal, (iii) pre-existing affinity with the product, and (iv) visibility of the product. Notably, the child-targeted milk ad (featuring an animated cookie character) was less well-received, with some children finding it "creepy" or confusing.
3. **Purchase Intent:** Most children expressed "negative purchase intent" for all ads due to pre-existing aversion to the product. Even children who liked the product often expressed negative purchase intent because they preferred other brands or flavors.
4. **Perceived Target Audience:** Children considered the type of product over marketing techniques when determining who the ad was for. Themes included "product for everyone" and "product for people that like the product."

**Conclusions:** Children's perceptions, purchase intent, and perceived targeted audience did not differ significantly between child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads. The study underscores the critical role of the product itself (rather than marketing techniques) in influencing children's responses to ads. The authors recommend that public policies and advertising regulations focus on restricting promotions of unhealthy products rather than solely addressing marketing techniques or target audiences.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: How bad is ultra-processed food for the planet? ---
URL: https://www.soilassociation.org/blogs/2022/august/24/how-bad-is-ultra-processed-food-for-the-planet

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published August 24, 2022) by the Soil Association examines the environmental impacts of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), based on a paper published by researchers from CSIRO and Deakin University in Australia. The paper reviewed 52 studies on UPF environmental impacts.

Key findings include that UPFs account for 17-39% of total diet-related energy use, 36-45% of diet-related biodiversity loss, up to a third of diet-related greenhouse gas emissions/land use/food waste, and up to a quarter of diet-related water use in high-income countries. UPF production relies on commodity ingredients like palm oil, soya, wheat, maize, milk, eggs, and meat, which have driven ecosystem destruction (e.g., rainforest clearing for palm oil in Indonesia, Cerrado conversion for soya in Brazil). UPFs contribute significantly to climate change, plastic pollution, and food waste.

The authors conclude that UPFs are "potentially counterproductive" to sustainable food system objectives and call on policymakers to regulate UPF production, availability, and consumption. Countries including Brazil, Canada, Chile, Ecuador, France, Israel, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay already encourage limiting UPF intake through dietary guidance and labeling. The UK is one of the highest consumers of UPFs, with these products making up over half of average weekly shopping baskets. The article calls for UK government action including reduction targets, consumer guidance, UPF labeling, and support for transition to agroecology and organic farming.

--- SOURCE 6: Measuring Progress | Healthy Food Policy Project ---
URL: https://healthyfoodpolicyproject.org/towards-equitable-and-just-food-systems/measuring-progress

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the "Towards Equitable and Just Food Systems" resource from the Healthy Food Policy Project. It examines common terms used to measure progress in food systems—food security, food deserts, food swamps, and hunger—along with their definitions, uses in policy and research, and significant limitations.

**Food Security** is defined as consistent access to sufficient, safe, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food. The USDA measures it on a spectrum from high to very low food security. However, the term is limiting as an ultimate goal because it does not address nutritional quality or root causes of inequity. Related terms include nutrition security, community food security, food access (with five dimensions: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability, accommodation), and food system resilience.

**Food Desert** refers to areas with low access to grocery stores. The term is being phased out at the federal level in favor of "low-income and low-access areas." It is criticized for implying scarcity is natural, masking deliberate policy decisions (e.g., redlining, suburbanization), ignoring racial disparities, and not reflecting community vibrancy. Baltimore, Maryland has shifted to using "Healthy Food Priority Areas."

**Food Swamp** describes areas where unhealthy food outlets (fast food, convenience stores) outnumber healthy options. Research suggests food swamps predict obesity better than food deserts and disproportionately impact low-income and Black communities. Root causes include redlining, white flight, and zoning policies. Critiques note the term still does not adequately address root causes, with some advocating for "food apartheid" as a better descriptor.

**Hunger** is an individual-level physical sensation from insufficient food intake, often conflated with food insecurity in surveys. It is difficult to measure directly, so food insecurity is used as a proxy. The Committee on National Statistics has recommended USDA stop using "hunger" to describe food insecurity indicators.

The page includes policy examples for each term and discussion questions for reflection.
</summary>

URL: https://sdohplace.org/guides/measuring-food-access-on-a-neighborhood-level

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the SDOH & Place Project provides a guide on measuring food access at the neighborhood level. It covers the background, key dimensions, data collection methods, and analysis tools.

**Background:** Food access measures how easily people can reach and afford food. Communities with poor access experience more obesity, poorer health outcomes, and worse academic performance.

**Key Dimensions of Food Access:**
1. **Availability** – Measured via the "container method" (counting food retailers per area) or distance-based approaches. Distance must account for travel routes, public transit, walking paths, safety, and daily mobility patterns. Low-income households face additional barriers like lack of car access, social discomfort, and time constraints. Delivery services are changing the importance of physical distance.
2. **Acceptability** – Considers food quality, including whether food is healthy, fresh, safe, and culturally appropriate. Distinguishes between access to healthy foods and exposure to unhealthy "Energy Dense, Nutrient Poor" (EDNP) foods. Different store types (supermarkets vs. convenience stores) offer different ratios of produce to EDNP foods.
3. **Affordability** – Noted as beyond the scope of the guide but relevant when fresh foods are available at a premium price, forcing trade-offs.

**Data Collection:** Recommends using both quantitative and qualitative data. Large national datasets are often free but outdated. The U.S. Census Bureau provides demographic and socioeconomic data at the zip code and census tract level. Focus groups and surveys provide qualitative insights. Table 1 lists validated survey tools (e.g., NEMS-SS), composite indices (USDA Food Access Research Atlas, Healthy Food Availability Index), and proprietary/commercial datasets.

**Data Processing Tools:**
- **Geographic Information Systems (GIS):** Used for spatial analysis of access, distance, and centrality. Advanced metrics like the Aggregated Accessibility Index account for route quality and effort.
- **Nexus Analysis:** A qualitative method for analyzing social dimensions of food access using observational data, interviews, and focus groups.
- **Machine Learning Algorithms:** Can process large datasets to categorize foods and assess menu balance across many outlets, enabling frequent, low-cost surveillance.

**Conclusion:** The field is evolving rapidly. The choice of measurement approach depends on the research question. Rigorous analysis of food environments benefits students, researchers, and government/nonprofit professionals.

The law requires front-of-package warning labels (black octagons reading "high in" sugar, sodium, saturated fat, or calories), restricts marketing to children, and bans sales of these products in schools. The law was implemented in three progressively stricter phases (2016, 2018, 2019).

**Methods:** Longitudinal data from 2,381 Chilean households (Kantar WorldPanel Chile) from January 2015 to December 2017 were used. Products were categorized as "high-in" if they exceeded Phase 1 nutrient thresholds. Fixed-effects models compared post-policy purchases to a counterfactual based on pre-policy trends.

**Results:** Compared to the counterfactual:
- Overall calories purchased declined by 16.4 kcal/capita/day (4%)
- Overall sugar declined by 11.5 kcal/capita/day (10%)
- Saturated fat declined by 2.2 kcal/capita/day (4%)
- Sodium declined by 27.7 mg/capita/day (5%)

Among "high-in" products specifically, there were larger declines: 24% reduction in calories, 37% in sodium, and 27% in sugar purchased. These declines were partially offset by increases in "not-high-in" purchases. Beverage purchases showed a 10% decline in calories and 13% decline in sugar. Food purchases showed significant declines in sugar, sodium, and saturated fat, though overall calories from food alone did not decline significantly.

**SES differences:** Results were complex. Highest-educated households showed larger declines in overall and high-in calories, while lowest-asset households had larger decreases in high-in calories but smaller increases in not-high-in calories.

**Conclusions:** Chile's Phase 1 policies were associated with reduced purchases of high-in products, leading to small but significant declines in purchased nutrients of concern. The authors anticipate greater changes after Phases 2 and 3 with stricter thresholds. The study builds on previous evaluations showing the law improved the food supply, reduced marketing to children, and reduced unhealthy food availability in schools.
</summary>

Overall sugar declined 11·5 kcal/capita/day (–14.6, –8·4; p<0·0001) or 10%, and saturated fat declined 2·2 kcal/capita/day (–3·8, –0·5; p=0·0097) or 4%. --- SOURCE 31: The UN Decade of Nutrition, the NOVA food classification and the trouble with ultra-processing ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10261019

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Public Health Nutrition in 2017, presents the NOVA food classification system developed by researchers at the University of São Paulo, which categorizes foods based on the nature, extent, and purpose of industrial processing. The authors argue that the UN Decade of Nutrition (2016-2025) and Sustainable Development Goals require understanding which foods are healthy and which are not, and that NOVA effectively addresses this need.

The NOVA system classifies all foods into four groups: (1) Unprocessed or minimally processed foods (fresh fruits, vegetables, meat, milk, eggs, etc.); (2) Processed culinary ingredients (oils, butter, sugar, salt); (3) Processed foods (canned vegetables, cheeses, breads); and (4) Ultra-processed foods - formulations made mostly from industrial ingredients and additives with little intact food, such as soft drinks, packaged snacks, reconstituted meat products, and pre-prepared frozen dishes.

The article documents that ultra-processed products now dominate food supplies in high-income countries and are rapidly increasing in middle- and low-income countries. Sales of ultra-processed foods in upper-middle-income countries grew from one-third to more than half of high-income country levels between 2000 and 2015. Studies using NOVA across Brazil, USA, Canada, UK, Australia, Chile, Mexico, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Spain, and 79 other countries show that higher consumption of ultra-processed products is associated with unhealthy nutrient profiles (higher energy density, saturated/trans fats, free sugars; lower fiber and micronutrients) and increased risks of obesity, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, and dyslipidemias.

The authors conclude that the ever-increasing production and consumption of ultra-processed products constitutes a world crisis that needs to be addressed as part of the UN Sustainable Development Goals and Decade of Nutrition. The article also notes that the Brazilian and Uruguayan national dietary guidelines are based on NOVA's four food groups, recommending avoidance of ultra-processed products.
</summary>

Fifteen years later, they were more than half.", "The overall purpose of ultra-processing is to create branded, convenient (durable, ready to consume), attractive (hyper-palatable) and highly profitable (low-cost ingredients) food products designed to displace all other food groups.", "We conclude that the ever-increasing production and consumption of these products is a world crisis, to be confronted, checked and reversed as part of the work of the UN Sustainable Development Goals and its Decade of Nutrition."

--- SOURCE 34: NOVA Food Classification Framework - metabolicmatrix.info ---

The NOVA system shows high inter-rater reliability, though concerns about definition imprecision remain.

--- SOURCE 35: The NOVA classification system: A critical perspective in food science ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0924224421004970

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a commentary article published in Trends in Food Science & Technology (Volume 116, October 2021, Pages 603-608) by researchers from the University of São Paulo (Brazil), providing a critical analysis of the NOVA food classification system from the perspective of Food Science, Technology, and Engineering (FSTE).

**Main Argument:** The NOVA classification system, which categorizes foods into four groups based on processing level (unprocessed/minimally processed, processed culinary ingredients, processed foods, and "ultra-processed" foods), is fundamentally flawed from a food science perspective. The authors argue that NOVA does not truly classify by processing level but rather by ingredient count, leading to misleading and pejorative connotations about commercially manufactured foods.

**Key Points:**
- Food processing has existed for ~2 million years since early hominoids discovered cooking, and essential foods like bread, olive oil, and wine are all processed.
- Many crops (soy, coffee, cocoa, barley, wheat, olives) cannot be consumed without processing.
- The term "ultra-processed" (UPF) was created by Monteiro (2009) and has been adopted by media with a negative connotation, creating consumer confusion.
- NOVA is inconsistent: pasteurized milk and powdered milk are classified as "minimally processed," while sweetened yogurt is "ultra-processed," despite both undergoing significant processing.
- The authors argue that healthiness has no direct correlation with the number of ingredients, processing intensity, or whether food is homemade vs. industrially produced.
- Homemade food can be a source of foodborne disease, while processed foods offer safety, shelf-life extension, and nutritional benefits.
- The classification neglects well-established food science concepts and dismisses benefits of diets incorporating foods at all processing levels.
- The NOVA system could be acceptable if based only on health concerns, but it is not accurate as a food processing classification.

**Citation Impact:** The article has been cited 161 times, indicating significant influence in the ongoing debate about food processing classification systems.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

NOVA could be acceptable if it were based only on health concerns, but this was not the case., The NOVA classification does not truly consider only food processing levels. Clarifications are needed to avoid pejorative connotations to industrialized foods., NOVA is based on the erroneous assumption that all commercially manufactured foods have low nutritional value, promote weight gain and chronic diseases to consumers because they contain sugar, salt and additives., Terms like UPF are more misleading than explanatory. The prefix 'ultra' refers to what is extreme or excessive, which would not in itself necessarily be a problem., Consumers need to be correctly informed that healthiness has no direct or absolute correlation either with the number of ingredients, intensity, or number of processes or with the fact that the food has been processed in households or a large industrial plant.

--- SOURCE 38: Variation in low food access areas due to data source inaccuracies ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3869099

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Applied Geography (2013), examined how inaccuracies in secondary commercial data sources (InfoUSA and Dun & Bradstreet) affect the designation of Census tracts as low food access areas (food deserts). The researchers replicated two U.S. government measures—the USDA ERS food desert (FD) measure and the CDC non-healthier food retail tract (NHFRT) measure—across 169 Census tracts in eight counties in South Carolina, comparing secondary data sources against a ground-truthed field census (reference data) conducted from September 2008 to July 2009.

**Key findings:** For the USDA ERS food desert measure, secondary data sources showed 94% concordance, but only 50–65% sensitivity and 60–64% positive predictive value (PPV). For the CDC NHFRT measure, secondary data showed 88–91% concordance, 80–86% sensitivity, and 78–82% PPV. Secondary data sources consistently undercounted low food access areas, with D&B more prone to undercount supermarkets in low-income areas, leading to greater under-ascertainment of food deserts. The CDC NHFRT measure was less affected because it relied solely on food outlet data without income criteria.

**Conclusions:** The authors concluded that while inaccuracies in secondary data sources may be acceptable for large-scale surveillance, verification with field work is advisable for local community efforts aimed at identifying and improving food access. The under-ascertainment of low food access areas was a more pronounced problem than incorrect assignment of high access areas as low access.
</summary>
