Prevention: Tax and pricing

# Countries and jurisdictions that have taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs)

Last updated 27-03-2025

Over 130 jurisdictions across nearly 120 countries and territories have implemented taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) to date. In some of these countries, the effects of these taxes on consumption and reformulation of SSBs has been extensively studied.

## Key Evidence

Data from the United Kingdom (UK), Mexico, South Africa and other countries indicate that SSB taxes successfully reduce sugar consumption from SSBs

SSB taxes have led to reformulation of products in the UK and other countries, reducing the amount of sugar in these beverages

03

Over 130 jurisdictions have introduced a tax on SSBs, as listed in the table below

With many countries introducing an SSB tax over the past decade, research is now showing the benefits of these policies. High-quality studies, particularly from Mexico,[1](#cite927)[2](#cite2006) the UK[3](#cite1543)[4](#cite1956) and South Africa,[5](#cite2012)[6](#cite8583) as well as a systematic review and meta-analysis of SSB taxes around the world,[7](#cite8585) show that these policies increased prices of SSBs, reduced their sale and consumption, and led to reformulation of products to reduce sugar levels. Most of the current data looks at impacts up to three years after the introduction of the tax, with longer-term studies needed to measure the effects of SSB taxes on health. Emerging longitudinal evidence and modelling studies suggest that SSB taxes can reduce body weight and type 2 diabetes prevalence, while improving outcomes related to quality-of-life.[8](#cite6897)[9](#cite926)[10](#cite2008)

## Impact of SSB taxes: international case studies

### Mexico

Mexico introduced a volumetric SSB tax in 2014 at a rate of 1 peso per L. This tax has led to a price rise of about 11% for soft drinks, and a slightly smaller increase for other sweetened beverages.[1](#cite927) In turn, the price increase reduced both purchases and consumption of SSBs. Studies of the effects of this tax on obesity are ongoing. Below is a summary of the major results to date:

1. **Reduction in the volume of SSBs purchased.** By 2016, there was a 37% reduction in the total volume of SSBs purchased, compared to the year before the tax was introduced.[2](#cite2006)
2. **Reductions in SSB purchases were greatest among poorer households and those that previously purchased high amounts of SSBs.**[1](#cite927)[11](#cite2007)
3. Over 10 years, **the SSB tax is predicted to prevent 239,900 cases of obesity**; of these, 39% would be in children. This drop in obesity is expected to prevent 5,840 disability-adjusted life-years.[10](#cite2008)
4. **The tax is predicted to be highly cost effective.** By reducing costs such as healthcare, the tax would save almost $4 per $1 spent on its implementation.[10](#cite2008)

### The United Kingdom

An SSB tax, called the Soft Drinks Industry Levy (SDIL), was introduced in the UK in April 2018. The UK tax is a two-tiered levy that taxes producers according to a drink’s sugar concentration, with higher rates for sugar levels above a certain threshold: drinks containing 5 to 8 g per mL of sugar are taxed at £0.18 per L, while those containing more than 8 g of sugar per 100 mL are taxed at £0.24 per L.[12](#cite930) Manufacturers responded to the UK tax with widespread reformulation of their products to reduce sugar levels. Where sugar levels remained above the taxation threshold, prices were not always raised to reflect the taxed amount: the tax was only passed onto consumers for drinks with more than 8 g of sugar per 100 mL, which underwent an average price increase of £0.075 per L.[3](#cite1543)

The success of the UK tax in reducing sugar consumption has been demonstrated by high-quality research, with major findings summarised below:

1. **The tax led to widespread reformulation to reduce sugar levels in SSBs**. This was the equivalent of removing a total of 45 million kg of sugar from soft drinks each year.[13](#cite931) More information on reformulation is available from [Reformulation of food products to reduce sugar consumption](https://www.obesityevidencehub.org.au/collections/prevention/reformulation-of-food-products-to-reduce-sugar-consumption).
2. **The proportion of drinks available in supermarkets with high sugar content dropped after the tax.** Between 2015 and 2019, the percentage of drinks in supermarkets with sugar content of more than 5 g per 100 mL fell from 49% to 15%.[3](#cite1543)
3. **Sugar levels in SSBs were reduced after the tax was introduced.** The sugar content of drinks subject to the tax decreased by nearly 45% four years after the tax was introduced.[4](#cite1956)
4. **Sugar purchased from taxed drinks decreased by 35%.** This reduction was largest (38.5%) in the households where the main wage earner was in a skilled manual occupation.[4](#cite1956)
5. **Sugar consumption decreased in both children and adults.** Nearly one year after the tax, daily free sugar intakes from food and soft drinks were nearly 5 g and 11 g lower in these populations, respectively. Sugar consumption from soft drinks alone decreased by about 3 g and 5 g in each population, demonstrating their significant contribution of sugar to the diet.[14](#cite8604)
6. **The tax is predicted to improve the health of children and adolescents, particularly in low socioeconomic areas.** One modelling study reported that 10 years after implementation, the tax could reduce dental caries and overweight/obesity prevalence among those under 18 years by 3,600 and over 64,000 cases, respectively, while increasing quality of life and life expectancy. These changes were greatest in areas of lower socioeconomic status, suggesting the SDIL may reduce health inequalities.[15](#cite8587)
7. **The majority of fruit juices, juice drinks and smoothies targeted to children and in children's lunch boxes were not eligible for the UK tax.** Most of these drinks did not meet eligibility requirements for the UK tax, usually because they were made with fruit juice or pureed fruit without other added sugar, despite having over 5 g of sugar per 100 mL. As a result, researchers suggested adapting the UK tax to include these drinks.[16](#cite2011)

### South Africa

In 2018, South Africa introduced a 10% tax, called the Health Promotion Levy (HPL), on sugary drinks, excluding fruit juices. The tax of 0.021 ZAR per g of sugar was applied to drinks with over 4 g of sugar per 100 mL.[5](#cite2012) While prices of taxable non-carbonated drinks did not increase after the policy’s introduction, prices of both low- and high-sugar carbonated drinks increased by an average of 1.006 ZAR per L.[17](#cite2013)

The success of the HPL has been described by a number of studies:

1. **Fewer carbonated drinks were purchased in urban areas.** Purchases of carbonated drinks by households fell by an average of 29% after the tax was introduced. The amount of sugar purchased in these drinks fell by 51% due to both behaviour change and reformulation.[17](#cite2013)[5](#cite2012)[18](#cite2014)
2. **People in lower socioeconomic groups purchased considerably less sugar in drinks that were subject to the tax**. There was a 57% drop in the g of sugar purchased in taxed drinks by people in lower socioeconomic urban households.[5](#cite2012)[19](#cite2015) In addition to reformulation, the total volume of taxed drinks purchased was reduced, indicating a behaviour change.[19](#cite2015)
3. **Beyond changes in consumer purchases, manufacturers reformulated drinks to contain lower sugar levels.** Reformulation began after the pre-tax announcement and continued one year after implementation, with sugar content decreasing by nearly 5 g per capita per day (-32%). While researchers could not determine whether these changes resulted from the policy itself or consumer demand after its implementation (e.g., wanting lower priced items), this finding suggests that SSB taxes can motivate manufacturers to develop healthier drink options.[6](#cite8583)

## SSB taxes in other countries

Research on the effects of SSB taxes is continuing in many other countries, with some highlights presented below:[20](#cite2016)

**Portugal:** A two-tiered SSB tax was introduced in Portugal in 2017 at a rate of €0.8 per L and €0.16 per L for drinks with sugar contents of <80 g per L and ≥80 g per L, respectively. Nearly 100% of the tax was passed on to consumers.[21](#cite2017) A 7% reduction in SSB sales was reported in the first year, with reformulation leading to an 11% reduction of total energy intake through SSB consumption.[22](#cite1979)

**Chile:** Until 2013, Chile had a 13% tax on non-alcoholic drinks. In 2014, this tax was raised to 18% for soft drinks with at least 6.25 g of sugar per 100 mL and decreased to 10% for soft drinks under this threshold of sugar.[23](#cite1980) The prices of high-sugar soft drinks increased by an average of 1.9% and decreased by 1.7% for the low-sugar soft drinks.[23](#cite1980) After one year, there was a 22% reduction in the volume of higher-taxed drinks sold, but no change in the overall purchase of soft drinks; this indicates that some consumers switched to drinks with lower sugar content.[23](#cite1980)

**United States (US) regional and city-based taxes:** SSB taxes have been introduced in specific regions and cities in the US.[20](#cite2016)

* A 1¢ per fl oz SSB tax was introduced in Berkeley, California in 2015, resulting in an average price increase of 0.83¢ per fl oz.[24](#cite939) One year after the introduction of the tax, there was a 20% decrease in SSB consumption.[24](#cite939) These reductions were maintained for at least three years and occurred in demographically diverse neighbourhoods.[25](#cite1981)
* A 1.5¢ per oz tax on SSBs (including diet soft drinks but excluding fruit juices and milk drinks) was introduced in the city of Philadelphia in 2017. The tax was fully passed on to consumers, leading to a price increase of 21% for the taxed drinks one year later.[26](#cite1982) There was an average reduction of 8.5 oz (251 mL) of taxed beverages purchased per shopping trip in Philadelphia the year after the tax,[26](#cite1982) with sustained reductions in volume sales of SSBs after two years.[27](#cite8589) Even after accounting for cross-border shopping (e.g. from nearby towns without the tax), there was a 35% overall reduction in SSB sales across the city.[27](#cite8589) Adults in Philadelphia reduced their consumption of sugars from SSBs by an average of 6 g per day after one year of the tax, but the same effect was not seen in children.[26](#cite1982) There was also reduced availability of SSBs in stores the year after the tax, as stocks of taxed drinks decreased, while stocks of water increased.[28](#cite2018)

## List of countries and jurisdictions with an SSB tax

Collectively, over 130 jurisdictions have implemented SSB taxes at the national or subnational level. For more information on these taxes around the world, visit the [World Bank’s Global SSB Tax Database](https://ssbtax.worldbank.org/).

The countries and jurisdictions that have SSB taxes are listed below, with details including the implementation date and type of tax used. Some locations have adopted a tiered tax design, which applies different tax rates depending on factors such as the sugar content or beverage type.

The table below uses the following definitions:

**Type of tax**

* Excise tax – a tax levied on a particular product at point of manufacture. An excise tax can be:
  + Specific – based on quantity (e.g. volume or sugar content);
  + Ad valorem – calculated on a percentage of the wholesale or retail price[29](#cite1967); OR
  + Mixed – containing both specific and ad valorem elements.
* Value-added tax/Goods and services tax – a consumption tax placed on a product whenever value is added at each stage of the supply chain, from production to point of sale.
* Import tax – a tax placed on a product imported for domestic consumption and usually collected at the port of entry.
* Sales tax – a tax levied on the sale of a product and often calculated as a percentage of the retail price.

**Tax design**

A specific excise tax can be calculated on the volume of the drink (volumetric), its sugar content, or a combination of both the volume and sugar levels.

**Tiers**

A tiered excise tax applies different rates depending on factors such as sugar content or beverage type. For example, the United Kingdom’s SDIL has different rates for drinks containing 5-8 g and over 8 g of sugar per 100 mL, while Mali taxes carbonated sweetened waters at 10% versus juices and concentrates at 12%.

See [How should an Australian tax on sugar-sweetened beverages be designed](https://www.obesityevidencehub.org.au/collections/prevention/how-should-an-australian-tax-on-sugar-sweetened-beverages-ssbs-be-designed) for more details.

args.summary:
This webpage from the Obesity Evidence Hub provides a comprehensive overview of sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) taxes globally, last updated 27-03-2025. It reports that over 130 jurisdictions across nearly 120 countries and territories have implemented SSB taxes, with evidence showing these policies successfully reduce sugar consumption and drive product reformulation.

**Key Evidence from International Case Studies:**

**Mexico** (2014): Introduced a 1 peso/L volumetric tax, leading to ~11% price rise on soft drinks. By 2016, there was a 37% reduction in SSB purchases. Over 10 years, the tax is predicted to prevent 239,900 cases of obesity and save almost $4 per $1 spent on implementation.

**United Kingdom** (2018): The Soft Drinks Industry Levy (SDIL) is a two-tiered tax based on sugar concentration (£0.18/L for 5-8g sugar/100mL; £0.24/L for >8g/100mL). It led to reformulation removing 45 million kg of sugar annually. The proportion of high-sugar drinks in supermarkets fell from 49% to 15% (2015-2019). Sugar purchased from taxed drinks decreased by 35%. The tax is predicted to reduce dental caries by 3,600 cases and overweight/obesity by over 64,000 cases among under-18s.

**South Africa** (2018): The Health Promotion Levy (10% tax on sugary drinks, excluding fruit juices) led to a 29% reduction in carbonated drink purchases in urban areas and 51% reduction in sugar purchased. Lower socioeconomic groups showed a 57% drop in sugar from taxed drinks.

**Other Countries:** Portugal (7% reduction in SSB sales, 11% reduction in energy intake), Chile (22% reduction in higher-taxed drinks volume), and US cities Berkeley (20% decrease in SSB consumption), Philadelphia (35% overall reduction in SSB sales).

The page includes a comprehensive table listing countries/jurisdictions with SSB taxes, detailing implementation dates, tax instruments (excise, VAT/GST, import, sales taxes), structures (specific, ad valorem, mixed), tax bases (volume, sugar content), and whether they are tiered.

# Lessons Learned from Implementing a Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Tax in Berkeley, California By Jennifer Falbe, UC Davis; Anna H. Grummon, Harvard University; Nadia Rojas, ChangeLab Solutions; Suzanne Ryan-Ibarra, Public Health Institute; Lynn D. Silver, Public Health Institute; and Kristine A. Madsen, UC Berkeley

[![](/sites/main/files/imagecache/profile/main-images/falbe_beverage_image.jpg?1601212752)](/sites/main/files/imagecache/lightbox/main-images/falbe_beverage_image.jpg)

In 2014, Berkeley, California became the first US jurisdiction to tax distribution of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs). In a recent study, we interviewed city stakeholders and SSB distributors and retailers and analyzed records in order to identify lessons learned from the implementation of this tax. Our findings emphasized the importance of investing tax revenues back into the community through programs that advance health equity. Other findings include the need for thorough and timely communications with distributors and retailers, adequate lead time for implementation, advisory commissions for revenue allocations, and funding of staff, communications, and evaluation before tax collection begins. We concluded that the policy package, context, and implementation process facilitated translating policy into public health outcomes, and that the Berkeley example could, and should, inform the success of future taxes. As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, the need to fund public health and food security is more pressing than ever. SSB taxation not only contributes to reducing risk factors for severe COVID-19 illness, such as type 2 diabetes, but also generates revenues that can support the families and communities hit hardest by the pandemic.

> **Key Facts**
>
> * Policymakers and public health experts have argued that the sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) industry should be taxed for the health-harms their products cause, and that revenues should fund public health programs, especially ones that address health disparities.
> * Berkeley’s SSB tax ordinance generated more than $9 million, which was allocated for public health and equity from 2015 to 2021.
> * Within one year, SSB consumption declined in Berkeley’s lower-income neighborhoods, and SSB purchasing dropped 10 percent in supermarkets.
> * Key lessons include the importance of thorough and timely communications with business, adequate lead time for implementation, and the need to immediately fund new staff, communications, outreach, and evaluation before implementation.

The Berkeley ordinance, which garnered 76 percent of the vote in a 2014 referendum and was implemented the following year, levied a $0.01 per ounce excise tax on SSB distribution. Although SSB taxes evoke higher support when revenues are designated for health or education, Berkeley’s measure appropriated revenues to the general fund. This was a strategic decision made by SSB tax proponents and City Council to keep the vote threshold at a simple majority, since California requires a two-thirds vote for earmarked taxes.[1] However, to promote revenue allocations aligned with public health, the ordinance established an SSB Product Panel of Experts (SSBPPE) to advise the city on funding “programs to further reduce [SSB] consumption. . . [and its] consequences.”

Within one year, SSB consumption declined in Berkeley’s lower-income neighborhoods,[2] and SSB purchasing dropped 10 percent in supermarkets.[3] These results are consistent with findings of lower consumption and sales of taxed beverages following enactment of beverage taxes in Mexico (in 2013), Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (2016), and Seattle, Washington (2017). With eight further US jurisdictions now having implemented such taxes, the evidence base for SSB taxation has strengthened. Given this, it is critical to use implementation science to identify barriers, facilitators, and resources required to translate taxation policy into public health outcomes.[4]

### Support, Simplicity, and Synergy

From June 2015 to April 2017, we conducted 48 semi-structured interviews with city staff, its tax administrator, SSB distributors, Berkeley retailers, and SSBPPE commissioners. We audio-recorded interviews and transcribed them verbatim, or took detailed notes when subjects declined recording, and used both deductive and inductive analysis to interpret our results. We analyzed these data using implementation science frameworks.

In [our study](https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2020.305795)[5], we identified three policy characteristics that facilitated implementation of Berkeley’s SSB tax. The first was the legitimacy of the policy source, based on the emphatic referendum result plus support for the tax from a diverse coalition including parents, health professionals, the Berkeley NAACP, Latinos Unidos, and others. The second was the simplicity of the tax calculation ($0.01/oz) when compared with, for example, tobacco tax rates, which vary from one product to the next. The third was the policy “package” that combined a tax with a community and expert advisory commission tasked with identifying the best uses for the revenue. These two components worked synergistically: the excise tax reduced SSB consumption while generating revenue which the commission directed to new public health programs.

In terms of outer setting, characteristics of Berkeley’s history, institutions, and residents were conducive to public support for SSB tax enactment and implementation. Meanwhile, the inner setting—City officials—placed a high priority on implementation. This took the form of early leadership engagement across multiple city departments, especially Finance, the City Attorney’s Office, and, later, Public Health, with leadership from the City Manager’s Office. A lesson learned in this area was the importance of funding and hiring personnel in advance of implementation.

Regarding implementation, Berkeley’s tax collection was divided into phases focusing on (1) distributors (e.g., Pepsi and Coca Cola bottling companies) and (2) self-distributors (e.g., retailers that make their own SSBs or buy SSBs from wholesale stores). City officials and the tax administrator perceived successful execution of the first phase, noting a wide-reaching communication strategy, high attendance at education sessions, and timely execution of tax collection.

The second phase (self-distributors) began in January 2016, 10 months after enforcement for distributors began. Though the city and the administrator engaged potential self-distributors in November 2015 through a mailing and phone call, inviting them to attend two education sessions. Although few attended, those who did found the sessions useful. Most self-distributors did not recall receiving mailed session notifications and said that e-mail and in-person visits were preferable modes of communication. Overall, a lesson learned from this phase was the need for more widespread outreach.

### Retailers and Revenue

Although SSB distributors could assume the costs of the excise tax, most raised prices to retailers, according to interviews. When asked if and how retailers were making up for these costs, most reported raising SSB prices only, with some absorbing or delaying beverage price increases. No retailers reported raising food prices, indicating that beverage industry claims that SSB taxes are “grocery taxes” are false and deceptive . Many retailers regretted the lack of early retailer-specific outreach from the city, which contributed to some confusion about whether artificially sweetened drinks and sugar-sweetened coffee and fruit drinks were taxable. Many retailers were highly supportive of the tax, mentioning benefits for children or health. Approval was lower, however, among small retailers bordering other cities. Several of these wanted the tax to cover a larger jurisdiction, such as the whole state of California, so that they were not at a competitive disadvantage on price.

Regarding SSBPPE and revenue allocation, commissioners recommended getting money quickly to the community (which the City Council did by advancing funds before revenues accrued), and quickly funding a robust media campaign. Both actions would facilitate widespread understanding of the rationale for the tax and disseminate information on programs funded, which can sustain public support. Commissioners noted the importance of advisory commissions for making revenue allocations consistent with the intent of the law, ensuring that funded programs are within the scope of the ordinance and that new funding not replace existing funding.

### Lessons for Future Implementations

Berkeley’s SSB tax ordinance generated more than $9 million in funding allocated for [public health and equity](https://www.thepraxisproject.org/ssb#ssb-multimedia) from 2015 to 2021, facilitated by the SSBPPE Commission, which represented community and expert voices and provided accountability over revenue allocations. Key lessons from Berkeley include the importance of thorough and timely communications with business, adequate lead time for implementation, and the need to immediately fund new staff, communications, outreach, and evaluation before implementation. Early and robust outreach to the public and retailers about the tax and programs funded may promote public support, correct misinformation, educate residents about healthy beverage consumption, reduce friction, and facilitate any beverage price increases only on SSBs.

These lessons provide a starting place for other jurisdictions considering SSB taxes. The policy package, context, and implementation process, including stakeholder engagement, were key for translating tax policy into public health behavioral outcomes. However, more research is needed to understand the long-term facilitators and barriers to sustaining the public health benefits of Berkeley’s SSB tax, and also how those differ from facilitators and barriers in other jurisdictions, such as Philadelphia and Cook County, which faced aggressive industry-funded repeal campaigns.

***Anna H. Grummon** is a David E. Bell Fellow at the Harvard Center for Population and Development Studies and a research fellow at the Division of Chronic Disease Research Across the Lifecourse (CoRAL).*

***Nadia Rojas**, formerly a research associate at the UC Berkeley School of Public Health, is a Policy Analyst at ChangeLab Solutions.*

***Suzanne Ryan-Ibarra** is a Principal Investigator and Senior Research Scientist at Survey Research Group, a program of the Public Health Institute.*

***Lynn D. Silver**is a pediatrician and public health expert who serves as senior advisor at the Public Health Institute.*

***Kristine A. Madsen** is Associate Professor at the School of Public Health and the Faculty Director for the Berkeley Food Institute.*

**References**

[1] Hagenaars LL, Jeurissen PPT, Klazinga NS. The taxation of unhealthy energy-dense foods (EDFs) and sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs): an overview of patterns observed in the policy content and policy context of 13 case studies. *Health Policy*. 2017;121(8):887–894.

[5] Falbe J, Grummon AH, Rojas N, Ryan-Ibarra S, Silver LD, Madsen KA. Implementation of the First US Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Tax in Berkeley, CA, 2015–2019. Am J Public Health. 2020;110(9):1429-1437. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2020.305795

[![](/sites/main/files/imagecache/thumbnail/main-images/falbe_pic.jpg?1576469422)](/profile/jennifer-falbe)

Dr. Falbe’s research focuses on studying programmatic, policy, and environmental interventions to prevent chronic disease and reduce health disparities. Dr. Falbe led an evaluation of the nation’s first soda tax in Berkeley, California. Her research has also examined primary care nutrition and physical activity interventions for youth, healthy retail programs, and multi-sector community interventions to prevent obesity. Dr. Falbe received a dual doctorate in Nutrition and Epidemiology in 2013 from Harvard University.

- Berkeley's SSB tax generated over $9 million allocated for public health and equity from 2015-2021.
- Within one year, SSB consumption declined in Berkeley's lower-income neighborhoods and SSB purchasing dropped 10% in supermarkets.
- The tax was strategically directed to the general fund (not earmarked) to require only a simple majority vote, but an SSB Product Panel of Experts (SSBPPE) was established to advise on revenue allocation.

**Lessons Learned:**
1. **Policy characteristics that facilitated implementation:** Legitimacy from the strong referendum result and diverse coalition support; simplicity of the tax calculation ($0.01/oz); and the synergistic policy package combining the tax with a community advisory commission.
2. **Importance of thorough and timely communications** with distributors and retailers, adequate lead time for implementation, and funding staff, communications, outreach, and evaluation before tax collection begins.
3. **Retailers did not raise food prices** (contrary to industry claims that SSB taxes are "grocery taxes"), with most raising SSB prices only.
4. **Advisory commissions** are critical for ensuring revenue allocations align with the intent of the law.
5. The need for early and robust public and retailer outreach to promote support, correct misinformation, and facilitate beverage price increases only on SSBs.

The authors note that as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, the need to fund public health and food security is more pressing than ever, and SSB taxation contributes to reducing risk factors for severe COVID-19 illness while generating revenues to support affected communities.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854)Abstract

### Background

International trade and investment liberalization impact national food environments via changes to the availability and affordability of foods, and may encourage the trade of ultra-processed foods (UPF). This study describes New Zealand (NZ) food and beverage imports over time, in terms of their level of food processing.

### Methods

United Nations Comtrade data was gathered for years 1990–2023. All Harmonized System (HS) codes related to food or non-alcoholic beverages (_N_ = 898) were categorized according to the Nova classification system into unprocessed and minimally processed foods (G1), processed culinary ingredients (G2), processed foods (G3) and UPF (G4). The food-derivatives/additives (e.g. industrial sugars and modified oils, flavourings, texture enhancers) that are UPF inputs were classified as a subgroup of G4. Total and per capita (p.c.) imports (by volume) were calculated for all years by Nova group and subgroup. Annual tariff rates from 1996 to 2023 were obtained from the World Trade Organisation Tariff & Trade Data platform.

### Results

The share of G4 in total food and beverage imports increased over the study period, from 15.7 kg p.c. (8.7% of food imports) in 1990 to 103.8 kg p.c. (21.8%) in 2023. Of all G4 subgroups, the p.c. import volume of food-derivatives/additives (UPF inputs) increased dramatically since 1990, surpassing all other UPF subgroups since 2011. Other Nova subgroups with notable import growth included wheat cereals and flours (G1), plant oils (G2), processed vegetables and fruit (G3), and sweetened/flavoured drinks (G4). Tariff rates were reduced to zero or low levels for all food products between 1990 and 2023, with notable reductions around 1996-98, and 2007/08. Tariffs were generally higher on G3 and G4 product subgroups than G1 throughout the study period, though the difference was minimal.

### Conclusions

The 34 years of progressive trade liberalization in NZ were characterised by an increasing proportion of imported products being ultra-processed foods/beverages and their inputs, underscoring the need for policy interventions to counteract the impact of these trends on food environments and population nutrition.

### Supplementary Information

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12992-026-01203-1.

**Keywords:**International trade, Food environments, Food systems, Ultra-processed foods, New Zealand

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854)Background

International trade and investment agreements (TIAs) are legally binding economic treaties that aim to increase the flow of goods, services, and capital across borders. These agreements have undeniably shaped the design of food systems, including the degree of global integration and corporate concentration [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR1)].

TIAs shape domestic food environments through several mechanisms, such as reducing the tariffs (border taxes) on food imports, opening new areas of the food environment (e.g. food manufacturing, retail, and service/restaurants) to foreign investment, and harmonizing food standards, rules, and policy procedures. In addition, TIAs and their associated governance processes – including the Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is the main international standards-setting institution for food – can constrain governments’ freedom to regulate food environments [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR2), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR3)].

A growing body of literature has raised concerns that trade and investment liberalization, through TIAs, has facilitated the development of unhealthy, less equitable and environmentally unsustainable food environments and food systems [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR3)–[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR12)].

Surveillance and monitoring provide an opportunity to understand and develop appropriate policy and research interventions aimed at creating healthier food environments. To this end, in 2013, the International Network for Food and Obesity/noncommunicable disease Research, Monitoring and Action Support (INFORMAS), published a series of protocols to monitor key elements of food environments across several domains including food trade and investment [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR13)]. Monitoring changes to the food environment alongside trade and investment liberalization, according to the INFORMAS approach, can help guide healthier trade policy decisions, improving policy coherence.

New Zealand (NZ) provides a unique case study to examine how rapid and comprehensive trade liberalization has shaped the food environment. As an island nation in the South Pacific, NZ is highly reliant on international trade for its food supply, however it also has a strong agricultural sector and is one of the largest global producers of dairy and lamb products [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR14)]. In 1965, NZ entered into a pioneering economic agreement with neighbouring Australia, updated in 1983, establishing a comprehensive free trade arrangement for goods and services. This was followed by a series of neoliberal economic reforms (1984-88) including complete removal of agricultural subsidies and major tariff reductions as part of an ideological shift within government. The country joined the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 1994 alongside 143 other countries. The following decades saw further development of bilateral and regional TIAs, increasingly focusing on facilitating trade with regional blocs. Including the seven major WTO agreements, NZ had 23 TIAs in force as of 2025 (see Fig. [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig1) and Supplementary Table [S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#MOESM1)]).

Fig. 1Timeline of New Zealand’s free trade agreements, by date of entry into force. Countries included in regional agreements are listed. Many of New Zealand’s trade agreements include investment chapters. This list does not include separate bilateral investment treaties

### Ultra-processed foods and the Nova classification system

This study examined NZ’s inward food and non-alcoholic beverage trade by level of food processing, according to the Nova classification. The Nova food classification assesses foods according to the degree of food processing, categorizing them into four main groups. Group 1 (G1) refers to ‘unprocessed and minimally processed foods’, including animal and plant based fresh foods or those that have undergone minimal processing such as cleaning, drying, grinding, pasteurization, freezing or refrigeration. Group 2 (G2) refers to ‘processed culinary ingredients’ such as cooking oils, butter, lard, sugar and salt. Group 3 (G3) refers to ‘processed foods’ which are made by combining products from G1 and G2 and following processes for preservation, cooking or fermentation [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)].

Group 4 (G4), ultra-processed foods and beverages (UPF), are “_industrial food and drink formulations made of food-derived substances and additives_,_often containing little or no whole foods_” [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)]. The presence of industrial additives is a key marker for UPF and what sets the Nova classification apart from previous classifications of unhealthy food and drinks, based on nutritional characteristics like energy-density or containing high amounts of fat, salt or sugar, though there is considerable overlap between these classifications [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR16)]. UPF typically contain high levels of added sugars, salt, and/or fats, as well as additives to enhance appeal and palatability, while lacking in essential micronutrients, food matrix and fibre. Common UPF examples include packaged sweet and savoury snacks, soft drinks, sugary breakfast cereals, confectionery, reconstituted meat products, and many ready-meals.

Not all additives are markers of UPF; those which prolong product duration, protect original properties and prevent the growth of bacteria may be used in both processed and ultra-processed foods, as well as in processed culinary ingredients, and, less frequently, in minimally processed foods [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)]. In contrast, ingredients that are characteristic of UPF include _food substances of no or rare culinary use_ and classes of additives whose function is to make the final product palatable or often hyper-palatable (‘cosmetic additives’) [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)]. Food substances of no or rare culinary use, i.e. used only in the manufacture of UPF, include industrial varieties of sugars (fructose, high-fructose corn syrup, ‘fruit juice concentrates’, invert sugar, maltodextrin, dextrose, lactose), modified oils (hydrogenated or interesterified oils) and protein sources (hydrolysed proteins, soya protein isolate, gluten, casein, whey protein and ‘mechanically separated meat’). Cosmetic additives, also used exclusively in the manufacture of UPF, include flavours, flavour enhancers, colours, emulsifiers, emulsifying salts, sweeteners, thickeners, and anti-foaming, bulking, carbonating, foaming, gelling and glazing agents [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)]. These classes of additives are known to “_disguise undesirable sensory properties created by ingredients_,_processes or packaging used in the manufacture of ultra-processed foods_,_or else give the final product sensory properties especially attractive to see_,_taste_,_smell and/or touch._” [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)].

Ultra-processing creates branded, convenient, hyper-palatable, cheap to purchase and highly profitable (cheap to produce) food and beverage products [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR17)], which may have addictive properties for some people [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR18), [19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR19)]. Increasing consumption of UPF displaces unprocessed/minimally processed foods (G1) and processed foods (G3) in the diet. UPF are predominantly produced by large, often transnational, corporations with the power to dictate what is grown, produced, marketed, and sold in global food systems [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR20)]. Evidence on the global expansion in the types and quantities of UPF sold indicates that, as countries become wealthier, there is a parallel rise in both the availability and variety of these products. This pattern is strongly linked to the industrialization of food systems, technological advancements, and globalization — including the expanding commercial and political power of transnational food corporations and the absence of robust regulatory frameworks to protect public nutrition in these changing environments [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR21)].

A diet high in UPF compromises health by impairing multiple dimensions of diet quality. Elevated consumption of UPF is associated with increased intake of free sugars, total and saturated fats, and decreased intake of fibre, protein, potassium, zinc, magnesium, and vitamins A, C, D, E, B12, and niacin [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR22)]. The global rise in diet-related chronic disease is closely linked to the displacement of traditional diets brought about by UPF [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR23)]. Systematic reviews have shown that dietary patterns high in UPF are associated with weight gain and obesity [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR24)], with a robust body of evidence linking UPF consumption to several adverse health outcomes, including cardiometabolic disorders, common mental illnesses, and increased mortality [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR25)]. Moreover, studies indicate that UPF production and consumption generate negative environmental impacts, including high plastic use, waste generation, biodiversity loss, and water consumption [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR20), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR26)–[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR28)], and together contribute to a substantial environmental burden [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR29)].

Though UPF have only become available on a truly global scale during the current era (post-1970s) of globalized food systems [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR30)], they are now dominant in global food systems and diets [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR31)], making up a large (stable) proportion of energy intake in many high-income countries, with consumption growing rapidly in several middle- and low-income country populations [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR17)]. Previous research indicates that UPF consumption in NZ is high [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR21), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR32)], and not decreasing despite clear evidence of serious negative health impacts [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR25), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR33), [34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR34)]. In NZ, the trend matches what is seen in other high-income countries like the United States, Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom, where UPF represent between 40 and 60% of adult populations’ caloric intake [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR35)–[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR38)], though consumption is consistently higher among children, adolescents and youth [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR34)].

Though NZ lacks up-to-date national dietary consumption data [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR39)], UPF constituted the majority of household food purchases in 2019, accounting for more than half of the total available dietary energy [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR40)]. Previous research has shown that over two thirds of the packaged food available in NZ supermarkets is ultra-processed [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR41)], and present the poorest nutritional profile [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR42)]. Most concerning is that NZ children under five years appear to consume approximately half their energy intake from UPF [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR43)], and the known health and wellbeing impacts of UPF consumption are disproportionately borne by Māori and Pasifika children, and those living in the most deprived areas [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR44)].

### Aims and objectives

This study aimed to monitor the nature of NZ food imports over time, as broadly defined by Nova, alongside progressive trade liberalization. Specific objectives were (1) to determine the proportion of all food and beverage imports represented by different Nova groups, and compare this over time; and (2) to track per capita changes in import volumes, and changes in tariff rates, of key food and beverage product categories (Nova subgroups) over time.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854)Methods

This study applied the INFORMAS framework for monitoring international trade and investment and food environments [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR9)], focusing on indicators for trade in goods:

_Total and per capita food import volumes, by category (Nova groups and subgroups)_._Most favoured nation (MFN) tariff rates for all food categories (Nova subgroups)_._Tariff differential between healthy and unhealthy food categories (Nova groups and subgroups)_.

Notably, this framework also recommends monitoring foreign direct investment in the food and beverage sectors, however there was insufficient data to carry this out for NZ.

### Volume of trade

Import data was downloaded from the UN Comtrade database [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR45)] for years 1990–2023, selecting all Harmonized System (HS) codes at the 6-digit level related to food and non-alcoholic beverages (broadly, from codes beginning in 02 to those beginning 25). Any HS codes designated “not for human consumption” (e.g. live plants, commodities designated for animal feed, seeds of the variety used for sowing, live fish and animals, and waste products used in alcohol production) were removed. The lead author (KG) categorised each HS code by Nova classification (Groups 1–4 and subgroups) according to best practice guidance [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR46)]. The categorisations were checked by the second author (GLC) and any discrepancies discussed and resolved among the research team. In the ultra-processed food literature, ‘subgroups’ typically refer to groups of final food products (e.g., reconstituted meat products, soft drinks, etc.), as most studies focus on dietary intake, food purchases, or food availability. In this study, which includes not only food-based groups but food manufacturing ingredients that would not be directly purchased or consumed, we define an additional ‘subgroup’ for UPF markers (‘food-derivatives/additives’). These are distinct from Group 2 processed ingredients, as they are by definition exclusively used in UPF production. The majority of categories were easily classified using this system. When in doubt, we developed the following two strategies to achieve an accurate classification.

Ingredients were searched within the Codex Alimentarius, to determine the functional definition and purpose, e.g. bulkener, thickening agent, emulsifier, etc. If the ingredient would primarily be an industrial _additive_ for food manufacturing (even if ‘natural’ or derived from plant or animal sources), as a cosmetic additive and/or not home or restaurant cooking, then it was classified as an UPF ingredient/marker, in G4. This includes all flavours, emulsifiers, modified thickeners, colours and _industrial oils and sugars_. For oils, crude (or not) oils and their fractions that were described as “whether or not refined, but not chemically modified” were classified as G2 ingredients (e.g. soy oil, sunflower oil, olive oil, coconut oil). We made the distinction of _industrial oils_ from a G2 ingredient when the oils were labelled as having been _chemically modified_ (e.g. described as “oxidised, boiled or otherwise chemically modified”; or “partly or wholly hydrogenated, inter-esterified, re-esterified or elaidinised, whether or not refined, but not further prepared”), classifying these as G4 ‘food-derivatives/additives’. For sugars, those described as “raw, in solid (or liquid) form, not containing added flavouring or colouring matter” or molasses from sugar cane or sugar beet, “resulting from the extraction or refining of sugar” were classified as G2 ingredients, as these may all be used in home food preparation. In contrast, lactose and lactose syrup, fructose in solid form, glucose and glucose syrup, and sucrose described as “containing added flavouring or colouring matter” were classified as G4 ‘food-derivatives/additives’.

For HS codes where the products included could represent two or more Nova groups (e.g. breakfast cereals, yogurts, sausages and other meat preparations, juices, and chocolate), we cross-referenced these products with the Nutritrack database (2019) [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR47)], containing the ingredient list and nutrient content data for approximately 15,000 products sold in NZ supermarkets. We assigned the code the Nova group corresponding to the majority of products available for sale, using a threshold of 80%. For example, an HS code for apple juice would be determined to be majority G4 if at least 80% of these products in NZ supermarkets can be classified as UPF based on their ingredient list. If the 80% threshold was not met, or if it was still impossible to determine the composition of these products in the NZ market, such HS codes were classified as the lower (i.e. less processed) of the possible Nova Groups.

As described above, we collected food-derivatives of rare or no culinary use or commonly used as cosmetic additives (e.g. flavours and flavour enhancers, colours, emulsifiers) and classified them as Nova G4 because they are markers of UPF [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR15)]. However, we were only able to collect additives of ‘natural’ origin, i.e. derived from plant or animal products, that are exclusively used in food manufacturing. Thus, this study did not include artificial food and beverage additives as these fall under broader categories of chemicals that are not necessarily representative of their occurrence in food (i.e. they are also used in other products like medicines, toothpaste, varnishes, etc.). Notably, not included in this study were the non-nutritive artificial sweeteners that are often present in UPF, including:

aspartame, a common artificial sweetener, which can also be used in vitamin supplements and cough drops; other cyclic amides in the same HS code are used for various pharmaceuticals and in materials science.sucralose (aka Splenda); a common artificial sweetener, which can also be used to sweeten medicines.saccharin (aka Sucaryl); a common beverage sweetener, which can also be used in medicines, cosmetics, cattle feed and tobacco products.polyols e.g. mannitol, sorbitol, erythritol (alcohol sugar), which are used to sweeten food and beverages, but substances in this category are also employed in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, polyurethanes, paints and coatings, and construction materials.

Alternative sweeteners that are derived from food sources and primarily used in food, such as monk fruit extract, would be classified as G4 under “Vegetable saps and extracts”.

Likewise, other common UPF markers with non-food applications like xanthan gum (a thickening, stabilizing and emulsifying agent in food; classified under polysaccharide derivatives which are used in household and industrial products like paints, glazes, and cleaning agents), are not captured in this analysis.

Mass-produced packaged breads (typically classified as Nova G4, and a major contributor to dietary share of UPF consumption in NZ [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR40)]) were also not represented in this dataset, as NZ generally does not import or export these.

Using the Excel pivot table function, the contribution of each Nova group to total food and beverage import volumes were calculated for each year. Using population data from Statistics NZ, per capita import volumes were calculated for each year for the included HS commodity codes, organized into Nova groups and subgroups and plotted over time.

### Tariff rates

Bound tariff rates (the maximum tariff level for a given commodity according to the Most Favoured Nation [MFN] principle) were collected from the World Trade Organization (WTO) Tariff and Trade Data website ([http://ttd.wto.org](http://ttd.wto.org/)) for all Nova subgroups each year starting in 1996 (the first year they are reported) and plotted over time. Due to the large number of HS codes included in this study, tariff rates were collected only for the first available HS code in each Nova subgroup (codes with rates available across all years); this strategy has been applied in similar studies previously [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#CR48)]. We visually examined the tariff rate difference between Nova groups, noting the key periods of reductions over the study period.

### Proportion of Nova groups in total food and non-alcoholic beverage imports, and per capita import volumes

New Zealand’s imports are consistently dominated by Nova G1 products, which have accounted for no less than 40% of the country’s total food imports during the analysed period. The second largest group, by volume, was G2 processed culinary ingredients until the year 2014, when it was surpassed by G4 ultra-processed products; G2 and G4 represented 19.0% and 21.7% of the imports of this year, respectively. These two categories alternated as second- and third-highest contributors to total import volumes for the rest of the study period. Group 3 consistently represented the smallest proportion of NZ import volume, with only a modest increase from 4.9% of the total in 1990 to 6.9% in 2023.

The data shows a steady increase in the proportion of New Zealand’s food imports that were ultra-processed in the 34 years monitored in this study, from 8.7% in 1990 to 21.8% n 2023, peaking at 25.7% in 2016 (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig2)). There appears to be a large stepwise increase between the years 1995 (G4 then representing 7.9% of imports) to 1997 (representing 16.4%), while the share of G1 reduced from 52.9% to 41.8% of import volumes in that interval. Figure[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig3) shows import volumes of all food and beverages over time, per capita.

Fig. 3Import volumes of all food and beverage products over time, per capita

### Trends in per capita imports of Nova subgroups

Examining the patterns in per capita food imports of Nova subgroups provides a more detailed and meaningful representation of changes to the food environment.

#### Group 1 imports

Figure [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig4) shows the trends in per capita imports of G1, unprocessed or minimally processed foods and beverages. The subgroup representing by far the greatest per capita volume of G1 imports throughout the study period was cereal grains and flours, primarily consisting of wheat products; the cereal grains and flours group also demonstrated the most dramatic growth within G1, from 68 kg per capita in 1990 to 154 kg per capita in 2023. Fruit imports were the next most important subgroup of G1 imports, and remained relatively stable over the period despite peaking between 2005–2008. Removing these two categories, trends in the remaining subgroups were more apparent (Supplemental Figure [S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#MOESM2)), including a modest increase in per capita imports of pork, nuts and seeds, vegetables, and legumes over the study period.

Fig. 4Volume of Nova Group 1 imports (kg per capita), between 1990–2023

#### Group 2 imports

Sugars (including table sugar, cane sugar, beet sugar, maple sugar and syrup, honey, and molasses) represented the largest volume of imported culinary ingredients throughout the study period (Fig.[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig5)). The imported volume of these sugars increased from 40 kg per capita in 1990, reaching a peak of 114 kg per capita in 2008. After 2008, the import volume of sugars declined in almost equal measure, to a volume of 47 kg per capita in 2023. Of the remaining categories of imported G2 ingredients, vegetable oils represented a substantial proportion of the volume per capita. These include all virgin and cold-pressed vegetable oils, (crude or not) and their fractions, “whether or not refined, though not chemically modified.” The volume of imported vegetable oils increased substantially between 1996 (then 0.5 kg per capita) to 1997 (surging to 13.0 kg per capita), after which a more steady increase was observed, to 25.9 kg per capita in 2023. Butter and other fats derived from animal origin were a negligeable proportion of imported culinary ingredients. Salt was another significant ingredient within this category, though its volume fluctuated across the study period. There is only one HS code for salt, which includes table salt, but the reported data is likely to have included salt destined for other purposes (e.g. in animal feed), which could not be separated from this single commodity code.

Fig. 5Volume of Nova Group 2 imports (kg per capita), between 1990–2023

#### Group 3 imports

Figure [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig6) shows imports in processed food subgroups, including processed meats (such as bacon, ham, and other salted, smoked or canned meat or fish); most cheeses; vegetable-based food preparations; and fruit and nut preparations.

The study period saw dramatic growth in imports of plant-based food preparations (vegetable, fruit or nut-based). Major contributing products in the vegetable preparations category were frozen cooked potatoes, cooked legumes (e.g. canned beans) and other prepared vegetables, and tomato preparations (whole, in pieces or pureed, e.g. canned or bottled). Fruit and nut preparations included canned fruit such as peaches and pineapples; jams, jellies and marmalades; and sweetened or salted nuts. Other Group 3 subgroups (e.g. processed meats and fish, cheese) displayed little or modest growth.

Fig. 6Volume of Nova Group 3 imports (kg per capita), between 1990–2023

#### Group 4 imports

Figure [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig7) shows import volumes of Nova G4 ultra-processed products, such as biscuits and snacks, confectionery and ice cream, sauces and spreads, and ultra-processed drinks, as well as food-derivatives/additives that are UPF inputs. Among this Nova Group, the per capita volume of imported food-derivatives/additives (e.g. industrial sweeteners, flavourings, texture enhancers) increased dramatically since 1990, surpassing all other subgroups since 2011. After peaking in 2019 at more than 37 kg per capita, the volume of imported food derivatives was approximately 28 kg per capita in 2023, similar to 2015 levels. The second most notable category of G4 imports in terms of total volume and substantial growth over time was ultra-processed drinks, reaching a volume of 24.3 L per capita in 2023. Disaggregated trends for these two subgroups are presented below.

Fig. 7Volume of Nova Group 4 imports (kg per capita), between 1990–2023

#### Group 4 ‘food-derivatives / additives’: disaggregated trends

This subgroup included all food-derived industrial sweeteners, modified oils and proteins, flavourings, and texture enhancers, of the type that are not used in home or restaurant cooking. As shown in Fig.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Fig8), a large proportion of the growth in these UPF-markers may be explained by G4 ultra-processed sweeteners, of which 20.7 kg p.c. were imported in 2023. These include lactose and lactose syrups, glucose and glucose syrups, fructose, and sucrose that has been flavoured or coloured. The per capita import volume of G4 sweeteners increased sharply in 2011, and maintained a relatively steep increase until 2019, with a slight decline afterward.

Fig. 8Volume of Group 4 Food-derived substances subgroup (kg per capita), between 1990–2023. Food-derived additives have been disaggregated by their primary form and/or function (e.g. sweeteners, protein derivatives, modified oils, flavourings and flavour enhancers, and texture enhancers including emulsifiers/ thickeners/ humectants)

#### Group 4 drinks: disaggregated trends

This subgroup category encompasses fruit drinks, flavoured waters (including sweetened and flavoured carbonated drinks) and ‘other non-alcoholic beverages’ which primarily includes plant-based milks. The major contributing products in this category changed over time. In 1990, this was mostly fruit drinks, followed by flavoured waters and ‘other’ (NZ importing 2.3L p.c., 1.9L p.c., and 0.9L p.c., respectively) (see Figure [S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#MOESM3)). By 2012, the ‘other’ category surpassed the others, and by 2016 the order observed in 1990 had reversed so that ultra-processed drink imports were led by ‘other’/plant-based milks, followed by flavoured waters, and then fruit drinks. In 2023, NZ imported 12.8L p.c. of ‘other’ beverages such as plant-based milks, 7.3L p.c. of flavoured waters such as carbonated soft drinks, and 4.5L p.c. of fruit drinks.

### Tariff rates

Tariffs on foodstuffs were substantially reduced during the study period (Table[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13097854#Tab3)). Notable reductions for all subgroups occurred between 1996–99, and then between 2007–08. By 2023, tariffs were generally non-existent for Nova Groups 1 and 2, and they remained at a low ( < = 5%) level for most processed and ultra-processed food and beverage products.

This study published in *Global Health* (2026) examines New Zealand's food and beverage imports from 1990–2023, categorized by the Nova classification system, alongside progressive trade liberalization. The research analyzed 898 Harmonized System codes from UN Comtrade data, categorizing imports into unprocessed/minimally processed foods (G1), processed culinary ingredients (G2), processed foods (G3), and ultra-processed foods/beverages (G4), with a special subgroup for UPF inputs (food-derivatives/additives).

Key findings: The share of ultra-processed foods (G4) in total food imports rose dramatically from 8.7% (15.7 kg per capita) in 1990 to 21.8% (103.8 kg per capita) in 2023, peaking at 25.7% in 2016. Most notably, imports of food-derivatives/additives (UPF inputs like industrial sweeteners, modified oils, flavorings, and texture enhancers) increased dramatically since 1990, surpassing all other UPF subgroups since 2011. By 2023, NZ imported 28 kg per capita of these UPF inputs, with industrial sweeteners alone accounting for 20.7 kg per capita.

Other notable trends: Cereal grains and flours (G1) grew from 68 to 154 kg per capita; plant oils (G2) surged from 0.5 to 25.9 kg per capita; and ultra-processed drinks reached 24.3 L per capita in 2023. Tariff rates were reduced to zero or low levels for all food products between 1990–2023, with notable reductions around 1996-98 and 2007/08.

The authors conclude that 34 years of progressive trade liberalization in NZ were characterized by an increasing proportion of imported products being ultra-processed foods and their inputs, underscoring the need for policy interventions to counteract these trends' impact on food environments and population nutrition. The study notes that UPF consumption in NZ is high, with children under five consuming approximately half their energy from UPF, and health impacts disproportionately borne by Māori and Pasifika children and those in deprived areas.

## Abstract

### Background

The public health community has become increasingly critical of the role that powerful corporations play in driving unhealthy diets, one of the leading contributors to the global burden of disease. While a substantial amount of work has examined the political strategies used by dominant processed food manufacturers that undermine public health, less attention has been paid to their use of market strategies to build and consolidate power. In this light, this paper aimed to systematically review and synthesise the market strategies deployed by dominant processed food manufacturers to increase and consolidate their power.

### Methods

A systematic review and document analysis of public health, business, legal and media content databases (Scopus, Medline, ABI Inform, Business Source Complete, Thomas Reuters Westlaw, Lexis Advance, Factiva, NewsBank), and grey literature were conducted. Data extracted were analysed thematically using an approach informed by Porter’s ‘Five Forces’ framework.

### Results

213 documents met inclusion criteria. The market strategies (_n_=21) and related practices of dominant processed food manufacturers identified in the documents were categorised into a typological framework consisting of six interconnected strategic objectives: i) reduce intense competition with equivalent sized rivals and maintaining dominance over smaller rivals; ii) raise barriers to market entry by new competitors; iii) counter the threat of market disruptors and drive dietary displacement in favour of their products; iv) increase firm buyer power over suppliers; v) increase firm seller power over retailers and distributors; and vi) leverage informational power asymmetries in relations with consumers.

### Conclusions

The typological framework is well-placed to inform general and jurisdiction-specific market strategy analyses of dominant processed food manufacturers, and has the potential to assist in identifying countervailing public policies, such as those related to merger control, unfair trading practices, and public procurement, that could be used to address market-power imbalances as part of efforts to improve population diets.
