A new study from researchers at the Global Food Research Program at UNC-Chapel Hill and The George Institute for Global Health, published in Public Health Nutrition, reveals stark disparities in ultra-processed food (UPF) purchases among U.S. households. Using nationally representative NielsenIQ Homescan Consumer Panel data, researchers examined over 33 million packaged food and beverage purchases from 2020 across nearly 60,000 U.S. households, classifying items using the Nova food processing system.

Key findings include: nearly half of all packaged food purchases and over one-third of beverage purchases were ultra-processed. Specific categories were overwhelmingly ultra-processed—90% of carbonated soft drinks, 81% of mixed dishes and soups, and 71% of sweets and snacks fell into the UPF category, with these three categories making up 36% of total purchases. Only 12% of purchases were minimally processed items like fruits, vegetables, nuts, and oils.

Disparities were observed across socioeconomic groups: lower-income and lower-education households purchased more UPFs, while non-Hispanic White households purchased significantly more UPFs than Black, Hispanic, or other race/ethnic groups. The study underscores the need for policy interventions that address food processing levels, not just nutrient content, noting that current U.S. dietary guidelines do not make recommendations based on food processing levels unlike some other countries. The research was funded primarily by Bloomberg Philanthropies.

## Abstract

### Purpose

We quantified levels of ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption and investigated consumption patterns in a representative sample of UK adolescents.

### Methods

We used data from 4-day food diaries from adolescents in the UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey (NDNS) (2008/09–2018/19). UPF were identified using the NOVA classification. We estimated the percentage of Total Energy Intake (%TEI) and the absolute weight (grams). Linear regression models quantified differences in UPF consumption across survey years and its association with participant’s individual characteristics. This was an analysis of the repeated cross-sectional data from the UK NDNS Rolling Programme waves 1–11 (2008/09–2018/19). A total of 2991 adolescents (11–18y) with complete information on dietary intake were included.

### Results

Mean UPF consumption was 861 (SD 442) g/d and this accounted for 65.9% (SD 13.4%) of TEI. Between 2008 and 2019, mean UPF consumption decreased from 996 to 776 g/d [ – 211 (95%CI  – 302;  – 120)] and from 67.7% to 62.8% of TEI [ – 4.8% (95%CI  – 8.1;  – 1.5)]. Higher %TEI was consumed by adolescents with lower socioeconomic status; white ethnicity and living in England North. A higher weight of UPF consumption (g/d) was associated with being male, white, age 18y, having parents with routine or manual occupation, living in England North, and living with obesity.

### Conclusion

Average energy intake from UPF has decreased over a decade in UK adolescents. We observed a social and regional patterning of UPF consumption, with higher consumption among adolescents from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, from a white ethnicity and living in England North. Our findings suggest inequalities associated with UPF intake and factors that might lie beyond individual choice.

### Supplementary Information

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00394-024-03458-z.

**Keywords:** Ultra-processed food, Adolescents, National diet and nutrition survey, Food consumption

## Background

The consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPF) has been proposed as one of the key drivers of the global rise in chronic diet-related diseases [[1](#CR1)]. UPF are often manufactured from cheap industrial substances extracted or derived from foods, such as fats and oils, free sugars, and amino acids, which are then mixed with cosmetic additives, like colours, stabilisers, humectants, emulsifiers which are not used in domestic kitchens. Diets high in UPFs are linked to indicators of poor dietary quality, including elevated levels of added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, as well as increased energy density and decreased fibre, protein, and micronutrient content [[2](#CR2), [3](#CR3)]. Such unhealthy dietary patterns have been implicated in the rise of chronic diseases through inflammatory pathways [[4](#CR4)]. There is a growing body of evidence linking the consumption of UPF with poor dietary quality, and diet related diseases such as obesity in children, adolescents and adults [[7](#CR7)], and chronic non-communicable diseases, such as cardiovascular disease and cancer [[8](#CR8)] and all-cause mortality in adults [[9](#CR9)]. A recent systematic umbrella review of published meta-analyses found that increased consumption of UPFs is correlated with increased risks of negative health outcomes, particularly relating to cardiometabolic, common mental disorders, and mortality [[16](#CR16)]. Moreover, the detrimental health effects associated with UPFs may not be attributed to their nutrient profile and calorie density but also to physical alterations in the food matrix and chemical properties resulting from industrial processing methods, ingredients (such as additives and non-sugar sweeteners), and by-products [[5](#CR5)]. Some examples of UPF are soft drinks, breakfast cereals, reconstituted meat products, packaged breads, ready-to-eat foods. UPF are durable, convenient, ready-to-eat, hyper-palatable, have attractive packaging and are strongly marketed to children and adolescents [[6](#CR6)]. These results underscore the need to create and assess the efficacy of population-wide and public health interventions aimed at minimizing the intake of UPFs to enhance human health.

Adolescence is a key transitional stage when major changes in practices that influence health occur [[10](#CR10)]. Adolescents’ search for novelty and openness to change also makes them a vulnerable group for commercial marketing [[6](#CR6)]. Adolescents’ food patterns and practices are strongly driven by their food environments and eating contexts, their autonomy, peer influence and social norms [[11](#CR11)]. These food patterns can additionally be influenced by commercially targeted activities, such as marketing and advertising, product placement, and pricing strategies such as food promotions and discounts [[12](#CR12)].

Evidence across different countries suggests that adolescents are the highest consumers on average of UPF compared to other age groups [[13](#CR13)]. In Canada it is estimated that UPF contribute approximately 55% of the total caloric intake in children and adolescents (2–18y) versus 45% in adults [[14](#CR14)]. In the USA, children (6-11y) (69.0%) and adolescents (12–19y) (67.7%) consumed a significantly higher percentage of energy from UPF than those aged 2–5 years (61.1%) [[15](#CR15)].

Although consumption of UPF is becoming more prevalent worldwide [[1](#CR1), [17](#CR17)], there are notable cross-country and socioeconomic status (SES) differences [[18](#CR18)]. In nationally representative samples from high-income countries UPF contribute more than 50% of energy intake [[19](#CR19)], and up to 30% in middle-income countries [[20](#CR20)]. Even though consumption of UPF is much higher in high-income compared to upper-middle income countries, among these latter countries adolescents are still the highest UPF consumption age group. Evidence from high- and upper-middle income countries signals a distinction in social patterning of UPF consumption according to the nutritional transition stage of each country [[1](#CR1)].

Globally, the availability and sales of UPF have increased over time (2006–2019) [[1](#CR1)], and evidence from the USA (2010–2018) and Korea (1999–2018) suggests that consumption of UPF among adolescents has also increased over time [[15](#CR15), [21](#CR21)]. However, evidence from a representative sample of UK population (> 1.5 years) did not find evidence for an increase in the energy share of UPF between 2008 and 2019 [[22](#CR22)], yet changes in weight consumption (g/d) from UPF were not explored. Examining the changes in consumption of UPF over time can aid us in understanding the behavioural trends within a shifting food landscape. Considering that adolescents are the highest consumers of UPF, and considering evidence from other countries indicating an increase in consumption in this age group over time, we explored the 11 data waves in NDNS to determine if consumption patterns of energy (TEI%) and weight (g/d) followed similar trends.

Previous studies on UPF consumption have mostly expressed UPF as percentage of energy intake. However, the French NutriNet-Santé study [[23](#CR23)] proposed expressing UPF by weight (grams) given that this can capture non-nutritional factors relating to processing of food and foods and drinks that contribute little to energy intake (e.g., additives, non-sugar sweeteners, neo-formed contaminants and endocrine-disrupting chemicals from packaging materials [[24](#CR24)]. The associations observed between UPF and health might be influenced by various mechanisms. For example, research shows that weight measures (g/d) of UPF consumption have a stronger association with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Conversely, energy intake from UPF was found to be more strongly associated with body fat accumulation [[25](#CR25)]. Furthermore, research shows that UPF remains strongly associated with obesity and health-related outcomes after adjusting for quality and dietary pattern [[23](#CR23)].

Currently there is limited evidence on UPF consumption among adolescents. Quantifying levels of UPF consumption and exploring consumption patterns is essential to enable policies that prevent unhealthy dietary patterns in adolescent years and prevent diet-related diseases later in life. To address this research gap, this study aimed to quantify the levels UPF consumption and investigate consumption patterns in a representative sample of UK adolescents. To achieve this, we carried out the following objectives: we calculated UPF consumption and its contribution to relative energy intake (% kcal/day) and absolute food weight intake (g/day); we described UPF consumption across the 11 NDNS survey waves (2008–2019); and investigated the association between sociodemographic characteristics and UPF consumption.

## Methods

We conducted an analysis using repeated cross-sectional data from 11- to 18-year-old participants (adolescents) in the UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey Rolling Programme (NDNS) waves 1–11 (2008/09–2018/19). Data were downloaded from the UK Data Service [[26](#CR26)]. This study is reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational studies in Epidemiology – Nutritional Epidemiology (STROBE-nut). Parental consent was obtained for participants aged 11 to 15 and direct consent was obtained for participants aged 16 to 18 years. Additional ethical approval for this secondary analysis of anonymised data was not required.

### Study design and population

The NDNS is an annual rolling programme (RP) of cross-sectional surveys conducted in the UK (England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland) assessing the food consumption, nutrient intake and nutritional status of the general UK population aged 1.5 years and above living in private households. Additionally, data collected in England is presented by regions: England North, Central/Midlands, England South (including London). NDNS survey year starts in April and data collection runs from April until March the following year. Population, sampling and recruitment are described in detail elsewhere [[27](#CR27)]. Briefly, NDNS’s continuous rolling programme seeks to collect data from a representative sample of the UK population with 1000 participants every year (500 adults, 500 children and adolescents) with provision of an additional sample to achieve country-level representativeness.

Sampling follows a multistage probability design to generate a new random sample of private households in the UK every year. Each year a random sample from small geographical areas [(i.e., primary sampling units (PSUs)] is selected. Within these PSUs, private addresses are randomly selected from the Postcode Address File and the selected households receive a visit by the study team. Among the participating household one child and one adult are randomly selected to take part. Participants within households are then asked to complete a food diary across 4 days to record all foods and beverages consumed inside and outside of the house. Those who record at least 3 days are then invited for further physical measurements.

### Inclusion criteria

Individuals were included in the analysis if they took part in NDNS waves 1 to 11, were aged between ≥ 11 and ≤ 18 years at data collection and completed at least three out of four food diary days.

The current study combines NDNS data from waves 1 to 11 (2008/09 to 2018/19). Overall, at an individual level, 53% of those selected to take part, including adults and children, completed at least three food diary days. From the sample of included individuals, 3,270 were adolescents (11- to 18-year-olds).

### Dietary data collection & processing

Dietary assessment in NDNS waves 1–11 was designed to provide full description, detail and quantification of all food and drink consumed during the dietary assessment period, with the ability to capture habitual consumption when conducted over a number of days. Seasonal variations in food and drink consumption are addressed by the continuous fieldwork design.

Trained interviewers collected sociodemographic information through interviews and administered the food diaries to adolescent participants. Adolescents were instructed (in the case of 11- and 12-year-olds, their parent or carer) by the trained interviewer to record location, time and quantity of all the food and drink they consumed inside and outside of the home over four consecutive days. Recording of the four-day food diary would start on selected days to ensure even representation of all days of the week across the whole sample. After the food diaries were completed, the interviewer returned to collect the diary, reviewed the data with the participant and added missing details to improve completeness. Participants received monetary gift vouchers following completion of at least three of the four dietary recordings. Household measures and nutritional information from labels were used to estimate portion sizes consumed. Food diaries were entered in the Dietary assessment system DINO (Diet In Nutrients Out) that uses food composition data from the NDNS Nutrient Databank [[28](#CR28), [29](#CR29)]. Additional details of the coding of food intake data and calculation of energy intakes and food composition in NDNS data are described in detail elsewhere [[28](#CR28)–[31](#CR31)].

Across the 11 years of data collection, NDNS participants reported on 60 main food groups, 154 subsidiary food groups and 4,944 food items. Classification of foods and beverages according to their level of processing was conducted using the NOVA food classification system which considers the nature, extent and purpose of industrial food manufacturing processing [[32](#CR32)]. The NOVA classification includes four categories: (1) unprocessed or minimally processed foods, (2) processed culinary ingredients, (3) processed foods and (4) UPF. Figure [1](#Fig1) shows these four classifications and examples of each food group. More details on the NOVA classification can be found elsewhere [[4](#CR4), [32](#CR32)].

#### Fig. 1.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig1/)

The 4 groups in the NOVA food classification system [based on information from [[33](#CR33)]]

All foods and drinks in the NDNS Nutrient Databank were coded and grouped independently by two researchers (YCU and ZC) based on main food group first (e.g., ‘Pasta rice and other cereals’), then coded according to subsidiary food groups (e.g., pasta, manufactured products and ready meals) and then by individual food item (e.g., pasta, spaghetti, canned in tomato sauce) based on their recipe information and the ingredient list if the classification of a whole main or subgroup was not possible (e.g., composite dishes). This allowed us to classify each underlying or main constituent ingredient into the corresponding NOVA group as previously suggested on how to disaggregate composite food codes in NDNS data [[30](#CR30), [31](#CR31)]. Food supplements (i.e., vitamins and minerals) were not coded. Previous studies that have used either the NOVA classification system and/or NDNS data served as a useful coding framework to classify dietary data in this study [[7](#CR7), [34](#CR34), [35](#CR35)].

This study was specifically interested in the consumption of UPF. Thus, we classified group 1, 2 and 3 as non-UPF, and group 4 as UPF and focused on the UPF category (NOVA 4) to describe UPF consumption among UK adolescents.

### NOVA classification level of agreement

The level of agreement between both coders was 97% after independently classifying all food and drink items using the full NOVA classification system (NOVA 1, 2, 3 and 4). Most of this disagreement (152 of 4,784 food and drink items, 3.1%) was between NOVA categories 1, 2 and 3. Only 10 of 4,784 (0.2%) food items caused a disagreement in UPF classification (NOVA 4). These 10 UPF were mainly composite dishes (i.e., beef curry takeaway, cottage pie with instant mash potato, black pudding in batter takeaway, fish pie with crust flaky pastry, vegetable pie with crust, *vol au vents* made with mushroom sauce and pastry), sauces (i.e., chilli pickle sweet, golden syrup), and ice-cream (i.e., ice-cream with double cream and purchased sorbet). These 10 food items categorised as NOVA 4 (UPF) by the first researcher (YCU) based on the individual food name and searches for lists of ingredients in branded products, whilst the second researcher (ZC) classified them based on the food name without searching for list of ingredients in branded items. Once the lists of ingredients were reviewed and discussed both researchers reached a 100% agreement.

### Variables of interest

The outcomes of interest were the relative energy intake from UPF (NOVA 4) (% kcal/d) and the absolute weight of UPF consumed (g/d). These were calculated based on the relative energy and total absolute weight of foods and drinks classified as UPF in the NDNS food individual level dietary dataset reported by each participant. Individual-level sociodemographic characteristics included sex at birth, age, parent’s occupation social class, ethnic group and UK region. Other individual characteristics included weight categories derived from standardised body mass index (zBMI), survey year, and moderate-to-vigorous-physical activity (MVPA).

BMI was calculated from nurse measured height and weight. BMI values were standardised for sex and age and categorised [normal weight (< = 1 standard deviation (sd)), overweight (> 1 sd) and obese (> 2 sd)] based on the 1990 British Growth Reference (UK90).

MVPA data was self-reported using the Recent Physical Activity Questionnaire (RPAQ) [[36](#CR36)], which assessed type, amount of physical activity and screen time, and is validated for use in older adolescents and adults. Data was therefore collected only in 16–18-year-olds, and among these, only 56% provided MVPA data (18% of the entire sample, n = 575 out of n = 3270). Daily time spent in MVPA was summed in each individual (min/day). As MVPA was not normally distributed we created quartiles (< 21 min/day; 21–52 min/day; 52–124 min/day; > 124 min/day).

Other sociodemographic variables were categorised as follows: sex (male and female), age in completed whole years (8 categories from 11 to 18 years), parent’s occupation social class (higher managerial, administrative, and professional occupations; intermediate occupations; routine and manual occupations; we used the three level National Statistics Socioeconomic classification (NS-SEC) [[37](#CR37)]), ethnic group (white, non-white), and region [England North, England Central/Midlands, England South (including London), Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland].

### Statistical analysis

Study weights were provided by NDNS, and datasets were re-scaled and adjusted for the adolescent subsample based on NDNS study weights guide documentation [[38](#CR38)]. These weights were applied using the *svy* prefix in Stata for all analysis to account for non-response and sampling error and to provide estimates representative of the UK adolescent population.

For the description of the sample, we reported weighted percentages (with 95%Cis) of the distribution of individual sociodemographic characteristics alongside the distribution and means of relative UPF energy consumption (%kcal/day) and absolute weight of UPF consumption (g/d) in the overall sample and for each sociodemographic characteristic. We displayed the mean of all available days of food diary for each individual.

We pooled all survey years and used multivariable linear regression models to test if each of our two outcome variables – dietary contribution of UPF (%kcal/d and g/d) – differed across each of the variables of interest by doing individual stepwise models (i.e., sociodemographic categories and individual characteristics separately) adjusting for age, sex and survey year as covariates. Each category within a variable was compared to the reference group (i.e., sex (male), age (11 years) parent’s occupation social class (higher managerial, administrative, and professional occupations), ethnic group (white), and region (England North). We also used linear regression analysis to evaluate if mean UPF consumption (%kcal/d and g/d) changed across NDNS survey years by comparing each survey year (2 to 11) vs year 1 (2008/09) and adjusting for age and sex. Given the clustered regional sampling design of NDNS, we used survey analysis procedures to incorporate sample weights in these models.

### Missing data

Variables with complete data (n = 3,270) were sex, age, survey year, and region. Variables with missing data were ethnicity (0.1%), parents’ occupation (4.5%), BMI z-score (4.3%), and MVPA (82.4%). We used a complete case analysis for all analyses (n = 2,991 for all variables, except for MVPA n = 534, for which a separate analysis was done using this subsample).

### Additional analysis

We ran an analysis adjusting for total energy intake in addition to the primary analysis to explore whether individual characteristics were associated with relative energy (%kcal/d) and absolute weight (g/d) independently from total energy intake.

All data analysis was conducted in Stata Statistical Software: Release 17.0 (StataCorp LP., College Station, TX, USA).

## Results

Table [1](#Tab1) presents descriptive data of the 2991 participants with complete data for the variables of interest except MVPA (n = 534). Of all adolescents, 51.3% were females, 42.9% had parents with a higher managerial, administrative and professional occupation, 66% had normal weight, 83.3% were from a white ethnic group, 43.7% lived in England South (including London), and of participants with physical activity data (16 to 18 year olds) 26.7% reported more than 124 min/day of MVPA.

### Associations of UPF consumption with time and sociodemographic variables

#### UPF consumption across NDNS survey years

Figures [2](#Fig2) and [3](#Fig3) (and Supplementary Table [S1](#MOESM1)) show mean UPF consumption and CI’s across NDNS survey years (2009/09 – 2018/19) (adjusted for age and sex). There was evidence for a difference in relative energy (%kcal/day) and absolute weight (g/day) consumption from UPF across survey years (*p* < 0.001).

##### Fig. 2.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig2/)

Mean relative energy consumption (%kcal/day) and CI’s from UPF across NDNS survey years (adjusted for age and sex)

##### Fig. 3.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig3/)

Mean grams of UPF consumption (plus 95% confidence interval) across NDNS survey years (adjusted for age and sex)

In Fig. [2](#Fig2) we observed that comparing survey year 2 (2009/10) through 7 (2014/15) versus survey year 1 (i.e., reference year) there was no evidence of a difference in the absolute UPF as percentage of total energy intake (%TEI). However, %TEI from UPF was significantly lower from survey year 8 (2015/16) through 10 (2017/19) (vs year 1 – 2008/09) with the largest reduction in survey year 8 (-5.8%kcal/day).

In Fig. [3](#Fig3) we observed that the highest absolute weight from UPF consumed (g/d) was seen in year 1 (2008/09) (993.7 g/d). Similar to relative energy intake (%kcal/d), we observed a steady decline with some random variation in UPF weight across survey years.

### Individual characteristics and %TEI from UPF

After adjusting for age, sex and survey year, results show (Fig. [4](#Fig4) and Supplementary Table [S1](#MOESM1)) that parents’ occupation, ethnic group and UK region were associated with percentage of energy consumption from UPF. A higher %TEI from UPF was consumed by adolescents whose parents had routine and manual occupations or intermediate occupations compared to adolescents with parents who had higher managerial occupations [intermediate: 2.0% (95%CI 0.4; 3.5); routine and manual parental occupation: 4.6% (95%CI 3.2; 6.1)]. Adolescents from a non-white ethnicity (vs white) reported lower %TEI from UPF [ – 8.0% (95%CI  – 9.8;  – 6.1)] as well as those living in England South (including London) (vs England North) [ – 3.2% (95%CI  – 4.9;  – 1.5)].

#### Fig. 4.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig4/)

Linear regression of the adjusted associations between participants’ characteristics (vs reference category) and consumption of UPF defined as relative energy (%kcal/day) (adjusted for age, sex and survey year)

### Individual characteristics and absolute weight from UPF

Figure [5](#Fig5) (and Supplementary Table [S1](#MOESM1)) shows that higher weight of UPF consumption (g/d) was associated with age between 17 and 18 years (vs 11-year-olds), with the highest consumption observed in 18-year-olds [115.1 g/day, (95%CI 26.6; 203.5)]. Adolescents whose parents had a routine and manual occupation (vs higher managerial) [78.9 g/day, (95%CI 34.6; 123.3)], and adolescents living with obesity (vs normal weight) [90.3 g/day (95%CI 39.0; 141.5)] reported a higher UPF weight consumption. In contrast, lower weight of UPF consumption (g/d) was associated with female sex (vs male) [ – 169.2 g/day, (95%CI  – 206.8;  – 131.7)], non-white ethnicity (vs white) [ – 247.2, (95%CI  – 292.8;  – 201.6)], and living in South England and Northern Ireland (vs. North England) [ – 99.2, (95%CI  – 150.6;  – 47.8);  – 76.8, (95%CI  – 135.0;  – 18.6)].

#### Fig. 5.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig5/)

Linear regression of the adjusted associations between participants’ characteristics (vs reference category) and consumption of UPF defined as absolute weight (g/day) (adjusted for age, sex and survey year)

### Additional analysis

After additionally adjusting for total energy intake, all associations with %TEI from UPF persisted and in addition 18-year-olds (vs. 11-year-olds) had a lower %TEI ( – 3.0%TEI, 95%CI  – 5.7,  – 0.3). For UPF weight consumption, after adjusting for total energy intake associations were attenuated for age, survey years 4, 5, 6 and 10, and for MVPA > 124 min/day (Supplementary Table S2).

## Discussion

In this repeated cross-sectional study of a nationally representative sample of UK adolescents, we found that mean UPF among 11- to 18-year-olds was 861 g/day and accounted for 65.9% of their TEI. After adjusting for age and sex, mean consumption of UPF (both %TEI and weight) declined between 2008/09/ and 2018/19. Percentage of energy from UPF was lower by 5 percentage points and weight consumption from UPF was lower by 211.2 g per day when comparing the first vs last NDNS survey waves (wave 1: 2008/09 vs wave 11:2018/19). After adjusting for age, sex and survey year, adolescents with lower socioeconomic status (having parents in an intermediate or routine and manual occupations), from a white ethnicity, and living in England North had higher %TEI from UPF. Additionally, being male, being between 17 and 18 years, having a lower socioeconomic status (having parents in a routine and manual occupation), living with obesity, from a white ethnicity, and living in England North were associated with a higher weight of UPF consumption (g/d). This increased consumption in weight of UPFs but not calories from UPFs could be explained by health behaviour changes and increased health awareness as adolescents age, and by adolescents living with obesity consuming a larger weight of UPFs that are low in fat, sugar and/or calories (e.g., zero calorie soft drinks) (22). In additional analysis, adjusting for total energy intake, patterns of association with UPF weight became more consistent to those with %TEI from UPF.

These findings are consistent with previous analyses of the same NDNS data in 11 to 18-year-olds using survey years 2008/16 and 2008/17 (68% contribution of UPF to total energy intake [[35](#CR35), [39](#CR39)] and with analyses of data from adolescents living in other high-income countries (55% in Canada [[14](#CR14)], and 68% in USA [[15](#CR15)]). Although UPF are becoming more prevalent worldwide [[1](#CR1), [17](#CR17), [18](#CR18)], there are cross-country differences that should be acknowledged. A recent multi-country study assessing adolescents’ UPF consumption in upper-middle and high-income countries found that consumption across these countries ranged between 19 to 36% in upper-middle-income countries (i.e., Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, and Mexico), and from 34 to 68% in high-income countries (i.e., Australia, Chile, USA and UK) with UK adolescents being the highest consumers of UPF [[40](#CR40)]. The high consumption of UPF among HIC such as the UK may be partly explained by a combination of social, cultural, economic, and marketing factors [[18](#CR18)]. Urbanisation in the UK, as in other HIC, can increase access to a greater diversity of and cheaper foods, including UPF, and increased exposure to commercial marketing with a wide offer of ready-to-eat products [[41](#CR41)]. These offer convenient solutions to longer working hours, changes in family structure and contribute to shifting from home food preparations to more ready-to-consume foods [[42](#CR42)]. An analysis of household availability of UPF in nineteen European countries showed that in the UK 50.4% of total purchased dietary energy comes from UPF, in contrast with 10.2% in Portugal, 13.4% in Italy and 46.2% in Germany [[43](#CR43)].

Our findings suggest a decline of UPF consumption (%TEI and weight) between survey years 1 and 11 in the NDNS (2008/09 – 2018/19). Time trend analysis in NDNS (years 1 to 9) show a decline in total energy intake in this age group, especially between survey years 7 and 8 (2014/15). Additionally, the general downward trend in energy consumption from UPF is consistent with other study findings; a study using a controlled interrupted time series analysis between 2014 and 2019 found a 10% reduction in free sugars purchased per household per week from SSBs between 2014 and 2019 [[44](#CR44)], however they did not find a reduction in volume (mL) purchased from SSBs. Another study using data from adults and children in NDNS found a reduction in energy share by 1.4% from sweetened beverages between 2008/09 to 2018/19, also without a reduction in volume (mL) consumed [[22](#CR22)]. We hypothesise that this reduction could be partly explained by an increased public awareness and health concerns associated with sugar consumption, government-led campaigns and SSB reformulation to reduce sugar content. However, in this study we did not analyse UPF subgroup consumption and cannot attribute this drop in consumption exclusively to SSBs or free sugars. The reduction in UPF weight consumption in this study might be attributable to other UPF subgroups, or alternatively to a change in NDNS main food group classification or subsidiary group classification in the NDNS Nutrient Databank.

Interestingly, in our sample UPF contributed proportionately more to TEI (65%) than to food weight (43%), which reflects the overall higher energy density of UPF. Energy density is associated with weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and obesity [[45](#CR45)]. Some associations were apparent with food weight but not with %TEI from UPF, for example with sex (higher in males vs. females) and age (higher in older adolescents). These differences largely reflect the higher TEI consumed by males and older adolescents. However, after accounting for TEI we still observed an independent significant effect. We need to understand mechanisms of harm, if any, to help guide finding a correct metric of exposure.

Similar to other findings, we observed that being from a white ethnicity is associated with a significantly higher consumption of UPF [[15](#CR15), [39](#CR39)]. However, the relationship between ethnicity and UPF is complex and multifactorial, and the observed higher UPF consumption among white ethnicity adolescents could be due to other factors associated with ethnicity, for example, cultural and other economic factors (e.g., home ownership [[46](#CR46)].

Our findings add to the body of knowledge that in HIC, lower socioeconomic groups consume higher levels of UPF [[1](#CR1)]. This may be partly due to the greater affordability (i.e., price per calorie) of food with less nutritional value across country incomes and regions [[47](#CR47)] alongside targeted marketing to specific population subgroups [[48](#CR48)]. Additionally, reduced at-home facilities for food preparation and lack of time to cook at home may lead to an increased consumption of more processed and convenience foods (e.g., pre-prepared meals) [[49](#CR49)]. Whilst in HIC most UPF are relatively cheaper than less processed foods, the opposite patterns are seen in LMIC. As an example, soft drinks are relatively inexpensive in HIC, whilst they are relatively expensive in LMIC [[1](#CR1), [18](#CR18)].

There is currently no universally agreed “safe” levels of dietary share from UPF. Therefore, future research to understand the mechanisms of harms to health may substantially improve nutritional quality of adolescent diets and contribute to the prevention of diet related NCDs.

## Strengths and limitations

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to characterise and present data associating to both %TEI and weight of UPF consumption (g/d) in a representative sample of UK adolescents.

This study has several additional strengths. Due to the consistent methods of data collection over time, the data across waves could be mixed resulting in a relatively large sample size. This study used individual-level dietary data, had 3 or 4 food diary days for each individual and had relatively high numbers of individuals among each group, which is likely to give a more accurate assessment of total dietary intake versus other methods [[50](#CR50), [51](#CR51)]. For example, food records allow researchers to have high levels of detail on dietary intake, they were completed in real-time, which avoids reliance on recall, a common limitation of food frequency questionnaires and 24-h recalls. Additionally, food records, when compared to direct observation and doubly labelled water, perform much better than other self-reported methods and capture about 80% of energy intake [[50](#CR50), [52](#CR52)]. Weighting of the sample was applied to reduce non-response and sampling bias, therefore, the study results can be generalisable to the UK adolescent population. Additionally, this study included a weight measure of UPF to capture non-nutritional factors relating to processing of food (i.e., additives, non-sugar sweeteners, neo-formed contaminants), and foods and drinks that do not contribute to energy intake (e.g., artificially sweetened beverages). Our results show that there were more individual characteristics associated with weight of UPF consumption (g/d) than UPF contribution to TEI. The inclusion of this measure could further enhance our knowledge about the risks involved by diets high in UPF beyond their contribution to TEI, but this should be systematically tested in studies of UPF and health outcomes.

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed scientific study published in 2024 examining ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption among UK adolescents using data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey (NDNS) spanning 2008/09 to 2018/19. The study analyzed 2,991 adolescents aged 11-18 years, using 4-day food diaries and the NOVA food classification system to identify UPF.

**Key Findings:**
- Mean UPF consumption was 861 g/day, accounting for 65.9% of total energy intake (TEI)
- Between 2008 and 2019, UPF consumption decreased from 996 to 776 g/day (a drop of 211 g/day) and from 67.7% to 62.8% of TEI (a 4.8% decrease)
- Higher %TEI from UPF was consumed by adolescents with lower socioeconomic status, white ethnicity, and those living in England North
- Higher weight of UPF consumption (g/day) was associated with being male, white, age 18, having parents with routine/manual occupations, living in England North, and living with obesity
- Adolescents from non-white ethnicities reported 8% lower TEI from UPF compared to white adolescents
- Those living in England South (including London) consumed 3.2% less TEI from UPF compared to those in England North

**Methodology:** The study used repeated cross-sectional data from NDNS waves 1-11, applying survey weights for representativeness. UPF classification was done independently by two researchers with 97% initial agreement and 100% final agreement. Linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, and survey year.

**Conclusions:** While average UPF consumption has declined over a decade in UK adolescents, consumption remains high (roughly two-thirds of energy intake). The study found significant social and regional patterning of UPF consumption, suggesting inequalities associated with UPF intake and factors beyond individual choice. The authors note there is no universally agreed "safe" level of dietary share from UPF.

--- SOURCE 1: Ultra-Processed Foods, Gut Microbiota, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Critical Review of Emerging Evidence ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/16/2677

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Nutrients (2025, 17(16), 2677) titled "Ultra-Processed Foods, Gut Microbiota, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Critical Review of Emerging Evidence." The review examines the influence of ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption on gut microbiota composition and function and its potential link to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Key findings include: (1) UPFs account for up to 58% of daily caloric intake in high-income countries and are associated with intestinal dysbiosis, reduced microbial diversity, decreased short-chain fatty acid production, impaired barrier integrity, and mucus layer disruption. (2) Consuming 10% of calories from UPFs per day is associated with a 19% increased risk of developing Crohn's disease. (3) Food additives like emulsifiers (e.g., carboxymethyl cellulose, polysorbate 80) can promote proinflammatory changes in the gut microbiota, enhance LPS release, and impair the mucus layer. (4) The persistent low-grade inflammation driven by UPF consumption can lead to "leaky gut" and increased intestinal permeability. The review notes that serum LPS levels are reportedly six times higher in patients with active Crohn's disease compared to healthy controls. The article concludes that high UPF consumption is associated with intestinal dysbiosis characterized by overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria such as Clostridium and Enterococcus, triggering inflammatory responses in the host.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: The Science of Ultra-Processed Foods and Mental Health ---
URL: https://www.news-medical.net/health/The-Science-of-Ultra-Processed-Foods-and-Mental-Health.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from News-Medical (dated April 3, 2025) explores the growing evidence linking ultra-processed foods (UPFs) to mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, and cognitive decline. UPFs—defined by the NOVA classification system as industrially processed foods like packaged snacks, sugary drinks, instant noodles, and processed meats—now constitute a significant portion of daily caloric intake in many countries.

**Key Evidence:**
- A 2020 study of over 10,000 US adults found that those consuming the most UPFs had a 35% greater likelihood of depressive symptoms.
- Harvard Medical School research found higher UPF consumption was associated with a 50% increased risk of depression, particularly with artificially sweetened beverages and processed snacks.
- A large cohort study of over 25,000 individuals followed for more than five years linked increased UPF intake to higher rates of depressive episodes, independent of lifestyle factors.

**Proposed Mechanisms:**
1. **Gut-brain axis dysfunction** – UPFs lack dietary fiber, disrupting gut microbiota and impairing production of mood-regulating neurotransmitters like serotonin and GABA.
2. **Chronic inflammation** – Refined carbohydrates, unhealthy fats, and additives promote systemic inflammation, with elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) linked to depression.
3. **Blood sugar fluctuations** – High glycemic index foods cause glucose spikes and crashes, affecting mood stability and cognitive function.
4. **Artificial additives** – Sweeteners like aspartame may alter neurotransmitter activity; emulsifiers can disrupt gut microbiota and influence neuroinflammatory pathways.

**Global Trends & Industry Response:** The food industry continues expanding UPF production due to cost-effectiveness and convenience demand. Some companies are reformulating products, but health impacts remain uncertain. Public health initiatives promoting whole-food diets (e.g., Mediterranean, DASH) are increasingly advocated.

**Limitations:** Most studies are observational, making causality difficult to establish. Reverse causality (people with depression may consume more UPFs as a coping mechanism) is possible. Self-reported dietary data is subject to recall bias, and confounding factors like socioeconomic status and genetics may influence outcomes.

**Future Directions:** Research should focus on elucidating mechanisms using microbiome analysis, neuroimaging, and biomarker assessments. Longitudinal studies with diverse populations are needed to establish causality. Public health policies should aim to reduce UPF consumption and promote whole-food-based diets.
</summary>

Diets high in UPFs often lack dietary fiber and essential nutrients, leading to an imbalance in gut microbiota.", "Markers of inflammation, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), are often elevated in individuals consuming diets high in UPFs.", "While the associations between UPFs and mental health concerns are evident, it is unclear whether UPF consumption directly causes mental health disorders or if individuals with pre-existing depression and anxiety are more likely to consume these foods as a coping mechanism."

--- SOURCE 3: The Detrimental Impact of Ultra-Processed Foods on the Human Gut Microbiome and Gut Barrier - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11901572

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific review article, published February 28, 2025, in Nutrients journal (PMCID: PMC11901572, PMID: 40077728), examines the detrimental impact of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) on the human gut microbiome and gut barrier. Authored by researchers from Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore and Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Gemelli IRCCS in Rome, Italy, the review covers the following key areas:

**NOVA Classification System:** UPFs (NOVA4) are defined as industrially manufactured products with 5+ ingredients, including additives not commonly found in kitchens (e.g., hydrogenated oils, emulsifiers, artificial colors). Examples include soft drinks, packaged snacks, processed meats, and ready-to-eat meals.

**Gut Microbiome Overview:** The healthy gut microbiome is dominated by Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes phyla. Key beneficial bacteria include Akkermansia muciniphila, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Bifidobacteria. The microbiome produces essential short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like acetate, propionate, and butyrate, which maintain gut barrier integrity, modulate immunity, and regulate metabolism.

**UPF-Driven Gut Alterations:** UPF consumption is associated with decreased microbial α-diversity, reduced beneficial bacteria (Akkermansia muciniphila, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Lachnospira, Roseburia), and increased pro-inflammatory microorganisms (Granulicatella, Blautia, Bacteroidaceae). Emulsifiers (carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate 80) alter microbiota composition, promote pro-inflammatory environments, and compromise the mucus layer, leading to increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut").

**Health Implications:** UPF-induced dysbiosis contributes to systemic low-grade inflammation and is linked to metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and colorectal cancer. UPFs may also alter the gut-brain axis, potentially affecting cognitive function and mental health.

**Mitigation Strategies:** Dietary modifications incorporating fiber, fermented foods, and probiotics can help mitigate UPF effects. The authors advocate for stricter regulations on UPFs and well-defined food labels. The review notes that Latin American countries have already integrated NOVA into dietary guidelines, and France aims to reduce UPF consumption by 20%.
</summary>

UPFs, characterized by a high content of synthetic additives and emulsifiers, and low fiber content, are associated with a decrease in microbial diversity, lower levels of beneficial bacteria like Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and an increase in pro-inflammatory microorganisms., Commonly utilized emulsifiers, including carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), polysorbate 80 (P80), carrageenan, and gums, are known to alter gut microbiota composition, thereby promoting a pro-inflammatory microbial environment that may contribute to the development of metabolic disorders such as obesity and T2DM., Individuals who consumed high levels of UPFs exhibited an elevated presence of potentially harmful bacterial groups... including Granulicatella, which is linked to metabolic disorders, as well as Blautia, Carnobacteriaceae, Bacteroidaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Bacteroidia, and Bacteroidetes., The germ-free mice colonized with emulsifier-treated microbiotas exhibited low-grade inflammation, increased metabolic markers, higher fasting blood glucose levels and increased adiposity, indicative of MetS., Dietary modifications incorporating fiber, fermented foods, and probiotics can help mitigate the effects of UPFs. Furthermore, the public needs stricter regulations for banning UPFs, along with well-defined food labels.

--- SOURCE 4: How ultra-processed foods affect our gut microbiome ---
URL: https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20260220-how-ultra-processed-foods-influence-our-gut-microbiome

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This BBC article examines how additives in ultra-processed foods (UPFs), particularly emulsifiers, affect the gut microbiome — the trillions of microbes in our digestive system. A healthy, diverse microbiome is linked to better mood, metabolism, brain health, sleep, and longevity. 

Key findings include:
- Emulsifiers, which help mix oils/water and extend shelf life, are found in about half of UK supermarket products (6,640 products analyzed).
- Animal studies (led by Benoit Chassaing at Institut Pasteur) show emulsifiers cause gut bacteria to move closer to the gut wall, eroding the protective mucus layer and triggering inflammation.
- Human correlational studies link emulsifier exposure to increased risk of type 2 diabetes (over 100,000 adults, 2024 French study) and breast/prostate cancers (over 90,000 adults).
- A clinical trial on Crohn's disease patients found those on a restricted emulsifier diet were three times more likely to experience reduced symptoms.
- A randomized control trial (Melissa Lane, Deakin University) found that a high-UPF diet reduced gut microbe diversity and increased constipation compared to a low-UPF diet with similar nutrients, likely due to differences in fiber types and additive content.
- Emulsifiers are approved for safety (tested for toxicity and DNA damage) but have not been tested for their direct effects on the microbiome. The "cocktail effect" of multiple additives is difficult to study.

Experts recommend cooking from scratch with fresh ingredients, eating more fiber and polyphenols, and practicing moderation rather than completely avoiding UPFs. The article emphasizes that food processing methods matter for gut health beyond just nutrient content.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"You can think of gut diversity as like a forest. The more microbes that you have and the different types of microbes in your forest, the greater resilience you have to any perturbations," says Melissa Lane, a nutritional epidemiologist at Deakin University., "They are only tested for the toxicity effect or for the ability to induce DNA damage. And for those two aspects, they are perfectly fine. But they were never tested in the past for the direct effect on the microbiome," says Benoit Chassaing., "The higher ultra-processed food diet had mixtures of additives and, very low amounts of minimally processed ingredients, whilst the low-UPF diet had many different types of fibre coming from whole foods, and far fewer additives," said Melissa Lane., "I wouldn't want to be saying to the general public, 'never eat anything that has a food additive in it', I certainly don't do that and I'm not recommending people do it," says Kevin Whelan, professor of dietetics at King's College London.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Quadram Institute, published March 22, 2024, explores how processed foods affect the microbiota-gut-brain axis. The microbiota-gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication network between gut microorganisms, gut cells, and the brain, facilitated by nerves and hormones. A varied diet rich in fibers promotes beneficial gut microbes, while a diet high in refined sugars and low in fiber reduces microbial diversity.

The article notes that processed foods can include both unhealthy options (high sugar, salt, saturated fat) and healthier options (wholegrain bread high in fiber). The research was conducted on mice, so caution is needed in extrapolating to humans, but it provides insights into how diet affects the gut-brain axis and highlights bile acid concentrations as a potential area for future therapeutic targets.

SUMMARY:

This PEN (Practice-based Evidence in Nutrition) article, posted April 17, 2025, examines the evidence on whether dietary emulsifiers affect the gut microbiome. For individuals at high risk of IBD, 2023 ESPEN guidelines recommend excluding ultra-processed foods and CMC (Grade C evidence).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is a narrative review published in Nutrients (June 2024) examining the impact of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) on the human gut microbiome and variations in UPF classification methods, particularly the NOVA system. 

**Key Points:**

**UPFs and Gut Microbiome:** The review summarizes four observational studies that used the NOVA classification system and 16S rRNA sequencing to examine associations between UPFs and gut microbiota. Findings include:
- Increased UPF consumption was associated with higher Prevotella spp. (2 studies) and decreased Lachnospira spp. (2 studies) and Ruminococcus spp. (2 studies).

- Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios were not significantly correlated with UPF consumption in three studies.

**Additional Dietary Context:** The review discusses how plant-based diets (Mediterranean, DASH, WCRF/AICR) and fast-food meals affect the gut microbiome. Fast-food diets (4-day crossover trial) increased bile-tolerant bacteria (Collinsella, Parabacteroides, Bilophila wadsworthia) and decreased fiber-fermenting bacteria (Lachnospiraceae, Butyricicoccus). Military ready-to-eat meals (UPFs with high nutritional value) altered gut microbiota and fecal metabolome over 21 days.

**Food Additives:** The review notes that most UPFs contain food additives, which may contribute to health effects through the gut microbiome. Some additives (e.g., emulsifiers E471, carrageenans) have been associated with increased cancer risk, while others (polydextrose) showed potential cognitive benefits.

**NOVA Classification Challenges:** The NOVA system categorizes foods into 4 groups based on processing extent. The review highlights significant methodological heterogeneity across studies, including differences in dietary collection tools (FFQs vs. 24h recalls), classification rules for ambiguous foods, and cut-off values for comparing UPF consumption levels. This makes cross-study comparisons difficult, though conclusions appear robust despite classification challenges.

**Conclusions:** More studies are needed to understand the mechanisms by which UPFs affect health, including through the microbiome and metabolome. Standardizing UPF classification methods remains difficult but important.

--- SOURCE 12: A toxic relationship: ultra-processed foods & plastics ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This commentary published in *Globalization and Health* (Oct 24, 2024) by Yates et al. from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and other institutions explores the toxic relationship between ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and plastics. The authors argue that these two industries are co-dependent, generating substantial profits for agri-food and petrochemical companies at high costs for human and planetary health.

**Key findings:**

- UPFs are defined by the Nova system as industrially processed formulations of food-derived substances and additives, designed to displace whole foods. They form a high share of diets in high-income countries and are rapidly expanding in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
- Over 75 prospective cohort studies show associations between UPF consumption and adverse health outcomes including premature mortality, cancer, and mental, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and metabolic ill health.
- The plastics industry is worth over $700 billion annually, with production projected to triple from 460 million metric tons (2019) to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060.
- Plastics are deeply intertwined with UPFs across the supply chain - from agricultural plastics on farms, to food contact materials (FCMs) in processing and packaging.
- Thousands of plastic food contact chemicals (FCCs) migrate into foodstuffs, including known hazardous substances like bisphenol A (BPA), ortho-phthalates, and PFAS. Many are endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs).
- A recent report identified over 16,000 plastic chemicals, with almost 60% (over 9,000) lacking specific information on their use or hazard properties.
- UPF consumption is associated with higher levels of urinary phthalates, bisphenols, and PFAS, including in children and pregnant women.

**Four propositions from the authors:**
1. More systems thinking in agenda setting to realize co-benefits of tackling common drivers of climate change, UPF-related illness, and plastic/chemical pollution.
2. Interdisciplinary research collaboration across food production and consumption, with standardized indicators and data sharing.
3. Clear safety, sustainability, transparency, and essentiality criteria for plastics, centered on a precautionary, hazard-based approach.
4. Scrutinize and address commercial determinants of health, with government-led statutory regulations to limit power of health-harming industries.

--- SOURCE 1: Ultra-Processed Foods and Metabolic Dysfunction: A Narrative Review of Dietary Processing, Behavioral Drivers and Chronic Disease Risk ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12734455

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review (published December 2025 in Metabolites) from Oklahoma State University examining the relationship between ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and metabolic dysfunction. The review synthesizes evidence on UPF definitions (via the NOVA classification system), global consumption patterns, behavioral drivers of overconsumption, nutrient composition, and mechanistic links to metabolic dysfunction, obesity, and chronic disease.

Key findings include:
- **NOVA Classification**: UPFs (Group 4) are industrial formulations with little resemblance to whole foods, including sugar-sweetened beverages, reconstituted meats, and packaged snacks. Critiques of NOVA include its focus on processing over formulation and lack of differentiation within Group 4.
- **Dietary Quality**: Higher UPF consumption is associated with lower diet quality scores (AHA diet score, HEI-2015). UPFs are high in added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, and artificial additives, while low in fiber, protein, vitamins, and minerals. Over 90% of US adults do not meet fiber recommendations.
- **Energy Consumption**: UPFs are energy-dense (>2 kcal/g), with low water content, and are consumed at faster eating rates due to soft textures. Both factors drive overconsumption. Energy-dense foods classified as UPF increased from 67% to 77% of the food supply over 30 years.
- **Consumption Trends**: UPFs now make up ~57-58% of average US adult daily calories (up from 53.5% in 2001-2002). Unprocessed/minimally processed foods contribute only 27.6% of calories. Obesity prevalence rose from 30.5% to 42.4% between 1999-2000 and 2017-2018.
- **Mechanisms**: UPFs promote overconsumption through hyperpalatability, reward pathway activation, blunted satiety signals, disruption of flavor-nutrient associations, and altered gut microbiome from additives. The "cocktail effect" of combined additive exposure is a growing concern.
- **Limitations**: While cross-sectional and cohort evidence is extensive, causal intervention trials and mechanistic human work remain limited. The Hall et al. clinical trial faced critiques regarding variability between processed and unprocessed diets.
- **Future Directions**: The authors call for real-world intervention studies examining effects of reduced UPF consumption on energy balance, inflammation, and gut health.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: The collapse of the food matrix: how ultra-processed foods impact satiety ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2026.1737280/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article, published in Frontiers in Nutrition on May 5, 2026, proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the primary health threat of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) stems not merely from their poor nutritional composition but from the industrial collapse of their physical "food matrix." The authors, led by Xinna Wang and colleagues from Chinese medical universities, hypothesize that this structural disintegration triggers a top-down cascade of dysregulation across multiple physiological systems.

The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This leads to metabolic dysregulation including insulin resistance, de novo lipogenesis, and mitochondrial stress. Finally, the impoverished matrix combined with chemical additives causes gut microbiome imbalance, compromised intestinal barrier function, and systemic low-grade chronic inflammation via metabolic endotoxemia.

Key evidence cited includes Hall's landmark randomized controlled trial showing that participants on nutrient-matched ultra-processed diets consumed ~500 kcal/day more and gained weight. Epidemiological data show UPF consumers have 15% increased all-cause mortality risk (HR=1.15), 11% increased cardiovascular disease risk (HR=1.11), and each 10% increase in UPF intake associates with 10% higher type 2 diabetes risk (RR=1.10).

The review critiques "nutritionism" and fortified UPFs, arguing that adding isolated nutrients to a collapsed matrix cannot restore health value. It calls for methodological innovation, multi-omics research, clinical translation studies, and development of "gentle" processing technologies that preserve food matrix integrity. The authors conclude that food processing degree, particularly physical matrix integrity, must be given equal importance to nutrient composition in dietary guidelines and public health policy.
</summary>

Merely playing an 'arithmetic game' with nutrients on top of an already collapsed industrial matrix is a misleading marketing strategy."

--- SOURCE 3: Dietary impact on fasting and stimulated GLP-1 secretion in different metabolic conditions – a narrative review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10972717

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific narrative review published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (January 2024) examining the impact of diet on fasting and postprandial GLP-1 secretion across different metabolic conditions. 

**Key Points:**

- **GLP-1 Overview:** Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) is a gastrointestinal peptide secreted by intestinal L cells in response to food intake. It plays a central role in glucose metabolism by stimulating insulin secretion, promoting satiety, and slowing gastric emptying. GLP-1 analogs are used pharmacologically for treating type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

- **GLP-1 Secretion Mechanisms:** Postprandial GLP-1 secretion is triggered by nutrient-sensing via G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and membrane transporters (e.g., SGLT1). Nutrients (peptides, amino acids, fatty acids, SCFAs) and fermentable dietary fibers can stimulate secretion.

- **Metabolic Condition Differences:** The evidence is conflicting. Some studies show diminished GLP-1 response in individuals with obesity/overweight (OW), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), or T2DM compared to normal glucose tolerance (NGT), while others report elevated or unchanged responses. --- SOURCE 16: Brain dopamine responses to ultra-processed milkshakes are ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11302720

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study published in medRxiv (2024) investigated whether ultra-processed milkshakes high in fat and sugar elicit postingestive brain dopamine responses similar to drugs of abuse, and whether such responses relate to adiposity. Researchers used [11C]raclopride PET displacement methods to measure striatal dopamine responses in 50 young, healthy adults across a wide BMI range (20–45 kg/m²). Contrary to the hypothesis, milkshake consumption did not result in significant postingestive dopamine response in the striatum (p=0.62) or any subregion (p>0.33), and interindividual variability was not significantly related to adiposity (BMI: r=0.076, p=0.51; %body fat: r=0.16, p=0.28). The study involved participants who underwent dietary stabilization (3-5 days outpatient, then 5 days inpatient) on a eucaloric standardized diet. After an overnight fast, participants completed a PET scan, then consumed a 418 kcal vanilla milkshake (60% fat, 33% carbohydrate), followed by a second PET scan 30 minutes later.

Exploratory analyses revealed that participants who showed dopamine responses in the expected direction ("Responders") perceived the milkshake as more pleasant (73.3 vs 48.2, p=0.010), wanted more of it (56.4 vs 25.8, p=0.003), and tended to be hungrier in the fasted state. Perceived hunger was weakly correlated with whole striatal dopamine response (r=0.288, p=0.055). Ad libitum cookie intake from ultra-processed chocolate chip cookies was correlated with dopamine response in the left putamen (r=-0.323, p=0.031) and left pallidum (r=-0.332, p=0.026).

The authors conclude that postingestive striatal dopamine responses to the milkshake were likely substantially smaller than those produced by many addictive drugs and below the limits of detection using standard PET methods. They suggest that the narrative that ultra-processed foods high in fat and sugar can be as addictive as drugs of abuse based on exaggerated dopamine responses was not supported by their data. They note that the observed dopamine responses may be closer in magnitude to nicotine (~5% reduction in D2BP) rather than psychostimulants (~10-20% reduction). The study is a US Government work under a CC0 license.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: How bad is ultra-processed food for the planet? ---
URL: https://www.soilassociation.org/blogs/2022/august/24/how-bad-is-ultra-processed-food-for-the-planet

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published August 24, 2022) by the Soil Association examines the environmental impacts of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), based on a paper published by researchers from CSIRO and Deakin University in Australia. The paper reviewed 52 studies on UPF environmental impacts.

Key findings include that UPFs account for 17-39% of total diet-related energy use, 36-45% of diet-related biodiversity loss, up to a third of diet-related greenhouse gas emissions/land use/food waste, and up to a quarter of diet-related water use in high-income countries. UPF production relies on commodity ingredients like palm oil, soya, wheat, maize, milk, eggs, and meat, which have driven ecosystem destruction (e.g., rainforest clearing for palm oil in Indonesia, Cerrado conversion for soya in Brazil). UPFs contribute significantly to climate change, plastic pollution, and food waste.

The authors conclude that UPFs are "potentially counterproductive" to sustainable food system objectives and call on policymakers to regulate UPF production, availability, and consumption. Countries including Brazil, Canada, Chile, Ecuador, France, Israel, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay already encourage limiting UPF intake through dietary guidance and labeling. The UK is one of the highest consumers of UPFs, with these products making up over half of average weekly shopping baskets. The article calls for UK government action including reduction targets, consumer guidance, UPF labeling, and support for transition to agroecology and organic farming.
</summary>

URL: https://www.aleph2020.org/human-health/ultra-processed-foods

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from ALEPH2020 presents a detailed critique of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), arguing that they are a major driver of health deterioration, environmental harm, and socio-economic inequity. It distinguishes between traditional processing (beneficial) and ultra-processing (harmful), and uses the NOVA classification system as a reference point.

Key points include:

- **Definition of UPFs**: Products made from deconstructed and recombined ingredients (starches, sugars, oils, protein isolates) with cosmetic additives, engineered for hyperpalatability, low satiety, and market dominance. 70-90% of products from global food corporations are UPFs.

- **Prevalence**: Annual per capita consumption is ~100 kg in Western Europe, ~120 kg in North America/Australasia, plus 120-180 kg of ultra-processed drinks. In high-income countries, UPFs make up 15-60% of adult caloric intake. US children get 61-67% of energy from UPFs (1999-2018). In France, UPFs account for 46% of children's and 35% of adults' diets.

- **Trends**: UPF consumption is rising globally, disproportionately affecting lower socioeconomic groups. Plant-based "alternatives" and Nutrient Profiling Systems (e.g., Nutri-Score) are criticized for minimizing UPF risks while exaggerating flaws in traditional animal foods.

- **Health impacts**: UPFs are linked to higher risks of mortality, mental disorders, obesity, type-2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer. Mechanisms include dysregulation of satiety, endocrine disruption, gut microbiota harm, chronic fructose excess, cosmetic additives, and misleading sensory information that disrupts the body's appestatic control.

- **Environmental impacts**: UPFs account for up to one-third of diet-related climate emissions in wealthy countries. In Belgium, they drive ~50% of dietary climate and land impacts; in the Netherlands, 45% of food-related emissions; in France, ~25% of dietary climate, energy, water, and land impacts. Reducing UPF consumption is presented as a priority for lowering environmental damage.

--- SOURCE 4: Ultra-Processed Foods and Health Outcomes: A Narrative Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7399967

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review published in *Nutrients* (2020) by Elizabeth, Machado, Zinöcker, Baker, and Lawrence that systematically examines the associations between ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption and health outcomes. The review is based on a systematic search of 43 studies, with 37 finding that dietary UPF exposure was associated with at least one adverse health outcome.

**Key Content:**
- **NOVA Classification:** UPFs are defined as "formulations of ingredients, mostly of exclusive industrial use, resulting from a series of industrial processes." They include items like sweet and savoury snacks, reconstituted meats, pizza dishes, and confectionery.
- **Prevalence:** UPFs contribute up to >50% of energy intake in high-income countries and up to 30% in middle-income countries, with consumption rapidly increasing.
- **Health Outcomes in Adults:** UPF consumption was associated with overweight, obesity, cardio-metabolic risks (e.g., metabolic syndrome, hypertension), cancer, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, irritable bowel syndrome, depression, frailty conditions, and all-cause mortality.
- **Health Outcomes in Children/Adolescents:** Associations were found with cardio-metabolic risks (e.g., higher total cholesterol, LDL-C, triglycerides, waist circumference) and asthma.
- **No Beneficial Associations:** No study reported an association between UPF and beneficial health outcomes.
- **Key Study Findings:** A randomized controlled trial (Hall et al. 2019) showed that participants on a UPF diet consumed ~508 more kcal/day and gained 0.9 kg, while losing 0.9 kg on an unprocessed diet. Ecological studies across 80 countries linked UPF sales volume increases with rising mean BMI trajectories.
- **Conclusion:** The authors conclude there is considerable evidence supporting the use of UPFs as a scientific concept to assess the healthiness of foods within dietary patterns and to inform dietary guidelines and nutrition policy.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of an NIH Office of Disease Prevention (ODP) webinar titled "Ultra-Processed Foods and Health Outcomes: State of the Research to Inform Practice," part of the Prevention in Focus Webinar Series, recorded on July 8, 2026. The webinar features three expert speakers: Dr. Josiemer Mattei (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health), Dr. Lauren O'Connor (Texas A&M AgriLife Research), and Professor Jerold Mande (Nourish Science/Harvard).

**Key Points from Dr. Josiemer Mattei (UPF Overview and Epidemiology):**
- Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are defined using the Nova framework, which classifies foods into four categories (unprocessed/minimally processed, culinary ingredients, processed foods, and ultra-processed foods) based on the extent and purpose of industrial processing rather than nutritional composition.
- 73% of the U.S. food supply is ultra-processed, and UPFs comprise nearly 60% of total energy intake among U.S. adults, with consumption increasing over the past two decades.
- UPF intake varies by race/ethnicity (higher in Black individuals, lower in Hispanic/Latino individuals) and socioeconomic status (higher intake among lower income and education groups).
- Meta-analyses show direct associations between UPF consumption and 71% of health parameters studied, including mortality, cancer, mental health, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity. The most convincing evidence is for cardiovascular disease mortality, type 2 diabetes, and anxiety.
- Not all UPFs are equal: subgroup analyses show sugary beverages and animal-based products as the main drivers of adverse health outcomes, while some UPFs (cereals, yogurt, dark breads) show inverse associations with disease risk.
- A pivotal randomized controlled trial by Kevin Hall showed that people on an ultra-processed diet consumed more calories and gained weight compared to an unprocessed diet, even when meals were matched for calories, macronutrients, and fiber.

**Key Points from Dr. Lauren O'Connor (Research Challenges and Causality):**
- Nutrition research faces unique challenges compared to drug trials, including confounding by energy intake, complexity of food matrices, and the impact of comparison foods on study conclusions.
- The heterogeneity of UPFs (ranging from cookies and hot dogs to tofu and whole grains) amplifies these challenges, making it difficult to isolate mechanisms.
- Many proposed mechanisms linking UPFs to disease (e.g., fructose, whey protein, additives) already have decades of existing research that predates the UPF framework.
- The speaker recommends organizing existing evidence through systematic reviews and evidence mapping (e.g., using tools like EpiMapper) to identify true research gaps.
- A metabolomics analysis of samples from Kevin Hall's controlled feeding trial found that metabolites related to benzoate (preservatives) and acesulfame (artificial sweeteners) were higher after the UPF diet, while fruit and vegetable metabolites were lower.

**Additional Context:**
- Dr. Drew Bremer (NIH Office of Nutrition Research) provided opening remarks, emphasizing the need to understand biological, behavioral, and environmental mechanisms linking UPFs to disease.
- The webinar was approved for 1.5 Continuing Professional Education Units (CPEUs) for registered dietitian nutritionists through June 1, 2026.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Measuring Progress | Healthy Food Policy Project ---
URL: https://healthyfoodpolicyproject.org/towards-equitable-and-just-food-systems/measuring-progress

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the "Towards Equitable and Just Food Systems" resource from the Healthy Food Policy Project. It examines common terms used to measure progress in food systems—food security, food deserts, food swamps, and hunger—along with their definitions, uses in policy and research, and significant limitations.

**Food Security** is defined as consistent access to sufficient, safe, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food. The USDA measures it on a spectrum from high to very low food security. However, the term is limiting as an ultimate goal because it does not address nutritional quality or root causes of inequity. Related terms include nutrition security, community food security, food access (with five dimensions: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability, accommodation), and food system resilience.

**Food Desert** refers to areas with low access to grocery stores. The term is being phased out at the federal level in favor of "low-income and low-access areas." It is criticized for implying scarcity is natural, masking deliberate policy decisions (e.g., redlining, suburbanization), ignoring racial disparities, and not reflecting community vibrancy. Baltimore, Maryland has shifted to using "Healthy Food Priority Areas."

**Food Swamp** describes areas where unhealthy food outlets (fast food, convenience stores) outnumber healthy options. Research suggests food swamps predict obesity better than food deserts and disproportionately impact low-income and Black communities. Root causes include redlining, white flight, and zoning policies. Critiques note the term still does not adequately address root causes, with some advocating for "food apartheid" as a better descriptor.

**Hunger** is an individual-level physical sensation from insufficient food intake, often conflated with food insecurity in surveys. It is difficult to measure directly, so food insecurity is used as a proxy. The Committee on National Statistics has recommended USDA stop using "hunger" to describe food insecurity indicators.

The page includes policy examples for each term and discussion questions for reflection.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Food Swamps Predict Obesity Rates Better Than Food Deserts in the United States ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5708005

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2017), investigates the effect of food environments on adult obesity rates across U.S. counties, comparing "food swamps" (areas with high-density of fast food/junk food outlets relative to healthy options) with "food deserts" (areas with limited access to affordable, nutritious food). 

Key findings include:
- Food swamps are a stronger predictor of obesity rates than food deserts across U.S. counties.
- Even after controlling for food desert effects, food swamps had a positive, statistically significant effect on adult obesity rates.

- An instrumental variables (IV) approach using highway exits corrected for endogeneity (people self-selecting into neighborhoods) and revealed a stronger effect of food swamps than ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates would suggest.
- The food swamp effect was stronger in counties with greater income inequality (p<0.05) and where residents are less mobile (p<0.01).
- OLS estimates underestimated the food swamp effect; IV estimates suggested policies like zoning laws could lower obesity rates by about three percent.
- The traditional RFEI (ratio of fast food restaurants and convenience stores to grocery stores/supermarkets) had the strongest relationship with obesity rates.

The authors recommend local government policies such as zoning laws that simultaneously restrict access to unhealthy food outlets and incentivize healthy food retailers in underserved neighborhoods to increase health equity. Data sources included the USDA Food Environment Atlas, American Community Survey, and CDC BRFSS data for all 3,141 U.S. counties.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Food Access Research Atlas (FARA) webpage, published by the USDA Economic Research Service, documents data and methodology for mapping food access across the 50 U.S. states and D.C. (excluding U.S. territories). It covers two main components:

**1. SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM) - 2025**: Uses SNAP-authorized food retailer locations from STARS (excluding farmers markets and delivery routes), LandScan USA 2020 nighttime gridded population data at ~90-meter resolution, and 2020–24 ACS data. Distance calculations use both Euclidean (straight-line) and network-based (driving) methods at four thresholds (0.5, 1, 10, and 20 miles). **2. Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM) - 2019**: Based on a merged directory of 45,233 foodstores from STARS and TDLinx (supermarkets, supercenters, large grocery stores). **Methodology**: Population is mapped onto high-resolution grids using LandScan data, then overlaid with food access zones to identify low-access populations. Tract-level aggregation follows. The page also lists strengths, limitations, and references (Rhone et al. 2017, 2019, 2022; Ver Ploeg et al. 2009, 2012; Dutko et al. 2012; and others).
