- The term "ultra-processed" (UPF) was created by Monteiro (2009) and has been adopted by media with a negative connotation, creating consumer confusion.

- Homemade food can be a source of foodborne disease, while processed foods offer safety, shelf-life extension, and nutritional benefits.
- The classification neglects well-established food science concepts and dismisses benefits of diets incorporating foods at all processing levels.

--- SOURCE 1: Why 2026 could see the end of the Farm Bill era of American agriculture policy | The Invading Sea ---
URL: https://www.theinvadingsea.com/2026/01/08/farm-bill-subsidies-snap-climate-smart-agriculture-organic-maha-trump-one-big-beautiful-bill

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This opinion piece by Christopher Neubert and Kathleen Merrigan (Arizona State University) argues that the traditional five-year Farm Bill era of American agriculture policy may be ending, with 2026 marking a critical juncture. The last comprehensive Farm Bill passed in 2018; its provisions expired in 2023 and have been renewed only year-to-year since.

The July 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" fundamentally disrupted the historic bipartisan compromise that paired farm subsidies with nutrition assistance (SNAP). It slashed SNAP spending by $186 billion over ten years (with about one-third of cuts shifted to state budgets), while boosting farm subsidies for key crops like corn, soybeans, and wheat by $60 billion, plus an additional $12 billion in December 2025 to offset tariff-related export losses. Anti-hunger advocates are furious, and farmers say subsidies are insufficient to cover low commodity prices and high input costs.

The authors believe a comprehensive five-year Farm Bill is unlikely in 2026 due to midterm elections and deep divisions in Congress. Instead, smaller extension bills may be pursued. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act's $20 billion for climate-smart agriculture was cut and repurposed. The Trump administration's "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) agenda offers some potential alignment with sustainable agriculture advocates (e.g., $700 million committed for regenerative practices in December 2025), but faces pushback from conventional agriculture allies. The authors conclude that advocates for food and agriculture reform will need new strategies without the Farm Bill framework.
</summary>

"Farm bills are massive pieces of legislation that address a diverse constellation of topics, including agricultural commodities, conservation, trade, nutrition, rural development, energy, forestry and more.", "The July 2025 enactment of the so-called 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act'... included a 20% cut in funding to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program... and doubled support for the largest farm subsidy programs.", "For decades, political conventional wisdom has held that sweeping federal farm bills are able to pass only because farmers seeking subsidies and anti-hunger advocates wanting increased SNAP dollars recognize the mutual advantage in working together.", "Instead of a complete five-year farm bill, the House and Senate committees on agriculture might take up a series of smaller bills... Doing so would be an effective declaration that a permanent five-year farm bill is on indefinite hold.", "Overall, in this new political environment, we believe advocates for changes in agriculture and food aid will likely need to rethink how to advance their agendas without the promise of a farm bill coming anytime soon."

--- SOURCE 3: CAP at a glance - Agriculture and rural development - Europa.eu ---
URL: https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/cap-overview/cap-glance_en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The common agricultural policy (CAP) is a partnership between agriculture and society, and between Europe and its farmers. Launched in 1962, the CAP aims to support farmers and ensure Europe's food security. It is a common policy for all EU countries, managed and funded at European level from the EU's budget.

The CAP 2023-27 entered into force on 1 January 2023, representing a modernised policy with emphasis on results and performance. It seeks to ensure a sustainable future for European farmers, provide more targeted support to smaller farms, and allow greater flexibility for EU countries to adapt measures to local conditions.

The CAP upholds environmental rules and encourages green farming, supports rural communities, and ensures sustainable agriculture and forestry can be profitable and competitive. It focuses on ten specific objectives linked to EU goals for social, environmental, and economic sustainability. Each EU country designed a national CAP Strategic Plan combining funding for income support, rural development, and market measures.

The CAP is financed through two funds: the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF) at €291.1 billion, and the European Agricultural Rural Development Fund (EAFRD) at €95.5 billion, totalling €387 billion for the 2021-27 period. Payments are managed at national level.

Key benefits include food production (ensuring safe, affordable, high-quality food), rural community development (supporting rural areas and creating jobs), and environmentally sustainable farming (protecting biodiversity and natural resources).

The legal basis is established in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The CAP 2023-27 is covered by three regulations, generally applicable since 1 January 2023. The Commission carries out impact assessments when planning new legislation, and the EU Court of Auditors supervises expenditure in agriculture.

Historical milestones include: the CAP's birth in 1962; 1992 reforms shifting from market support to producer support; 2003-2008-2011 reforms; 2014-20 programming period focusing on competitiveness and sustainability; the 2021 transitional regulation; and the current CAP 2023-27 period.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from TraceGains provides a comprehensive overview of the UK's HFSS (High Fat, Sugar, and Salt) regulations, which are among the most significant food marketing legislation changes in the UK. The regulations aim to combat obesity by restricting how products high in saturated fat, sugar, and salt can be marketed, advertised, and promoted.

**Timeline of Regulations:**
- **October 1, 2022**: Placement restrictions took effect in England, banning HFSS products from prominent retail positions (aisle ends, checkouts) in larger retailers (over 2,000 sq. ft., 50+ staff).
- **October 2025**: Volume promotions ban (e.g., "Buy One, Get One Free") took effect in England as planned.
- **January 5, 2026**: Advertising restrictions (TV pre-9 PM watershed ban and paid online advertising limitations) will come into force UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland).
- **Spring 2026**: Wales intends to implement placement and promotion restrictions.
- **Autumn 2026**: Scotland expected to implement its own measures.
- Northern Ireland has not yet confirmed similar legislation.

**How HFSS Classification Works:**
Products are scored using the Government Nutrient Profile Model. Points are added for calories, fats, sugars, and sodium. Points are subtracted for beneficial nutrients like fiber, protein, and fruit/vegetable content. A score of 4+ for foods or 1+ for drinks earns HFSS designation.

**Affected Product Categories (13 categories):**
Soft drinks, crisps/savory snacks, breakfast cereals, chocolates/sweets, ice cream/frozen desserts, cakes/cupcakes, sweet biscuits/snack bars, morning goods (pastries/scones), desserts/puddings, sweetened yogurt/fromage frais, pizza, chips/potato products, ready meals/breaded products.

**Impact Data:**
End-of-aisle promotions increased sugary drink sales by 51.7%. Early restrictions have shown healthier product sales up 5.6% and non-compliant product sales down 5.1% (per The Grocer and Kantar data).

**Compliance Strategies for Brands:**
1. Reformulate recipes to reduce saturated fat, sugar, or salt.
2. Develop alternative healthier product lines alongside traditional offerings.
3. Innovate entirely new compliant products.

The article promotes TraceGains' NutriCalc tool as a solution for calculating HFSS scores, experimenting with ingredient substitutions, and generating nutrition information.

--- SOURCE 11: Impact of the Berkeley Excise Tax on Sugar-Sweetened ... - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5024386

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This peer-reviewed study published in the American Journal of Public Health (October 2016) evaluates the impact of Berkeley, California's sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) excise tax—the first such tax in the United States—implemented in March 2015 at $0.01 per ounce.

**Methods:** Researchers used a repeated cross-sectional design with interviewer-administered beverage frequency questionnaires in low-income neighborhoods in Berkeley versus comparison cities (Oakland and San Francisco). Data were collected from 990 participants before the tax (April–July 2014) and 1,689 after the tax (April–August 2015, approximately 8 months after the vote and 4 months after implementation).

**Key Findings:**
- SSB consumption decreased 21% in Berkeley while increasing 4% in comparison cities (p=0.046), a statistically significant difference.
- Regular soda consumption dropped 26% in Berkeley versus a 10% increase in comparison cities (p=0.05).
- Sports drink consumption decreased 36% in Berkeley versus a 21% increase in comparison cities (p=0.02).
- Water consumption increased 63% in Berkeley compared to 19% in comparison cities (p<0.01).
- Only 5% of Berkeley residents who previously bought SSBs in the city reported switching purchases to another city; only 2% cited the tax or prices as the reason.
- Among those reporting behavioral changes, 82% reported drinking SSBs less frequently and 40% reported drinking smaller sizes.

**Context:** Previous research by the same authors found that 69% of the tax was passed through to higher soda prices and 47% to higher prices of SSBs overall. The 21% reduction in SSB consumption represents a price elasticity of -2.6, larger than the average elasticity of -1.2 found in other studies. The authors suggest this greater-than-expected reduction may reflect the tax campaign's effects on social norms, greater price sensitivity among low-income populations, or early reaction to the tax.

**Limitations:** Berkeley is a single city with relatively high socioeconomic status; results may not generalize. The study used self-reported data and reflected short-term impacts (less than 6 months post-implementation).

**Conclusions:** Berkeley's excise tax reduced SSB consumption in low-income neighborhoods. The authors note the tax has already generated $1.5 million for public health programs and argue that widespread adoption of SSB excise taxes could have considerable fiscal and public health benefits.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: The Incidence of Taxes on Sugar-Sweetened Beverages ---
URL: https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w21465/revisions/w21465.rev0.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NBER working paper (No. 21465, August 2015) by John Cawley and David Frisvold examines the pass-through of the first city-level sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) tax in the U.S., enacted by Berkeley, California voters in November 2014 at a rate of one cent per ounce. The study collected price data from a near-census of convenience stores and supermarkets in Berkeley and a control city (San Francisco, where a similar tax failed to pass) both before (December 2014) and after (June 2015) the tax took effect.

**Methodology:** The authors employ difference-in-differences (DD) models comparing Berkeley to San Francisco, DD models comparing regular (taxed) versus diet (untaxed) versions of the same products in Berkeley, and difference-in-difference-in-differences (DDD) models using both comparisons. They examine homogenous products at the brand-item-size level (Coke, Diet Coke, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Dasani, Red Bull, Snapple) across three sizes.

**Key Findings:** Across all models, the authors consistently find that retail prices rose by less than half of the tax amount. The DDD models pooling all sizes of Coke and Pepsi indicate only 21.7% pass-through to consumers. For 20-oz bottles, pass-through ranged from 41.1% (Coke) to 45.8% (Pepsi) in DD models. For 2-liter bottles, pass-through ranged from 33.8% to 50.6%. The authors can reject full pass-through (100%) for almost all estimates. They note that the vast majority of stores charged identical prices for regular and diet versions even after the tax, with only a small handful passing through the tax fully.

5) **Not all UPFs are unhealthy**: Perelman notes that some ultra-processed foods (like Cheerios) can be more nutrient-dense than others. 3. **Food reinforcement:** A significant difference was observed for rs1800497, where homozygous A1A1 showed less reinforcement (p=0.01), particularly in males (p=0.03).

4. **Bilocus score distribution:** 11.7% "very low" dopaminergic signaling, 24.4% "under", 49.7% "intermediate", 12.7% "high", and 1.4% "very high".

SUMMARY:

This is a qualitative research article published in BMC Public Health (2025) examining how children aged 6–12 perceive child-targeted versus non-child-targeted food advertising. The study, conducted by researchers from the University of Ottawa, Université Laval, and University of Calgary, involved 17 children (11 girls, 6 boys) who participated in online interviews where they were shown four advertisements: child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads for both healthy (plain milk) and unhealthy (chocolate) products.

--- SOURCE 1: The collapse of the food matrix: how ultra-processed foods impact satiety ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2026.1737280/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article, published in Frontiers in Nutrition on May 5, 2026, proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the primary health threat of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) stems not merely from their poor nutritional composition but from the industrial collapse of their physical "food matrix." The authors, led by Xinna Wang and colleagues from Chinese medical universities, hypothesize that this structural disintegration triggers a top-down cascade of dysregulation across multiple physiological systems.

The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This leads to metabolic dysregulation including insulin resistance, de novo lipogenesis, and mitochondrial stress. Finally, the impoverished matrix combined with chemical additives causes gut microbiome imbalance, compromised intestinal barrier function, and systemic low-grade chronic inflammation via metabolic endotoxemia.

Key evidence cited includes Hall's landmark randomized controlled trial showing that participants on nutrient-matched ultra-processed diets consumed ~500 kcal/day more and gained weight. Epidemiological data show UPF consumers have 15% increased all-cause mortality risk (HR=1.15), 11% increased cardiovascular disease risk (HR=1.11), and each 10% increase in UPF intake associates with 10% higher type 2 diabetes risk (RR=1.10).

The review critiques "nutritionism" and fortified UPFs, arguing that adding isolated nutrients to a collapsed matrix cannot restore health value. It calls for methodological innovation, multi-omics research, clinical translation studies, and development of "gentle" processing technologies that preserve food matrix integrity. The authors conclude that food processing degree, particularly physical matrix integrity, must be given equal importance to nutrient composition in dietary guidelines and public health policy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The core threat of UPFs to health may originate profoundly from the industrial collapse of their physical 'food matrix.'", "This supraphysiological nutrient flux imposes a significant challenge on core metabolic organs, driving insulin resistance and hepatic de novo lipogenesis.", "The integrity of the food matrix is an indispensable dimension for evaluating the health value of food.", "This review calls for a fundamental shift in perspective within nutritional science and public health policy: from focusing solely on 'what is in our food' to equally considering 'what has been done to our food.'", "The health value of food arises from the organic unity of its structure and composition. Merely playing an 'arithmetic game' with nutrients on top of an already collapsed industrial matrix is a misleading marketing strategy."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Ultra-Processed Foods and Metabolic Dysfunction: A Narrative Review of Dietary Processing, Behavioral Drivers and Chronic Disease Risk ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2218-1989/15/12/784

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review article published in *Metabolites* (2025, Volume 15, Issue 12, 784) by Tyler J. Godsey, Travis Eden, and Sam R. Emerson from Oklahoma State University. The review synthesizes evidence on how ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and dietary processing interact with dietary quality, energy balance, and biological pathways to influence metabolic health.

**Key findings:**
- UPFs (defined via the NOVA classification system - Group 4) are industrially manufactured, ready-to-eat products that are highly energy dense, typically high in added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, and low in protein and fiber.
- UPFs now make up ~57-58% of the average US adult's daily caloric intake, up from 53.5% in 2001-2002, with annual per capita consumption increasing ~142% since 1960.
- High UPF intake is consistently associated with reduced diet quality, increased energy density, faster eating rates, and activation of reward pathways, leading to excessive energy intake and adiposity.
- The article traces the history of UPFs back to the Malthusian Trap concerns and 20th-century agricultural/industrial advancements, including US government incentives for commodity crops.
- Key critiques of the NOVA system include its focus on processing over formulation, lack of evidence that UPF reduction is more beneficial than other dietary guidelines, and inconsistencies in food categorization.
- UPFs promote overconsumption through hyperpalatability, altered nutrient profiles (high saturated fat, added sugar, sodium), low water content, high energy density, faster eating rates (especially soft-textured and liquid UPFs), and disruption of evolved nutrient-flavor associations.
- Over 10,000 food additives have been approved over the last 60 years, with concerns about the "cocktail effect" of cumulative exposures.
- While cross-sectional and cohort evidence is extensive linking UPFs to obesity, metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and gut microbiome alterations, causal intervention trials and mechanistic human work remain limited.
- The review concludes that UPFs may influence chronic disease risk through both their unbalanced nutrient profiles AND additional effects introduced by industrial processing, calling for real-world intervention studies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The 2025 Levels guide to hunger — and how to manage it | Levels | Levels ---
URL: https://www.levels.com/blog/levels-guide-to-hunger

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive Levels guide (updated April 23, 2025) about the science of hunger and how to manage it. The article explains that hunger is a complex survival mechanism driven by physical, neurological, and hormonal signals influenced by food intake, body fat, physical activity, stress, and sleep. It details the roles of hormones like ghrelin (the "hunger hormone"), leptin (the "satiety hormone"), and others such as orexin, MCH, and INSL5 that drive appetite, as well as CCK, PYY, and GLP-1 that promote fullness. The guide covers how different macronutrients affect hunger: protein is most satiating (especially ~30g per meal), fiber-rich foods promote fullness via gastric stretch receptors and SCFAs, fats can suppress hunger when consumed with whole foods, and refined carbohydrates/sugars can spike blood sugar and lead to cravings. Solid foods are more satiating than liquids. Ultra-processed foods are linked to overeating. Lifestyle factors like exercise, sleep, stress management, hydration, and eating slowly also help regulate appetite. The article notes that GLP-1 agonist drugs (e.g., Ozempic, Wegovy) mimic natural GLP-1 but at much higher levels, which can cause side effects like nausea. Key recommendations include focusing on whole, minimally processed foods rich in fiber, protein, and healthy fats; limiting ultra-processed foods; staying hydrated; exercising regularly; managing stress; and prioritizing sleep.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Hunger is a natural (and essential) feeling, but it shouldn't rule your life. Here's why you might feel hungry all the time and how to manage it with specific nutrients, foods, and habits.", "Different macronutrients and levels of food processing impact hunger and fullness in various ways, with protein, fiber, and whole foods generally being more satiating than refined carbohydrates, added sugars, and ultra-processed foods.", "Eating slowly, chewing thoroughly, and consuming solid foods rather than liquids can enhance feelings of fullness and reduce overall calorie intake.", "Regular exercise and adequate sleep can help regulate appetite by suppressing hunger hormones and increasing feelings of fullness, while chronic stress may drive overeating, particularly of hyperpalatable foods.", "To best manage hunger, focus on whole, minimally processed foods rich in fiber, protein, and healthy fats; limit ultra-processed foods; stay hydrated; exercise regularly; manage stress; and prioritize sleep."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: The Science of Appetite Control: How Hormones Regulate Hunger and Satiety ---
URL: https://www.news-medical.net/health/The-Science-of-Appetite-Control-How-Hormones-Regulate-Hunger-and-Satiety.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from News-Medical, written by Vijay Kumar Malesu (Ph.D. in Biotechnology) and last updated February 23, 2026, explains the science of appetite control through the lens of hormonal regulation via the gut–brain axis. It covers how dietary protein, carbohydrates, fats, and fiber influence key appetite-regulating hormones including GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, CCK, and leptin.

**Key points:**
- **Hormonal control:** Appetite is regulated by bidirectional communication between the GI tract, adipose tissue, and the central nervous system (hypothalamic arcuate nucleus and brainstem). GLP-1 and PYY (from enteroendocrine L-cells) reduce hunger after eating, while ghrelin is the primary hunger hormone that rises preprandially.
- **Protein:** High-protein meals increase GLP-1 and PYY release and may suppress postprandial ghrelin, though ad libitum energy intake at subsequent meals may not differ significantly when calories and volume are matched.
- **Carbohydrates:** High glycemic index foods cause rapid glucose/insulin spikes and earlier hunger onset; low glycemic index foods prolong satiety. Dietary fiber (especially viscous fiber) slows digestion and enhances satiety.
- **Fats:** Fat intake stimulates CCK release. In an 8-week trial, postprandial CCK decreased in both low-carb and low-fat diet groups, suggesting energy restriction, rather than fat content per se, drives CCK responses.
- **Fiber:** Viscous fibers slow gastric emptying and glucose absorption. Fermentable fibers (resistant starch, beta-glucans) produce SCFAs that may alter GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, and leptin in animal models, but effects vary.
- **Human studies:** A randomized crossover trial found high-protein meals increased GLP-1 and PYY but did not significantly reduce subsequent ad libitum intake. An 8-week trial showed low-carb diets led to greater weight loss, reduced postprandial ghrelin, and increased subjective fullness.
- **Translational insights:** A balanced diet rich in protein, high-fiber/low-glycemic carbohydrates, and fats can regulate multiple satiety hormones. Leptin resistance is common in obesity. Fermentable fibers affect appetite through viscosity, fermentability, and gut hormone modulation rather than SCFA production alone.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Appetite regulation refers to the complex physiological processes that control hunger, satiety, and energy balance through coordinated central and peripheral signals.", "GLP-1 delays gastric emptying, controls blood sugar levels, and reduces food intake by acting on appetite-regulating centers in the hypothalamus and brainstem.", "High-protein meals facilitate the release of GLP-1 and PYY, which reduce hunger; controlled feeding studies demonstrate that protein-rich meals produce higher, more sustained circulating levels of GLP-1 and PYY than isocaloric meals rich in fat or carbohydrates.", "In an eight-week randomized trial comparing low-carbohydrate and low-fat, low-energy diets, postprandial CCK decreased in both groups, suggesting that energy restriction, rather than dietary fat content per se, influenced CCK responses.", "Consuming a balanced diet rich in various nutrients is an effective way to simultaneously regulate multiple satiety hormones to support weight management."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Gut Hormones and Appetite Control: A Focus on PYY and GLP-1 as Therapeutic Targets in Obesity ---
URL: https://www.gutnliver.org/journal/view.html?uid=331&vmd=Full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage is a review article published in Gut and Liver (2012) by Akila De Silva and Stephen R. Bloom titled 'Gut Hormones and Appetite Control: A Focus on PYY and GLP-1 as Therapeutic Targets in Obesity.' The article addresses the global obesity epidemic and the limited medical treatments available. It focuses on two gut hormones, PYY (peptide tyrosine tyrosine) and GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide 1), which are elevated after gastric bypass surgery and reduce food intake.

Key points include:
- Nearly 2 billion adults are overweight and 500 million are obese globally.
- Bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) is the most effective treatment, leading to ~30% sustained weight loss, but carries a 0.5% mortality rate.
- Lifestyle modification results are disappointing, and drug treatments have been limited (orlistat is the only licensed pharmacological treatment in the UK).
- PYY3-36, a form of PYY, inhibits appetite by acting on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) via the Y2 receptor, increasing activity of anorexigenic POMC/α-MSH neurons while suppressing orexigenic NPY neurons.
- In human studies, intravenous PYY3-36 reduced ad libitum food intake by up to 36% compared to saline, with comparable effects in lean and obese subjects.
- GLP-1 is released post-prandially and acts via the GLP-1 receptor. A meta-analysis found that GLP-1 infusion reduced energy intake by ~13% in lean subjects and ~10.5% in overweight/obese subjects.
- GLP-1 analogues (exenatide, liraglutide) are licensed for type 2 diabetes and promote weight loss. Liraglutide 3 mg once daily in non-diabetic obese patients led to 7.2 kg mean weight loss over 20 weeks.
- Combination therapy based on PYY and GLP-1 is being explored to better mimic the physiological fed state.
- Challenges include nausea (especially with PYY3-36) and the rapid degradation of these peptides by DPP-IV.
- Gut and Liver is an international journal of gastroenterology indexed in SCIE, MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Scopus, and other databases, with a 2025 Impact Factor of 4.1.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Obesity and the MC4R Gene ---
URL: https://www.gbhealthwatch.com/GND-Obesity-MC4R.php

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from GB HealthWatch provides a comprehensive overview of the relationship between the MC4R gene and obesity. The MC4R gene codes for the melanocortin 4 receptor, primarily found in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and satiety. Mutations in the MC4R gene are the most common genetic cause of obesity, accounting for 6-8% of severe inheritable obesity cases. A common variant (rs17782313, C-allele), carried by about 22% of the general population, increases obesity risk by 8% per copy and is associated with a BMI increase of 0.22. Carriers experience increased appetite and decreased satiety, leading to larger food intake, more frequent snacking, and preference for fatty foods.

The article explains the biological mechanism: hunger signals (like ghrelin) and satiety signals (like leptin and insulin) both function through MC4R via competitive binding of AgRP and α-MSH. When AgRP prevails, hunger results; when α-MSH prevails, satiety results.

To date, 166 MC4R mutations have been documented, with about 0.66% of the general population carrying one. In early-onset severe obesity populations, 6-8% carry MC4R loss-of-function mutations. These individuals typically develop obesity by age 3-4, with meals containing about three times the calories of non-carriers. Female carriers gain about twice the weight as male carriers.

Two gain-of-function mutations (V103I/rs2229616 and I251L/rs52820871) have protective effects against obesity, reducing risk by 20% and 48% respectively.

For management, the most effective approach for common variant carriers is calorie restriction through portion control and smart food choices. For loss-of-function mutation carriers, low-calorie dietary interventions, multidisciplinary approaches, and bariatric surgery are options, though weight regain is common.

The article also notes an evolutionary perspective: reduced MC4R activity may have provided survival advantages during food scarcity but is disadvantageous in modern food-abundant environments.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Fat mass and obesity-associated gene (FTO) rs9939609 (A ... ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1321355874/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in BMC Nutrition (2023), investigated the relationship between the FTO rs9939609 (A/T) polymorphism and food preferences in two distinct groups: 36 obese individuals with low-calorie intake (consuming less than 50% of required calories) and 41 non-obese individuals with high-calorie intake (consuming more than 50% of required calories). The study was conducted at Zanjan University of Medical Sciences between June 2020 and September 2021. Using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) with 147 food items, researchers calculated sweet and fatty food propensity scores. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples and genotyped via ARMS-PCR.

Key findings: There were no significant differences between the two groups in sweet food preference (15.64±10.53 in obese vs. 14.72±7.95 in non-obese, p=0.711) or fatty food preference (16.81±8.84 vs. 17.27±8.75, p=0.833). No significant correlation was found between FTO rs9939609 polymorphism and sweet or fatty food preferences in fully adjusted models (p>0.05). The study concludes that the results do not support the hypothesis that FTO rs9939609 polymorphism influences different food preferences. The authors note limitations including self-reported dietary assessment methods and a relatively small sample size, and call for larger studies to confirm these findings.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: How does FTO gene affect obesity and how to reduce genetic risk through diet? – PlexusDx ---
URL: https://plexusdx.com/blogs/learn/how-does-fto-gene-affect-obesity-and-how-to-reduce-genetic-risk-through-diet

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from PlexusDx explains the role of the FTO (fat mass and obesity-associated) gene in obesity and how dietary choices can mitigate genetic risk. The FTO gene is the most researched gene related to body weight and the first genetic discovery linked to obesity. It acts as a "master switch" controlling multiple weight-related genes and pathways, affecting appetite regulation, emotional eating, food preferences, fat metabolism, and energy expenditure.

The key SNP rs9939609 is strongly correlated with obesity across age groups and ethnicities. Carriers of the 'A' allele show higher weight gain, obesity prevalence, elevated ghrelin levels, increased food consumption, preference for calorie-rich foods, less meal satisfaction, emotional/binge eating, greater insulin resistance, and higher blood sugar. The 'T' allele carriers typically maintain normal weight with greater satiety and healthier food choices.

Dietary interventions can help 'A' allele carriers: low-fat diets or replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated/monounsaturated fats reduce weight, abdominal fat, cholesterol, inflammation, and insulin resistance. Higher protein intake improves appetite regulation and food craving control. A three-year study showed 'AA' genotype carriers experienced better weight loss on a Mediterranean diet and may be protected from diabetes. However, some meta-analyses do not support FTO-BMI associations, and findings vary across populations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: TAS1R2/TAS1R3 Single-Nucleotide Polymorphisms Affect Sweet Taste Receptor Activation by Sweeteners: The SWEET Project ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/6/949

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access scientific article published in *Nutrients* (2025, Volume 17, Issue 6, 949) as part of the SWEET Project. The study investigates how single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 genes—which encode the human sweet taste receptor—affect receptor activation by 12 different sweeteners.

**Background:** Previous studies hypothesized that SNPs in TAS1R2/TAS1R3 may alter sweet compound detection and eating habits, potentially increasing obesity risk. This in vitro study aimed to measure the impact of polymorphisms on sweet taste receptor response to various sweeteners and identify new SNPs in an obese population.

**Methods:** The researchers used functional cellular assays (calcium mobilization assays in HEK293T cells) to test 12 human TAS1R2-SNPs and 16 human TAS1R3-SNPs stimulated by 12 sweeteners (sucralose, acesulfame K, saccharin, cyclamate, NHDC, neotame, perillartine, RebA, RebM, mogroside V, thaumatin, and brazzein). Additionally, 162 blood samples were collected from an obese population (BMI 25–35 kg/m²) from 5 European centers involved in the SWEET project for SNP genotyping via DNA sequencing.

**Results:** Although certain TAS1R2/TAS1R3 SNPs showed reduced receptor response, they were not associated with particular phenotypes. The I595T and K689Q substitutions in TAS1R2 severely impaired responses to most sweeteners. The L95P and S551N substitutions in TAS1R3 completely abolished or decreased receptor response. The mouse TAS1R3-I60T variant (known to be associated with saccharin preference) led to significant decreases in overall functional activity. Seven SNPs were predicted to severely impair human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 response to sweeteners. However, some variants (e.g., R813K, G832R) showed higher potency/efficacy than wild-type for certain sweeteners.

**Conclusions:** Although some TAS1R2- and TAS1R3-SNPs have previously been associated with obesity, the cellular results do not confirm this association. The findings reinforce the hypothesis that sweet taste perception and sugar consumption are governed by factors other than the TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 genes alone.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Frontiers | Genetic Background of Taste Perception, Taste Preferences, and Its Nutritional Implications: A Systematic Review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/genetics/articles/10.3389/fgene.2019.01272/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This systematic review, published in Frontiers in Genetics (December 19, 2019), investigates the genetic background of taste perception, taste preferences, and their nutritional implications. The review was conducted by Diószegi et al. following the PRISMA statement, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published between January 1, 2000 and April 13, 2018.

**Methods:** Of 949 identified publications, 103 articles were included after screening. Quality was assessed using the Q-Genie tool: 43 studies were rated good quality, 47 moderate, and 13 low quality.

**Key Findings by Taste Modality:**

- **Bitter Taste (64 studies):** The most extensively studied. TAS2R38 variants (rs713598, rs1726866, rs10246939) were strongly associated with PTC/PROP sensitivity and bitterness perception of foods like vegetables, wine, and alcohol. PAV haplotype homozygotes showed greater sensitivity to bitter compounds. Other genes studied include TAS2R19, TAS2R31, TAS2R4, TAS2R5, TAS2R9, and CA6.

- **Sweet Taste (28 studies):** TAS2R38 polymorphisms were also associated with sweet taste preference and sugar intake. TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 variants showed inconclusive or limited associations. Other genes include GNAT3, SLC2A2, TAS1R1, ADIPOQ, ANKK1, DRD2, OPRM1, LEP, LEPR, and NPY1.

- **Fat Taste (22 studies):** The most convincing results were for CD36 polymorphisms (rs1761667, rs1527483) associated with oleic acid threshold and fat perception. IZUMO1 rs838145 variant was also associated with fat preference.

- **Umami Taste (6 studies):** Limited studies suggested TAS1R1 and TAS1R3 polymorphisms influence umami taster status.

- **Salty Taste (6 studies):** Very limited research. TRPV1 and SCNN1B variants were associated with salt perception.

- **Sour Taste (4 studies):** Minimal research identified associations with TAS1R1 variants and citric acid perception.

**Conclusions:** Significant associations exist between TAS2R38 variants and bitter/sweet taste preference, and between CD36 rs1761667 and fat taste responsiveness. The knowledge of genetic influences on taste preferences is important for developing tailored public health strategies to reduce nutrition-related diseases. Further research is needed, especially for umami, salty, and sour taste modalities.
</summary>

In addition to socio-economical, socio-cultural, psychological determinants, taste is one of the main factors that influence food choices.", "Our findings suggest that a significant association exists between TAS2R38 variants (rs713598, rs1726866, rs10246939) and bitter and sweet taste preference. Other confirmed results are related to rs1761667 (CD36) and fat taste responsiveness.", "Unfavorable dietary patterns referred to as the 'nutrition transition' can be characterized with an increased consumption of industrially processed foods with high salt, fat, and sugar content and contribute to the development of metabolic abnormalities and consequent NCDs of high public health significance...and have emerged as the biggest contributor to premature mortality around the world, accounting for 11 million deaths in 2017.", "Heritability estimates range from high to moderate for bitter tasting stimuli [0.72, 0.71, 0.34, for 6-n-propylthiouracil (PROP), phenylthiocarbamide (PTC), and quinine hydrochloride, respectively] and moderate for sweet tasting compounds (glucose: h2= 0.31, fructose: h2= 0.34).", "Knowledge of the extent to which genetic and environmental factors influence the development of individual taste preferences and eating patterns is important for public policy actions addressing nutritional behavior of populations."

--- SOURCE 14: Genetics of Taste Receptors ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4764331

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific review article, "Genetics of Taste Receptors" by Alexander A. Bachmanov et al., published in Current Pharmaceutical Design (2014), examines the genetic basis of taste receptors in vertebrates. The review covers five main taste qualities: sweet, umami, bitter, salty, and sour, plus noncanonical tastes like water, fat, and complex carbohydrates. 

Key findings include: Taste receptors for sweet and umami (T1R family), bitter (T2R family), and salty (ENaC) have been identified, but sour taste receptors remain unknown. T1R2+3 functions as a sweet taste receptor, while T1R1+3 functions as an umami receptor. T2R family members act as bitter taste receptors with broad ligand specificity.

The article emphasizes two types of genetic variation: between-species variation (orthologous genes) and within-species variation (allelic variation). --- SOURCE 1: How bad is ultra-processed food for the planet? ---
URL: https://www.soilassociation.org/blogs/2022/august/24/how-bad-is-ultra-processed-food-for-the-planet

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published August 24, 2022) by the Soil Association examines the environmental impacts of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), based on a paper published by researchers from CSIRO and Deakin University in Australia. The paper reviewed 52 studies on UPF environmental impacts.

Key findings include that UPFs account for 17-39% of total diet-related energy use, 36-45% of diet-related biodiversity loss, up to a third of diet-related greenhouse gas emissions/land use/food waste, and up to a quarter of diet-related water use in high-income countries. UPF production relies on commodity ingredients like palm oil, soya, wheat, maize, milk, eggs, and meat, which have driven ecosystem destruction (e.g., rainforest clearing for palm oil in Indonesia, Cerrado conversion for soya in Brazil). UPFs contribute significantly to climate change, plastic pollution, and food waste.

The authors conclude that UPFs are "potentially counterproductive" to sustainable food system objectives and call on policymakers to regulate UPF production, availability, and consumption. Countries including Brazil, Canada, Chile, Ecuador, France, Israel, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay already encourage limiting UPF intake through dietary guidance and labeling. The UK is one of the highest consumers of UPFs, with these products making up over half of average weekly shopping baskets. The article calls for UK government action including reduction targets, consumer guidance, UPF labeling, and support for transition to agroecology and organic farming.
</summary>

URL: https://healthyfoodpolicyproject.org/towards-equitable-and-just-food-systems/measuring-progress

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the "Towards Equitable and Just Food Systems" resource from the Healthy Food Policy Project. It examines common terms used to measure progress in food systems—food security, food deserts, food swamps, and hunger—along with their definitions, uses in policy and research, and significant limitations.

**Food Security** is defined as consistent access to sufficient, safe, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food. The USDA measures it on a spectrum from high to very low food security. However, the term is limiting as an ultimate goal because it does not address nutritional quality or root causes of inequity. Related terms include nutrition security, community food security, food access (with five dimensions: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability, accommodation), and food system resilience.

**Food Desert** refers to areas with low access to grocery stores. The term is being phased out at the federal level in favor of "low-income and low-access areas." It is criticized for implying scarcity is natural, masking deliberate policy decisions (e.g., redlining, suburbanization), ignoring racial disparities, and not reflecting community vibrancy. Baltimore, Maryland has shifted to using "Healthy Food Priority Areas."

**Food Swamp** describes areas where unhealthy food outlets (fast food, convenience stores) outnumber healthy options. Research suggests food swamps predict obesity better than food deserts and disproportionately impact low-income and Black communities. Root causes include redlining, white flight, and zoning policies. Critiques note the term still does not adequately address root causes, with some advocating for "food apartheid" as a better descriptor.

**Hunger** is an individual-level physical sensation from insufficient food intake, often conflated with food insecurity in surveys. It is difficult to measure directly, so food insecurity is used as a proxy. The Committee on National Statistics has recommended USDA stop using "hunger" to describe food insecurity indicators.

The page includes policy examples for each term and discussion questions for reflection.
</summary>

Key findings include:
- Food swamps are a stronger predictor of obesity rates than food deserts across U.S. counties.
- Even after controlling for food desert effects, food swamps had a positive, statistically significant effect on adult obesity rates.

The authors argue that NOVA does not truly classify by processing level but rather by ingredient count, leading to misleading and pejorative connotations about commercially manufactured foods.

**Key Points:**

--- SOURCE 1: Why 2026 could see the end of the Farm Bill era of American agriculture policy | The Invading Sea ---
URL: https://www.theinvadingsea.com/2026/01/08/farm-bill-subsidies-snap-climate-smart-agriculture-organic-maha-trump-one-big-beautiful-bill

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This opinion piece by Christopher Neubert and Kathleen Merrigan (Arizona State University) argues that the traditional five-year Farm Bill era of American agriculture policy may be ending, with 2026 marking a critical juncture. The last comprehensive Farm Bill passed in 2018; its provisions expired in 2023 and have been renewed only year-to-year since.

The July 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" fundamentally disrupted the historic bipartisan compromise that paired farm subsidies with nutrition assistance (SNAP). It slashed SNAP spending by $186 billion over ten years (with about one-third of cuts shifted to state budgets), while boosting farm subsidies for key crops like corn, soybeans, and wheat by $60 billion, plus an additional $12 billion in December 2025 to offset tariff-related export losses. Anti-hunger advocates are furious, and farmers say subsidies are insufficient to cover low commodity prices and high input costs.

The authors believe a comprehensive five-year Farm Bill is unlikely in 2026 due to midterm elections and deep divisions in Congress. Instead, smaller extension bills may be pursued. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act's $20 billion for climate-smart agriculture was cut and repurposed. The Trump administration's "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) agenda offers some potential alignment with sustainable agriculture advocates (e.g., $700 million committed for regenerative practices in December 2025), but faces pushback from conventional agriculture allies. The authors conclude that advocates for food and agriculture reform will need new strategies without the Farm Bill framework.
</summary>

Doing so would be an effective declaration that a permanent five-year farm bill is on indefinite hold.", "Overall, in this new political environment, we believe advocates for changes in agriculture and food aid will likely need to rethink how to advance their agendas without the promise of a farm bill coming anytime soon."

--- SOURCE 3: CAP at a glance - Agriculture and rural development - Europa.eu ---
URL: https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/cap-overview/cap-glance_en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The common agricultural policy (CAP) is a partnership between agriculture and society, and between Europe and its farmers. Launched in 1962, the CAP aims to support farmers and ensure Europe's food security. It is a common policy for all EU countries, managed and funded at European level from the EU's budget.

The CAP 2023-27 entered into force on 1 January 2023, representing a modernised policy with emphasis on results and performance. It seeks to ensure a sustainable future for European farmers, provide more targeted support to smaller farms, and allow greater flexibility for EU countries to adapt measures to local conditions.

The CAP upholds environmental rules and encourages green farming, supports rural communities, and ensures sustainable agriculture and forestry can be profitable and competitive. It focuses on ten specific objectives linked to EU goals for social, environmental, and economic sustainability. Each EU country designed a national CAP Strategic Plan combining funding for income support, rural development, and market measures.

The CAP is financed through two funds: the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF) at €291.1 billion, and the European Agricultural Rural Development Fund (EAFRD) at €95.5 billion, totalling €387 billion for the 2021-27 period. Payments are managed at national level.

Key benefits include food production (ensuring safe, affordable, high-quality food), rural community development (supporting rural areas and creating jobs), and environmentally sustainable farming (protecting biodiversity and natural resources).

The legal basis is established in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The CAP 2023-27 is covered by three regulations, generally applicable since 1 January 2023. The Commission carries out impact assessments when planning new legislation, and the EU Court of Auditors supervises expenditure in agriculture.

Historical milestones include: the CAP's birth in 1962; 1992 reforms shifting from market support to producer support; 2003-2008-2011 reforms; 2014-20 programming period focusing on competitiveness and sustainability; the 2021 transitional regulation; and the current CAP 2023-27 period.
</summary>

## 1. FOOD DESERTS AND FOOD SWAMPS: Definitions, Measurement Methods, and Health Outcomes

### Definitions and Terminology

**Food Deserts** are geographic areas where residents have few to no convenient options for securing affordable and healthy foods, especially fresh fruits and vegetables [31]. The term refers to "low-income and low-access areas" where residents face barriers to healthy food due to geography, limited income, transportation, and availability [33]. The term is being phased out at the federal level in favor of "low-income and low-access areas" [6]. It is criticized for implying scarcity is natural, masking deliberate policy decisions (e.g., redlining, suburbanization), ignoring racial disparities, and not reflecting community vibrancy. Baltimore, Maryland has shifted to using "Healthy Food Priority Areas" [6]. The term "food desert" is rooted in deficit and does not accurately reflect the vibrancy of communities experiencing low access to healthy food [6].

**Food Swamps** are "areas in which large relative amounts of energy-dense snack foods, inundate healthy food options" (Donald Rose et al.) [6]. Food swamps are neighborhoods characterized by an abundance of fast-food restaurants and convenience stores that primarily offer ultra-processed, high-calorie foods, while healthy options remain scarce [33]. The term describes areas where unhealthy food outlets (fast food, convenience stores) outnumber healthy options [6].

**Food Security** is defined as consistent access to sufficient, safe, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food, according to the United Nations' Committee on World Food Security [6]. Food security includes the dimensions of 1) Availability; 2) Access; 3) Use; and 4) Stability of these three dimensions [6]. The term is limiting as an ultimate goal because it does not address nutritional quality or root causes of inequity [6].

**Hunger** is "an uncomfortable or painful physical sensation caused by insufficient consumption of dietary energy" (FAO) [6]. It is difficult to measure directly, so food insecurity is used as a proxy. The Committee on National Statistics has recommended USDA stop using "hunger" to describe food insecurity indicators [6].

### USDA Food Access Research and Measurement Methods

The **Food Access Research Atlas (FARA)** from the USDA Economic Research Service presents a spatial overview of food access indicators for low-income and other census tracts using different measures of supermarket accessibility [36][39]. FARA includes two measures of retail food access: the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM) and the Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM) [39]. These measures can help highlight neighborhoods where distance and transportation barriers may limit access to food retailers [39]. Low-income census tracts are defined based on their poverty rates or median family income, and low access refers to being far from a SNAP-authorized retailer or a large food retailer (supermarkets, supercenters, and large grocery stores) [39].

The SRAM for 2025 uses SNAP-authorized food retailer locations from STARS, LandScan USA 2020 nighttime gridded population data at ~90-meter resolution, and 2020–24 ACS data. Distance calculations use both Euclidean (straight-line) and network-based (driving) methods at four thresholds (0.5, 1, 10, and 20 miles). 101 stores were excluded from drive-distance calculations due to accessibility issues [10]. The LRAM for 2019 is based on a merged directory of 45,233 foodstores from STARS and TDLinx (supermarkets, supercenters, large grocery stores), excluding military commissaries, warehouse clubs, drug stores, dollar stores, and convenience stores [10]. Urban tracts (>2,500 people) use 0.5 and 1-mile thresholds; rural tracts (<2,500 people) use 10 and 20-mile thresholds [10].

Low food access is defined as living more than 1 mile (urban) or 10 miles (rural) from the nearest supermarket, supercenter, or large grocery store [37]. Stores met the definition of a supermarket or large grocery store if they reported at least $2 million in annual sales and contained all the major food departments found in a traditional supermarket [37].

The **Food Environment Index** from County Health Rankings & Roadmaps accounts for both proximity to healthy foods and income, considering distance to grocery stores and barriers like cost and transportation. It equally weights two indicators: (1) Limited Access to Healthy Foods – percentage of low-income population (≤200% federal poverty threshold) not living close to a grocery store; and (2) Food Insecurity – percentage of the population without reliable food access in the past year. Data sources include the USDA Food Environment Atlas and Feeding America's Map the Meal Gap [8].

### Key Dimensions of Food Access

Food access is measured by several dimensions: (1) **Availability** – measured via the "container method" (counting food retailers per area) or distance-based approaches, accounting for travel routes, public transit, walking paths, safety, and daily mobility patterns; (2) **Acceptability** – considers food quality, including whether food is healthy, fresh, safe, and culturally appropriate, distinguishing between access to healthy foods and exposure to unhealthy "Energy Dense, Nutrient Poor" (EDNP) foods; and (3) **Affordability** – when fresh foods are available at a premium price, forcing trade-offs [23].

### Prevalence and Geographic Distribution

Nearly 39.5 million people (13% of the U.S. population) live in low-income, low-access areas, more than 1 mile (urban) or 10 miles (rural) from the nearest supermarket. Almost 19 million people (6% of the population) have limited access to a supermarket [31]. A report from the USDA Economic Research Service estimated that 7.3 million Americans live in low-income census tracts that are distant from a fully stocked grocery store or supermarket [32].

Among states with the greatest share of residents living in low-income, low-food-access areas, nine of the top 10 are located in the South. Mississippi ranks first with 30% of residents in food deserts, followed by New Mexico (29%) and Arkansas (26%) [31]. Among large metro areas, Memphis has the highest share (32%), followed by San Antonio and Riverside, CA (26% each) [31].

### Food Swamps vs. Food Deserts: Health Outcomes

Research increasingly demonstrates that food swamps are stronger predictors of obesity and diet-related disease than food deserts alone [33]. A seminal study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2017) found that food swamps are a stronger predictor of obesity rates than food deserts across U.S. counties. Even after controlling for food desert effects, food swamps had a positive, statistically significant effect on adult obesity rates. The study used three measures of food swamps (Traditional Retail Food Environment Index and two expanded versions), all showing positive associations with obesity. The food swamp effect was stronger in counties with greater income inequality (p<0.05) and where residents are less mobile (p<0.01). The traditional RFEI (ratio of fast food restaurants and convenience stores to grocery stores/supermarkets) had the strongest relationship with obesity rates [7].

A 2023 study found that counties with the highest food swamp scores had a 77% increase in obesity-related cancer mortality compared with counties with lower food swamp scores (Bevel et al., 2023) [33].

There is strong evidence that food deserts are correlated with high prevalence of overweight, obesity, and premature death [8]. Communities with less access to healthy foods experience more obesity, poorer physical and mental health, and worse outcomes in school [23].

### Recent Trends (2003-2023)

A new study published in the American Journal of Public Health (June 2026) reveals that between 2003 and 2023, nearly five million Americans lived in food deserts (areas with no grocery stores), predominantly in poor, rural areas and communities reliant on public transit. The results showed a considerable increase in the percentage of food swamps and no substantial progress in reducing food deserts [9][34]. Food swamps increased from 80.2% to 88.5% of census tracts (2003 to 2023). Food deserts declined only slightly, from 6.1% to 5.5% over the same period. Food deserts were substantially higher in rural, economically disadvantaged (persistent poverty) areas and among public transit users. If only relying on public transit, over 7.4 million people would be living in food deserts. The researchers used longitudinal data on all licensed food retailers, geocoded to census-tract level [34].

Lead author Dr. Daniel Wiese (principal scientist, cancer disparity research at ACS) stated: "Everyone in the United States should be living in a food oasis rather than a food desert. Unfortunately, our findings show many neighborhoods where healthy food options, especially fresh fruits and vegetables, are almost nonexistent, and fast-food restaurants and corner stores with only a few healthy options are dominating the landscape in these same neighborhoods. This needs to change" [34].

### Data Source Limitations and Accuracy

A study published in Applied Geography (2013) examined how inaccuracies in secondary commercial data sources (InfoUSA and Dun & Bradstreet) affect the designation of Census tracts as low food access areas. For the USDA ERS food desert measure, secondary data sources showed 94% concordance, but only 50–65% sensitivity and 60–64% positive predictive value (PPV). For the CDC NHFRT measure, secondary data showed 88–91% concordance, 80–86% sensitivity, and 78–82% PPV. Secondary data sources consistently undercounted low food access areas, with D&B more prone to undercount supermarkets in low-income areas, leading to greater under-ascertainment of food deserts [38][35]. The authors concluded that while inaccuracies in secondary data sources may be acceptable for large-scale surveillance, verification with field work is advisable for local community efforts aimed at identifying and improving food access [38][35].

### Urban and Rural Comparisons

Low-income, minority, and rural neighborhoods have the poorest access to supermarkets and healthful foods. A national study of 28,000 ZIP codes found rural areas had 14% fewer chain supermarkets than urban areas; low-income areas had 75% as many as middle-income areas; predominantly Black neighborhoods had half as many chain supermarkets as white neighborhoods; and Hispanic neighborhoods had 32% as many [26]. Residential segregation by income, race, and ethnicity contributes to health disparities in the U.S. Poor dietary patterns and obesity have been linked to neighborhood deprivation, neighborhood minority composition, and low area population density [26].

### GIS Applications

GIS enables researchers to map food deserts, analyze variables like income and car ownership, and uncover spatial patterns. A study published in Health & Place examined Chicago supermarkets (2007-2014), finding lower-income neighborhoods consistently had worse food access [32]. A study from the National Bureau of Economic Research found that a greater supply of nutritional foods could only have a limited effect on dietary inequality, unless a demand for these items also increased [32]. A Rand Health study in Pittsburgh found that a supermarket opening in 2013 improved diets and cholesterol but also brought broader community benefits like reduced food insecurity, rising incomes, and greater neighborhood satisfaction [32].

### Causes of Food Deserts

Causes include food distribution systems favoring convenience stores in low-income areas, supermarket disinvestment in lower-income neighborhoods, transportation challenges, and income inequality (healthier diets cost ~$1.50 more per day) [31]. Root causes of food swamps include redlining, white flight, and zoning policies [6]. Critics note the term "food swamp" still does not adequately address root causes, with some advocating for "food apartheid" as a better descriptor [6].

## 2. ECONOMIC INEQUALITY AND FOOD PRICING

### Cost Differentials Between UPFs and Whole Foods

Americans pay 40% more for fruits and vegetables due to supply chain costs [15]. A 2022 survey found 46% cited high cost of healthy food as the biggest barrier to a healthier diet [15]. 18 million U.S. households experienced food insecurity in 2023 [15]. Americans scored an average of just 58 out of 100 on the USDA's Healthy Eating Index [15].

Processed foods are cheaper, more shelf-stable, and aggressively marketed, but contribute to chronic diseases like diabetes, heart disease, and obesity [15]. There's evidence that inflation continues to shape food choices, particularly for low-income Americans who prioritize price over healthfulness [15]. Higher food prices often increase food insecurity. "These shifts increase the risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and obesity" [15].

### Cost and Affordability of Healthy Diets Globally

The Food Prices for Nutrition DataHub, a World Bank-hosted platform, provides global statistics on the cost and affordability of healthy diets across over 170 countries. It tracks 51 indicators covering diet cost and diet affordability. Key findings from the SOFI 2025 report indicate that approximately 2.6 billion people (about one-third of the global population) could not afford a healthy diet in 2024, representing a reduction from the COVID-19 pandemic peak in 2020, though recovery has been uneven with worsening trends in low-income countries and sub-Saharan Africa [14]. Earlier reports found that over 3 billion – or two in five people on the planet – could not afford a healthy diet in 2017 [14]. The indicators use the least-cost combination of locally available foods to meet the needs of a representative adult requiring 2,330 kcal per day at three diet quality levels: a healthy diet; a nutrient adequate diet; and an energy sufficient diet [14].

### Price Elasticity of Demand and Fiscal Policies

A study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine (July 2024) by Pourya Valizadeh and Shu Wen Ng examined the impact of nationwide taxes on unhealthy ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) and subsidies for minimally processed foods (MPFs) for low-income households. Using 2017–2018 Nielsen Homescan Panel data (11,152 low-income and 47,518 higher-income U.S. households), the study found that a sugar-based tax on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) would lower both volume and calories purchased, with the largest impact on low-income households without children. Targeted subsidies would increase fruit, vegetable, and healthier drink purchases without substantially increasing calories. Under tax simulations, low-income households would make larger reductions in absolute volume and calorie purchases of taxed foods/beverages than higher-income households, suggesting the policies could help narrow nutritional disparities. The authors concluded: "Levying national taxes on unhealthy ultraprocessed foods/beverages and offering targeted subsidies for minimally processed foods/beverages could promote healthier food choices among low-income households. Such policies have the potential to benefit low-income households financially and at a relatively low cost for the federal government annually" [13].

### UPF Demand Across the Lifecycle

A working paper by Awad, Ehmke, McCluskey, and Okrent (May 2024) investigates the relationship between ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption and obesity in the U.S., using household-level scanner data from IRI-Circana (2008–2012, over 120,000 households). The authors classify foods using the NOVA system and employ a structural demand approach (EASI demand system) to estimate demand elasticities for UPFs across age groups. They note that structural shifts in food retail have led to UPF dominance in food deserts, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations like the elderly. The paper hypothesizes that consumers allocating a higher proportion of their food budget to UPFs are at greater risk of obesity [11].

### Agricultural Subsidies and the US Farm Bill

The US Farm Bill is a massive piece of legislation that addresses agricultural commodities, conservation, trade, nutrition, rural development, energy, forestry, and more [1]. The last comprehensive Farm Bill passed in 2018; its provisions expired in 2023 and have been renewed only year-to-year since [1].

The July 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" fundamentally disrupted the historic bipartisan compromise that paired farm subsidies with nutrition assistance (SNAP). It slashed SNAP spending by $186 billion over ten years (with about one-third of cuts shifted to state budgets), while boosting farm subsidies for key crops like corn, soybeans, and wheat by $60 billion, plus an additional $12 billion in December 2025 to offset tariff-related export losses [1].

Of the $1.4 trillion in the Congressional Budget Office's baseline projected outlays (2027–36) for farm and nutrition programs, nutrition programs account for more than 70 percent—with most of the remaining spending directed to crop insurance, commodity programs, and conservation [5]. Mandatory nutrition-program spending was projected to account for 72 percent ($985 billion) of the 10-year projected outlays from 2027–2036 [5]. Crop-insurance-program expenditures are projected to comprise 11 percent ($156 billion) of total outlays over 2027–36. The 2025 OBBBA raised subsidy rates across different levels of crop insurance coverage, beginning in crop year 2026 [5].

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act's $20 billion for climate-smart agriculture was cut and repurposed. The Trump administration's "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) agenda offers some potential alignment with sustainable agriculture advocates (e.g., $700 million committed for regenerative practices in December 2025), but faces pushback from conventional agriculture allies [1]. The authors conclude that advocates for food and agriculture reform will need new strategies without the Farm Bill framework [1].

### European Union Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)

The common agricultural policy (CAP) is a partnership between agriculture and society, and between Europe and its farmers. Launched in 1962, the CAP aims to support farmers and ensure Europe's food security. It is a common policy for all EU countries, managed and funded at European level from the EU's budget [3]. The CAP 2023-27 entered into force on 1 January 2023, representing a modernised policy with emphasis on results and performance. It seeks to ensure a sustainable future for European farmers, provide more targeted support to smaller farms, and allow greater flexibility for EU countries to adapt measures to local conditions [3].

The CAP is financed through two funds: the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF) at €291.1 billion, and the European Agricultural Rural Development Fund (EAFRD) at €95.5 billion, totalling €387 billion for the 2021-27 period [3]. The CAP has been criticized for alleged anti-development effects, funding of animal farming, oversupply and redistribution issues, artificially high food prices, negative impacts on public health, harming smaller farms, and environmental problems [4].

## 3. MARKETING TARGETING AND FOOD ENVIRONMENT INEQUITIES

### Scale of Unhealthy Food Marketing

Food, beverage, and restaurant companies spend nearly $14 billion annually on advertising in the U.S., with 80% promoting fast food, sugary drinks, candy, and unhealthy snacks [16][19]. Fast-food companies spent approximately $5 billion on U.S. advertising in 2019, with disproportionate targeting of Black and Hispanic youth compared to white youth (per University of Connecticut's Rudd Center for Food Policy and Health) [16].

### Targeted Marketing to Communities of Color

U.S. food companies disproportionately target Black and Hispanic consumers with marketing for high-calorie, low-nutrient products including candy, sugary drinks, snacks, and fast food. The more than $1 billion spent on this targeted marketing exacerbates inequities in poor diet and diet-related diseases in communities of color, including heart disease, obesity, and diabetes (Rudd Center for Food Policy & Obesity; Council on Black Health, November 2022) [20].

A 2022 Rudd Center report found that U.S. food companies spend over $1 billion on targeted marketing to Black and Hispanic consumers, exacerbating inequities in diet and diet-related diseases [20]. A 2019 Rudd Center report documented increasing disparities in unhealthy food advertising targeted to Hispanic and Black youth [20]. Research from 2016 found Black children are exposed to junk food ads significantly more than white children [20].

"Companies often put their money behind their least healthy products and target those to Black and Latino young consumers. We have evidence that there are disproportionate effects of diet-related disease among those groups. It's higher. So when you target those groups with your least healthy products, you are making the problem worse," said the Rudd Center's Director of Marketing Initiatives Frances Fleming-Milici [16].

African American children and teens see more than twice as many ads for sugary drinks as their white peers [19]. In 2019, kids and teens saw an average of two fast-food ads per day on television alone [19].

A 2022 study in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that "Overall greater health-adverse and fewer health-beneficial advertisements are broadcasted on Spanish-language than on English-language TV. Unchecked corporate marketing strategies may serve as a commercial determinant of health disparities for Latino populations by Spanish-language TV" [20].

### Marketing Tactics and Strategies

Corporations use sophisticated tactics including celebrity endorsements (e.g., Bad Bunny), sports sponsorships (FIFA World Cup, Olympics), QR code promotions, school partnerships, social media influencers, and algorithmic micro-targeting based on ZIP codes, ethnicity, and online behavior [16]. The concept of "cradle-to-grave" marketing aims to hook children young for lifelong consumption [16].

Clay Venetis, a policy associate at the Center for Science in the Public Interest: "These unhealthy food companies use cultural moments and important milestones or events in kids' lives as Trojan horses to sneak in their advertising. The goal is to hit people at the exact moment they're most likely to be moved emotionally" [16].

Marion Nestle, a public health advocate and professor at NYU: "Of course it's a Trojan horse. That's the whole point of community support and funding community activities. If you get kids to like and want a product, they will pester their parents for it and consume it for life" [16].

Tyra Willis of the Food Empowerment Project: "Advertising has always been used as a tool of colonization, teaching BIPOC and low-income communities to view certain products as necessary for health, even when those products may harm their bodies" [16].

"Children are raised inside a system of misinformation from the start, making them easy targets for future consumers rather than supporting them as a whole human, worthy of health and the tools to thrive. Parents and our youth are blamed for food choices that they were groomed to make through corporate manipulation, colonialism, and racism" [16].

### Marketing to Children

The average Australian 5 to 8-year-old is exposed to at least 827 unhealthy food TV ads per year [18]. Australian adolescents are exposed to almost 100 promotions per week from online sources [18]. Children aged 4 to 6 believe a product tastes better with a cartoon character on the pack [18]. Children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds face higher exposure to unhealthy food marketing [18]. For every hour online, children aged 13-17 are exposed to 17 unhealthy food ads [18]. Techniques include data-driven targeted ads, influencer marketing (including "kidfluencers"), user-generated content campaigns on TikTok, advergames, and rewarded video advertising [18]. The WHO notes that online advertisers build deep individual profiles using data from multiple sources to deliver highly targeted messages [18].

Child-directed marketing is commonly used to market unhealthy food. Brands use 'fun' to make unhealthy food more appealing to children [18].

### School Food Environments

Under the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010, schools may only feature advertising for foods and drinks that meet "Smart Snacks" nutrition guidelines [19].

### Food Industry Lobbying and Political Strategies

Food companies spend millions lobbying to block regulations on child-targeted advertising, soda taxes, and warning labels [16]. Federal agencies (HHS, CDC, FTC) classify targeted food marketing as a significant public health concern, with "racialized marketing" linked to higher rates of diet-related diseases (obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease) among Black and Hispanic youth [16].
