[70] According to Bellinger et al. [55], LP-exposed rats consumed less chow than controls but became hyperphagic when allowed to self-select their diet, and then consumed significantly more high-fat food. This preference was more marked in female than male adults. These effects were observed at 12 weeks of age but no longer at 30 weeks and did not impact on body weight. The timing of the LP exposure (early, mid, late or all gestation) induced different patterns of food intake alterations: a higher intake in males and females exposed during mid-gestation, but a lower intake in males and females exposed throughout gestation or females exposed during late gestation [56]. Surprisingly, in this study, long-term effects on food intake were observed (18 months), whereas it was only a short-term effect (3 months) in the previous study. Plagemann et al. [62] found that specifically restricting maternal protein during pregnancy and lactation resulted in hypophagia on a chow diet and reduced body weights in the offspring. In our laboratory, in two independent studies, we showed that LP-exposed males demonstrated hyperphagia from weaning to the age of 35 days [60, 61], resulting from an enhanced meal size rather than an increase in the number of meals. When they got older (6 months), LP-exposed male rats did not eat more, but either spent more time eating than control rats or eating faster and resting longer [60, 61], suggesting long-lasting alterations in the feeding pattern. At a young age, this was associated with significantly higher expression levels of orexigenic neuropeptides [60, 61], suggesting a high drive toward food intake in order to catch up faster. At adulthood, LP-exposed male rats that demonstrated catch-up growth, preferred fatty food and became leptin resistant (Parnet P., unpublished results). Rats exposed to severe in utero global undernutrition were also hyperphagic after birth [64, 67], an effect that lasted until adulthood and was amplified when the offspring were fed a hypercaloric diet in the post-weaning period which suggests that the set point of the regulation of appetite in these offspring is permanently reset at an elevated level. Early Life Nutrition and Long Term Appetite Regulation 289 The latter was associated with hyperleptinemia and hyperinsulinism, suggesting a state of leptin and insulin resistance which may be involved in the development of a metabolic syndrome. Impact of Early Nutrition on Neurodevelopment of Feeding Regulation Pathways Early life events (prenatal and postnatal) can significantly impact the development of metabolic systems, including hypothalamic circuitry, causing long-term consequences on body-weight and energy homeostasis in adult life. All peripheral and central pathways involved in food intake regulation have their own pattern of development either during prenatal or postnatal periods and differ among species. The neuronal circuitry linking the different regions of the hypothalamus is present before birth in the sheep and non-human primate, as well as in the human [71, 72]. In the rodent, however, this neuronal circuitry is not fully established until 16 days after birth. It is therefore clear that the critical windows of development, during which exposure to altered levels of nutrients, will have long-term effects on the development of this axis and are different in rodents from those observed in large animal models and humans. In the rodent, NPY mRNA is present in the brainstem and forebrain as early as embryonic day 14 (E14) [73]. NPY mRNA expression does increase from birth, to peak around P15–16, and subsequently slowly declines to adult levels by P30 [74]. However, the efferent projection of the NPY neurons originating from the ARH develops only during the postnatal period. It is not until P5–6 that a significant number of NPY/AgRP-ir fibers are present outside of the ARH. By P10–11 NPY/AgRP projections to the DMH appear to be near complete development, while projections to the PVH do not fully develop until P15–16. It has been expected that a mutation resulting in the lack of NPY during critical developmental stages would result in stunted growth and development. In fact, mice can develop to a normal stature without NPY and/or AgRP but lack the ability to adapt to metabolic challenges, such as fasting and diet-induced obesity [71]. In contrast to rodents, in both the human and non-human primate, NPY neurons appear during the middle of the 2nd trimester [75]. ARH–NPY projections begin to develop in the late 2nd trimester, and they continue to develop throughout the 3rd trimester and into the early postnatal period. In adult animals of most species, AgRP is exclusively colocalized in ARH–NPY neurons; therefore, development of AgRP projections follows the same pattern of innervation by NPY. POMC neurons are present within the hypothalamus in the developing rat at E12–13 [76]. At birth, and unlike AgRP, αMSH fibers are evident throughout the hypothalamus, including the PVH [76]. Although the projections of POMC neurons become evident towards the end of gestation, they do not reach their full maturity until weaning. In primates, POMC neurons are readily detectable during early 2nd trimester and the development of ARH– POMC projections occurs during the 3rd trimester [75]. In direct contrast to hypothalamic circuit maturation in the rodent, the brainstem neurocircuitry (i.e., the relay site for short-acting gastrointestinal signals) matures prenatally and is functional at birth. Therefore, in the rodent, these circuits are conceivably far more sensitive to the maternal, in utero environment in comparison to the hypothalamic development which appears to be influenced more by the postnatal nutrient environment. Valerie Amarger and Patricia Parnet 290 Impact of Early Nutrition on Leptin Neurotrophic Action Leptin cannot modulate food intake or energy expenditure through actions in the ARH until after the 3rd postnatal week of life in the rodents when all neural pathways are fully distributed in the hypothalamus. However, remarkably high plasma levels of this hormone have been reported during the early postnatal period in both mice and rats [77-79] and suggest its critical role as a major trophic factor associated with early developmental processes of ARH efferent. The group of Simerly [72, 80, 81] clearly demonstrated that leptin exerts a potent neurotrophic action during this period. These authors have observed that ob/obmice, genetically deficient in leptin, have an altered hypothalamic development characterized by a dramatic decrease in neuronal fiber density in the hypothalamic structures, possibly accounting for their obesity. Leptin administration to these animals during the early postnatal period restored the neuronal organization of hypothalamic circuits in terms of fiber density in the paraventricular nucleus, and induced a long-term reduction of food intake [80]. These results were followed by a number of studies on the role of the leptin surge around birth. Several animal models have clearly shown that either severe undernutrition during pregnancy or placental insufficiency induce intra-uterine growth retardation (IUGR), leading to a low birth weight associated with low plasma leptine levels [82, 83]. Vickers et al. [84] have reported that the subcutaneous delivery of leptin (from P3to P13) to growth-restricted offspring of nutrient-restricted rat dams in the early postnatal period attenuated postnatal hyperphagia, and prevents the later development of obesity and hyperleptinemia. Offspring of dams placed on a 50% food restriction during gestation have a blunted leptin surge during the first two postnatal weeks in comparison to control animals and have a reduced expression of the anorexigenic peptide POMC as well as a reduction in endorphin immunoreactive fibers in the hypothalamus at weaning [68, 83]. The same result was obtained for IUGR rats obtained from LP dams in our laboratory. Expression screening performed on hypothalami from IUGR rats at birth and at postnatal day 12 identified changes in the gene expression of neurodevelopmental processes (cell differentiation and cytoskeleton organization), a slight reduction of AgRP, and a strong reduction of α-MSH-immunoreactive efferent fibers in the PVN suggesting a profound disorganization of his regulatory center [82]. Interestingly, in rats born with IUGR, rapid catch-up growth had a positive effect on neurodevelopmental factors and on neuronal projections emanating from ARH without any beneficial effect on the feeding pattern, suggesting that other metabolic alterations override the beneficial effect of catch-up growth on brain development. Plagemann et al. found that specifically restricting maternal protein during pregnancy and lactation that resulted in hypophagia and reduced body weight in the offspring appeared to be the consequence of hypoplasia of neurons expressing NPY and galanin in the ARC, PVN and LHA at weaning [62, 69, 85]. Concerning leptin action, it is tempting to speculate that leptin absorbed by the newborn via the milk may be an important factor, which participates in the maturation of various organs such as the intestine or hypothalamic structures involved in food intake regulation. Experimental data supports this hypothesis. In our laboratory we showed that formula-fed newborn rats have very low circulating leptin and an impaired hypothalamic neurocircuitry compared to pups nursed by their mothers [86]. Indeed, it has been reported that breast-fed infants have higher serum leptin levels than formula-fed infants [87] and that breast-fed infants may show a better protection toward the risk of developing obesity. Early Life Nutrition and Long Term Appetite Regulation 291 Impact of Early Nutrition on the Food Reward System In the field of appetite programming, the concept of food preferences, and not just control of appetite, is worth studying. The group of Reyes hypothesized that dopamine- and opioid-related gene expressions within the mesocorticolimbic circuitry, underlying the processing associated with the rewarding properties of food, may be altered in offspring from high fat-fed or protein-restricted dams [88, 89]. Indeed, they reported a hypo-dopaminergic state, with an increased re-uptake of DA that could be linked to an increased consumption of rewarding food in an effort to restore homeostasis within this circuitry [89, 90]. The importance of the Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Adrenals (HPA) axis in fetal programming was evidenced in several studies in humans and animal models and is associated with both response to stress and metabolic outcomes. Meaney et al. [91] proposed that the HPA axis is an important target of prenatal environment via epigenetic mechanisms. The HPA axis, essentially through corticoids, plays a role in many outcomes related to fetal and postnatal growth, energy metabolism, stress response, and food intake regulation [92]. It is influenced by a large set of maternal insults during and after pregnancy (stress, alcohol, tobacco, nutrition, maternal care). Undernutrition during Early Development Alters Circadian Rhythm System A wide range of animal and clinical studies clearly indicate that some of the features of the metabolic syndrome arise from a disruption of the circadian clock [15]. A study performed in our laboratory recently demonstrated that feeding a low-protein diet during gestation and lactation induces a long lasting disruption of the diurnal expression pattern of several genes involved in the regulation of food intake and energy metabolism. Seventeen-day-old pups exposed to perinatal undernutrition exhibited significant alterations in the circadian expression profile of the transcripts encoding diverse genes regulating food intake, the metabolic enzymes fatty acid synthase and glucokinase as well as the clock genes BMAL1 and Period1. These effects persisted after weaning, were associated with hyperphagia and mirrored the results of the behavioral analysis of feeding [93]. In a similar model, Sutton et al. [94] found abnormal daily rhythms in food intake and metabolism and an increased lipogenesis, associated at the molecular level with an arrhythmic expression of circadian oscillator genes in the brain, liver, and muscles at 8 weeks of age. In particular, the expression of the clock-associated nuclear receptor and transcription repressor Rev-erb was reduced, with a concordant increased expression of its downstream targets Bmal1 and Per2 in the liver and muscles. This disruption in the circadian rhythm is a potential mechanism for altered feeding behavior which may contribute to an increased diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance. It is generally accepted that preterm infants lack circadian rhythms. Babies born prematurely complete their development in an artificial environment devoid of maternal cues in which their daily light/dark cycles and feeding rhythms are aligned to the working schedule of the nursing staff. In adulthood, both light and food signals act as a potent zeitgeber. At birth, the circadian clock is refractory to the light entrainment such that only feeding or parental care schedule impacts on its rhythmicity, and only 3 months after birth does the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the newborn become responsive to the environmental Valerie Amarger and Patricia Parnet 292 light/dark cycle. In most neonatal intensive care units, a regular light/dark cycle has been introduced as routine practice to improve the circadian synchronization of preterm infants. It will be important in future studies to determine whether metabolic and sleep disorders that have been associated with a disrupted rhythm of the circadian clock is programmed in utero or result from the influence of the post-natal environment. The Early Postnatal Environment and Epigenetic Regulation Molecular mechanisms underlying the long-term effects of the early environment are still poorly characterized. The field of epigenetic research has been tremendously expanding over the last decade and the epigenetic regulation of gene expression appears to be a key mechanism in the persistent adaptation to the prenatal and early postnatal environment. All the different types of cells that make up an organism share an identical genotype, yet each cell type has well defined, specific and stable profiles of gene expression, largely controlled and regulated by the epigenotype. Epigenotypes are set up early during embryonic development and maintained through cell division. However, they also have an inherent flexibility because they can undergo changes in response to particular stimuli; thus, they largely contribute to the plasticity and adaptability of living organisms [95]. The role of epigenetics in programming is supported by studies in both humans and animal models, and has been the subject of many reviews over the last few years [95-102] even though experimental evidence is still scarce. A major obstacle to study epigenetics in humans is the inherent tissue specificity of epigenetic regulation and, consequently, the availability of biological material to conduct these studies. Few studies on post-mortem tissues have been conducted, but they face the limitation of the number of subjects and the potential impact of death circumstances and sampling. Epigenetic studies on the post-mortem hippocampus from adult suicide victims showed that people who experienced childhood abuse many years earlier present modifications in the level of methylation of the promoter region of the Glucocorticoid Receptor (GR) gene [103] as well as the rRNA gene promoter [104]. Epigenetic studies on people who suffered from the Dutch famine were conducted but limited to the analysis of whole blood cells. Differences in the methylation profiles of several candidate genes involved in growth and metabolism were observed in comparison to unexposed, same-sex siblings [105, 106]. This data suggests that permanent changes in DNA methylation may result from a prenatal famine exposure, and this is sex-dependent and varies with the time of exposure, the early gestation being the most sensitive period. Interestingly, the same modifications were not observed in a population of adults born small for gestational age (SGA) (i.e., who suffered from growth restriction early in development) [107]. This is not surprising though, since preterm birth and SGA do not necessarily have a nutritional origin in the population of Western countries. These studies suffer from several limitations, including, as stated before, scarce tissue availability. Second, so far, the observed effects are relatively small (absolute difference in DNA methylation up to 2.5%) [99, 105] which might reflect the biological reality, but requires the choice of highly reliable methods for their detection. Moreover, the number of individuals is usually rather small. Technology and bioinformatics are progressing fast in the field, and it is tempting to think that high-throughput methods will soon allow genome-wide analysis of the epigenome. However, the interpretation of this data will require a better understanding of the epigenetic regulation of the genome. Early Life Nutrition and Long Term Appetite Regulation 293 Epigenetic studies on animal models are exempt from a number of these limitations: 1) A strict control of the environment makes it possible to study the effect of a given environmental insult; 2) The genetic variability is low; 3) It is possible to analyze epigenetic profiles of specific tissues. Of course, findings in animal models are not directly applicable to humans, but they should provide fundamental information regarding the way environmental factors may modify the epigenome and how the epigenome influences the phenotype, domains that are still largely unknown. The most striking epigenetic effect of an environmental factor identified so far is probably the impact of maternal care on the promoter of the glucocorticosteroid receptor (GR) gene, confirming the fact the HPA axis may be a major target in nutritional programming [91]. Maternal care during the first days of life strongly influences the methylation status of the GR gene’s promoter in hippocampus [108]. This affects the expression of the GR gene, persists into adulthood and influences response to stress [109] but is potentially reversible by cross-fostering or by directly injecting L-methionine in the hippocampus [108, 110]. The impact of maternal nutrition on the epigenome was demonstrated for a number of genes in the liver of offspring who experience protein restriction during fetal development. The PPAR and the GR gene promoters were less methylated in offspring exposed to the LP maternal diet from conception to delivery, and this effect lasted until adulthood [111, 112]. A global transcriptomic analysis revealed that a maternal LP diet affects the expression of several hundred genes in the liver of the offspring [113], among which the DNA methyl transferase DNMT1, involved in the maintenance of DNA methylation throughout fetal development [114]. Global DNA methylation and histone acetylation were altered in the brain and liver of rats rendered IUGR by uterine artery ligation [115, 116]. Epigenetic alterations after maternal peri-conceptual under nutrition were also observed in a number of cases. Decreased promoter methylation and modification of histone acetylation levels were noticed for the POMC and GR genes in sheep hypothalami after maternal peri-conceptual under nutrition [117]. Methylation was also reduced at the hypothalamic POMC promoter in rats suffering from a maternal LP diet [82], whereas it was increased in rats overnourished after birth in the small-litter model [118]. The leptin gene promoter methylation level was affected in both mice adipose tissue [119] and rat liver [120] after LP maternal diet exposure. The Igf2 gene methylation was higher in the liver of rats exposed to the maternal LP diet [120]. Dopamine and opioid-related genes (DAT, MOR and PENK) are hypomethylated in the brains of offsprings from dams that consumed a high fat diet, possibly explaining their increased long-term expression [90, 121]. Experimental evidence of epigenetic modifications in response to peri-conceptual and perinatal environment is accumulating, but one must be mindful that the magnitude of the expected effects is usually small, therefore requiring both careful experimental design and highly sensitive and reliable techniques. Moreover, the way environmental factors act on the epigenome is still very poorly understood, and will require more knowledge on how the different components of the epigenetic regulation interact with each other, and how much, where, and how they might be Valerie Amarger and Patricia Parnet 294 reversible [96]. One carbon metabolic pathway clearly plays an important role in the way early nutrition may affect epigenetic mechanisms, and the reversibility of the food restriction by supplementation with various components of the one-carbon cycle was evidenced in many cases [57, 110, 122-124]. Perspectives and Conclusion Feeding behavior and life style are certainly major contributors to human health and are largely involved in the on-going obesity epidemic. Because of its multifactor determinants, the improvement of eating habits is a complex task that requires the involvement of social and industrial partners as well as health professionals. Hence, it follows that:  Maternal health and nutrition during the peri-conceptual period, pregnancy and lactation should be a major concern for women themselves as well as the social and medical staff involved in their management and care (weight control, nutritional advice, appropriate dietary supplementation). This is already a major topic of the WHO Global Strategy For Women’s and Children’s Health (www.who.int).  As breastfeeding is considered the gold standard of early nutrition [125], it should be encouraged and young mothers provided with help and counselling. Parents should receive appropriate advice regarding the way to feed their babies and young children. This is particularly important for preterm and/or IUGR babies who experience feeding difficulties and implies that neonatologists and pediatricians be aware of nutritional issues in terms of health promotion and obesity prevention.  Public policies should include interventions for promoting healthier eating for children and adolescents (reduce advertising and availability of unhealthy food, improve food quality in schools, and promote physical exercise). Several countries have initiated social and education programs promoting good feeding habits, such as the PNNS (National Plan for Health and Nutrition) in France (www.manger. bouger.fr). In addition to these social and medical parameters, there is still a wide gap in the knowledge associated with the physiological and molecular mechanisms of programming, thus requiring extensive research on human cohorts and populations as well as animal models. Hence, it follows that:  Randomized intervention trials on at-risk populations should be carefully designed in order to provide information regarding (1) critical windows during which environmental parameters may have an impact; (2) the effect of a given nutritional intervention (maternal diet supplementation or supplemented formulas). For instance, the prospect of leptin-supplemented formulas as a potential strategy for reducing childhood obesity has already been raised [126, 127] but requires a better understanding of its biological implications.  The effect of early nutrition on the development of ARH circuits is actually largely studied, but more efforts need to be spent on other areas of the brain (reward circuits) Early Life Nutrition and Long Term Appetite Regulation 295 and how the complete integrated circuit develops, including peripheral metabolic systems in such an environment. The understanding of a possible gut-brain axis alteration should also be emphasized.  Differences between species in the development of metabolic systems should be precisely analyzed and considered when interpreting data from animal models.  The way a temporal shift in a specific nutrient or hormone is able to induce permanent structural changes in a tissue is still poorly known.  There is a crucial need for biomarkers that are not only predictive of a later effect but which remain measurable once the initial exposure has ceased. A major problem is to identify biomarkers that can be characterized from non-invasive samples. References [1] Elmquist, J. K., Elias, C. F. and Saper, C. B. (1999). This academic book chapter (Chapter XIII) by Valerie Amarger and Patricia Parnet from INRA and the University of Nantes, France, examines how early-life nutrition influences long-term appetite regulation and feeding behavior. The chapter presents a comprehensive review of the physiological, environmental, and genetic determinants of feeding behavior, with a focus on nutritional programming during critical developmental windows.

Key topics covered include:
1. **Physiological Regulation**: The homeostatic control of appetite involves complex interactions between the hypothalamus (especially the arcuate nucleus), peripheral organs (gut, pancreas, adipose tissue), and various signaling peptides (leptin, ghrelin, NPY, AgRP, POMC, etc.). The hedonic/reward system can override homeostatic regulation.

2. **Environmental and Social Determinants**: Fetal exposure to flavors via amniotic fluid, breastfeeding's positive effect on food acceptance, parental feeding practices, and socioeconomic context all shape feeding behavior from early life.

3. **Evidence from Human Studies**: Studies on Dutch famine survivors show conflicting results regarding later food preferences (some show preference for high-fat diets). Preterm and SGA (small for gestational age) infants often experience feeding difficulties that persist through early childhood. A pilot study in Nantes found SGA babies showed greater feeding difficulties and preference for unhealthy foods at age 2.

4. **Animal Models**: Maternal protein restriction and global nutrient restriction in rodents produce varied effects on offspring feeding behavior including hyperphagia, altered feeding patterns, and preference for high-fat foods. These effects are often gender-specific and depend on timing of exposure.

5. **Neurodevelopmental Mechanisms**: The hypothalamic circuitry develops differently across species (postnatal in rodents, prenatal in humans). Leptin plays a critical neurotrophic role in hypothalamic development during early postnatal periods. Perinatal undernutrition can disrupt circadian rhythm systems and alter the development of food reward pathways.

6. **Epigenetic Regulation**: Early nutrition can induce persistent epigenetic changes (DNA methylation, histone modifications) affecting genes involved in metabolism, stress response, and feeding regulation. Notable examples include glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene methylation in hippocampus, and altered methylation of POMC, leptin, and IGF2 genes.

7. **Conclusions and Recommendations**: The chapter emphasizes the importance of maternal nutrition, breastfeeding support, public health policies promoting healthy eating, and the need for further research on biomarkers, critical windows, and intervention strategies.

It presents the stark reality of American children’s declining health, backed by compelling data and long-term trends. More importantly, it seeks to unpack the potential dietary, behavioral, medical, and environmental drivers behind this crisis. By examining the root causes of deteriorating child health, this assessment establishes a clear, evidence-based foundation for the policy interventions, institutional reforms, and societal shifts needed to reverse course. To turn the tide and better protect our children, the United States must act decisively. During this administration, we will begin reversing the childhood chronic disease crisis by confronting its root causes—not just its symptoms. This means pursuing truth, embracing science, and enacting pro-growth policies and innovations to restore children’s health. Today’s children are tomorrow’s workforce, caregivers, and leaders—we can no longer afford to ignore this crisis. After a century of costly and ineffective approaches, the federal government will lead a coordinated transformation of our food, health, and scientific systems. This strategic realignment will ensure that all Americans—today and in the future—live longer, healthier lives, supported by systems that prioritize prevention, wellbeing, and resilience. But real transformation requires more than vision—it requires clarity. Before we act, we must fully understand the scope of the crisis, the conditions that created it, and the mechanisms through which it continues to grow. Without this foundation, interventions risk being reactive, fragmented, or ineffective. To Make Our Children Healthy Again, we must begin with a shared understanding of the magnitude of the crisis and subsequently what’s likely driving it. This assessment provides that foundation— grounding future efforts in a common scientific basis that identifies four potential drivers behind the rise in childhood chronic disease that present the clearest opportunities for progress:  Poor Diet: The American diet has shifted dramatically toward ultra-processed foods (UPFs), leading to nutrient depletion, increased caloric intake, and exposure to harmful additives. Nearly 70% of children’s calories now come from UPFs, contributing to obesity, diabetes, and other chronic conditions.  Aggregation of Environmental Chemicals: Children are exposed to an increasing number of synthetic chemicals, some of which have been linked to developmental issues and chronic disease. The current regulatory framework should be continually evaluated to ensure that chemicals and other exposures do not interact together to pose a threat to the health of our children.  Lack of Physical Activity and Chronic Stress: American children are experiencing unprecedented levels of inactivity, screen use, sleep deprivation, and chronic stress. These 6 factors significantly contribute to the rise in chronic diseases and mental health challenges.  Overmedicalization: There is a concerning trend of overprescribing medications to children, often driven by conflicts of interest in medical research, regulation, and practice. This has led to unnecessary treatments and long-term health risks. By examining each of these drivers, this assessment equips MAHA Commission stakeholders and partners with the facts needed to identify where and how policy interventions will likely have the most impact. Rising rates of childhood chronic disease are likely being driven by a combination of factors, including the food children are eating, the chemicals they are exposed to, the medications they are taking, and various changes to their lifestyle and behavior, particularly those related to physical activity, sleep and the use of technology. This report focuses on these four major drivers. The food American children are eating The American food system is safe but could be healthier. Most American children’s diets are dominated by ultra-processed foods (UPFs) high in added sugars, chemical additives, and saturated fats, while lacking sufficient intakes of fruits and vegetables. This modern diet has been linked to a range of chronic diseases, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain cancers.44 The excessive consumption of UPFs has led to a depletion of essential micronutrients and dietary fiber, while increasing the consumption of sugars and carbohydrates, which negatively affects overall health.45  Nearly 70% of an American child’s calories today comes from ultra-processed foods46 (increased from zero 100 years ago), many of which are designed to override satiety mechanisms and increase caloric intake.  UPFs makeup over 50% of the diets of pregnant and postpartum mothers.47 American children’s exposure to environmental chemicals The cumulative load of thousands of synthetic chemicals that our children are exposed to through the food they eat, the water they drink, and the air they breathe may pose risks to their long-term health, including neurodevelopmental and endocrine effects.  Over 40,000 chemicals are registered for use in the U.S.48  Pesticides, microplastics, and dioxins are commonly found in the blood and urine of American children and pregnant women—some at alarming levels.49 50 51  Children are particularly vulnerable to chemicals during critical stages of development—in utero, infancy, early childhood, and puberty. args.summary:
This document is the "Make Our Children Healthy Again: Assessment" report, established by President Trump's Executive Order 14212 (February 13, 2025) via the President's Make America Healthy Again Commission. Chaired by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the report is a call to action addressing the childhood chronic disease crisis in the United States.

Key findings: Over 40% of America's 73 million children (aged 0-17) have at least one chronic health condition. The U.S. ranks last in life expectancy among high-income countries despite spending more than double per capita on healthcare. Over 75% of youth aged 17-24 are ineligible for military service primarily due to obesity, poor fitness, and mental health challenges.

The report identifies four major drivers of the crisis:

1. **Poor Diet**: Nearly 70% of children's calories come from ultra-processed foods (UPFs), up from virtually zero 100 years ago. Childhood obesity has increased over 270% since the 1970s, with severe obesity up over 500%. The U.S. obesity rate is more than double the G7 average.

2. **Environmental Chemicals**: Over 40,000 chemicals are registered for use in the U.S. Children are uniquely vulnerable during critical developmental stages. Pesticides, microplastics, and dioxins are commonly found in American children's blood and urine.

3. **Lack of Physical Activity and Chronic Stress**: Teens average nearly 9 hours of non-school screen time daily. Over 70% of children fail to meet federal physical activity guidelines. Teenage depression rates nearly doubled from 2009-2019, and suicide is the second leading cause of death in teens aged 15-19.

4. **Overmedicalization**: Stimulant prescriptions for ADHD increased 250% from 2006-2016. Antidepressant prescriptions in teens increased 14-fold between 1987-2014. Antipsychotic prescriptions for children increased eight-fold between 1995-2005. Over 35% of childhood antibiotics are unnecessary.

The report also highlights "corporate capture" and conflicts of interest, noting that 95% of the 2020 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee had financial ties to food and pharmaceutical companies, the pharmaceutical industry spent $4.7 billion on federal lobbying (1999-2018), and 9 of 10 recent FDA commissioners went on to work for the pharmaceutical industry.

The assessment calls for reversing the crisis by confronting root causes through policy interventions, institutional reforms, and societal shifts—putting American farmers at the center of health, prioritizing prevention over symptom management, and pursuing gold-standard scientific research.

Conduct a comprehensive literature review on the biological mechanisms by which ultra-processed foods (UPFs) affect human physiology, metabolism, and neurology. This is for a scholarly scientific report. Focus on the following subtopics:

1. GUT-BRAIN AXIS DISRUPTION: How emulsifiers, artificial sweeteners, and other food additives disrupt the gut-brain axis signaling pathways. Include research on vagus nerve signaling alterations, changes in gut hormone secretion (GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, leptin), and how these affect satiety signaling.

2. MICROBIOME ALTERATIONS: How UPF consumption alters gut microbiome composition and diversity. Include studies on how emulsifiers (carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate-80), artificial sweeteners (saccharin, sucralose, aspartame), and lack of fermentable fibers affect microbial ecology, intestinal barrier integrity, and metabolic endotoxemia.

3. ENDOCRINE DISRUPTION: How food contact chemicals (bisphenols, phthalates, PFAS), preservatives, and additives interfere with endocrine signaling, including thyroid function, sex hormones, insulin/IGF-1 signaling, and metabolic hormone regulation.

4. NEUROINFLAMMATION AND NEURODEGENERATION: How UPF components promote systemic and central nervous system inflammation. URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/16/2677

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Nutrients (2025, 17(16), 2677) titled "Ultra-Processed Foods, Gut Microbiota, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Critical Review of Emerging Evidence." The review examines the influence of ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption on gut microbiota composition and function and its potential link to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Key findings include: (1) UPFs account for up to 58% of daily caloric intake in high-income countries and are associated with intestinal dysbiosis, reduced microbial diversity, decreased short-chain fatty acid production, impaired barrier integrity, and mucus layer disruption. (2) Consuming 10% of calories from UPFs per day is associated with a 19% increased risk of developing Crohn's disease. (3) Food additives like emulsifiers (e.g., carboxymethyl cellulose, polysorbate 80) can promote proinflammatory changes in the gut microbiota, enhance LPS release, and impair the mucus layer. (4) The persistent low-grade inflammation driven by UPF consumption can lead to "leaky gut" and increased intestinal permeability. The review notes that serum LPS levels are reportedly six times higher in patients with active Crohn's disease compared to healthy controls. The article concludes that high UPF consumption is associated with intestinal dysbiosis characterized by overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria such as Clostridium and Enterococcus, triggering inflammatory responses in the host.
</summary>

URL: https://www.news-medical.net/health/The-Science-of-Ultra-Processed-Foods-and-Mental-Health.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from News-Medical (dated April 3, 2025) explores the growing evidence linking ultra-processed foods (UPFs) to mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, and cognitive decline. UPFs—defined by the NOVA classification system as industrially processed foods like packaged snacks, sugary drinks, instant noodles, and processed meats—now constitute a significant portion of daily caloric intake in many countries.

**Key Evidence:**
- A 2020 study of over 10,000 US adults found that those consuming the most UPFs had a 35% greater likelihood of depressive symptoms.
- Harvard Medical School research found higher UPF consumption was associated with a 50% increased risk of depression, particularly with artificially sweetened beverages and processed snacks.
- A large cohort study of over 25,000 individuals followed for more than five years linked increased UPF intake to higher rates of depressive episodes, independent of lifestyle factors.

**Proposed Mechanisms:**
1. **Gut-brain axis dysfunction** – UPFs lack dietary fiber, disrupting gut microbiota and impairing production of mood-regulating neurotransmitters like serotonin and GABA.
2. **Chronic inflammation** – Refined carbohydrates, unhealthy fats, and additives promote systemic inflammation, with elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) linked to depression.

SUMMARY:
<summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Ultra-Processed Foods and Metabolic Dysfunction: A Narrative Review of Dietary Processing, Behavioral Drivers and Chronic Disease Risk ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12734455

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review (published December 2025 in Metabolites) from Oklahoma State University examining the relationship between ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and metabolic dysfunction. The review synthesizes evidence on UPF definitions (via the NOVA classification system), global consumption patterns, behavioral drivers of overconsumption, nutrient composition, and mechanistic links to metabolic dysfunction, obesity, and chronic disease.

Key findings include:
- **NOVA Classification**: UPFs (Group 4) are industrial formulations with little resemblance to whole foods, including sugar-sweetened beverages, reconstituted meats, and packaged snacks. Critiques of NOVA include its focus on processing over formulation and lack of differentiation within Group 4.
- **Dietary Quality**: Higher UPF consumption is associated with lower diet quality scores (AHA diet score, HEI-2015). UPFs are high in added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, and artificial additives, while low in fiber, protein, vitamins, and minerals. Over 90% of US adults do not meet fiber recommendations.
- **Energy Consumption**: UPFs are energy-dense (>2 kcal/g), with low water content, and are consumed at faster eating rates due to soft textures. Both factors drive overconsumption. Energy-dense foods classified as UPF increased from 67% to 77% of the food supply over 30 years.
- **Consumption Trends**: UPFs now make up ~57-58% of average US adult daily calories (up from 53.5% in 2001-2002). Unprocessed/minimally processed foods contribute only 27.6% of calories. Obesity prevalence rose from 30.5% to 42.4% between 1999-2000 and 2017-2018.
- **Mechanisms**: UPFs promote overconsumption through hyperpalatability, reward pathway activation, blunted satiety signals, disruption of flavor-nutrient associations, and altered gut microbiome from additives. The "cocktail effect" of combined additive exposure is a growing concern.
- **Limitations**: While cross-sectional and cohort evidence is extensive, causal intervention trials and mechanistic human work remain limited. The Hall et al. clinical trial faced critiques regarding variability between processed and unprocessed diets.
- **Future Directions**: The authors call for real-world intervention studies examining effects of reduced UPF consumption on energy balance, inflammation, and gut health.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have become a dominant component of the modern diet, paralleling the rise in obesity and chronic disease prevalence worldwide.", "The average US adult's diet has a majority of daily calories (~57%) from UPFs, a number that has increased throughout the years.", "The NOVA system consists of four categories: unprocessed/minimally processed foods (Group 1), processed culinary ingredients (Group 2), processed foods (Group 3), and UPFs (Group 4).", "Analysis of the 2017–2018 What We Eat in America (WWEIA), NHANES data, NOVA category 4 foods make up 58.2% of the average US adult's daily caloric intake.", "From 1999–2000 to 2017–2018, the prevalence of obesity has risen from 30.5% to 42.4% just in under two decades."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The collapse of the food matrix: how ultra-processed foods impact satiety ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2026.1737280/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article, published in Frontiers in Nutrition on May 5, 2026, proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the primary health threat of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) stems not merely from their poor nutritional composition but from the industrial collapse of their physical "food matrix." The authors, led by Xinna Wang and colleagues from Chinese medical universities, hypothesize that this structural disintegration triggers a top-down cascade of dysregulation across multiple physiological systems.

The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This leads to metabolic dysregulation including insulin resistance, de novo lipogenesis, and mitochondrial stress. Finally, the impoverished matrix combined with chemical additives causes gut microbiome imbalance, compromised intestinal barrier function, and systemic low-grade chronic inflammation via metabolic endotoxemia.

Key evidence cited includes Hall's landmark randomized controlled trial showing that participants on nutrient-matched ultra-processed diets consumed ~500 kcal/day more and gained weight. Epidemiological data show UPF consumers have 15% increased all-cause mortality risk (HR=1.15), 11% increased cardiovascular disease risk (HR=1.11), and each 10% increase in UPF intake associates with 10% higher type 2 diabetes risk (RR=1.10).

The review critiques "nutritionism" and fortified UPFs, arguing that adding isolated nutrients to a collapsed matrix cannot restore health value. It calls for methodological innovation, multi-omics research, clinical translation studies, and development of "gentle" processing technologies that preserve food matrix integrity. The authors conclude that food processing degree, particularly physical matrix integrity, must be given equal importance to nutrient composition in dietary guidelines and public health policy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The core threat of UPFs to health may originate profoundly from the industrial collapse of their physical 'food matrix.'", "This supraphysiological nutrient flux imposes a significant challenge on core metabolic organs, driving insulin resistance and hepatic de novo lipogenesis.", "The integrity of the food matrix is an indispensable dimension for evaluating the health value of food.", "This review calls for a fundamental shift in perspective within nutritional science and public health policy: from focusing solely on 'what is in our food' to equally considering 'what has been done to our food.'", "The health value of food arises from the organic unity of its structure and composition. Merely playing an 'arithmetic game' with nutrients on top of an already collapsed industrial matrix is a misleading marketing strategy."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Dietary impact on fasting and stimulated GLP-1 secretion in different metabolic conditions – a narrative review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10972717

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific narrative review published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (January 2024) examining the impact of diet on fasting and postprandial GLP-1 secretion across different metabolic conditions. 

**Key Points:**

- **GLP-1 Overview:** Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) is a gastrointestinal peptide secreted by intestinal L cells in response to food intake. It plays a central role in glucose metabolism by stimulating insulin secretion, promoting satiety, and slowing gastric emptying. GLP-1 analogs are used pharmacologically for treating type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

- **GLP-1 Secretion Mechanisms:** Postprandial GLP-1 secretion is triggered by nutrient-sensing via G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and membrane transporters (e.g., SGLT1). Nutrients (peptides, amino acids, fatty acids, SCFAs) and fermentable dietary fibers can stimulate secretion.

- **Metabolic Condition Differences:** The evidence is conflicting. Some studies show diminished GLP-1 response in individuals with obesity/overweight (OW), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), or T2DM compared to normal glucose tolerance (NGT), while others report elevated or unchanged responses. The meta-analysis of 18 studies found small and heterogeneous variations.

- **Glucose-Stimulated GLP-1 (OGTT):** 13 studies reviewed. Time to peak GLP-1 ranged 20-90 min, with peaks of 10.5-69 pmol/L. NGT groups peaked earlier (20-30 min) than IGT (30-45 min) or T2DM (30-90 min). Results were mixed: some found higher fasting/AUC in T2DM, others found lower, and some found no significant differences.

- **Food-Stimulated GLP-1 (MMTT/Meal Challenges):** 7 studies reviewed. Most reported impaired GLP-1 response in (pre)diabetes, though some found no differences. Meal composition, especially macronutrient ratios and meal size, impacted secretion.

- **Key factors influencing GLP-1:** BMI (inverse relationship), sex (higher in females), age, glucose tolerance status, and antidiabetic treatment.

- **Conclusion:** The review highlights the potential of nutritional and physiologic stimulation of GLP-1 secretion as a preventive or synergistic method for improving glucose metabolism. Further research is needed to account for confounding factors like BMI and sex.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), a gastrointestinal peptide and central mediator of glucose metabolism, is secreted by L cells in the intestine in response to food intake.", "Postprandial secretion of GLP-1 is triggered by nutrient-sensing via transporters and G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).", "Some studies showed diminished glucose- or meal-stimulated GLP-1 response in participants with T2DM, IGT, or OW compared with those with NGT, whereas other studies have reported an elevated or unchanged GLP-1 response in T2DM or IGT.", "Meal composition, especially the relationship between macronutrients and interventions targeting the microbiome can impact postprandial GLP-1 secretion, although it is not clear which macronutrients are strong stimulants of GLP-1.", "The results presented in this review highlight the potential of nutritional and physiologic stimulation of GLP-1 secretion."

SUMMARY:

# Summary: The GLP-1 Effect on Food Reformulation

This article (published January 15, 2026) from Ingredion examines how GLP-1 medications (e.g., Ozempic®, Wegovy®, Mounjaro®) are fundamentally reshaping consumer eating patterns and creating new demands for nutrient-dense, high-protein, high-fiber, portion-controlled foods. Approximately 1 in 8 U.S. adults has used a GLP-1 drug, with ~6% (15+ million people) currently using a prescription. The global anti-obesity drug market is projected to reach $82.55 billion by 2032 (18.01% CAGR).

## Key Consumer Types & Nutritional Needs

Three distinct consumer groups emerge:
1. **Current GLP-1 users** – face appetite suppression, GI side effects, muscle loss concerns
2. **Exiting GLP-1 users** – seeking maintenance solutions (39% stop within 3 months, 50% within 12 months)
3. **Health-inspired consumers** – adopting GLP-1-like eating patterns without medication

--- SOURCE 1: Hall 2019 UPF Study: 500 Hidden Calories Nobody Tasted — FitChef ---
URL: https://fitchef.com/studies/hall-2019-ultra-processed-food-study

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Hall 2019 UPF Study: The NIH Ultra-Processed Food Trial

**Core Finding:** A landmark randomized controlled trial from the NIH (Hall et al., 2019, *Cell Metabolism*) demonstrated that ultra-processed food causes overeating and weight gain through eating **speed** — not taste preference.

**Methodology:** 20 adults (10 men, 10 women; average age 31, BMI ~27) lived in an NIH metabolic ward for 28 days. They spent 2 weeks on an ultra-processed diet and 2 weeks on an unprocessed diet in random order. Both diets were matched for calories offered, macronutrients, fiber, sugar, and sodium. Participants ate ad libitum (as much as they wanted).

**Key Results:**

- **508 extra calories per day** consumed on ultra-processed food (p = 0.0001) — despite both diets rated equally pleasant and familiar.
- **Weight change:** 0.9 kg gained on ultra-processed food; 0.9 kg lost on unprocessed food — in just 14 days each.
- **Eating speed:** Ultra-processed food consumed 17 calories/minute faster. At a 20-minute meal, that's ~340 calories before gut satiety hormones can signal fullness.
- **Satiety hormones:** PYY (appetite-suppressing hormone) was significantly higher after unprocessed food.
- **Weight gain was mostly body fat**, fully reversible by switching to real food.
- Extra eating occurred almost entirely at **breakfast and lunch** — dinner and snacking barely budged.
- Unprocessed diet cost **42% more** ($151 vs $106/week per person).

**The Mechanism:** The key driver is not taste or addiction, but **physics** — ultra-processed food is softer, requires fewer chews, is eaten faster, and clears the plate before the body's satiety signals can respond. A separate analysis of 327 foods across 5 countries confirmed the gradient: unprocessed foods at 36 kcal/min, processed at 54, ultra-processed at 69.

**Replications:** Three international replications confirmed the direction:
- **Japan (Hamano 2024):** 9 men gained 1.1 kg more, ate 814 extra kcal/day, with significantly **lower chewing frequency** on UPF.
- **UK (Dicken 2025):** 55 adults — even "healthy" ultra-processed food (meeting government guidelines) produced less weight loss.
- **Forde 2020:** Eating rate gradient confirmed across 327 foods from 5 countries.

**Criticisms Addressed:** The ultra-processed diet had slightly less protein (14% vs 15.6%), which could explain ~half the gap via protein leverage. The other half aligns with the eating-speed data. The NOVA classification system is broad, but the nutrient-matching design already accounts for this.

**Practical Implications:** 55% of American calories come from ultra-processed food (62% for children). The solution isn't willpower — it's changing what's on the plate. Swapping the fastest-disappearing items (e.g., packaged cereal for eggs/cut fruit) at breakfast and lunch targets the meals where the speed mechanism is strongest.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Nobody preferred the ultra-processed meals. Then the data showed they ate five hundred extra calories a day of food they didn't even like more.", "The food doesn't taste better. It just disappears faster than your body can count.", "Ultra-processed food was consumed seventeen calories per minute faster than unprocessed food — and the gut's 'stop eating' hormones couldn't keep pace.", "Three-quarters of what's on American grocery shelves is ultra-processed — and it costs roughly half as much as the alternative.", "When both sides ate real food, low-carb and low-fat lost the same weight."

- Negative correlations between food addiction symptoms and connectivity in executive control regions (e.g., left DLPFC).

**Conclusions:** There was a lack of consistency in activation across studies, likely due to heterogeneity in study designs, participant characteristics, food cues, and paradigms. The review notes that few studies reported nutritional composition of food cues or standardized fasting protocols. ## Systematic Review: Neurobiological Insights into the Effects of Ultra-Processed Food on Lipid Metabolism and Associated Mental Health Conditions

**Published:** Frontiers in Nutrition, 21 January 2026, Volume 12 - 2025  
**Authors:** Emily Poon, Christine Li, Daniel Schweitzer, Isaac Akefe (University of Queensland, Mater Hospital, Charles Darwin University)

### Background & Objectives
Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) account for approximately 38% of the adult diet. This scoping review aimed to uncover the association between UPF consumption, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and increased risk of mental illnesses including depression, anxiety, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), eating disorders, and food addiction. It also explored underlying biological and behavioral mechanisms.

### Methodology
Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive search across PubMed, Web of Science, and EMBASE was conducted. Of 1,567 studies identified, 123 studies published between 2020-2025 were included after screening. English-language studies involving participants without significant comorbidities were included.

### Key Findings

**Depression:** Multiple studies demonstrated a significant, dose-dependent association between UPF consumption and increased depression risk. Individuals in the highest quartile of UPF intake had significantly greater risk of depression. UPF consumption during pregnancy was associated with increased odds of depressive symptoms in offspring. Specific UPF types implicated included sugar-sweetened beverages, energy drinks, fast foods, fried foods, processed meat, and smoked foods.

**Proposed Mechanisms:**
1. **Systemic low-grade inflammation:** Saturated fatty acids activate TLR4 receptors on macrophages and microglia, triggering NF-κB signaling and pro-inflammatory cytokine production (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, CRP)
2. **Altered neuronal signaling:** Particularly dopamine and serotonin pathways
3. **Gut-brain axis disruption:** High UPF intake decreases SCFA production, compromising BBB integrity
4. **Neuroinflammation:** Inflammatory cytokines cross BBB, leading to microglial activation and impaired neurogenesis
5. **HPA axis dysregulation:** Hyperpalatability contributes to stress hormone dysregulation
6. **Advanced glycation end products (AGEs):** Formed during high-temperature processing, contributing to neuroinflammation and neurotoxicity
7. **Hormonal dysregulation:** BPA and contaminants from food packaging alter gut microbiome

**Lipid Metabolism & Mental Health:** Key lipid subtypes implicated included saturated fatty acids, trans-fatty acids, monounsaturated fatty acids, polyunsaturated fatty acids (omega-3 and omega-6), and cholesterol. UPFs alter blood lipid profiles, reduce membrane fluidity, and impair neurotransmission.

**Geographic Distribution:** Studies originated from Brazil (most), China, USA, Australia, UK, Iran, Spain, and others, suggesting global interest.

**Publication Trend:** Most studies published between 2022-2025, with peak in 2024.

### Conclusions
There is a strong association between UPF consumption, disrupted lipid metabolism, and increased risk of mental disorders in populations without significant comorbidities. Diets rich in minimally processed foods appear protective. The findings support public health initiatives aimed at reducing UPF consumption to mitigate mental health burden. Future studies should focus on mechanistic pathways to provide evidence for targeted dietary and policy interventions.

### Therapeutic Implications
- Promote Mediterranean and DASH diets
- Encourage substitution of UPFs with minimally processed foods
- Implement food labeling, taxation, and marketing regulation
- Consider sex-specific and age-specific dietary recommendations
- Low-AGE cooking methods (boiling, steaming instead of frying)
</summary>

URL: https://www.foodtimes.eu/consumers-and-health/bliss-effect-ultra-processed-food

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The article examines the "Bliss effect" in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) — a phenomenon where combinations of fats, sugars, and salt create synergistic sensory experiences that override normal satiety mechanisms and drive overconsumption. Originally developed in pharmacology, the Bliss independence model describes how combined stimuli produce effects greater than the sum of individual components.

Investigative journalist Michael Moss, in his book "Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us" (2013), revealed how food corporations like Kraft, Coca-Cola, Frito-Lay, and Nestlé deliberately engineer products to hit the "bliss point" — the precise combination of salt, sugar, and fat that triggers maximum dopamine release and craving. Research by Fazzino et al. (2019) identified three hyper-palatable food clusters: fat + sodium, fat + simple sugars, and carbohydrates + sodium, with consumption increases of up to 30%.

The article covers neurobiological mechanisms, including dopamine release in the mesolimbic pathway, though a 2024 study by Darcey et al. found highly variable individual dopamine responses to UPFs. The Yale Food Addiction Scale indicates approximately 15-20% of adults may meet criteria for food addiction.

--- SOURCE 30: The power of product: how food advertising affects children’s perceptions of child and non-child targeted food advertising? ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487379

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a qualitative research article published in BMC Public Health (2025) examining how children aged 6–12 perceive child-targeted versus non-child-targeted food advertising. The study, conducted by researchers from the University of Ottawa, Université Laval, and University of Calgary, involved 17 children (11 girls, 6 boys) who participated in online interviews where they were shown four advertisements: child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads for both healthy (plain milk) and unhealthy (chocolate) products.

**Key Background:** The study notes that approximately 30% of Canadian children aged 5–17 have overweight or obesity, and ultra-processed foods account for 49.1% of caloric intake among children aged 2–5 and 54.2% among those aged 6–12. Children are exposed to nearly 2,000 unhealthy food ads annually on television and over 4,000 on digital platforms in Canada.

**Methods:** Open-ended interviews were conducted via Zoom, with thematic analysis using a hybrid deductive-inductive coding approach. The ads featured brands not readily available in Canada (Milka, Dove, Arla) to minimize prior brand familiarity.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Awareness:** Most children could identify the product being advertised but showed no brand awareness, as expected with unfamiliar brands.
2. **Attitudes:** Most children expressed positive perceptions of the ads, regardless of whether they were child-targeted or non-child-targeted. Reasons for liking included: (i) seeing people eating the product, (ii) positive emotional appeal, (iii) pre-existing affinity with the product, and (iv) visibility of the product. Notably, the child-targeted milk ad (featuring an animated cookie character) was less well-received, with some children finding it "creepy" or confusing.
3. **Purchase Intent:** Most children expressed "negative purchase intent" for all ads due to pre-existing aversion to the product. Even children who liked the product often expressed negative purchase intent because they preferred other brands or flavors.
4. **Perceived Target Audience:** Children considered the type of product over marketing techniques when determining who the ad was for. Themes included "product for everyone" and "product for people that like the product."

**Conclusions:** Children's perceptions, purchase intent, and perceived targeted audience did not differ significantly between child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads. The study underscores the critical role of the product itself (rather than marketing techniques) in influencing children's responses to ads. The authors recommend that public policies and advertising regulations focus on restricting promotions of unhealthy products rather than solely addressing marketing techniques or target audiences.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: The collapse of the food matrix: how ultra-processed foods impact satiety ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2026.1737280/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article, published in Frontiers in Nutrition on May 5, 2026, proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the primary health threat of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) stems not merely from their poor nutritional composition but from the industrial collapse of their physical "food matrix." The authors, led by Xinna Wang and colleagues from Chinese medical universities, hypothesize that this structural disintegration triggers a top-down cascade of dysregulation across multiple physiological systems.

The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This leads to metabolic dysregulation including insulin resistance, de novo lipogenesis, and mitochondrial stress. Finally, the impoverished matrix combined with chemical additives causes gut microbiome imbalance, compromised intestinal barrier function, and systemic low-grade chronic inflammation via metabolic endotoxemia.

Key evidence cited includes Hall's landmark randomized controlled trial showing that participants on nutrient-matched ultra-processed diets consumed ~500 kcal/day more and gained weight. Epidemiological data show UPF consumers have 15% increased all-cause mortality risk (HR=1.15), 11% increased cardiovascular disease risk (HR=1.11), and each 10% increase in UPF intake associates with 10% higher type 2 diabetes risk (RR=1.10).

The review critiques "nutritionism" and fortified UPFs, arguing that adding isolated nutrients to a collapsed matrix cannot restore health value. It calls for methodological innovation, multi-omics research, clinical translation studies, and development of "gentle" processing technologies that preserve food matrix integrity. The authors conclude that food processing degree, particularly physical matrix integrity, must be given equal importance to nutrient composition in dietary guidelines and public health policy.
</summary>

Merely playing an 'arithmetic game' with nutrients on top of an already collapsed industrial matrix is a misleading marketing strategy."

--- SOURCE 2: Ultra-Processed Foods and Metabolic Dysfunction: A Narrative Review of Dietary Processing, Behavioral Drivers and Chronic Disease Risk ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2218-1989/15/12/784

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review article published in *Metabolites* (2025, Volume 15, Issue 12, 784) by Tyler J. Godsey, Travis Eden, and Sam R. Emerson from Oklahoma State University. The review synthesizes evidence on how ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and dietary processing interact with dietary quality, energy balance, and biological pathways to influence metabolic health.

**Key findings:**
- UPFs (defined via the NOVA classification system - Group 4) are industrially manufactured, ready-to-eat products that are highly energy dense, typically high in added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, and low in protein and fiber.
- UPFs now make up ~57-58% of the average US adult's daily caloric intake, up from 53.5% in 2001-2002, with annual per capita consumption increasing ~142% since 1960.
- High UPF intake is consistently associated with reduced diet quality, increased energy density, faster eating rates, and activation of reward pathways, leading to excessive energy intake and adiposity.
- The article traces the history of UPFs back to the Malthusian Trap concerns and 20th-century agricultural/industrial advancements, including US government incentives for commodity crops.
- Key critiques of the NOVA system include its focus on processing over formulation, lack of evidence that UPF reduction is more beneficial than other dietary guidelines, and inconsistencies in food categorization.
- UPFs promote overconsumption through hyperpalatability, altered nutrient profiles (high saturated fat, added sugar, sodium), low water content, high energy density, faster eating rates (especially soft-textured and liquid UPFs), and disruption of evolved nutrient-flavor associations.
- Over 10,000 food additives have been approved over the last 60 years, with concerns about the "cocktail effect" of cumulative exposures.
- While cross-sectional and cohort evidence is extensive linking UPFs to obesity, metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and gut microbiome alterations, causal intervention trials and mechanistic human work remain limited.
- The review concludes that UPFs may influence chronic disease risk through both their unbalanced nutrient profiles AND additional effects introduced by industrial processing, calling for real-world intervention studies.
</summary>

The article notes that GLP-1 agonist drugs (e.g., Ozempic, Wegovy) mimic natural GLP-1 but at much higher levels, which can cause side effects like nausea. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from News-Medical, written by Vijay Kumar Malesu (Ph.D. in Biotechnology) and last updated February 23, 2026, explains the science of appetite control through the lens of hormonal regulation via the gut–brain axis. It covers how dietary protein, carbohydrates, fats, and fiber influence key appetite-regulating hormones including GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, CCK, and leptin.

**Key points:**
- **Hormonal control:** Appetite is regulated by bidirectional communication between the GI tract, adipose tissue, and the central nervous system (hypothalamic arcuate nucleus and brainstem). GLP-1 and PYY (from enteroendocrine L-cells) reduce hunger after eating, while ghrelin is the primary hunger hormone that rises preprandially.
- **Protein:** High-protein meals increase GLP-1 and PYY release and may suppress postprandial ghrelin, though ad libitum energy intake at subsequent meals may not differ significantly when calories and volume are matched.
- **Carbohydrates:** High glycemic index foods cause rapid glucose/insulin spikes and earlier hunger onset; low glycemic index foods prolong satiety. Dietary fiber (especially viscous fiber) slows digestion and enhances satiety.
- **Fats:** Fat intake stimulates CCK release. In an 8-week trial, postprandial CCK decreased in both low-carb and low-fat diet groups, suggesting energy restriction, rather than fat content per se, drives CCK responses.
- **Fiber:** Viscous fibers slow gastric emptying and glucose absorption. Fermentable fibers (resistant starch, beta-glucans) produce SCFAs that may alter GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, and leptin in animal models, but effects vary.
- **Human studies:** A randomized crossover trial found high-protein meals increased GLP-1 and PYY but did not significantly reduce subsequent ad libitum intake. An 8-week trial showed low-carb diets led to greater weight loss, reduced postprandial ghrelin, and increased subjective fullness.
- **Translational insights:** A balanced diet rich in protein, high-fiber/low-glycemic carbohydrates, and fats can regulate multiple satiety hormones. Leptin resistance is common in obesity. Fermentable fibers affect appetite through viscosity, fermentability, and gut hormone modulation rather than SCFA production alone.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Obesity and the MC4R Gene ---
URL: https://www.gbhealthwatch.com/GND-Obesity-MC4R.php

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from GB HealthWatch provides a comprehensive overview of the relationship between the MC4R gene and obesity. The MC4R gene codes for the melanocortin 4 receptor, primarily found in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and satiety. Mutations in the MC4R gene are the most common genetic cause of obesity, accounting for 6-8% of severe inheritable obesity cases. A common variant (rs17782313, C-allele), carried by about 22% of the general population, increases obesity risk by 8% per copy and is associated with a BMI increase of 0.22. Carriers experience increased appetite and decreased satiety, leading to larger food intake, more frequent snacking, and preference for fatty foods.

The article explains the biological mechanism: hunger signals (like ghrelin) and satiety signals (like leptin and insulin) both function through MC4R via competitive binding of AgRP and α-MSH. When AgRP prevails, hunger results; when α-MSH prevails, satiety results.

To date, 166 MC4R mutations have been documented, with about 0.66% of the general population carrying one. In early-onset severe obesity populations, 6-8% carry MC4R loss-of-function mutations. These individuals typically develop obesity by age 3-4, with meals containing about three times the calories of non-carriers. Female carriers gain about twice the weight as male carriers.

Two gain-of-function mutations (V103I/rs2229616 and I251L/rs52820871) have protective effects against obesity, reducing risk by 20% and 48% respectively.

For management, the most effective approach for common variant carriers is calorie restriction through portion control and smart food choices. For loss-of-function mutation carriers, low-calorie dietary interventions, multidisciplinary approaches, and bariatric surgery are options, though weight regain is common.

The article also notes an evolutionary perspective: reduced MC4R activity may have provided survival advantages during food scarcity but is disadvantageous in modern food-abundant environments.
</summary>

Unhealthy dietary behaviors have led to a rise in nutrition-related noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), accounting for 11 million deaths in 2017. Taste is one of the main factors influencing food choices, and individual differences in taste perception may be explained by genetic variations.

- **Quality assessment:** Conducted using the validated Q-Genie tool

--- SOURCE 6: Food Addiction Debate: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment ---
URL: https://www.news-medical.net/health/Food-Addiction-Debate-Symptoms-Causes-and-Treatment.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from News-Medical discusses the ongoing debate surrounding food addiction, which describes addiction-like responses to ultra-processed foods (UPFs) but is not yet a formal diagnosis in the DSM-5 or ICD-11.

**Key points:**

- **Prevalence:** Meta-analytic data suggests 14% of adults and 12% of children globally exhibit addictive-like eating phenotypes, comparable to alcohol use disorder rates. However, estimates vary widely (e.g., 2.78% in a Rio de Janeiro household survey).

- **Symptoms:** Include intense cravings, loss of control, continued use despite negative consequences, and withdrawal-like symptoms (irritability, anxiety, anhedonia) when abstaining from refined carbohydrates.

- **Proposed mechanisms:** Dysregulation of mesolimbic dopaminergic reward pathways; UPFs combine high fat and refined sugar to engage reward pathways. Genetic factors, childhood traumatic experiences (CTEs), attachment insecurity, and emotional dysregulation are risk factors.

- **Debate:** Evidence supports each DSM-5 SUD criterion in the context of food. However, there is no consensus on diagnostic validity, as symptoms overlap with binge eating disorder and bulimia nervosa. Some researchers propose "ultra-processed food addiction" or "ultra-processed food use disorder" as potential diagnostic terms.

- **Treatment:** No established standard treatment exists. Current approaches include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), dietary modifications (harm reduction model), and emerging research on GLP-1 receptor agonists for reducing cravings. Abstinence-based approaches for specific trigger UPFs are discussed but not yet validated.

- **Assessment:** Should consider co-occurring eating disorders, trauma histories, and mental health concerns rather than focusing only on weight or willpower.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Current Status of Evidence for a New Diagnosis: Food Addiction-A Literature Review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2021.824936/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Frontiers in Psychiatry review article (published January 10, 2022) by Octavian Vasiliu systematically examines the current evidence for "food addiction" as a potential new diagnosis. The review evaluates five key dimensions: clinical criteria, validated instruments, epidemiology, pathophysiology, and treatment options.

Key findings include:
- **Definition**: Food addiction involves overconsumption of hyperpalatable foods (high in saturated fat, sugar, artificial flavors, sodium) in an addiction-like manner, activating similar neural pathways as drugs of abuse.
- **Diagnostic Criteria**: Largely extrapolated from DSM substance dependence criteria, including consuming more than intended, craving, preoccupation, and continued use despite negative consequences.
- **Prevalence**: Approximately 20% in the general population based on meta-analytic research using the Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS). Higher in females (12% vs 6.4%), older adults (age >35), and obese/overweight individuals (25% vs 11%).
- **Psychometric Instruments**: The YFAS (and its variants YFAS 2.0, mYFAS, YFAS-C) have been validated for measuring food addiction severity across adult and child populations.
- **Pathophysiology**: Involves reward dysfunction (dopamine D2 receptor abnormalities), impulsivity, and emotion dysregulation. Similar neural activation patterns found in food addiction and substance use disorders, including elevated activity in reward circuitry and reduced activity in inhibitory control regions.
- **Treatment**: No clinical trials specifically for food addiction exist. Potential treatments are extrapolated from related disorders and include pharmacotherapy (lorcaserin, naltrexone/bupropion, topiramate), psychotherapy (CBT, interpersonal therapy, dialectical behavior therapy), neuromodulation (tDCS, rTMS), and lifestyle interventions.

The article concludes that while food addiction is not currently recognized in DSM-5 or ICD-10, substantial evidence supports its existence as a clinical entity, though more research is needed on diagnostic criteria and treatment.
</summary>

The paper addresses the evolutionary paradox of why humans are predisposed to addictive behaviors despite their detrimental effects on health and reproductive success. It reviews biological and psychological mechanisms of both substance and behavioral addictions through an evolutionary lens.

- Behavioral addictions (e.g., video games, social media, gambling) emulate ancestrally beneficial behaviors, making them appealing yet often irrelevant to contemporary success—a concept known as evolutionary mismatch.
- The article explores emerging and future addictions, including potential addictions related to AI romantic relationships.
- Evolutionary insights have implications for how addiction is criminalized and stigmatized, and propose novel avenues for interventions.
- The emerging potential of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonists (targeting obesity) is noted as a possible natural counter to overactivation of the reward system via satiation mechanisms.
