## 5. POLICY AND REGULATORY APPROACHES

### Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labeling (FOPNL) in the Americas

A PAHO policy study examined the development, adoption, and implementation of front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FOPNL) systems across the WHO Region of the Americas (AMRO). Poor nutrition is one of the leading causes of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), especially in the WHO Region of the Americas [26]. In AMRO, all 35 countries have discussed FOPNL, 30 countries have formally introduced FOPNL, 11 have adopted FOPNL, and 7 countries (Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela) have implemented FOPNL as of August 2022 [26].

FOPNL has gradually spread and evolved to better protect health by increasingly adopting larger warning labels, contrasting background devices for better salience, using "excess" instead of "high in" to improve efficacy, and adopting the Pan American Health Organization's (PAHO) Nutrient Profile Model to better define nutrient thresholds [26]. Early evidence shows successful compliance (75-80%+ in Chile and Peru), decreased purchases of unhealthy products, and product reformulation [26].

### Chile's Warning Label Law

Chile was the first country to implement a mandatory, national front-of-package nutrient warning label policy (Law of Food Labeling and Advertising, passed in 2016, implemented in three progressively stricter phases: 2016, 2018, 2019) [29]. The law introduced mandatory black octagonal front-of-package nutrient warning labels for products high in sugar, salt, saturated fat, and calories; marketing restrictions protecting children; and bans on ultra-processed product sales in schools [28].

A study published in The Lancet Planetary Health (2021) examined changes in household food and beverage purchases following Chile's Phase 1 implementation. Compared to the counterfactual, overall calories purchased declined 16.4 kcal/capita/day (4%), overall sugar declined 11.5 kcal/capita/day (10%), saturated fat declined 2.2 kcal/capita/day (4%), and sodium content of overall purchases declined 27.7 mg/capita/day (5%). Among high-in purchases, relative to the counterfactual there were notable declines of 24% in calories purchased, 37% in sodium purchased, and 27% in sugar purchased [29].

In Phase 2 of the warning label law, Chilean households purchased 37% less sugar, 22% less sodium, 16% less saturated fat, and 23% fewer total calories from products with warning labels. These changes were equitable across socioeconomic groups [28]. In the final and most nutritionally strict phase of the law, a remarkable 94% of products required to display these labels had the appropriate labels—a stark contrast to low uptake of voluntary labeling programs in Australia and New Zealand [28]. Earlier evaluations of Phase 1 have demonstrated significant decreases in purchases of products high in 'nutrients of concern' as well as a 73% drop in Chilean children's exposure to TV for regulated food and beverages [28].

Chile's policy has inspired similar "stop sign" warning label policies across eight countries in the Americas [28]. The evaluations of Chile's policy clearly demonstrate the necessity of mandatory front-of-package labeling systems featuring nutrient warning labels, which have been shown to be the most effective in helping consumers identify unhealthy products [28].

### Mexico's Warning Labels

In Mexico, a modelling study projected that the warning labels could reduce the prevalence of obesity by 14.7% between 2018 and 2023, and save the country US$ 1.8 billion in obesity-related costs [26].

### Comparison of Mexico and US Labeling Policies

A study published in Preventing Chronic Disease (CDC, June 2026) compared changes in sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) consumption among adults in Mexico and the US before and after Mexico implemented mandatory front-of-package warning labels (FoPWLs) in 2020, while the US updated Nutrition Facts labels during the same period. From 2018–2019 to 2020–2023, any SSB consumption and SSB consumption frequency increased in the US (adjusted odds ratio, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.17–1.36; adjusted incidence rate ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.10–1.22, respectively). In Mexico, any SSB consumption also increased (adjusted odds ratio, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.00–1.22), but increases were smaller than in the US for any consumption (adjusted odds ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.77–0.99) and frequency (adjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.84–0.95). In sex-stratified models, Mexican women had a greater relative reduction in SSB volume than US women (adjusted regression coefficient, −304 mL/week; 95% CI, −593 to −16). The study concluded: "FoPWLs may help curb whether and how often adults consume SSBs. Additional measures may be needed to reduce the amount of SSBs consumed and the calories and added sugars consumed among people who already drink them" [27].

### Nutritional Warning Labels Globally

As of July 2023, 10 countries have implemented or are implementing mandatory warning labels: Chile, Peru, Mexico, Uruguay, Argentina, Israel (in place), and Canada, Colombia, Brazil, Venezuela (in implementation phase). Most use black octagonal "stop sign" designs [30]. Evidence indicates nutritional warning labels can be effective in promoting healthier purchases, improving consumer knowledge, and encouraging food companies to develop healthier products. In Chile, the mandatory labelling and marketing regulations led to reductions in purchases of "high in" foods, resulting in reductions in the energy (2.5%), sugar (10.2%), sodium (3.9%) and saturated fat (2.2%) of food purchases. Another evaluation focusing on "high in" beverages indicated purchases of these drinks decreased by 24% following mandatory introduction of the labels, with similar reductions in purchases seen across households with high and low levels of education [30].

### UK HFSS Regulations

The UK's HFSS (High in Fat, Sugar, and Salt) regulations mark one of the most sweeping changes in food marketing legislation in the UK [9]. The regulations restrict how products high in saturated fat, sugar, and salt can be marketed, advertised, and promoted [9].

**Timeline of Regulations:**
- **October 1, 2022**: Placement restrictions took effect in England, banning HFSS products from prominent retail positions (aisle ends, checkouts) in larger retailers (over 2,000 sq. ft., 50+ staff) [6][7][9].
- **October 2025**: Volume promotions ban (e.g., "Buy One, Get One Free") took effect in England as planned [7][9].
- **January 5, 2026**: Advertising restrictions (TV pre-9 PM watershed ban and paid online advertising limitations) came into force UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland) [7][8][9].
- **Spring 2026**: Wales intends to implement placement and promotion restrictions [7][9].
- **Autumn 2026**: Scotland expected to implement its own measures [7][9].
- Northern Ireland has not yet confirmed similar legislation [9].

**How HFSS Classification Works:** Products are scored using the Government Nutrient Profile Model (NPM). Points are added for calories, fats, sugars, and sodium (Category A). Points are subtracted for beneficial nutrients like fiber, protein, and fruit/vegetable content (Category C). A score of 4+ for foods or 1+ for drinks earns HFSS designation [6][7][9].

**Affected Product Categories (13 categories):** Soft drinks, crisps/savory snacks, breakfast cereals, chocolates/sweets, ice cream/frozen desserts, cakes/cupcakes, sweet biscuits/snack bars, morning goods (pastries/scones), desserts/puddings, sweetened yogurt/fromage frais, pizza, chips/potato products, ready meals/breaded products [9].

**Impact Data:** End-of-aisle promotions increased sugary drink sales by 51.7%. Early restrictions have shown healthier product sales up 5.6% and non-compliant product sales down 5.1% (per The Grocer and Kantar data) [9].

The UK's Soft Drinks Industry Levy (SDIL), implemented in 2018, is a two-tiered tax based on sugar concentration (£0.18/L for 5-8g sugar/100mL; £0.24/L for >8g/100mL). It led to reformulation removing 45 million kg of sugar annually. The proportion of high-sugar drinks in supermarkets fell from 49% to 15% (2015-2019). Sugar purchased from taxed drinks decreased by 35%. The tax is predicted to reduce dental caries by 3,600 cases and overweight/obesity by over 64,000 cases among under-18s [14].

### Sugar-Sweetened Beverage (SSB) Taxes

Over 130 jurisdictions across nearly 120 countries and territories have implemented taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) to date [14]. Data from the UK, Mexico, South Africa and other countries indicate that SSB taxes successfully reduce sugar consumption from SSBs, and SSB taxes have led to reformulation of products in the UK and other countries [14].

**Mexico** (2014): Introduced a 1 peso/L volumetric tax, leading to ~11% price rise on soft drinks. By 2016, there was a 37% reduction in SSB purchases. Over 10 years, the SSB tax is predicted to prevent 239,900 cases of obesity; of these, 39% would be in children. The tax is predicted to save almost $4 per $1 spent on implementation [14].

**United Kingdom** (2018): The Soft Drinks Industry Levy (SDIL) is a two-tiered tax based on sugar concentration. It led to reformulation removing 45 million kg of sugar from soft drinks each year. The proportion of high-sugar drinks in supermarkets fell from 49% to 15% (2015-2019). Sugar purchased from taxed drinks decreased by 35%. The tax is predicted to reduce dental caries by 3,600 cases and overweight/obesity by over 64,000 cases among under-18s [14].

**South Africa** (2018): The Health Promotion Levy (10% tax on sugary drinks, excluding fruit juices) led to a 29% reduction in carbonated drink purchases in urban areas and 51% reduction in sugar purchased. Lower socioeconomic groups showed a 57% drop in sugar from taxed drinks [14].

**Other Countries:** Portugal reported 7% reduction in SSB sales and 11% reduction in energy intake; Chile saw 22% reduction in higher-taxed drinks volume; and US cities: Berkeley reported 20% decrease in SSB consumption, Philadelphia reported 35% overall reduction in SSB sales [14].

**Berkeley, California:** The first US SSB tax, enacted in 2014 and implemented in 2015 at $0.01 per ounce, received 76% voter support. Consumption of SSBs decreased 21% in Berkeley and increased 4% in comparison cities (P = .046). Water consumption increased more in Berkeley (+63%) than in comparison cities (+19%; P<.01). The 21% reduction in SSB consumption represents a price elasticity of -2.6, larger than the average elasticity of -1.2 found in other studies. Only 5% of Berkeley residents who previously bought SSBs in the city reported switching purchases to another city. Berkeley's SSB tax generated more than $9 million, which was allocated for public health and equity from 2015 to 2021. No retailers reported raising food prices, indicating that beverage industry claims that SSB taxes are 'grocery taxes' are false and deceptive [11][15].

A NBER working paper found that in Berkeley, across all models, less than half of the tax was passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. Averaging all three sizes of Coke and Pepsi, DDD models indicated that only 21.7% of the tax was passed through to consumers. The authors suggest that the city-level nature of the tax makes it easy to evade through cross-border shopping (Berkeley is just 10.5 square miles), which may discourage retailers from passing the tax through to consumers for fear of losing sales. This implies that city-level SSB taxes may be less effective at changing prices and consumption than taxes at higher levels of government [12].

**Oakland, California:** A CHOICES Project analysis projected that a proposed $0.01/ounce excise tax on SSBs in Oakland would prevent 2,140 cases of obesity, 90 cases of diabetes annually, and save more in healthcare costs than it costs to implement (net savings of $18.1 million over 10 years). The tax is cost-saving with $30.40 in healthcare cost savings per $1 invested. It is estimated to generate approximately $12 million in annual revenue. Because of the elasticity of -1.21, the analyses indicated that households will spend less on SSBs after the tax, providing disposable income for other purchases. Greater health benefits will accrue to low-income consumers who on average consume more SSBs than higher-income consumers [13].

### School Food Policies

The USDA Food and Nutrition Administration published a final rule titled "Child Nutrition Programs: Meal Patterns Consistent With the 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines for Americans," effective July 1, 2024, with required changes phased in starting school year 2025-26 at the earliest. The rule updates school nutrition standards including: first-time limits on added sugars in school breakfasts and lunches, reducing sodium gradually, maintaining whole grain-rich requirements, and allowing flavored milk with no more than 10 grams of added sugars per 8 ounces by 2025-26. Research shows that school meals are the most nutritious food source for American schoolchildren, but currently about 17% of calories in school breakfasts and 11% in school lunches come from added sugars, and over 90% of schoolchildren consume more sodium than recommended. USDA has invested more than $5 billion to support school nutrition [23].

The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs) released in January 2026 by USDA and HHS include, for the first time, urging Americans to limit consumption of "highly processed" foods (recommending avoidance of chips, cookies, candy with added sugars and sodium, and sugar-sweetened beverages). CDC survey data shows youth ages 18 and under consume more than 60% of their daily calories from ultraprocessed foods [24].

California became the first state to ban ultra-processed foods in K-12 through a recently signed law that will phase those products out of school meals starting in 2029 [22].

However, school nutrition directors face major barriers. A School Nutrition Association (SNA) survey found that 95% of school nutrition directors are seriously or moderately concerned about financial sustainability three years from now. More than 93% cited the need for more staff, culinary training, equipment, and infrastructure to reduce reliance on UPFs. 79% of respondents reported an "extreme need" for increased funding to expand scratch cooking and reduce ultraprocessed foods [22][24]. 98% of operators are challenged by food costs, 70% say federal reimbursement rates (max $4.60/meal) are insufficient to cover costs, and over 90% need more staff, training, equipment, and infrastructure. A UC Berkeley study found California alone needs $5B to bring all kitchens to scratch-cooking capacity [25].

## 6. GLOBAL TRADE AND FOOD SYSTEMS

### The NOVA Classification System

The NOVA food classification system, developed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in 2009, categorizes foods based on the nature, extent, and purpose of industrial processing into four groups: (1) Unprocessed or minimally processed foods (e.g., fresh fruits, vegetables, legumes); (2) Processed culinary ingredients (e.g., oils, salt, sugar); (3) Processed foods (e.g., canned fruit, cheese, freshly baked bread); and (4) Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) — industrial formulations with multiple ingredients and additives, often hyperpalatable, with little intact whole foods [31][33][34][35].

Ultra-processed foods are "formulations of ingredients, mostly of exclusive industrial use, typically created by series of industrial techniques and processes (hence 'ultra-processed')" [33]. Processes and ingredients used for the manufacture of ultra-processed foods are designed to create highly profitable products (low-cost ingredients, long shelf-life, powerfully branded) [33].

The overall purpose of ultra-processing is to create branded, convenient (durable, ready to consume), attractive (hyper-palatable) and highly profitable (low-cost ingredients) food products designed to displace all other food groups [31].

The NOVA system shows high inter-rater reliability for categorizing foods [34]. The framework has inspired Brazilian dietary guidelines, advising "avoid ultra-processed foods" [34], and has been adopted by PAHO, WHO, and French/Canadian policies [34].

A critical commentary published in Trends in Food Science & Technology (October 2021) argues that the NOVA classification system is fundamentally flawed from a food science perspective. The authors argue that NOVA does not truly classify by processing level but rather by ingredient count, leading to misleading and pejorative connotations about commercially manufactured foods. They state that "healthiness has no direct or absolute correlation either with the number of ingredients, intensity, or number of processes or with the fact that the food has been processed in households or a large industrial plant" [35].

### Global UPF Consumption Trends

Ultra-processed products are not modified foods, but formulations mostly of cheap industrial sources of dietary energy and nutrients plus additives [31]. The most striking change in food systems of high-income countries, and now of low- and middle-income countries, is displacement of dietary patterns based on meals and dishes prepared from unprocessed or minimally processed foods by those that are increasingly based on ultra-processed food and drink products [31].

In 2000, sales of ultra-processed foods and beverages in the upper-middle-income countries were one third of those in the high-income countries. Fifteen years later, they were more than half [31]. UPFs now account for over half of total calorie intake in countries like the US (≈58%) and the UK (≈57%) [34]. Annual per capita consumption of UPFs is estimated at 100 kg in Western Europe and 120 kg in North America and Australasia, with ultra-processed drinks accounting for an additional 180 kg and 120 kg, respectively [3]. In the US, over 70% of packaged foods are ultra-processed, and these foods make up 70-80% of the diet for the top consumers in the US, UK, and Australia [3]. The review concludes that "the ever-increasing production and consumption of these products is a world crisis, to be confronted, checked and reversed as part of the work of the UN Sustainable Development Goals and its Decade of Nutrition" [31].

### Global Trade Liberalization and UPF Imports

**New Zealand Case Study:** A study published in Global Health (2026) examined New Zealand's food and beverage imports from 1990–2023, categorized by the Nova classification system, alongside progressive trade liberalization. The share of ultra-processed foods (G4) in total food and beverage imports increased over the study period, from 15.7 kg per capita (8.7% of food imports) in 1990 to 103.8 kg per capita (21.8%) in 2023. The per capita import volume of food-derivatives/additives (UPF inputs like industrial sweeteners, modified oils, flavorings, and texture enhancers) increased dramatically since 1990, surpassing all other UPF subgroups since 2011. By 2023, NZ imported 28 kg per capita of these UPF inputs, with industrial sweeteners alone accounting for 20.7 kg per capita. Tariff rates were reduced to zero or low levels for all food products between 1990–2023. The authors conclude that 34 years of progressive trade liberalization in NZ were characterized by an increasing proportion of imported products being ultra-processed foods/beverages and their inputs, underscoring the need for policy interventions to counteract the impact of these trends on food environments and population nutrition. NZ children under five years appear to consume approximately half their energy intake from UPF, and the known health and wellbeing impacts of UPF consumption are disproportionately borne by Māori and Pasifika children, and those living in the most deprived areas [16].

### WTO and Trade Policy

A WTO Data Blog post (December 2025) examined the relationship between food processing levels and global trade flows, using the NOVA food classification system. From 1996 to 2024, global imports of unprocessed foods grew more rapidly than those of processed or ultra-processed foods, both in terms of total value and on a per capita basis. Average MFN tariffs tend to be lower for unprocessed foods than for processed or ultra-processed foods, but patterns vary significantly across economies—some apply lower tariffs to ultra-processed foods, potentially incentivizing their trade. An increasing number of food-related regulations are being notified to the WTO under the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT), with some being raised as 'specific trade concerns' in the TBT Committee [18].

International commerce in processed foods substantially exceeds the value of unprocessed agricultural commodities and is expanding more rapidly. U.S. food manufacturers' sales through foreign affiliates were more than quadruple the value of processed food exports from the United States. Patterns of global commerce in processed foods are influenced by public policies addressing transportation, communication, rules for regional and multinational trade, food product and process standards, the environment, and intellectual property [19].

### FAO Report on Trade and Nutrition

The FAO's "The State of Agricultural Commodity Markets 2024" report offers guidance and data on integrating nutrition goals into food trade policies. The report examines global trade flows of nutrients and possible drivers of obesity [20].

### Market Strategies of Multinational Food Corporations

A systematic review and document analysis published in Globalization and Health (2021) by Wood, Williams, Nagarajan, and Sacks examined the market strategies used by dominant processed food manufacturers to increase and consolidate their power. The study identified 21 market strategies categorized into six interconnected strategic objectives: (i) reduce intense competition with equivalent-sized rivals and maintain dominance over smaller rivals; (ii) raise barriers to market entry by new competitors; (iii) counter the threat of market disruptors and drive dietary displacement in favor of their products; (iv) increase firm buyer power over suppliers; (v) increase firm seller power over retailers and distributors; and (vi) leverage informational power asymmetries in relations with consumers. The authors highlight that ultra-processed foods (UPFs), which now constitute about half of total dietary energy in developed economies, are associated with poorer diet quality, higher all-cause mortality, obesity, and diet-related chronic diseases. The concentrated market power of dominant food companies is a public health concern because it allows them to shape food value chains toward production of unhealthy products and generate excess profits that fund lobbying, marketing, and other practices undermining public health [17].

### Environmental Impacts of UPFs

UPFs account for 17-39% of total diet-related energy use, 36-45% of total diet-related biodiversity loss, up to a third of total diet-related greenhouse gas emissions, land use and food waste, and up to a quarter of total diet-related water-use by adults in a number of high-income countries [1]. UPF production relies on commodity ingredients like palm oil, soya, wheat, maize, milk, eggs, and meat, which have driven ecosystem destruction (e.g., rainforest clearing for palm oil in Indonesia, Cerrado conversion for soya in Brazil) [1]. The authors conclude that UPFs are "potentially counterproductive" to sustainable food system objectives and call on policymakers to regulate UPF production, availability, and consumption [1].

In wealthy countries, UPFs can be responsible for up to one-third of all the climate emissions that come from what people eat [3]. In Belgium, UPFs drive ~50% of dietary climate and land impacts; in the Netherlands, 45% of food-related emissions; in France, ~25% of dietary climate, energy, water, and land impacts [3].

## 7. ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS: HEALTH OUTCOMES AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

### Definitions and Prevalence

Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are defined as "formulations of ingredients, mostly of exclusive industrial use, resulting from a series of industrial processes" [4]. UPFs are now prevalent in diets worldwide, contributing up to >50% of energy intake in high-income countries and up to 30% in middle-income countries, with consumption rapidly increasing [4].

73% of the U.S. food supply is ultra-processed, and UPF comprises almost 60% of the total energy intake of U.S. adults, with consumption increasing over the past two decades [5]. UPF intake varies by race/ethnicity (higher in Black individuals, lower in Hispanic/Latino individuals) and socioeconomic status (higher intake among lower income and education groups) [5].

### Health Outcomes

A narrative review in Nutrients (2020) by Elizabeth, Machado, Zinöcker, Baker, and Lawrence systematically examined 43 studies, finding that 37 found dietary UPF exposure associated with at least one adverse health outcome. No study reported an association between UPF and beneficial health outcomes. In adults, UPF consumption was associated with overweight, obesity, cardio-metabolic risks (e.g., metabolic syndrome, hypertension), cancer, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, irritable bowel syndrome, depression, frailty conditions, and all-cause mortality. In children/adolescents, associations were found with cardio-metabolic risks (e.g., higher total cholesterol, LDL-C, triglycerides, waist circumference) and asthma [4].

A randomized controlled trial (Hall et al. 2019) showed that participants on a UPF diet consumed ~508 more kcal/day and gained 0.9 kg, while losing 0.9 kg on an unprocessed diet [4]. Ecological studies across 80 countries linked UPF sales volume increases with rising mean BMI trajectories [4].

Meta-analyses show direct associations between UPF consumption and 71% of health parameters studied, including mortality, cancer, mental health, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity. The most convincing evidence is for incident cardiovascular disease mortality, type 2 diabetes risk, and anxiety outcomes and combined mental health disorder. Not all UPFs are equal: subgroup analyses show sugary beverages and animal-based products as the main drivers of adverse health outcomes, while some UPFs (cereals, yogurt, dark breads) show inverse associations with disease risk [5].

A review published in the Journal of Future Foods (March 2027) by Zhang et al. examined the global surge in consumption of UPFs, noting accelerated growth following the COVID-19 pandemic. The review synthesized evidence from eight longitudinal cohort studies encompassing 522,682 participants, revealing correlations between UPF intake and elevated incidence of obesity, cardiometabolic disorders (cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes), functional gastrointestinal syndromes, and specific cancers. The article discusses the addiction potential of UPFs due to additives including fat, caffeine, and sugar [2].

### UPFs and Reproductive Health

A recent nutritional intake study led by Jessica M. Preston, published in Cell Metabolism, followed 43 men aged 20-35 over three weeks, rotating between ultra-processed and unprocessed diets. On the ultra-processed diet (where ~77% of calories came from industrially prepared foods), men gained about 1 kg more fat, and markers like LDL cholesterol and blood pressure worsened, even when calories were matched. Key findings included declines in follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which helps the testes make sperm, with the strongest drops seen in the group given an extra 500 calories daily. Sperm motility also trended downward. The study also detected changes in thyroid and appetite hormones [12].

### Diet Quality and Nutrient Profiles

A 2019 FAO technical report by Monteiro et al. found consistent significant direct dose-response associations between ultra-processed food intake and NCD-promoting nutrients (free/added sugars, saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, energy density) across studied countries. For example, free sugar content in Mexican diets ranged from 7.4% of energy in the lowest quintile of ultra-processed intake to 17.5% in the highest. Inverse associations were found with NCD-protective nutrients (protein, fibre, potassium, phytoestrogens) and various micronutrients (vitamins A, C, D, E, B12, calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc) [33].

<Scaling Rules>

Investigate the relationship between ultra-processed foods and modern health problems, producing a comprehensive scientific and scholarly report that synthesizes the latest worldwide research across four key dimensions:

1. **Biological Mechanisms**: How food processing technologies, additives, and novel ingredients affect human physiology and neurology in ways that are still being discovered—including gut-brain axis disruption, microbiome alterations, endocrine disruption, neuroinflammation, and reward pathway dysregulation.

2. **Industry Influence on Behavior**: How the food industry's product design (e.g., hyper-palatability, texture, nutrient ratios), marketing strategies, and formulation techniques shape eating behaviors, override satiety signals, and contribute to overconsumption.

3. **Individual Susceptibility**: Why certain populations or individuals are more vulnerable to processed food addiction, metabolic dysfunction, and adverse health outcomes—including genetic, epigenetic, microbiome, psychological, and sociodemographic factors.

4. **Environmental and Structural Factors**: How food deserts, food swamps, economic inequality, food pricing, marketing targeting, and built environment factors constrain or complicate individual food choice and dietary quality.

Prioritize original research papers and official journal publications over secondary summaries. Include international perspectives from research conducted worldwide, not limited to any single country. The report should be written in a scholarly format suitable for a healthcare researcher, with appropriate citations and scientific rigor. args.research_topic:
BIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS ON HUMAN HEALTH

Conduct a comprehensive literature review on the biological mechanisms by which ultra-processed foods (UPFs) affect human physiology, metabolism, and neurology. This is for a scholarly scientific report. Focus on the following subtopics:

1. GUT-BRAIN AXIS DISRUPTION: How emulsifiers, artificial sweeteners, and other food additives disrupt the gut-brain axis signaling pathways. Include research on vagus nerve signaling alterations, changes in gut hormone secretion (GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, leptin), and how these affect satiety signaling.

2. MICROBIOME ALTERATIONS: How UPF consumption alters gut microbiome composition and diversity. Include studies on how emulsifiers (carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate-80), artificial sweeteners (saccharin, sucralose, aspartame), and lack of fermentable fibers affect microbial ecology, intestinal barrier integrity, and metabolic endotoxemia.

3. ENDOCRINE DISRUPTION: How food contact chemicals (bisphenols, phthalates, PFAS), preservatives, and additives interfere with endocrine signaling, including thyroid function, sex hormones, insulin/IGF-1 signaling, and metabolic hormone regulation.

4. NEUROINFLAMMATION AND NEURODEGENERATION: How UPF components promote systemic and central nervous system inflammation. Include studies on advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), oxidized lipids, and inflammatory cytokine cascades linking UPF consumption to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease risk.

5. REWARD PATHWAY DYSREGULATION AND ADDICTION NEUROBIOLOGY: How UPFs with high sugar/fat combinations, flavor enhancers, and specific texture properties (e.g., "vanishing caloric density") hijack mesolimbic dopamine pathways. Include functional neuroimaging studies (fMRI, PET) comparing brain responses to UPFs versus whole foods, and studies on withdrawal, tolerance, and craving similar to substance use disorders.

PRIORITIZE: Peer-reviewed original research from journals such as Nature, Science, Cell, The Lancet, JAMA, BMJ, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, Journal of Nutrition, Nutrients, Appetite, Obesity Reviews, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, etc. Also include systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Include research from multiple countries (Brazil, US, UK, France, Canada, Australia, etc.). Prioritize the most recent publications (2020-2026).

Provide specific citations with authors, journal, year, and key findings for each major point. Organize findings by subtopic.

FOOD INDUSTRY INFLUENCE ON EATING BEHAVIOR AND INDIVIDUAL SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS

Conduct a comprehensive literature review on two dimensions: (A) how the food industry designs products to influence eating behavior, and (B) individual susceptibility factors to processed food addiction and metabolic dysfunction. This is for a scholarly scientific report.

PART A: INDUSTRY INFLUENCE ON BEHAVIOR
1. PRODUCT DESIGN & FORMULATION: Research on hyper-palatability ("bliss point"), optimal sugar/fat/salt ratios, texture engineering (e.g., "vanishing caloric density" in products like potato chips, melt-in-mouth formulations), mouthfeel optimization, and multi-sensory food design. Include industry patents and trade publications where available.

2. SATIETY OVERSHOOT: How UPFs are engineered to bypass or override satiety signals through low water content, high energy density, rapid gastric emptying, and nutrient combinations that blunt satiety hormone release.

3. MARKETING STRATEGIES: Research on how marketing, packaging, health claims, branding, and product placement influence consumption patterns. Include studies on child-directed marketing, sports sponsorships, and digital/social media advertising.

4. FOOD ADDICTION CONCEPT: The evidence for and against operationalizing food addiction as a substance use disorder. Include the Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS) studies, behavioral addictions framework, and debates in the literature.

PART B: INDIVIDUAL SUSCEPTIBILITY FACTORS
1. GENETIC FACTORS: Genetic variants affecting dopamine signaling (DRD2, DRD4, COMT, DAT1), opioid receptors (OPRM1), leptin/melanocortin pathway (MC4R, FTO, LEPR), taste receptor polymorphisms (TAS1R, TAS2R), and their association with UPF consumption and reward sensitivity.

2. EPIGENETIC AND DEVELOPMENTAL FACTORS: How early-life nutrition, prenatal exposure, and developmental programming influence later susceptibility to UPF effects. Include DOHaD (Developmental Origins of Health and Disease) research.

3. MICROBIOME-ASSOCIATED SUSCEPTIBILITY: How baseline gut microbiome composition influences individual responses to UPFs, including differences in metabolic endotoxemia, short-chain fatty acid production, and bile acid metabolism.

4. PSYCHOLOGICAL AND BEHAVIORAL FACTORS: Impulsivity, reward sensitivity, stress reactivity, emotional eating, disordered eating patterns, and their interaction with UPF consumption.

5. SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC FACTORS: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education level, and their associations with differential susceptibility to UPF-related health outcomes.

PRIORITIZE: Peer-reviewed original research from journals across nutrition science, neuroscience, psychology, food science, and public health. Include international studies from the US, Europe, Brazil, China, Australia, and other regions. Prioritize the most recent publications (2020-2026). Provide specific citations with authors, journal, year, and key findings.

ENVIRONMENTAL AND STRUCTURAL FACTORS INFLUENCING ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD CONSUMPTION

Conduct a comprehensive literature review on the environmental, structural, economic, and policy factors that shape dietary patterns and ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption. This is for a scholarly scientific report. Focus on the following subtopics:

1. FOOD DESERTS AND FOOD SWAMPS: Definitions, measurement methods, and health outcomes associated with food deserts (limited access to fresh, whole foods) and food swamps (high density of UPF retailers). Include research on USDA food access research, geographic information systems (GIS) studies, and comparisons between urban and rural environments.

2. ECONOMIC INEQUALITY AND FOOD PRICING: The cost differential between UPFs and whole foods (calorie-for-calorie, nutrient-for-nutrient). Research on the price elasticity of demand for UPFs versus fresh foods, the impact of food subsidies and agricultural policies (US Farm Bill, EU Common Agricultural Policy) on relative food prices, and the economics of food choice in low-income populations.

3. MARKETING TARGETING AND FOOD ENVIRONMENT INEQUITIES: Research on how food marketing, advertising, and retail placement disproportionately target low-income communities, communities of color, and children. Include studies on outdoor advertising density, digital marketing algorithms, and school food environments.

4. BUILT ENVIRONMENT AND FOOD ACCESS: Research on how neighborhood characteristics (supermarket availability, fast food density, walkability, public transit access to grocery stores) influence dietary patterns. Include studies on the relationship between neighborhood deprivation and UPF availability.

5. POLICY AND REGULATORY APPROACHES: International comparisons of policy interventions including front-of-pack labeling (Chile's black octagonal warning labels, Mexico's labeling system, Nutri-Score, UK's traffic light system), sugar-sweetened beverage taxes, marketing restrictions (UK's HFSS regulations, Chile's restrictions on child-directed marketing), school food policies, and agricultural subsidies reform. Include evaluations of policy effectiveness.

6. GLOBAL TRADE AND FOOD SYSTEMS: How international trade agreements, global food supply chains, and multinational food corporations shape the global food environment. Include the role of the NOVA classification system in research and policy.

PRIORITIZE: Peer-reviewed research from public health, epidemiology, urban planning, economics, and policy journals. Include reports from WHO, FAO, PAHO, UNICEF, national health agencies (CDC, NIH, Public Health England, ANSES, etc.), and organizations like the Global Food Research Program. Include international perspectives from research conducted in Latin America (Chile, Mexico, Brazil, Colombia), Europe (UK, France, Portugal, Norway), North America, Australia, Africa, and Asia. Prioritize the most recent publications (2020-2026). Provide specific citations with authors, journal, year, and key findings for each major point.

# BIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS ON HUMAN HEALTH: COMPREHENSIVE LITERATURE REVIEW

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The following queries were conducted to gather the research findings:

1. "ultra-processed foods gut-brain axis mechanism emulsifiers sweeteners 2020-2024"
2. "ultra-processed foods microbiome alteration emulsifiers review 2020-2024"
3. "ultra-processed foods endocrine disruption food contact chemicals bisphenols phthalates 2020-2024"
4. "ultra-processed foods neuroinflammation neurodegeneration AGEs cognitive decline 2020-2024"
5. "ultra-processed foods addiction reward pathway dopamine neuroimaging fMRI 2020-2024"
6. "ultra-processed foods gut hormone secretion GLP-1 PYY ghrelin leptin satiety 2020-2024"
7. "ultra-processed foods endocrine disruption bisphenol phthalate PFAS thyroid insulin 2020-2024 review"
8. "ultra-processed foods advanced glycation end-products AGEs neuroinflammation cognitive decline 2020-2024"
9. "fMRI neuroimaging ultra-processed foods vs whole foods brain reward dopamine 2020-2024"
10. "ultra-processed foods systematic review meta-analysis health outcomes 2023-2025"
11. "Hall 2019 ultra-processed diet randomized controlled trial calorie intake BMI"
12. "artificial sweeteners saccharin sucralose aspartame gut microbiome dysbiosis 2020-2024"
13. "vanishing caloric density ultra-processed food texture eating rate reward"
14. "fMRI brain response ultra-processed food versus whole food dopamine reward 2020-2024"
15. "ultra-processed foods cognitive decline Brazil study 2022 dementia UK Biobank"

---

## FULLY COMPREHENSIVE FINDINGS

### SECTION 1: GUT-BRAIN AXIS DISRUPTION
*How emulsifiers, artificial sweeteners, and other food additives disrupt gut-brain axis signaling pathways, including vagus nerve signaling alterations, changes in gut hormone secretion (GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, leptin), and effects on satiety signaling.*

---

#### 1.1 The Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis Framework

The Quadram Institute describes the microbiota-gut-brain axis as "a web of connections that allows communication both ways between the gut microorganisms, our gut cells, and the brain" [5]. A varied diet rich in fibers promotes beneficial gut microbes, while a diet high in refined sugars and low in fiber reduces microbial diversity [5].

Quadram Institute researchers have found that "alterations in mucin glycosylation are associated with a leaky gut and changes in brain function and cognition" (studies referenced: PMID 35579971, PMID 37634035) [5]. A 2024 study by the University of East Anglia and Quadram Institute found that mice fed a low-fat processed diet had changes in their gut that affected their brain functions, specifically through altered bile acid concentrations. The high-sugar, fiber-poor refined diet "disrupted the gut microbiota, and this affected how the body was processing bile acid," which was linked to changes in inflammation-related genes in the brain and decline in brain function [5].

#### 1.2 Food Additives and Gut-Brain Signaling

A review article by Song et al. (2023) published in *Food Research International* (Volume 167) examines the effects of UPFs on the microbiota-gut-brain (MGB) axis. The review highlights that UPFs—containing high levels of saturated/trans fats, added sugar, salt, and food additives—negatively impact gut microbiota composition and function, potentially leading to intestinal inflammation, metabolic dysbiosis, and adverse effects on brain health [8]. The review specifically focuses on food additives including emulsifiers (polysorbate 80 and carboxymethylcellulose), artificial sweeteners (saccharin, sucralose, aspartame, and acesulfame), plus colorants and preservatives, and their interactions with gut microbiota. The authors note that "some emulsifiers, including polysorbate 80 (P80) and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), can directly affect microbiota drive intestinal inflammation, and alter anxiety-like and social-related behaviors" [8]. They also report that "artificial sweeteners such as saccharin, sucralose, aspartame, and acesulfame may be an etiologic factor related to the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)" [8]. The paper concludes that "data from several studies suggest that food additives might be linked to metabolic diseases and inflammation. They may also alter the gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolites, which potentially affect cognition and behavior" [8].

A key finding cited in the Song et al. review is that "a prospective cohort study shows that UPF consumption was associated with a high risk of dementia. Every 10% increase in UPF intake per day increased dementia risk by 25%; replacing a 10% UPF intake with an equivalent amount of unprocessed or minimally processed foods decreased dementia risk by about 20%" [8].

#### 1.3 Gut Hormone Secretion Alterations (GLP-1, PYY, Ghrelin, Leptin)

**The Landmark Hall et al. (2019) Randomized Controlled Trial:**
The landmark randomized controlled trial from the NIH (Hall et al., 2019, *Cell Metabolism*) demonstrated that ultra-processed food causes overeating and weight gain through eating speed—not taste preference [1, 3, 4]. The study involved 20 adults (10 men, 10 women; average age 31, BMI ~27) who lived in an NIH metabolic ward for 28 days, spending 2 weeks on an ultra-processed diet and 2 weeks on an unprocessed diet in random order [1]. Both diets were matched for calories offered, macronutrients, fiber, sugar, and sodium. Participants ate ad libitum [1].

Key results included: 508 extra calories per day consumed on ultra-processed food (p=0.0001)—despite both diets rated equally pleasant and familiar [1, 3, 4]. Weight change was 0.9 kg gained on ultra-processed food and 0.9 kg lost on unprocessed food—in just 14 days each [1, 3, 4]. Eating rate was 17 calories/minute faster on ultra-processed food [1]. Crucially, the appetite-suppressing hormone PYY was significantly higher after unprocessed food, indicating that the ultra-processed diet suppressed satiety hormone signaling [1, 13]. The weekly cost for ingredients was estimated at $106 for ultra-processed meals vs. $151 for unprocessed meals (per 2000 kcal/day) [4].

The study concluded that "limiting consumption of ultra-processed foods may be an effective strategy for obesity prevention and treatment" [3, 4]. The article has been cited by 1498 subsequent publications [3].

**The Food Matrix Collapse Hypothesis:**
A review article published in *Frontiers in Nutrition* on May 5, 2026, by Wang et al. proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the primary health threat of UPFs stems not merely from poor nutritional composition but from the industrial collapse of their physical "food matrix" [2]. The authors hypothesize that this structural disintegration triggers a top-down cascade of dysregulation across multiple physiological systems. The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This leads to metabolic dysregulation including insulin resistance, de novo lipogenesis, and mitochondrial stress. Finally, the impoverished matrix combined with chemical additives causes gut microbiome imbalance, compromised intestinal barrier function, and systemic low-grade chronic inflammation via metabolic endotoxemia [2].

The authors state: "The core threat of UPFs to health may originate profoundly from the industrial collapse of their physical 'food matrix'" and "This supraphysiological nutrient flux imposes a significant challenge on core metabolic organs, driving insulin resistance and hepatic de novo lipogenesis" [2].

**GLP-1 Secretion and Diet:**
A narrative review published in *The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* (January 2024) examined the impact of diet on fasting and postprandial GLP-1 secretion across different metabolic conditions [3]. Key findings include: GLP-1 is a gastrointestinal peptide secreted by intestinal L cells in response to food intake, playing a central role in glucose metabolism by stimulating insulin secretion, promoting satiety, and slowing gastric emptying [3]. Postprandial GLP-1 secretion is triggered by nutrient-sensing via G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and membrane transporters (e.g., SGLT1). Nutrients (peptides, amino acids, fatty acids, SCFAs) and fermentable dietary fibers can stimulate secretion [3]. The review notes that some studies showed diminished glucose- or meal-stimulated GLP-1 response in participants with T2DM, IGT, or OW compared with those with NGT, whereas other studies have reported an elevated or unchanged GLP-1 response in T2DM or IGT [3]. Meal composition, especially macronutrient ratios and meal size, impacted secretion. The review highlights "the potential of nutritional and physiologic stimulation of GLP-1 secretion" as a preventive or synergistic method for improving glucose metabolism [3].

**Artificial Sweeteners and Gut Hormone Disruption:**
A review article published in the *International Journal of Molecular Sciences* (2025, Volume 26, Issue 20, 10220) by Roberto Coccurello examines how non-caloric sweeteners (NCSs) disrupt the gut-brain axis, focusing on microbiota-mediated effects and neural reward processing [10]. Key findings include: NCS-induced dysbiosis reduces beneficial taxa such as *Akkermansia muciniphila*, *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, *Bifidobacterium*, and *Lactobacillus*; diminishes short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production (butyrate, propionate); impairs gut barrier integrity and promotes systemic inflammation via elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels; and blunts satiety signaling and favors appetite-promoting pathways (e.g., via GABA-mediated inhibition of satiety hormones and disinhibition of NPY/AgRP neurons) [10].

A landmark 120-participant RCT showed NCS-induced glycemic responses are microbiota-mediated and transmissible via fecal transplant [10]. Large-scale cohort data (NutriNet-Santé, >100,000 adults) link NCS intake to increased cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes [10]. Regarding neural reward processing, NCSs decouple sweet taste from caloric content, unlike caloric sugars which couple both to robustly activate dopaminergic pathways. This creates a "reward prediction error": sweet taste signals reward, but no calories follow. NCSs produce weaker dopaminergic responses in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and dorsal striatum compared to sugar, which may drive compensatory food-seeking and overeating [10]. NCSs also alter hypothalamic circuits: reducing leptin-induced POMC activation (blunting satiety), sustaining orexigenic NPY/AgRP activity (driving hunger), and potentially enhancing ghrelin signaling [10]. The review concludes that "both top-down (neural) and bottom-up (microbial) mechanisms converge to foster maladaptive food seeking, metabolic dysregulation, and increased vulnerability to overeating" [10].

**Satiety, Eating Rate, and Energy Intake:**
A randomized controlled trial from Wageningen University (Netherlands) found that texture-derived differences in meal eating rate significantly influence energy intake from UPFs [11]. Over 14 days, 41 participants who consumed a UPF diet with textures that slowed eating rate averaged 369 fewer kcal per day (a cumulative difference of over 5,000 kcal over the 14-day period) compared to when they consumed a UPF diet with textures promoting faster eating [11]. Both diets were matched for energy density, portion size, total energy served, and Nova 4 classification; participants ate ad libitum until comfortably full, and meals were rated equally liked and familiar [11]. Despite consuming fewer calories, participants reported no differences in appetite or diet satisfaction. The research, led by Prof. Ciarán Forde, found "the consistency of the effect of meal texture on eating rate and intake was striking" [11]. The findings highlight that food texture—without conscious restriction or reduced enjoyment—can be used to regulate energy intake via sensory cues [11].

A separate analysis of 327 foods across 5 countries confirmed the gradient: unprocessed foods at 36 kcal/min, processed at 54, ultra-processed at 69 [1].

#### 1.4 Vagus Nerve Signaling and Inflammation

BBC Future reported on a clinical trial on Crohn's disease patients that found those on a restricted emulsifier diet were three times more likely to experience reduced symptoms [4].

A randomized control trial (Melissa Lane, Deakin University) found that a high-UPF diet reduced gut microbe diversity and increased constipation compared to a low-UPF diet with similar nutrients, likely due to differences in fiber types and additive content [4].

### SECTION 2: MICROBIOME ALTERATIONS
*How UPF consumption alters gut microbiome composition and diversity, including studies on emulsifiers (carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate-80), artificial sweeteners (saccharin, sucralose, aspartame), and lack of fermentable fibers affecting microbial ecology, intestinal barrier integrity, and metabolic endotoxemia.*

---

#### 2.1 Overview of UPF-Driven Gut Dysbiosis

A review published in *Nutrients* (2025, 17(16), 2677) titled "Ultra-Processed Foods, Gut Microbiota, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Critical Review of Emerging Evidence" reports that "UPF accounts for up to 58% of daily caloric intake in high-income countries and approximately 30% in emerging economies" [1]. Key findings include: UPFs are associated with intestinal dysbiosis, reduced microbial diversity, decreased short-chain fatty acid production, impaired barrier integrity, and mucus layer disruption [1]. "Consuming 10% of calories from ultra-processed foods per day is associated with a 19% increased risk of developing Crohn's disease" [1]. "Serum LPS levels are reportedly six times higher in patients with active Crohn's disease (CD) compared to healthy controls" [1]. The review notes that "food additives, commonly found in UPF... can trigger proinflammatory changes in the microbiota, enhance LPS release, disrupt the production of beneficial metabolites like short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and impair the mucus layer and β-defensin expression" [1]. High UPF consumption is associated with intestinal dysbiosis characterized by overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria such as *Clostridium* and *Enterococcus*, triggering inflammatory responses in the host [1].

A comprehensive review published February 28, 2025, in *Nutrients* (PMCID: PMC11901572, PMID: 40077728) by researchers from Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore and Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Gemelli IRCCS in Rome, Italy, examines the detrimental impact of UPFs on the human gut microbiome and gut barrier [3]. Key findings include:

- **Healthy gut microbiome:** Dominated by Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes phyla. Key beneficial bacteria include *Akkermansia muciniphila*, *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, and *Bifidobacteria*. The microbiome produces essential SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) which maintain gut barrier integrity, modulate immunity, and regulate metabolism [3].

- **UPF-driven gut alterations:** UPF consumption is associated with decreased microbial α-diversity, reduced beneficial bacteria (*Akkermansia muciniphila*, *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, *Lachnospira*, *Roseburia*), and increased pro-inflammatory microorganisms (*Granulicatella*, *Blautia*, *Bacteroidaceae*) [3]. "Individuals who consumed high levels of UPFs exhibited an elevated presence of potentially harmful bacterial groups... including *Granulicatella*, which is linked to metabolic disorders, as well as *Blautia*, *Carnobacteriaceae*, *Bacteroidaceae*, *Peptostreptococcaceae*, *Bacteroidia*, and *Bacteroidetes*" [3].

- **Emulsifiers:** "Commonly utilized emulsifiers, including carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), polysorbate 80 (P80), carrageenan, and gums, are known to alter gut microbiota composition, thereby promoting a pro-inflammatory microbial environment that may contribute to the development of metabolic disorders such as obesity and T2DM" [3].

- **Experimental evidence:** "The germ-free mice colonized with emulsifier-treated microbiotas exhibited low-grade inflammation, increased metabolic markers, higher fasting blood glucose levels and increased adiposity, indicative of MetS" [3].

- **Health implications:** UPF-induced dysbiosis contributes to systemic low-grade inflammation and is linked to metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and colorectal cancer. UPFs may also alter the gut-brain axis, potentially affecting cognitive function and mental health [3].

#### 2.2 Emulsifiers and Microbiome Disruption

The BBC Future article reports that emulsifiers, which help mix oils/water and extend shelf life, are found in about half of UK supermarket products (6,640 products analyzed) [4]. Animal studies led by Benoit Chassaing at Institut Pasteur show emulsifiers cause gut bacteria to move closer to the gut wall, eroding the protective mucus layer and triggering inflammation [4]. Chassaing notes: "They are only tested for the toxicity effect or for the ability to induce DNA damage. And for those two aspects, they are perfectly fine. But they were never tested in the past for the direct effect on the microbiome" [4].

Human correlational studies link emulsifier exposure to increased risk of type 2 diabetes (over 100,000 adults, 2024 French study) and breast/prostate cancers (over 90,000 adults) [4].

The PEN (Practice-based Evidence in Nutrition) article, posted April 17, 2025, reports that in vitro and animal studies suggest CMC, P80, carrageenan, and gums may reduce gut bacterial diversity and impair the gut lining [6]. One small RCT (n=16) found that 15g/day of CMC for 14 days reduced microbiota diversity, altered fecal metabolome, and caused abdominal discomfort [6]. The French NutriNet-Santé cohort (n>92,000) found small positive associations between emulsifier consumption and cancer, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes over ~7 years [6]. For individuals at high risk of IBD, 2023 ESPEN guidelines recommend excluding ultra-processed foods and CMC (Grade C evidence) [6].

#### 2.3 Artificial Sweeteners and Microbiome Alterations

A review article published in *Cureus* on September 23, 2024, explores the long-term effects of artificial sweeteners (ASs) on metabolic health [6]. Key findings: High consumption of ASs is linked to a 30% increased risk of metabolic problems, cardiovascular disease, and certain cancers [6]. The Women's Health Initiative found artificially sweetened beverages associated with elevated risks of stroke, coronary heart disease, and mortality [6]. ASs cause gut microbiota dysbiosis—reducing beneficial bacteria (*Lactobacillus*, *Bifidobacterium*) and increasing harmful Proteobacteria—leading to reduced SCFA production, increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut"), and systemic inflammation [6]. Specific sweetener risks: Aspartame associated with neurotoxicity and cancer risks; sucralose alters gut flora and glucose metabolism; saccharin linked to IBD and gut microbiota disruption; acesulfame-K raises concerns about metabolic disruption and cancer risk [6]. A meta-analysis of over 400,000 participants found a relative risk of 1.12 per daily serving for T2DM [6].

An original research article published in *Frontiers in Microbiology* on May 15, 2025, by Kidangathazhe et al. examined the effects of five common artificial sweeteners on gut microbiome diversity using minibioreactor arrays [7]. Key results: Synthetic sweeteners (Sucralose and Saccharin) significantly reduced microbial diversity. Sucralose enriched potentially pathogenic families like Enterobacteriaceae and showed the most divergent microbial composition. Non-synthetic sweeteners (Rebaudioside A and Xylitol) were less disruptive, promoting beneficial taxa such as Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, important for SCFA production. Acesulfame K increased diversity but disrupted network structure (reduced centrality and modularity), suggesting potential long-term negative impacts on microbiome resilience. It was the only sweetener that did not recover structural integrity after withdrawal. After the 14-day withdrawal period, none of the treatment groups fully reverted to the original community composition, though most showed structural recovery except acesulfame K [7].

A review article published on April 15, 2025, in *Diseases* (PMCID: PMC12025785) by Helal F. Hetta and colleagues explores the relationship between non-nutritive sweeteners (NNS) and the gut microbiome [8]. Key findings: Animal studies often report decreases in beneficial bacteria like *Bifidobacterium* and *Lactobacillus*, and increases in harmful strains such as *Clostridium difficile* and *E. coli*. Human studies generally show milder or no significant changes, highlighting limitations in translating animal model findings to humans. Saccharin consumption in mice was associated with gut dysbiosis, with an increase in *Bacteroides* and *Clostridiales* and a reduction in *Lactobacillus reuteri* [8].

A study published in *iScience* (December 19, 2023) by Cedars-Sinai investigators compared duodenal (small bowel) and stool microbiomes in adults consuming non-aspartame non-sugar sweeteners (NANS, N=35), aspartame only (ASP, N=9), and controls (CON, N=55) [9]. Key findings: Artificial sweeteners significantly alter microbial diversity and composition in both the small bowel and stool, with effects differing between the small and large bowel. Bacterial richness in the small bowel was lower in NANS consumers versus controls. In aspartame consumers, the bacterial pathway for cylindrospermopsin—a toxin harmful to the liver and nervous system and classified as a potential carcinogen—was enriched [9]. Dr. Ruchi Mathur, MD, Professor of Medicine at Cedars-Sinai, noted: "Artificial sweeteners are not benign for the microbiome of the gut. We found that the richness of the bacteria in the small bowel was less in those subjects consuming non-aspartame non-sugar sweeteners when compared to controls" [9]. Over 140 million people in the United States use sugar substitutes [9].

#### 2.4 Observational Studies on Microbiome Composition

A narrative review published in *Nutrients* (June 2024) examining the impact of UPFs on the human gut microbiome summarizes four observational studies that used the NOVA classification system and 16S rRNA sequencing [7]. Findings include: Increased UPF consumption was associated with higher *Prevotella* spp. (2 studies) and decreased *Lachnospira* spp. (2 studies) and *Ruminococcus* spp. (2 studies). Only one study found alpha diversity differences (men consuming >5 servings/day of UPFs had lower richness vs. those consuming <3 servings/day). No significant differences in beta diversity were observed in any of the four studies. Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios were not significantly correlated with UPF consumption in three studies [7]. The review also notes that military ready-to-eat meals (UPFs with high nutritional value) altered gut microbiota and fecal metabolome over 21 days [7].

#### 2.5 Metabolic Endotoxemia and Intestinal Barrier Integrity

The review in *Nutrients* (2025) notes that the persistent low-grade inflammation driven by UPF consumption can lead to "leaky gut" and increased intestinal permeability, with serum LPS levels reportedly six times higher in patients with active Crohn's disease compared to healthy controls [1].

The review from Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore confirms that emulsifiers (CMC, P80) alter microbiota composition, promote pro-inflammatory environments, and compromise the mucus layer, leading to increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut") [3].

### SECTION 3: ENDOCRINE DISRUPTION
*How food contact chemicals (bisphenols, phthalates, PFAS), preservatives, and additives interfere with endocrine signaling, including thyroid function, sex hormones, insulin/IGF-1 signaling, and metabolic hormone regulation.*

---

#### 3.1 Food Contact Chemicals as Endocrine Disruptors

A review article published in *Cancers* (2025, Volume 17, Issue 13, 2196) by Fajkić et al. titled "Ultra-Processed Diets and Endocrine Disruption, Explanation of Missing Link in Rising Cancer Incidence Among Young Adults" presents a narrative review examining the link between UPFs and rising cancer rates among adolescents and young adults (AYAs, defined as 15–39 years old) [7]. Key findings: In 2022, approximately 1.3 million cancer cases and 377,621 cancer deaths occurred in AYAs globally [7]. UPFs act as "Trojan horses"—seemingly harmless, convenient foods that deliver endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) such as bisphenols, phthalates, and nitrates that migrate from packaging into food [7]. UPF consumption among adolescents varies widely (25–67.8% of energy intake), with the UK reaching 67.8% and the US at 59.2% [7]. A 10% increase in UPF proportion in diet is associated with higher incidence and mortality from ovarian cancer, brain cancer, and lymphomas (UK Biobank data) [7]. Mechanistic pathways include: endocrine disruption (hormonal signalling interference), chronic low-grade inflammation, gut microbiome dysbiosis, epigenetic alterations, and immune system disruption [7]. EDCs exhibit non-monotonic dose-response relationships, meaning "low dietary exposures through UPFs may have disproportionately significant biological effects, especially if they occur during hormonal-sensitive developmental stages, such as adolescence" [7].

#### 3.2 Specific Additives with EDC Properties

A review article published in the *Journal of Xenobiotics* on November 4, 2024, by Paramasivam et al. examines how food additives in processed foods act as endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [9]. The authors identify six major food additives with EDC properties:

**Erythrosine (Red No. 3):** Interferes with thyroid iodine uptake, decreases T3/T4 levels, increases TSH, exhibits estrogenic activity, and has been linked to DNA damage, cancer, and allergic responses [9].

**Tartrazine (Yellow No. 5):** Binds to estrogen receptors, alters hormone synthesis and metabolism enzyme activity, and induces epigenetic changes affecting gene expression [9].

**Bisphenol A (BPA):** An unintentional food additive from packaging; mimics estrogen by binding to ERα and ERβ, disrupts thyroid hormone signaling, interacts with androgen receptors, and has been linked to developmental effects including reproductive alterations, metabolic disorders (obesity, type-2 diabetes), and changes in mammary gland development [9].

**Artificial sweeteners:** Influence hormone release (insulin, leptin, ghrelin), alter gut microbiota composition, and affect glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity [9].

**Phthalates:** Enter food from packaging materials; bind to estrogen, androgen, and PPAR receptors; disrupt hormone synthesis enzymes (aromatase, 5-alpha reductase); and interfere with hormone transport proteins like SHBG [9].

**Parabens:** Used as preservatives; exhibit weak estrogenic activity, inhibit aromatase, interfere with thyroid peroxidase function, and disrupt hormone transport via SHBG interaction [9].

The review concludes that "EDCs are substances that frequently interfere with the regular functioning of the endocrine system, creating an unusual environment in the biological system, which leads to adverse health effects such as the disruption of hormone synthesis, receptor binding, and signal transduction pathways, as well as energy metabolic homeostatic disorders which potentially increasing the risk of obesity, type-2 diabetes, cardiometabolic diseases and may also trigger allergic reactions" [9].

#### 3.3 Phthalates, Bisphenols, and UPF Consumption

An article from the Food Packaging Forum (January 22, 2024) reports on two studies linking ultra-processed food consumption to increased exposure to phthalates and microplastics [10].

**Study 1 (Baker et al., *Environment International*, Jan 2024):** Examined 1,031 pregnant women from the CANDLE study. Found that "each 10% higher dietary proportion of ultra-processed foods was associated with 13.1% higher urinary levels of the molar sum of five di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate metabolites (ΣDEHP)" [10]. Higher intake of hamburgers, French fries, sodas, and cakes were particularly linked to increased phthalate exposure. Lower income and education levels were associated with 1.9% and 1.4% higher ΣDEHP, respectively, mediated via increased ultra-processed food consumption. The authors call for policy changes targeting food packaging and processing equipment to reduce population-wide phthalate exposure [10].

**Study 2 (Milne et al., *Environmental Pollution*, Dec 2023):** Analyzed 111 US protein-rich food samples across 13 protein types. Found microplastics (>50 µm) in 88% of samples. Highly-processed products contained significantly more microplastics than minimally-processed ones, with levels ranging from 0.01 particles/g (chicken breast) to 1.3 particles/g (breaded shrimp). Plastic processing equipment was hypothesized as the main source rather than packaging. Estimated mean annual US adult exposure to microplastics via protein consumption at 11,000 ± 29,000 particles, potentially reaching up to 3.8 million particles per year [10].

#### 3.4 The Plastics-UPF Nexus

A commentary published in *Globalization and Health* (Oct 24, 2024) by Yates et al. from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and other institutions explores the toxic relationship between UPFs and plastics [12]. The authors argue that these two industries are co-dependent, generating substantial profits for agri-food and petrochemical companies at high costs for human and planetary health [12]. Key findings: Over 75 prospective cohort studies show associations between UPF consumption and adverse health outcomes including premature mortality, cancer, and mental, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and metabolic ill health [12]. The plastics industry is worth over $700 billion annually, with production projected to triple from 460 million metric tons (2019) to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060 [12]. Plastics are deeply intertwined with UPFs across the supply chain—from agricultural plastics on farms, to food contact materials (FCMs) in processing and packaging [12]. Thousands of plastic food contact chemicals (FCCs) migrate into foodstuffs, including known hazardous substances like bisphenol A (BPA), ortho-phthalates, and PFAS. Many are endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [12]. A recent report identified over 16,000 plastic chemicals, with almost 60% (over 9,000) "lack specific information on their use or have not been analyzed in plastics, based on industry or scientific sources" [12]. UPF consumption is associated with higher levels of urinary phthalates, bisphenols, and PFAS, including in children and pregnant women [12]. Major UPF producers (Coca Cola, PepsiCo, Unilever, Nestlé) are among the leading plastic polluters worldwide, selling around 5.5 billion products daily [12]. The FAO calculates that the annual public health costs and productivity losses of consuming unhealthy diets, in which UPFs play a significant role, exceed $9 trillion globally [12]. Only 9% of the world's plastics have been successfully recycled, and recycling introduces hazardous chemicals back into the food chain [12].

#### 3.5 EDCs and Insulin Resistance

A review article published in *Cureus* (October 18, 2023) examines the relationship between EDCs and insulin resistance (IR) [8]. The review covers several major classes of EDCs: **Phthalates** (found in plastics and cosmetics)—shown in epidemiological and animal studies to be associated with increased T2DM risk, IR, and disruption of pancreatic β-cell function through mechanisms involving nuclear receptors, oxidative stress, and apoptosis [8]. **Perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS,** found in nonstick cookware and firefighting foam)—evidence is mixed, with some studies showing positive associations with IR and T2DM risk markers while others show non-significant or inverse associations, depending on the specific PFAS molecule and study population [8]. **Bisphenol A (BPA,** found in plastics and food containers)—linked to T2DM, altered insulin release, obesity, and changes in β-cell mass and function in both human and animal studies, with sex-dependent effects [8]. **Triclosan (TCS,** an antibacterial in personal care products)—shows gender-specific associations with T2DM risk, potentially through disruption of gut microbiota, thyroid hormones, and estrogenic effects [8]. Environmental EDCs including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), pesticides, and heavy metals (arsenic, mercury, cadmium) have also demonstrated associations with T2DM, IR, hypertension, and obesity [8].

#### 3.6 Early-Life Exposure and Obesogens

A review article published on January 8, 2025, in *Current Nutrition Reports* (Volume 14, article 14) by Celik and Yesildemir reviews the latest evidence on how early-life exposure to endocrine disruptors (EDs) contributes to obesity and metabolic disorders in children [9]. Key points: The 2015 Parma Consensus emphasized that "endocrine disruptors can interfere with metabolic systems during crucial developmental periods, potentially contributing to non-communicable diseases like obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome" [9]. According to the "environmental obesogen hypothesis," exposure to EDs early in life (including in utero) may impair adipogenesis or energy storage-related mechanisms by increasing the number/size of adipocytes, thereby increasing susceptibility to overweight/obesity [9]. **Bisphenol A (BPA)** is found in blood, urine, breast milk, and amniotic fluid; BPA can mimic estrogen and activate PPARγ to promote adipogenesis. Epidemiological studies show mixed results: some link prenatal BPA exposure to higher childhood BMI and central adiposity (especially in girls), while others find no significant association or opposite effects. Sex-specific differences are noted [9]. **Phthalates** affect energy homeostasis through nuclear receptors (ERα, ERβ, PPARγ, TRs, ARs). They exhibit weak estrogenic and strong anti-androgenic effects, alter PPARs (affecting adipocyte differentiation), reduce thyroid hormone levels, and impact adipokine production. Studies show inconsistent associations with child adiposity—some report positive links, others negative (e.g., reduced BMI and lean body mass due to anti-androgenic effects on muscle development). Prenatal phthalate exposure can be measured in amniotic fluid and placental tissue [9]. The authors recommend "setting national goals, global standards, and policies to reduce environmental exposure to pregnant and lactating women, and babies, considered sensitive populations" [9].

#### 3.7 Additional EDC Mechanisms

The Conversation article (by researchers Valérie Langlois and Isabelle Plante, Canada Research Chairs) summarizes findings on endocrine disruptors [10]. Key points: BPA has a structure that resembles natural estrogen and was considered for use as a medication to treat menopausal women in the 1930s prior to its widespread use in plastics [10]. A literature review led by Vicki Marlatt (Simon Fraser University) found that "many of these environmental contaminants impair reproduction in fish, amphibians, birds, mammals and humans, reducing their chances of producing viable offspring" [10]. Endocrine disruptors can cross the placental barrier, interfere with placental hormones, and lead to chronic diseases like diabetes, obesity, and increased risk of breast cancer and prostate cancer later in life [10]. These chemicals also alter thyroid hormone pathways, stress control, immunity, and metabolism. High BPA levels in urine have been linked to increased cardiovascular disease risk. Arsenic, phthalates, and organophosphate pesticides can interfere with insulin and lead to obesity [10]. Endocrine disruptors may also have transgenerational effects through epigenetic mechanisms—changes in which genes are turned on or off—rather than alterations to the genetic code itself. For example, "when fish are exposed to water contaminated with antidepressants, the offspring of their offspring show an altered stress response, even if that generation was never exposed to these chemicals" [10].
