### SECTION 4: NEUROINFLAMMATION AND NEURODEGENERATION
*How UPF components promote systemic and central nervous system inflammation, including studies on advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), oxidized lipids, and inflammatory cytokine cascades linking UPF consumption to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease risk.*

---

#### 4.1 UPFs and Cognitive Decline: Epidemiological Evidence

**The Brazilian Study (Gonçalves et al., 2022, *JAMA Neurology*):**
A study analyzing data from 10,775 Brazilian public servants (average age 52, 55% women, 57% college-educated) from the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Adult Health, across three waves from 2008-2019, found that individuals consuming more than 20% of daily calories from ultraprocessed foods had a 28% faster rate of global cognitive decline and a 25% faster rate of decline in executive function compared to those with lower intake [20, 22, 23]. No significant association was found between ultraprocessed food consumption and changes in memory scores [20]. This study was cited by 199 subsequent publications [22, 23].

**The UK Biobank Study:**
A UK study of ~72,000 participants found that over 10 years, about 1 in 120 people in the highest ultra-processed food group developed dementia, versus 1 in 170 in the lowest consumption group [14, 11]. However, a third study found no such association in people over 60 [14, 11].

**The Song et al. (2023) Review:**
A prospective cohort study cited in the Song et al. review shows that every 10% increase in UPF intake per day increased dementia risk by 25%; substituting 10% UPF intake with an equivalent amount of unprocessed or minimally processed foods decreased dementia risk by about 20% [8].

**Harvard Study (Leung et al., *American Journal of Public Health*):**
A study led by researchers from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analyzing data from over 5,300 adults aged 50+ from the University of Michigan's Health and Retirement Study over an average of nine years, found that those who ate the highest amount of ultra-processed food daily had a 58% increased risk of developing dementia and a 46% increased risk for cognitive impairment compared to those who ate the least [18]. Processed meats like bacon carried the highest risk. Conversely, high consumption of minimally processed foods like whole grains, fruits, and vegetables was associated with lower risks. Senior author Cindy Leung noted that "there may not be a safe level" of moderate consumption [18].

**The Framingham Heart Study (2025, *Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease*):**
A study published in *The Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease* (Volume 12, Issue 2, February 2025, Article 100042) examined the association between UPF consumption and risk of all-cause dementia and Alzheimer's disease among 1,375 participants (mean age 68 ± 6 years, 54% female) from the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort [24]. During a mean follow-up of 12.7 ± 6.0 years, 224 individuals were diagnosed with all-cause dementia and 172 with Alzheimer's disease. An interaction between UPF consumption and age was observed (p for interaction = 0.02 for dementia, 0.007 for Alzheimer's). Among participants <68 years at baseline: each serving per day of UPF was associated with a 13% increased risk for Alzheimer's disease (HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.03-1.25); consumption of ≥10 servings/day vs. <10 servings/day was associated with a 2.7-fold increase in Alzheimer's disease risk (HR = 2.71, 95% CI: 1.18-6.24), after adjustment for age, sex, education, total energy, metabolic factors, and diet quality. No significant findings were observed when age at baseline was 68 years or above [24]. The study concludes that "consumption of ultra-processed food in middle-age may be linked with an increased risk for Alzheimer's disease" [24].

**Contrasting Evidence:**
A study published in the *European Journal of Nutrition* (February 19, 2026, Volume 65, article 66) by Buis et al. examined 1,371 participants from the Longitudinal Aging Study Amsterdam (LASA) and found "no associations... between UPF intake and cognitive function or decline with age for any of the cognitive domains" tested (global cognition, information processing speed, episodic memory, executive function) [21]. On average, UPFs contributed 20.1% of total dietary intake in grams per day among participants [21]. The authors note that "previous studies on UPF and cognition have shown mixed results; some found faster cognitive decline with higher UPF intake, while others found no association" [21].

#### 4.2 Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs) and Neurodegeneration

A narrative review article published in *Antioxidants* (2025, 14(9), 1044) by Boccardi, Mancinetti, and Mecocci from the University of Perugia and Karolinska Institutet examines the metabolic interplay between oxidative stress and advanced glycation end products (AGEs) in Alzheimer's disease (AD), particularly late-onset AD (LOAD) [14]. Key findings:

- **Background:** AD is the leading cause of dementia (60-80% of cases). LOAD is multifactorial, with advanced age as the primary risk factor. The review integrates oxidative stress and AGE-RAGE signaling as central drivers of neurodegeneration [14].

- **Oxidative Stress in AD:** The CNS is highly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high oxygen consumption, abundant polyunsaturated lipids, and limited antioxidant capacity. ROS damage lipids (4-HNE, MDA), proteins (carbonylation, nitration), and DNA (8-OHdG). Postmortem AD brains show elevated oxidative markers. Mitochondrial dysfunction creates a self-perpetuating cycle of ROS production and bioenergetic failure [14].

- **AGEs and the AGE-RAGE Axis:** AGEs form via the Maillard reaction and are accelerated by oxidative stress. Dietary AGEs from ultra-processed foods (UPFs constitute ~55% of US adult caloric intake) and high-temperature cooking contribute to systemic burden. AGE-RAGE signaling activates NADPH oxidase, NF-κB, and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6), promoting Aβ aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagic impairment, and BBB breakdown. This creates a feed-forward loop of chronic inflammation and oxidative stress [14]. The review states: "The AGE–RAGE interaction acts as a central node linking oxidative stress and inflammation in AD... the AGE–RAGE axis contributes to the increased amyloidogenic processing of APP, Tau hyperphosphorylation, mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagic impairment and cerebrovascular injury, and blood–brain barrier (BBB) compromise" [14].

- **Therapeutic Strategies:** Reviewed interventions include: (1) AGE formation inhibitors (aminoguanidine, pyridoxamine); (2) AGE cross-link breakers (ALT-711/Alagebrium); (3) enhancing detoxification via glyoxalase-1 activation (sulforaphane, resveratrol); (4) RAGE antagonists (azeliragon—phase II/III trials inconclusive; FPS-ZM1—preclinical promise); (5) soluble RAGE (sRAGE) as a decoy receptor; and (6) nutritional/lifestyle interventions (low-AGE diets, polyphenols like curcumin and quercetin, physical exercise) [14].

- **Conclusions:** Clinical translation remains limited due to AGE heterogeneity, lack of reliable biomarkers, and need for early intervention. Future directions include nanocarrier delivery systems, gene therapies, combinatorial approaches, and integration into precision medicine frameworks [14].

#### 4.3 Dietary AGEs and Cognitive Impairment

A NutritionFacts.org video (November 23, 2022) by Dr. Michael Greger reports that "those who consume meat, including poultry and fish, have 2 to 3 times the risk of developing dementia compared with vegetarians" [12]. "Increased saturated fat intake was associated with a 40% increased risk of cognitive impairment and nearly 90% higher risk of Alzheimer's disease" [12]. "A high-fat diet not only impairs the heart but also cognitive function" [12]. "Dietary advanced glycation end products are associated with a decline in memory" [12]. Major sources of AGEs include meat cooked with high, dry heat (broiling, grilling, frying, roasting). AGE accumulation can be measured non-invasively via skin autofluorescence, which is significantly lower in those eating more plant-based foods. "The more meat you eat, the more of the AGE skin autofluorescence you get, which then correlates with cognitive impairment" [12].

A 2022 article by D'Cunha et al. (cited by 89 subsequent publications) found that "decreasing dietary intake of AGEs may improve neurological and mental disorder outcomes" associated with cognitive impairment and depression [15].

#### 4.4 Systemic Inflammation and Neuroinflammation

A cross-sectional study published in *Frontiers in Nutrition* (June 2026) by Italian researchers examined the relationship between UPF consumption and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in 92 elderly participants (mean age 73.2 years) [15]. Key findings: Higher UPF consumption was significantly associated with lower cognitive scores (MMSE: 25.2 vs 27.2; MoCA: 21.2 vs 23.9). In adjusted models, high UPF intake was associated with significantly increased odds of MCI (Model 2 OR = 4.24, 95% CI: 1.05–17.13). After adjusting for inflammatory biomarkers (TGF-β1 and TNF-α), the association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (OR = 4.79, 95% CI: 0.73–31.24), though the direction remained positive. No significant associations were found for unprocessed, culinary processed, or processed foods with MCI. The study concludes that "higher consumption of UPFs may be associated with increased likelihood of MCI, and that this relationship may be partly explained by systemic inflammation" [15].

A scoping review published in *Frontiers in Nutrition* (January 21, 2026, Volume 12) by Poon et al. examined neurobiological insights into the effects of UPF on lipid metabolism and associated mental health conditions [18]. The review included 123 studies published between 2020-2025. Proposed mechanisms for all these increased risks included: systemic low-grade inflammation (saturated fatty acids activate TLR4 receptors on macrophages and microglia, triggering NF-κB signaling and pro-inflammatory cytokine production—IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, CRP); altered neuronal signaling, particularly dopamine and serotonin pathways; gut-brain axis disruption (high UPF intake decreases SCFA production, compromising BBB integrity); neuroinflammation (inflammatory cytokines cross BBB, leading to microglial activation and impaired neurogenesis); HPA axis dysregulation (hyperpalatability contributes to stress hormone dysregulation); advanced glycation end products (AGEs) formed during high-temperature processing, contributing to neuroinflammation and neurotoxicity; and hormonal dysregulation (BPA and contaminants from food packaging alter gut microbiome) [18].

#### 4.5 UPFs and Mental Health

A 2020 study examining dietary patterns in over 10,000 adults in the United States found that "individuals consuming the highest amounts of UPFs had a 35% greater likelihood of experiencing depressive symptoms compared to those with the lowest intake" [2]. Another study by Harvard Medical School researchers found that "higher UPF consumption was associated with a 50% risk of developing depression, particularly among individuals consuming high quantities of artificially sweetened beverages and processed snacks" [2]. A large cohort study of over 25,000 individuals followed for more than five years linked increased UPF intake to higher rates of depressive episodes, independent of lifestyle factors [2]. Markers of inflammation, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), are often elevated in individuals consuming diets high in UPFs [2].

#### 4.6 UPFs and Brain Development

A review article published in *Frontiers in Public Health* (2025) titled "The consequences of ultra-processed foods on brain development during prenatal, adolescent and adult stages" reports that UPFs constitute 17.2% of the total food intake among women in their third trimester of pregnancy [16]. The period from 24 to 42 weeks of gestation represents a critical window for child neurodevelopment, during which processes such as synapse formation and myelination are actively taking place [16]. Poor dietary patterns during pregnancy have been associated with an increased likelihood of developing chronic diseases later in life, including obesity, cardiovascular disorders, and type 2 diabetes mellitus [16]. Adolescence is a critical stage of brain maturation, particularly susceptible to the effects of micronutrient deficiencies, often exacerbated by diets high in UPFs [16]. The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis posits that adverse early-life exposures can permanently alter structure and function, predisposing to behavioral and cognitive disorders [16]. Early UPF exposure shapes long-term food preferences, with preferences for sweet/salty foods persisting into adulthood [16].

New research from Children's Hospital Los Angeles (published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2026.101350) found that "higher ultra-processed food intake had smaller volumes in brain regions tied to reward and emotion by age six" [18].

### SECTION 5: REWARD PATHWAY DYSREGULATION AND ADDICTION NEUROBIOLOGY
*How UPFs with high sugar/fat combinations, flavor enhancers, and specific texture properties (e.g., "vanishing caloric density") hijack mesolimbic dopamine pathways, including functional neuroimaging studies (fMRI, PET) comparing brain responses to UPFs versus whole foods, and studies on withdrawal, tolerance, and craving similar to substance use disorders.*

---

#### 5.1 The Food Addiction Framework

A review article published in *Pharmacological Research* (Volume 224, February 2026, 108097) by Hough, Friuli, Avena, and Romano (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai) explores the hypothesis that food addiction shares common clinical and neurochemical mechanisms with traditional substance use disorders [20, 21]. Key findings: "Emerging evidence suggests that ultra-processed foods (UPFs), particularly those high in refined sugars and saturated fats, may elicit neurobiological responses akin to those observed in substance use disorders" [20, 21]. Animal and human studies demonstrate that "excessive consumption of palatable foods can induce behaviors characteristic of addiction—bingeing, craving, tolerance, and withdrawal—accompanied by significant dopaminergic alterations within the mesolimbic reward circuitry" [20, 21]. "Chronic overconsumption of UPFs alters dopaminergic tone, disrupts prefrontal control, and activates stress pathways, thereby reinforcing compulsive intake" [20, 21]. The Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS) and its pediatric adaptations provide structured tools for identifying food addiction phenotypes in clinical and research settings. The review "underscores the need to reframe UPFs as potentially addictive agents and calls for integrative therapeutic strategies and policy-driven reforms aimed at mitigating their impact on public health" [20, 21].

#### 5.2 Neuroimaging Studies

**PET Study on Dopamine Responses (Darcey et al., 2025, *Cell Metabolism*):**
A study published in *Cell Metabolism* (2025) investigated whether ultra-processed milkshakes high in fat and sugar elicit postingestive brain dopamine responses similar to drugs of abuse [19, 16]. Researchers used [11C]raclopride PET displacement methods to measure striatal dopamine responses in 50 young, healthy adults across a wide BMI range (20–45 kg/m²) [19, 16]. Contrary to the hypothesis, "milkshake consumption did not result in significant postingestive dopamine response in the striatum (p=0.62) nor any striatal subregion (p>0.33)" and the highly variable interindividual responses were not significantly related to adiposity (BMI: r=0.076, p=0.51; %body fat: r=0.16, p=0.28) [19, 16]. The authors conclude that "postingestive striatal dopamine responses to an ultra-processed milkshake were likely substantially smaller than many addictive drugs and below the limits of detection using standard PET methods" and that "the narrative that ultra-processed foods high in fat and sugar can be as addictive as drugs of abuse based on their potential to elicit an outsized dopamine response in brain reward regions was not supported by our data" [19, 16]. The observed dopamine responses may be closer in magnitude to that of nicotine (~5% reduction in D2BP) rather than psychostimulants (~10-20% reduction) [19, 16]. However, exploratory analyses revealed that participants who showed dopamine responses in the expected direction ("Responders") perceived the milkshake as more pleasant (73.3 vs 48.2, p=0.010), wanted more of it (56.4 vs 25.8, p=0.003), and tended to be hungrier in the fasted state [19, 16].

**fMRI Study on UPF Diet and Brain Response (Preprint, May 2026):**
A preprint (not yet peer-reviewed, posted May 1, 2026) reports on a randomized controlled crossover trial investigating whether a high-UPF diet alters brain response to a milkshake reward in emerging adults (ages 18-25), compared to a nutrient-matched diet free of UPF [17]. Participants (n=22; 15 female; ages 18-25) completed two 14-day controlled feeding periods (81% UPF vs. 0% UPF), eucaloric and matched for macro/micronutrients, separated by a 4-week washout. Before and after each diet period, participants underwent fMRI while consuming a milkshake via a pump system [17]. In the entire cohort, no significant differences in brain response to milkshake were found between diet conditions. However, an exploratory analysis revealed a significant three-way interaction (diet × time × age) in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC): In adolescents (18-21 years), OFC response to milkshake decreased after the UPF diet and increased after the NonUPF diet; young adults (22-25 years) showed no significant change [17]. Habitual UPF intake (% grams) was positively correlated with OFC response to milkshake consumption, independent of diet condition or age. The authors conclude that "an acute UPF dietary intervention may only alter brain response in adolescents, not young adults" and that "the OFC—a region involved in food valuation that continues developing into the third decade of life—appears particularly sensitive to both acute dietary changes and habitual UPF intake" [17].

**Systematic Review of fMRI Studies (Pursey et al., 2024, *Current Addiction Reports*):**
A systematic review published in *Current Addiction Reports* (Volume 11, pages 173–190, 2024) by Pursey, Yokum, Brain, and Burrows synthesizes studies using fMRI to assess neural responses associated with food addiction as measured by the YFAS [16]. The review included 11 studies (7 task-related fMRI, 4 resting-state fMRI), involving 675 predominantly female participants. Key findings from task-related studies: Brain areas involved in reward, craving, and appetitive responses (left ACC, left medial OFC, left amygdala, basolateral amygdala, right SFG) were associated with YFAS-assessed food addiction in response to high-calorie processed foods. Impaired inhibition was found in non-food-related tasks (Go-No go tasks). Effect sizes were large for food-related tasks (d = 1.00–2.40) and medium to large for non-food tasks (d = 0.46–1.39). Key findings from resting-state studies: Altered connectivity in reward-related regions and cognitive control were commonly reported. Negative correlations between food addiction symptoms and connectivity in executive control regions (e.g., left DLPFC). Effect sizes ranged from small to large (d = 0.32–0.83). The review notes that "there was a lack of consistency in activation across studies" likely due to heterogeneity in study designs, participant characteristics, food cues, and paradigms. The prevalence of food addiction has been reported to be 15–20% across published studies and is higher in females, those of higher weight status, and clinical populations [16].

#### 5.3 Mechanisms of Hyperpalatability and Addictive Properties

**The Psych Scene Hub article by Dr. Sanil Rege** explores the neurobiology of food addiction, focusing on how salt, fat, sugar, and starch overstimulate brain reward circuits [22]. Key mechanisms: Salt activates opioid pathways and reinforces pleasure. Dietary fats trigger dopamine release through both taste receptors and gut-brain signalling, creating prolonged post-ingestive reward. Starch and sugar rapidly elevate glucose and insulin, producing dopamine surges independent of sweet taste. Ultra-processed foods exploit evolutionary survival cues, creating a mismatch between ancient brain wiring and modern food environments. Repeated dopamine overstimulation leads to receptor downregulation and compulsive reward-seeking, reinforcing craving patterns [22].

**The Veri article** explains how Big Food designs products to be addictive through three mechanisms: (1) Bliss points—optimal combinations of salt, sugar, and fat engineered to maximize pleasure; (2) Palatability—foods high in salt, sugar, and fat that target the brain's reward system via dopamine release, creating addiction-like deficits; (3) Vanishing caloric density—foods that melt quickly in the mouth, tricking the brain into thinking they have no calories, encouraging overconsumption [13]. The article notes that "foods that quickly 'vanish' in your mouth are more rewarding to the brain, reduce gastric satiety, and encourage overconsumption" [13].

**The Center for Nutritional Psychology (CNP)** reports on a conceptual paper published in the *Journal of Metabolic Health* by Vera I. Tarman, which proposes a five-stage model of ultra-processed food addiction [23]. The article explains that separate gut-brain signaling pathways for sugar and fat, when activated simultaneously, create intense reward experiences that can dysregulate brain systems. Approximately 14% of people worldwide display symptoms of food addiction. The five stages are: (1) Pre-addiction—increased reward activity in the brain (nucleus accumbens, VTA) with heightened dopamine and opioid signaling, though control is maintained; (2) Early addiction—receptors become less sensitive, opioid release decreases, excessive eating and cravings begin; (3) Mid-addiction—significantly reduced dopamine and opioid release, loss of control, frequent binge eating; (4) Late-stage—further reduced sensitivity, tolerance, severe withdrawal, metabolic disturbances, job/relationship loss; (5) End-stage—severe reward system deficits, dopamine/opioid depletion, compulsive eating with minimal pleasure, complete loss of control. The author suggests early-stage interventions (inhibitory control, hormonal balance) may suffice, but more intensive interventions are needed for middle and later stages [23].

#### 5.4 The Role of Food Texture and Eating Rate

The Wageningen University RCT (presented at NUTRITION 2025) demonstrated that texture-derived differences in meal eating rate significantly influence energy intake from UPFs [11]. Over 14 days, 41 participants who consumed a UPF diet with textures that slowed eating rate averaged 369 fewer kcal per day (a cumulative difference of over 5,000 kcal) compared to when they consumed a UPF diet with textures promoting faster eating [11]. Both diets were matched for energy density, portion size, total energy served, and Nova 4 classification. Despite consuming fewer calories, participants reported no differences in appetite or diet satisfaction. Prof. Ciarán Forde noted: "Almost all participants adjusted their eating behaviours in response to the meal textures served, without any guidance or instructions or the need to consciously restrict their intake or compromise on food enjoyment and satisfaction" [11].

The Hall et al. (2019) trial found that eating rate was 17 calories/minute faster on the ultra-processed diet, and at a 20-minute meal, that's ~340 calories before gut satiety hormones can signal fullness [1]. A separate analysis of 327 foods across 5 countries confirmed the gradient: unprocessed foods at 36 kcal/min, processed at 54, ultra-processed at 69 [1].

#### 5.5 DSM-5 Criteria and Food Addiction

The review by Hough et al. (2026) draws from DSM-5 diagnostic criteria and recent neuropharmacology findings, noting parallels between binge eating disorder and substance dependence that highlight overlapping neurobehavioral mechanisms [20, 21]. The Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS) and its pediatric adaptations provide structured tools for identifying food addiction phenotypes in clinical and research settings [20, 21].

The WSJ article (2025) reports that scientists are proposing a new mental-health condition called "ultra-processed food use disorder" [20].

### SECTION 6: CROSS-CUTTING EVIDENCE AND MAJOR SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS

#### 6.1 Umbrella Review in *The BMJ* (February 29, 2024)

A comprehensive umbrella review published in *The BMJ* analyzed 45 pooled meta-analyses from 14 review articles (involving nearly 10 million participants) and found consistent evidence linking UPF exposure to 32 damaging health outcomes [21, 22]. None of the reviewed studies were funded by UPF manufacturers [21, 22].

**Convincing evidence (Class I)** supported direct associations between greater UPF exposure and higher risks of:
- Cardiovascular disease-related mortality (risk ratio 1.50, 95% CI: 1.37 to 1.63)
- Type 2 diabetes (dose-response risk ratio 1.12, 1.11 to 1.13)
- Prevalent anxiety outcomes (odds ratio 1.48, 1.37 to 1.59)
- Combined common mental disorder outcomes (odds ratio 1.53, 1.43 to 1.63)

**Highly suggestive evidence (Class II)** indicated direct associations with:
- All-cause mortality (risk ratio 1.21, 1.15 to 1.27)
- Heart disease-related mortality (hazard ratio 1.66, 1.51 to 1.84)
- Type 2 diabetes (odds ratio 1.40, 1.23 to 1.59)
- Depressive outcomes (hazard ratio 1.22, 1.16 to 1.28)
- Adverse sleep-related outcomes (odds ratio 1.41, 1.24 to 1.61)
- Wheezing (risk ratio 1.40, 1.27 to 1.55)
- Obesity (odds ratio 1.55, 1.36 to 1.77)

Using GRADE, 22 pooled analyses were rated as low quality, 19 as very low quality, and 4 as moderate quality. 93% of pooled analyses showed point estimates in the same direction (greater than one), indicating consistent increased risk with greater UPF exposure [21, 22].

The accompanying editorial calls for "a UN framework convention on ultra-processed foods, modeled after the tobacco framework" [21].

#### 6.2 NIH Office of Disease Prevention Webinar (July 8, 2026)

Dr. Josiemer Mattei (Harvard) reported that "73% of the U.S. food supply is ultra-processed" and "UPF comprises almost 60% of the total energy intake of U.S. adults" [24]. Not all UPFs are the same: "sugary beverages, animal-based products, and artificial sweeteners showed the strongest adverse associations, while cereals, yogurt, and savory snacks showed inverse associations with disease risk" [24]. Dr. Lauren O'Connor (Texas A&M) noted that "nutrition research faces complex challenges: controlling for energy intake, selection of comparison foods, and the heterogeneous nature of UPFs (ranging from cookies to tofu to infant formula)" [24].

#### 6.3 Narrative Review in *Nutrients* (2020)

A narrative review by Elizabeth, Machado, Zinöcker, Baker, and Lawrence (2020, *Nutrients*) systematically examined 43 studies, with 37 finding that dietary UPF exposure was associated with at least one adverse health outcome [25]. No study reported an association between UPF and beneficial health outcomes [25]. The review found that UPF consumption was associated with overweight, obesity, cardio-metabolic risks (e.g., metabolic syndrome, hypertension), cancer, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, irritable bowel syndrome, depression, frailty conditions, and all-cause mortality. In children/adolescents, associations were found with cardio-metabolic risks (e.g., higher total cholesterol, LDL-C, triglycerides, waist circumference) and asthma [25].

#### 6.4 American College of Cardiology Report (January 2025)

The ACC reports that meta-analyses have revealed that total UPF intake at the highest vs. the lowest level (42.8-49.6% of daily caloric consumption vs. 15.3-20.8%) is associated with a 17% and 23% higher risk of cardiovascular disease and coronary heart disease, respectively [23]. UPFs also increase stroke and cognitive impairment risk, with greater stroke risk among Black individuals [23]. Nearly 18 million American households are experiencing food insecurity. Food companies disproportionately advertise their least nutritious foods to Black and Hispanic consumers from low-income neighborhoods [23]. Hospital system menus contain up to 25% UPF [23].

#### 6.5 Global Consumption Patterns

According to the narrative review published in *Metabolites* (December 2025) from Oklahoma State University, UPFs now make up ~57-58% of average US adult daily calories (up from 53.5% in 2001-2002) [1]. Unprocessed/minimally processed foods contribute only 27.6% of calories. Obesity prevalence rose from 30.5% to 42.4% between 1999-2000 and 2017-2018 [1]. Energy-dense foods classified as UPF increased from 67% to 77% of the food supply over 30 years [1]. Over 90% of US adults do not meet fiber recommendations [1].
