**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## PART A: INDUSTRY INFLUENCE ON BEHAVIOR

### A1. PRODUCT DESIGN & FORMULATION

**Hyper-palatability and the "Bliss Point"**

The combination of fats, sugars, and salt in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is designed to generate the "Bliss effect" and addiction in consumers [1]. The "bliss point" is the ideal amount of sugar, salt, and fat that is impossible to resist [1]. Investigative journalist Michael Moss, in his book "Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us" (2013), revealed how food corporations like Kraft, Coca-Cola, Frito-Lay, and Nestlé deliberately engineer products to hit the "bliss point" — the precise combination of salt, sugar, and fat that triggers maximum dopamine release and craving. Research by Fazzino et al. (2019) identified three hyper-palatable food clusters: fat + sodium, fat + simple sugars, and carbohydrates + sodium, with consumption increases of up to 30% [1].

The FoodTimes article notes that the "Bliss effect" in UPFs was originally described using the Bliss independence model from pharmacology, describing how combined stimuli produce effects greater than the sum of individual components [1]. A 2024 study by Darcey et al. found highly variable individual dopamine responses to UPFs [1].

UPFs are designed to be highly palatable, appealing, and energy dense with a unique combination of the main taste enhancer ingredients to generate a strong rewarding stimulus [12]. The reward circuitry is activated by both drugs and UPFs, triggering in both cases an escalation in consumption [12].

According to the Stanford Medicine article (July 15, 2025), featuring research dietitian Dalia Perelman from the Stanford Prevention Research Center, UPFs "are basically industrial formulations" containing "ingredients you wouldn't find in a typical kitchen — things like emulsifiers, colorings, flavor enhancers, bulking agents, gels" [2]. UPFs are formulated to hit the "bliss point" — the precise combination of sugar, salt, and fat maximizing palatability [2].

An Instagram post from "foodmeetsscience" (December 10, 2025) explains that these foods target the brain's reward system with a perfect mix of sugar, fat, and salt to hit the "bliss point," boosting cravings. Additives are used to shape flavor, color, and crunch to make the food feel fresher and more intense than it actually is [3]. The post concludes that these foods are designed for pleasure, not nutrition, which is why they are hard to resist [3].

**Food Matrix Collapse**

A landmark review article published in Frontiers in Nutrition on May 5, 2026 (Wang et al.) proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the primary health threat of UPFs stems not merely from their poor nutritional composition but from the industrial collapse of their physical "food matrix" [4]. The authors hypothesize that this structural disintegration triggers a top-down cascade of dysregulation across multiple physiological systems. The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This leads to metabolic dysregulation including insulin resistance, de novo lipogenesis, and mitochondrial stress. Finally, the impoverished matrix combined with chemical additives causes gut microbiome imbalance, compromised intestinal barrier function, and systemic low-grade chronic inflammation via metabolic endotoxemia [4].

The review critiques "nutritionism" and fortified UPFs, arguing that adding isolated nutrients to a collapsed matrix cannot restore health value. The authors conclude that the integrity of the food matrix is an indispensable dimension for evaluating the health value of food, and call for a fundamental shift in perspective from focusing solely on "what is in our food" to equally considering "what has been done to our food" [4].

**Industry Patents and Trade Publications**

A Canadian patent (CA2657130C) assigned to Frito Lay Trading Co GmbH describes a method for producing low-fat snack foods (such as potato or corn-based crisps) that have the appearance and taste of traditional fried snacks without using an oil-frying process [61]. The method involves: providing food slices from a starch-based food or dough; optionally blanching the slices; adding a controlled amount of oil to enhance organoleptic properties; and rapidly dehydrating the slices in a primary drying step that simulates conventional frying dehydration rates. The patent background notes that raw potato slices have 75-85% moisture, and conventional frying causes water to boil, bursting cell walls and allowing oil absorption, yielding oil contents ranging from 30% to 45% by weight. The goal of the patent is to produce a shelf-stable, ready-to-eat snack with low oil content while maintaining the texture and taste of fried products [61].

A comprehensive analysis of 14 original-cut potato chip brands in the Chinese market, published in Foods (December 2024, Cui et al.), examined physicochemical properties and sensory attributes [64]. Key findings include: Color difference (ΔE) strongly correlated with sensory scores (r = 0.73, p < 0.01), emphasizing the importance of visual appeal in consumer acceptance. Protein ranged from 5.19–8.51%, fat from 27.91–40.16%, and moisture from 0.67–3.78%. Acrylamide levels varied widely from 166.7 to 1101.78 µg/kg (mean 430.39 ± 283.29 µg/kg), with Brand M (1101.78 µg/kg) exceeding the EU benchmark of 750 µg/kg. Acrylamide positively correlated with sucrose content (r = 0.57, p < 0.05). Fracturability negatively correlated with sensory scores (r = −0.75, p < 0.01), suggesting that Chinese consumers prefer less brittle chips. Moisture negatively correlated with hardness (r = −0.63, p < 0.05) [64].

**Vanishing Caloric Density**

Chris van Tulleken explains the term "vanishing caloric density" in relation to foods such as chips, cookies, and other soft foods that are irresistible [62]. University of Queensland chemical engineers have developed a new method to analyze the physical characteristics of potato chips in a bid to keep the crunch in low-fat potato chips [63].

**Multi-Sensory Food Design and Mouthfeel Optimization**

Michael Moss revealed how food scientists calculate the "bliss point" of sugary beverages and enhance the "mouthfeel" of fat by manipulating its chemical structure, exposing marketing techniques borrowed directly from tobacco company playbooks [1].

**Historical Context**

Ultra-processing is not new. Artificial trans fats were invented in the early 1900s, and the major boom occurred after WWII due to military advances in food preservation [2]. The most striking change in food systems of high-income countries, and now of low- and middle-income countries, is displacement of dietary patterns based on meals and dishes prepared from unprocessed or minimally processed foods by those that are increasingly based on ultra-processed food and drink products [81].

**NOVA Classification System**

The NOVA food classification system, developed by researchers at the University of São Paulo (Carlos Monteiro et al.), categorizes foods based on the nature, extent, and purpose of industrial processing [81]. The four groups are: (1) Unprocessed or minimally processed foods; (2) Processed culinary ingredients; (3) Processed foods; and (4) Ultra-processed foods — formulations made mostly from industrial ingredients and additives with little intact food, such as soft drinks, packaged snacks, reconstituted meat products, and pre-prepared frozen dishes [81][82]. The overall purpose of ultra-processing is to create branded, convenient (durable, ready to consume), attractive (hyper-palatable) and highly profitable (low-cost ingredients) food products designed to displace all other food groups [81][82].

UPFs are "formulations of ingredients, mostly of exclusive industrial use" created through industrial techniques, containing substances like hydrogenated oils, protein isolates, and additives (flavours, colours, emulsifiers) that make them hyper-palatable, convenient, and highly profitable [82].

**Current Consumption Levels**

UPFs now account for nearly 60% of U.S. adults' calorie consumption and close to 70% of American children's intake [2]. 73% of the U.S. food supply is ultra-processed, according to estimation from a machine-learning algorithm that accurately predicted the degree of processing of any food [5]. The average US adult's diet has a majority of daily calories (~57%) from UPFs, a number that has increased throughout the years, up from 53.5% in 2001-2002, with annual per capita consumption increasing ~142% since 1960 [32]. Over half of the adults in the United States have at least one chronic disease, and roughly a quarter of adults have two or more [32].

Nearly 70% of an American child's calories today comes from ultra-processed foods (increased from zero 100 years ago) [89]. Over 40% of the roughly 73 million children (aged 0-17) in the United States have at least one chronic health condition, according to the CDC [89]. The U.S. obesity rate is, on average, more than double that of its G7 peers [89].

**Not All UPFs Are Equal**

Not all UPFs are the same or associated in the same way with disease [5]. Some ultra-processed foods (like Cheerios) can be more nutrient-dense than others [2]. The NOVA system has limitations, and some foods could fall into multiple categories. Perelman advocates for balance and moderation, not elimination, and suggests prioritizing fresh fruits, vegetables, beans, whole grains, nuts, and seeds while reading ingredient lists carefully [2]. Perelman states: "It's not like the industry is trying to kill us. They're trying to make food more affordable, more convenient, tastier" [2]. "You don't want to throw the baby out with the bathwater. Highly processed food has helped us feed a lot more people and reach populations that wouldn't otherwise get a lot of food" [2].

Sugary beverages, animal-based products, and artificial sweeteners showed the strongest adverse associations, while cereals, yogurt, and savory snacks showed inverse associations with disease risk [5]. The "plant-based = healthy" misconception is addressed: vegetarians and vegans often consume more UPFs (processed meat substitutes, protein bars, packaged snacks). The key factor is the degree of industrial processing, not whether food is plant or animal based [80].

### A2. SATIETY OVERSHOOT

**How UPFs Bypass Satiety Signals**

The collapse of the food matrix in UPFs is central to satiety disruption. The cascade begins with oral processing, where the soft matrix of UPFs accelerates eating rates and weakens early satiety signals. In the gastrointestinal tract, rapid nutrient absorption suppresses secretion of satiety hormones GLP-1 and PYY (the "ileal brake" mechanism). This supraphysiological nutrient flux imposes a significant challenge on core metabolic organs, driving insulin resistance and hepatic de novo lipogenesis [4].

UPFs promote overconsumption through hyperpalatability, altered nutrient profiles (high saturated fat, added sugar, sodium), low water content, high energy density, faster eating rates (especially soft-textured and liquid UPFs), and disruption of evolved nutrient-flavor associations [32]. Over 10,000 food additives have been approved over the last 60 years, with concerns about the "cocktail effect" of cumulative exposures [32].

A randomized controlled trial by NIH researcher Kevin D. Hall found that when calorie-matched, participants ate significantly more of ultra-processed foods than unprocessed foods, suggesting processing itself—not just nutrient content—influences appetite and weight regulation [5][80]. A 2019 study found participants on an ultra-processed diet ate 500 more calories per day and gained 2 pounds more than those on unprocessed diets [2]. The challenges faced in nutrition science "explode" when talking about UPFs because there are so many other components to these foods [5].

**Hormonal Mechanisms of Satiety**

Appetite regulation refers to the complex physiological processes that control hunger, satiety, and energy balance through coordinated central and peripheral signals [34]. Hunger is a natural (and essential) feeling driven by physical, neurological, and hormonal signals influenced by food intake, body fat, physical activity, stress, and sleep [33].

Key hormones include: ghrelin (the "hunger hormone"), leptin (the "satiety hormone"), orexin, MCH, and INSL5 that drive appetite, as well as CCK, PYY, and GLP-1 that promote fullness [33]. GLP-1 delays gastric emptying, controls blood sugar levels, and reduces food intake by acting on appetite-regulating centers in the hypothalamus and brainstem [34]. GLP-1 and PYY (from enteroendocrine L-cells) reduce hunger after eating, while ghrelin is the primary hunger hormone that rises preprandially [34].

High-protein meals facilitate the release of GLP-1 and PYY, which reduce hunger; controlled feeding studies demonstrate that protein-rich meals produce higher, more sustained circulating levels of GLP-1 and PYY than isocaloric meals rich in fat or carbohydrates [34]. High glycemic index foods cause rapid glucose/insulin spikes and earlier hunger onset; low glycemic index foods prolong satiety. Dietary fiber (especially viscous fiber) slows digestion and enhances satiety [34].

In an eight-week randomized trial comparing low-carbohydrate and low-fat, low-energy diets, postprandial CCK decreased in both groups, suggesting that energy restriction, rather than dietary fat content per se, influenced CCK responses [34]. Fermentable fibers (resistant starch, beta-glucans) produce SCFAs that may alter GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin, and leptin in animal models, but effects vary [34].

Different macronutrients and levels of food processing impact hunger and fullness in various ways, with protein, fiber, and whole foods generally being more satiating than refined carbohydrates, added sugars, and ultra-processed foods [33]. Eating slowly, chewing thoroughly, and consuming solid foods rather than liquids can enhance feelings of fullness and reduce overall calorie intake [33].

**PYY and GLP-1 as Therapeutic Targets**

Nearly 2 billion adults worldwide are overweight (BMI ≥25 kg/m²) and a further estimated 500 million are obese (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) [35]. Bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) is the most effective treatment, leading to ~30% sustained weight loss, but carries a 0.5% mortality rate [35].

PYY3-36, a form of PYY, inhibits appetite by acting on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) via the Y2 receptor, increasing activity of anorexigenic POMC/α-MSH neurons while suppressing orexigenic NPY neurons [35]. In human studies, intravenous PYY3-36 reduced ad libitum food intake by up to 36% compared to saline, with comparable effects in lean and obese subjects [35]. A meta-analysis found that GLP-1 infusion reduced energy intake by ~13% in lean subjects and ~10.5% in overweight/obese subjects [35]. GLP-1 analogues (exenatide, liraglutide) are licensed for type 2 diabetes and promote weight loss. Liraglutide 3 mg once daily in non-diabetic obese patients led to 7.2 kg mean weight loss over 20 weeks [35].

**GLP-1 Medications and UPF Consumption**

A notable section of the FoodTimes article discusses how GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy may disrupt Big Food's bliss point strategies by altering taste preferences and neurological reward pathways, with users reporting reduced food spending (11% decrease) and developing disgust for industrial foods [1]. The emerging potential of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonists (targeting obesity) is noted as a possible natural counter to overactivation of the reward system via satiation mechanisms [70].

**Metabolic Mechanism of Addiction**

A 2026 perspective paper in PLOS Medicine by Professor David Ludwig of Harvard Medical School argues that "hyperpalatability" may actually be the wrong explanation. The more compelling mechanism, Ludwig argues, is metabolic. When processed carbohydrates are rapidly digested, blood glucose spikes then crashes — and it's at that crash point, roughly three to four hours after eating, that a brain region linked to craving and reward (the nucleus accumbens) becomes significantly more active [9][20].

### A3. MARKETING STRATEGIES

**Child-Directed Marketing**

Food advertising has played a significant role in driving dietary shifts and maintaining poor dietary intake among children [30]. UPFs account for 49.1% of the total caloric intake among Canadian children aged 2-5 years old and 54.2% among Canadian children aged 6-12 years old [30]. In Canada, children (2-11 years old) are exposed to almost 2,000 advertisements (ads) for unhealthy foods annually on television and more than 4,000 on digital platforms [30].

Children's perceptions, purchase intent, and perceived targeted audience did not change between child-targeted and non-child-targeted ads [30]. This study underscores the critical role of the product itself in influencing children's responses to ads, highlighting the need for public policies and advertising regulations to focus on restricting promotions of unhealthy products rather than solely addressing marketing techniques or target audiences [30].

The average Australian 5 to 8-year-old is exposed to at least 827 unhealthy food advertisements on television each year [29]. Australian adolescents are exposed to almost 100 promotions per week from online sources [29]. Children aged 4 to 6 years believe a product tastes better if it has a cartoon character on the pack [29]. For every hour online, children aged 13-17 are exposed to 17 unhealthy food ads [29]. Children can view up to 37 unhealthy food ads each way to school [29].

Digital marketing targets children via data-driven personalized ads, influencer endorsements ('kidfluencers'), TikTok campaigns turning users into 'unofficial brand ambassadors', advergames, and in-game marketing [29]. Adolescents are especially vulnerable due to strong engagement with social media, gaming, and streaming services. Marketers build extensive profiles using browsing history, geo-location, and social network data to deliver highly targeted ads [29]. Commercial TV viewing is independently associated with childhood obesity, likely due to unhealthy food advertising [29].

Product packaging uses cartoon characters on packaging that significantly increase taste preferences [29]. Collectible toys can alter food preferences, with some evidence they can encourage healthier choices [29]. Sports sponsorship shows high awareness among children (ages 10-14) of food/beverage sponsors, with many receiving vouchers or certificates from these companies [29]. Outdoor advertising of unhealthy food ads is concentrated near schools, especially in lower socioeconomic areas [29]. Unhealthy foods are strategically placed at prominent store locations (end-of-aisles, checkouts), more so in disadvantaged areas. Price promotions also drive increased purchases [29]. Child-directed marketing uses 'fun' themes (playful names, bright colours, cartoon characters, e.g., McDonald's Happy Meal) to make unhealthy food appealing [29].

**Social Media and Digital Marketing**

A Cancer Research UK study found that more than half of the 4,000 young people aged 11 to 21 who took part in a survey had seen posts from businesses and influencers promoting products high in fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) on social media within a month [26]. These posts had a direct impact on young people's behavior, with many reporting feeling tempted, hungry, or craving specific foods after viewing [26]. Influencer marketing is particularly effective because it appears more relatable and trustworthy than corporate advertising, and young people often struggle to recognize when they are being targeted [26].

Children and adolescents are extensively exposed to digital marketing of unhealthy foods (high in unhealthy fats, sugars, salt, often highly processed), with exposure increasing with age [28]. A wide range of marketing techniques are used including influencers, branded hashtag challenges, cartoon/celebrity endorsements, engagement tools (likes, comments, shares), and product placement [28]. In a Canadian study, children were estimated to see 30 food marketing exposures/week and adolescents 189/week [28]. In Mexico, 69.5% of children/adolescents were exposed to food marketing during 45 min of screen time; 93.3% of promoted products were unhealthy [28]. 90.34% of food/drinks in kid influencer YouTube videos were unhealthy branded items [28]. Exposure to digital marketing of unhealthy foods appears to be linked to increased consumption, but evidence quality is limited [28].

The WHO recommends against marketing of these foods to children [28]. Mandatory comprehensive policies are needed; LAC countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Peru, Mexico) provide insights for policy development [28].

**UK and International Legislation**

New legislation entered into force in the UK in January 2026, banning paid-for online advertising of specific HFSS products, including on social media, and introducing a 9pm TV watershed for junk food ads [26]. SAFE (Safe Food Advocacy Europe) welcomed these measures and calls for the European Union to introduce comprehensive legislation to protect children from exposure to the marketing of HFSS and ultra-processed foods (UPFs) across all media channels [26].

Unhealthy food marketing creates social norms around food and eating, increases children's preference for and consumption of ultra-processed foods, and increases total energy intake [27].

**Marketing and Health Claims**

Michael Moss revealed how food scientists calculate the 'bliss point' of sugary beverages and enhance the 'mouthfeel' of fat by manipulating its chemical structure, exposing marketing techniques borrowed directly from tobacco company playbooks [1].

### A4. FOOD ADDICTION CONCEPT

**Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS)**

The Yale Food Addiction Scale (YFAS; Gearhardt, Corbin, & Brownell, 2009) is the first measure designed specifically to assess signs of addictive-like eating behavior, particularly regarding highly processed foods [7]. It includes 25 items based on DSM-IV criteria for substance dependence, with two scoring options: a symptom count (0-7) and a dichotomous diagnosis (3+ symptoms plus clinically significant impairment). It has received psychometric support across various populations, and has been translated into multiple languages including Arabic, Chinese, Finnish, French, German, Hindi, Iranian, Italian, Malay, Portuguese, Spanish, and Turkish [7].

The YFAS 2.0 (Gearhardt, Corbin, & Brownell, 2016) was developed to maintain consistency with the current diagnostic understanding of addiction (DSM-5 criteria) and to improve the psychometric properties of the original YFAS [7]. The YFAS 2.0 consists of 35 self-report items that assess eating behaviors and emotional responses associated with food consumption over the past 12 months, using an 8-point Likert scale [6]. It covers symptoms such as cravings, loss of control, continued use despite negative consequences, and withdrawal. The scale provides two scoring options: a symptom count score (0-11) and a dichotomous diagnosis (No Food Addiction, or Mild/Moderate/Severe Food Addiction, which requires both a symptom count threshold and clinical significance). The estimated completion time is 8-10 minutes [6]. Both versions of the YFAS are similarly associated with elevated body mass index, binge eating, and weight cycling [7].

Modified versions include the mYFAS (9 items for large epidemiologic studies) and mYFAS 2.0 (13 items) [7]. For children, the YFAS-C (2nd grade reading level), YFAS-C 2.0, dYFAS-C 2.0 (dimensional scoring, 3rd grade reading level), and mYFAS-C 2.0 (13-item brief version) are available [7]. Additional scales include the Highly Processed Food Withdrawal Scale (ProWS, 29 items), the ProWS-C (parent-report for children aged 3-11, 21 items), and the Anticipated Effects of Food Scale (AEFS) measuring food expectancies [7].

**Prevalence of Food Addiction**

According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse (2020), about 1 in 5 individuals with obesity meet the criteria for food addiction using this scale [8]. A World Health Organization-backed study using YFAS data found that nearly 15% of adolescents globally show signs of food addiction, with symptoms strongly correlated to increased intake of sugary beverages and snack foods [8]. A study by Flint et al., titled "Assessing the Short Version of the Yale Food Addiction Scale," published in Appetite (2014), reported a Cronbach's alpha of 0.84, confirming its high consistency in measuring food addiction symptoms across diverse populations [8].

The Yale Food Addiction Scale indicates approximately 15-20% of adults may meet criteria for food addiction [1]. Recent meta-analytic data cited in a 2025 commentary suggest that 14% of adults and 12% of children globally exhibit this addictive-like eating phenotype, a prevalence rate comparable to that of alcohol use disorders [66].

Using YFAS, a high prevalence of food addiction was found in the general population, up to 20% according to a meta-analytic research [67]. Higher prevalence in females (12% vs 6.4%), older adults (age >35), and obese/overweight individuals (25% vs 11%) [67].

**YFAS 2.0 Validation in Taiwan**

A validation study published in Frontiers in Psychiatry (November 25, 2022) validated the YFAS 2.0 and mYFAS 2.0 in a Taiwanese population of 687 university students [46]. Both scales demonstrated a satisfactory single-factor structure. Both scales showed good internal consistency (McDonald's ω = 0.96 for YFAS 2.0, 0.87 for mYFAS 2.0) and test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.71 for YFAS 2.0, 0.69 for mYFAS 2.0). Both scales were strongly associated with weight self-stigma (r = 0.54–0.57), and had small-to-moderate associations with BMI (r = 0.13–0.17) and physical activity (r = 0.23–0.25). The food addiction prevalence rate was 6.4% using both instruments. Both scales were invariant across sex, allowing valid comparisons between males and females [46].

**Clinical Data on YFAS 2.0**

Data from Creative Touch's own analysis of over 2,690 self-selected users shows an average symptom count of 4.7 out of 11 and 48.1% meeting the threshold for clinical significance [9]. BMI is identified as the strongest demographic predictor, with Obese Class III individuals averaging 6.8 symptoms (61% Severe Food Addiction) compared to 3.0 symptoms for those with normal BMI (19.7% Severe). Females report higher symptom severity (4.9 avg, 39.2% Severe) than males (4.04 avg, 27.6% Severe). Younger adults (18-24) show the highest symptom count (5.3, 45% Severe) [9].

**Evidence Base for Food Addiction**

In a systematic review of 52 studies, every DSM-5 SUD criterion was empirically supported in the context of food, with brain reward dysfunction and impaired control demonstrating the strongest evidence base [66]. Food addiction is associated with poorer quality of life, worse treatment prognosis, and greater psychopathology [69].

The pathogenesis of food addiction involves reward dysfunction (dopamine D2 receptor abnormalities), impulsivity, and emotion dysregulation. Similar neural activation patterns found in food addiction and substance use disorders, including elevated activity in reward circuitry and reduced activity in inhibitory control regions [67].

**The Food Addiction Debate**

Food addiction describes addiction-like responses to ultra-processed foods, but it is not yet a formal DSM-5 or ICD-11 diagnosis [66]. There currently remains no definitive consensus on diagnostic validity, as some researchers maintain that food craving, emotional eating, binge eating, body-image distress, and perceived loss of control may overlap with existing eating-disorder constructs rather than proving a distinct addiction diagnosis [66]. Considerable debate exists regarding the extent to which food may be addictive and whether food addiction might be an important entity [68].

The concept of food addiction remains debated in the scientific community, with overlaps with disordered eating and emotional eating [9]. Some researchers propose "ultra-processed food addiction" or "ultra-processed food use disorder" as potential diagnostic terms [66].

At behavioral level, food addiction has high degrees of similarity with other eating disorders, a phenomenon that creates difficulties in finding specific diagnostic criteria [67]. The article concludes that while food addiction is not currently recognized in DSM-5 or ICD-10, substantial evidence supports its existence as a clinical entity, though more research is needed on diagnostic criteria and treatment [67].

**Treatment Approaches**

There is no established standard treatment for food addiction itself, and evidence from broader eating-disorder treatment research suggests that CBT is often better than no treatment, but not consistently superior to other active interventions [66][67]. Current approaches include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), dietary modifications (harm reduction model), and emerging research on GLP-1 receptor agonists for reducing cravings [66]. Abstinence-based approaches for specific trigger UPFs are discussed but not yet validated [66]. Assessment should consider co-occurring eating disorders, trauma histories, and mental health concerns rather than focusing only on weight or willpower [66].

---

## PART B: INDIVIDUAL SUSCEPTIBILITY FACTORS

### B1. GENETIC FACTORS

**DRD2 (Dopamine D2 Receptor)**

The DRD2 gene encodes the dopamine D2 receptor. The primary SNP studied is rs1800497 (Taq1A). The 'A' (also known as the 'A1') allele correlates with a 30% lower number ('density') of D2 receptors [14][11]. According to a large meta-analysis of 33 trials, there was no strong or consistent correlation between this variant and body mass index (BMI). However, people with the 'A' allele may not respond well to (or comply with) weight-loss interventions [14]. Around 33% of European descendants carry the 'A' allele. However, this variant is up to twice as common among East Asian and African populations (64-65%) [14].

People with rs1800497-A crave tasty, energy-dense foods — but the feelings of 'reward' they experience upon consumption may be relatively weaker [14]. In five clinical trials with over 1,300 participants, the 'A' allele correlates with higher preference for carbohydrates, sugar, fast food, and high-fat fried foods [14]. Brain imaging studies show people with the 'A' allele have a blunted reward response to tasty food despite craving it. The variant is associated with uncontrolled eating, emotional eating, high food reinforcement (willingness to work harder for food), and consuming more calories [14].

The TaqA1 allele has a 30-40% reduction in D2 receptor density in the dorsal striatum [71]. Carriers (18% Caucasians, 38% Africans, 39% Asians) have reduced dopamine function, requiring more food to achieve the same reward, and have increased risk for addiction disorders and obesity [71].

A study in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience (March 31, 2023) evaluated the association between the bilocus genetic profile (rs1799732-rs1800497) of the dopaminergic pathway with food reinforcement and food addiction in Chilean adults [11]. The cross-sectional study of 221 adults (74% female) aged 18-54, comprising 44% obese, 11% overweight, and 45% normal weight, found that the genetic variants rs1799732 and rs1800497 were associated with anthropometric measurements but not with food addiction or food reinforcement in Chilean university students. Genotypic frequencies for rs1799732: 73.1% GG, 25.5% G/Del, 1.4% Del/Del. For rs1800497: 56.4% A2A2, 33.6% A1A2, 9.9% A1A1. In the normal weight group, individuals who were heterozygous for the rs1799732 variant (G/del) showed higher body weight (p=0.01) and abdominal circumference (p=0.01) compared to those who were homozygous (G/G). The bilocus score distribution showed: 11% "very low dopaminergic signaling", 24.4% "under", 49.7% "intermediate signaling", 12.7% "high" and 1.4% "very high". The authors suggest that other genotypes, such as rs4680 and rs6277, which affect DA signaling capacity through a multilocus composite score, should be studied [11].

Individuals who show reduced striatal activation during food intake have an increased risk of obesity, particularly those with genetic alterations in DA signaling [12]. Reduced striatal D2 receptor availability is seen in both obesity and drug addiction [12].

**DRD4 (Dopamine D4 Receptor)**

The DRD4 7R allele (7-repeat allele) is linked to novelty seeking, ADHD, impulsivity, and exploratory behaviors. Referred to as the "adventure gene," it leads to less responsive dopamine receptors, causing individuals to seek new and stimulating experiences. May contribute to overeating or impulsivity [13].

**COMT (Catechol-O-Methyltransferase)**

COMT is involved in regulating dopamine and stress response [13]. The authors of the Chilean study suggest that genotypes such as rs4680 (COMT) and rs6277 (DRD2) should be studied through a multilocus composite score for more comprehensive evaluation [11].

**MC4R (Melanocortin 4 Receptor)**

Mutations in the MC4R gene account for 6-8% of obesity cases and represent the most common genetic cause of human obesity [36]. A common variant of the MC4R gene (rs17782313, C-allele), distributed in about 22% of the population, increases the risk for weight gain by causing increased appetite and decreased satiety [36]. Each copy of the C-allele at this SNP correlates to a BMI increase of about 0.22 and an 8% increased risk for being overweight [36]. Carriers experience increased appetite and decreased satiety, leading to larger food intake, more frequent snacking, and preference for fatty foods [36].

The biological mechanism involves hunger signals (like ghrelin) and satiety signals (like leptin and insulin) both functioning through MC4R via competitive binding of AgRP and α-MSH. When AgRP prevails, hunger results; when α-MSH prevails, satiety results [36]. To date, 166 MC4R mutations have been documented, with about 0.66% of the general population carrying one. In early-onset severe obesity populations, 6-8% carry MC4R loss-of-function mutations. These individuals typically develop obesity by age 3-4, with meals containing about three times the calories of non-carriers. Female carriers gain about twice the weight as male carriers [36]. Two gain-of-function mutations (V103I/rs2229616 and I251L/rs52820871) have protective effects against obesity, reducing risk by 20% and 48% respectively [36].

**FTO (Fat Mass and Obesity-Associated Gene)**

FTO represents the fat mass and obesity-associated gene which holds the distinction of being the most researched gene related to body weight and obesity [40]. The FTO gene holds the distinction of being the initial genetic discovery connected to obesity and continues to have the greatest documented influence on body weight currently known [40]. Research indicates that FTO functions as a 'master switch' to control multiple weight-related genes and pathways in our bodies although its precise role remains unclear [40]. The key SNP rs9939609 is strongly correlated with obesity across age groups and ethnicities. Carriers of the 'A' allele show higher weight gain, obesity prevalence, elevated ghrelin levels, increased food consumption, preference for calorie-rich foods, less meal satisfaction, emotional/binge eating, greater insulin resistance, and higher blood sugar. The 'T' allele carriers typically maintain normal weight with greater satiety and healthier food choices [40].

A healthy diet provides individuals with the 'A' variant protection against its negative health effects [40]. A three-year investigation demonstrated that individuals with the 'AA' genotype experience better weight loss outcomes on a Mediterranean diet than those with the 'TT' genotype [40].

However, a study published in BMC Nutrition (2023) investigating the relationship between the FTO rs9939609 (A/T) polymorphism and food preferences found no significant differences between groups in sweet food preference (15.64±10.53 in obese vs. 14.72±7.95 in non-obese, p=0.711) or fatty food preference (16.81±8.84 vs. 17.27±8.75, p=0.833). The study concluded that the results do not support the hypothesis that FTO rs9939609 polymorphism influences different food preferences [38]. Some meta-analyses do not support FTO-BMI associations, and findings vary across populations [40].

**OPRM1 (Mu-Opioid Receptor)**

The OPRM1 gene provides instructions for making a protein called the mu (μ) opioid receptor [72]. The μ opioid receptor is the primary receptor for endogenous opioids called beta-endorphin and enkephalins, which help regulate the body's response to pain, among other functions [72]. The best-studied OPRM1 gene polymorphism, called A118G or rs1799971, changes a protein building block (amino acid) in a particular place in the μ opioid receptor protein [72]. This is a "gain-of-function" mutation with ~3-times greater affinity for endorphins [71]. The A118G polymorphism is much more common in certain populations, such as people of Asian or European ancestry, than in others, such as people of African or African American ancestry [72]. Carriers (38% Asians, 16% Caucasians, 1% Africans) show greater preference for sweet and fatty foods but paradoxically are less likely to gain weight due to heightened satisfaction [71].

Studies have found associations between the A118G polymorphism and a variety of other traits, including perception of physical and psychological pain, sensitivity to social rejection, a preference for sweet and fatty foods, and how the body responds to stress [72].

The A118G is the most common single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the human MOP-r (OPRM1) gene, found in approximately 15% of Caucasian and 40-60% of Asian populations [74]. The combination of the OPRM1 G-allele (118G) with the normal DRD2 A2A2 genotype creates the highest sensitivity toward palatable foods. This combination is found in 11% of Caucasians and 14% of Asians (less than 0.4% of Africans). These individuals have a dramatically increased risk for binge eating disorder when they frequently consume palatable foods [71].

The rewarding properties of foods, mainly the palatability, act like addictive substances in the reward system of the human brain to produce the feeling of pleasure. The function of foods in the reward system is independent of their calorie content. It is the palatability, not the calorie of the foods that modulate the reward system [71].

**Taste Receptor Polymorphisms (TAS1R, TAS2R, CD36)**

A systematic review published in Frontiers in Genetics (December 19, 2019, Diószegi et al.) investigated the genetic background of taste perception, taste preferences, and their nutritional implications [43][45]. Of 949 identified publications, 103 articles were included. Key findings by taste modality:

**Bitter Taste (64 studies):** The most extensively studied. TAS2R38 variants (rs713598, rs1726866, rs10246939) were strongly associated with PTC/PROP sensitivity and bitterness perception of foods like vegetables, wine, and alcohol. PAV haplotype homozygotes showed greater sensitivity to bitter compounds. Other genes studied include TAS2R19, TAS2R31, TAS2R4, TAS2R5, TAS2R9, and CA6 [43][45].

**Sweet Taste (28 studies):** TAS2R38 polymorphisms were also associated with sweet taste preference and sugar intake. TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 variants showed inconclusive or limited associations. Other genes include GNAT3, SLC2A2, TAS1R1, ADIPOQ, ANKK1, DRD2, OPRM1, LEP, LEPR, and NPY1 [43][45].

**Fat Taste (22 studies):** The most convincing results were for CD36 polymorphisms (rs1761667, rs1527483) associated with oleic acid threshold and fat perception. IZUMO1 rs838145 variant was also associated with fat preference [43][45].

**Umami Taste (6 studies):** Limited studies suggested TAS1R1 and TAS1R3 polymorphisms influence umami taster status [43][45].

Heritability estimates range from high to moderate for bitter tasting stimuli [0.72, 0.71, 0.34, for PROP, PTC, and quinine hydrochloride, respectively] and moderate for sweet tasting compounds (glucose: h² = 0.31, fructose: h² = 0.34) [43][45].

The SWEET Project (Nutrients, 2025, Volume 17, Issue 6, 949) investigated how SNPs in TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 genes affect receptor activation by 12 different sweeteners [42]. Although certain human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 SNPs showed reduced receptor response, they were not associated with particular phenotypes. Seven SNPs were predicted to severely impair the human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 response to sweeteners. The I595T and K689Q substitutions in TAS1R2 severely impaired the ability to respond to most of the tested sweeteners. The L95P and S551N substitutions completely abolished or decreased the receptor response to low-molecular sweeteners. The authors concluded that although some TAS1R2- and TAS1R3-SNPs have previously been associated with obesity, the cellular results do not confirm this association and reinforce the hypothesis that sweet taste perception and sugar consumption are governed by factors other than the TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 genes [42].

A T1R2+3 heterodimer functions as a sweet taste receptor, while a T1R1+3 heterodimer functions as an umami taste receptor [44]. T2R family members act as bitter taste receptors with broad ligand specificity [44]. The Tas1r2 gene is absent in the genomes of chicken, zebra finch, and horse; it is a pseudogene in four Felidae species (domestic cat, tiger, cheetah, and Asiatic lion), explaining the lack of attraction to sugars in cats [44].

**BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor)**

BDNF is involved in neuroplasticity and brain resilience [13].

### B2. EPIGENETIC AND DEVELOPMENTAL FACTORS

**Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) Paradigm**

The DOHaD hypothesis posits that environmental exposures during critical windows of early development—from preconception through infancy—have lasting effects on health and disease risk across the lifespan [23]. Originally conceptualized by Dr. David Barker in the 1980s through observations linking low birth weight to adult cardiovascular disease, the framework has expanded to encompass non-communicable diseases (NCDs) including obesity, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, neurodevelopmental disorders, and mental health conditions [23].

The DOHaD hypothesis proposes a link between periconceptual, fetal, and early infant phases of life and the long-term development of metabolic disorders [22]. According to the DOHaD hypothesis, epigenetic adaptations are made to the fetal/neonatal DNA in response to environmental influences [22]. The science of epigenetics is quickly growing with the understanding that the environment and individual lifestyle directly interact with the genome to influence epigenetic changes [22].

The core premise is that genetic heritage does not define one's destiny; rather, lifestyle choices and environmental factors influence gene expression through epigenetic modifications (methylation and other chemical changes) without altering the DNA sequence itself [22]. Research shows how external factors influence genetic function, resulting in altered longevity and the incidence of cancer and age-related diseases [22].

**Key Mechanisms of Developmental Programming**

Epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone changes) are influenced by one-carbon metabolism nutrients (folate, choline, methionine, vitamin B12) [21]. Hormonal signaling (cortisol, insulin, leptin) affects fetal HPA axis, metabolic regulation, and appetite [21]. Placental function adapts nutrient transport to maternal nutritional status [21]. The maternal microbiome influences infant microbial colonization and immune development [21]. Catch-up growth is linked to obesity and diabetes risk [21].

The "first 1000 days" of life, spanning preconception, pregnancy, and early infancy, represent a uniquely sensitive period of biological plasticity during which biological systems are established and calibrated [21]. The environmental mismatch concept—where prenatal adaptations to scarcity become maladaptive in postnatal abundance—is central to disease risk [21]. When fetal adaptations are mismatched with postnatal conditions, disease risk increases [21].

**Maternal and Paternal Influences**

Critical developmental windows include the third trimester of pregnancy (synapse formation, myelination), early childhood (taste preference formation), and adolescence (PFC and dopamine system development, continuing until ~age 25) [88].

Children of obese mothers are twice as likely to be obese at age 2. Infants of overweight/obese mothers have higher fat mass at birth and increased risk of metabolic disorders [22]. Undernutrition during prenatal life compromises the male germline, contributing to environmentally induced diseases (paternal transgenerational epigenetic inheritance). Men eating high saturated fat had 38% lower sperm concentrations and 41% lower sperm counts [22].

The Hertfordshire study (UK) found low birth weight (<2.5 kg) associated with coronary death, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome [22]. The Dutch Hunger Winter study showed that famine during pregnancy resulted in elevated rates of adult obesity, hyperlipidemia, and cardiovascular disease [22].

Mothers eating more animal protein had 39% higher infertility risk; those eating more vegetable protein had 22% less risk. Substituting 5% energy as vegetable protein lowered infertility risk by 50% [22].

**Early-Life Nutrition and Appetite Regulation**

Feeding behavior is a complex trait dedicated to the regulation of food intake in order to meet the physiological needs of the body. A strict regulation at the physiological level is maintained by the central nervous system which controls energy homeostasis and peripheral organs involved in food intake, and energy storage and expenditure [87]. It is now admitted that the early environment plays a major role in the establishment of feeding behavior both at the physiological and psychological levels [87].

Several animal models have clearly shown that either severe undernutrition during pregnancy or placental insufficiency induce intra-uterine growth retardation (IUGR), leading to a low birth weight associated with low plasma leptin levels [87]. The field of epigenetic research has been tremendously expanding over the last decade and the epigenetic regulation of gene expression appears to be a key mechanism in the persistent adaptation to the prenatal and early postnatal environment [87]. Maternal health and nutrition during the peri-conceptual period, pregnancy and lactation should be a major concern [87].

Fetal exposure to flavors via amniotic fluid, breastfeeding's positive effect on food acceptance, parental feeding practices, and socioeconomic context all shape feeding behavior from early life [87]. Studies on Dutch famine survivors show conflicting results regarding later food preferences (some show preference for high-fat diets). Preterm and SGA (small for gestational age) infants often experience feeding difficulties that persist through early childhood. A pilot study in Nantes found SGA babies showed greater feeding difficulties and preference for unhealthy foods at age 2 [87].

**Early-life UPF Exposure**

Poor dietary patterns during pregnancy have been associated with an increased likelihood of developing chronic diseases later in life, including obesity, cardiovascular disorders, and type 2 diabetes mellitus [88]. UPFs constitute 17.2% of the total food intake among women in their third trimester of pregnancy [88]. The period from 24 to 42 weeks of gestation represents a critical window for child neurodevelopment, during which processes such as synapse formation and myelination are actively taking place [88]. Adolescence is a critical stage of brain maturation, particularly susceptible to the effects of micronutrient deficiencies, often exacerbated by diets high in UPFs [88].

Prenatal UPF consumption is associated with adverse offspring outcomes including altered neurodevelopment, increased adiposity, and immune-related conditions. Mechanisms include nutritional deficiencies, metabolic dysregulation, inflammation, endocrine disruption, and microbiota alterations [86]. Early UPF exposure shapes long-term food preferences, with preferences for sweet/salty foods persisting into adulthood [88].

Shorter breastfeeding duration, excessive screen time, larger household size, and low parental nutrition literacy are associated with higher UPF consumption. Prolonged breastfeeding, shared family meals, and Mediterranean diet adherence are protective [86].

**Transgenerational Effects**

Transgenerational effects may occur through epigenetic modifications transmitted via germ cells [21]. Optimizing maternal nutrition represents a critical and modifiable determinant of lifelong health, with significant clinical and public health implications, offering a powerful strategy for reducing the global burden of non-communicable diseases across generations [21].

**Epigenetic Reversibility**

The take home message is that the genes people are born with can be significantly influenced to create either disease or wellness, and much of this influence relates to the lifestyle choices we make every day [22]. Epigenetic changes can be reversed by controlling lifestyle choices and environmental exposures, demonstrating that "genes are not always our destiny" [22].

### B3. MICROBIOME-ASSOCIATED SUSCEPTIBILITY

**UPF-Induced Gut Dysbiosis**

The consumption of UPFs may lead to the proliferation of pro-inflammatory microbial strains and reduced microbial α-diversity in the gut [16]. High UPF consumers show increased levels of potentially harmful bacterial groups including Granulicatella, Blautia, Carnobacteriaceae, Bacteroidaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Bacteroidia, and Bacteroidetes. Conversely, high UPF consumers showed decreased levels of Lachnospira and Roseburia, which are known producers of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [19].

UPFs, characterized by a high content of synthetic additives and emulsifiers, and low fiber content, are associated with a decrease in microbial diversity, lower levels of beneficial bacteria like Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and an increase in pro-inflammatory microorganisms [19]. These alterations in the microbial community contribute to persistent inflammation, which is associated with various chronic disorders including metabolic syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, type 2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer [19].

A randomized controlled study (RCT) conducted on human participants investigated the effects of CMC (carboxymethylcellulose) on the gut microbiome and metabolic processes. Participants who consumed CMC exhibited changes in gut microbiota composition, including decreases in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Ruminococcus sp. [19].

High-fat diets can lead to low levels of Eubacterium rectale, Bacteroides, Verrucomicrobia, Bifidobacterium, and Clostridium coccoides, as well as greater proliferation of Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, and pro-inflammatory cytokines [16]. Individuals who eat meals later in the day are more likely to consume UPFs than early eaters; a high intake of UPFs adversely impacts sleep duration and quality, irrespective of age [16].

**Metabolic Endotoxemia**

Metabolic endotoxemia is a condition in which blood lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels are elevated, regardless of the presence of obvious infection. It has been suggested to lead to chronic inflammation-related diseases such as obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), pancreatitis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease [18].

Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are large complex molecules found in gram-negative bacteria. LPS are endotoxins and when absorbed they can cause a very strong overreaction of the immune system [17]. Metabolic endotoxemia is an increased level of LPS in the bloodstream at two to three times higher than normal concentrations [17]. Through increasing inflammatory factors, it's believed LPS is the trigger for the onset of insulin resistance, obesity, and diabetes [17].

In 2007, Cani et al. showed that mice fed with a high-fat diet had higher blood LPS levels than normal chow-fed mice, resulting in inflammation of the liver and adipose tissue, which led to the development of NAFLD and insulin resistance, and the authors defined this condition as metabolic endotoxemia [18].

**Mechanisms of LPS Influx**

LPS enters the bloodstream through lipid absorption (via chylomicrons), increased intestinal permeability due to disrupted tight junctions, and potentially through constipation/peristalsis reduction. The colon is a key site for LPS absorption [18]. The LPS concentration in the portal blood is approximately 10 times higher than the LPS concentration in the peripheral blood, suggesting that a part of the LPS released in the intestinal tract is flowing from the portal vein [18]. LPS uptake in chylomicrons has been observed by immunoelectron microscopy. These results suggest that released-LPS in the intestine is taken up into micelles during lipid absorption, and then LPS is absorbed from the intestine together with lipids [18]. In mice, ingestion of a high-fat diet has been reported to increase intestinal permeability by inhibiting the mRNA expression of tight junction-related factors, zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin in intestinal epithelial cells [18].

LPS binds to various lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL, HDL), with different biological activities depending on the carrier. The liver is the primary site for LPS clearance, with Kupffer cells inactivating LPS [18].

**Dietary Factors that Decrease Blood LPS**

Prebiotics: Oligofructose, inulin, and galacto-oligosaccharides show significant reductions in blood LPS levels in human studies (8-12 weeks, 10-21 g/day) [18]. Probiotics: Mixed results in humans; animal studies show efficacy with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains [18]. Polyphenols: Limited human studies, but show potential for inhibiting postprandial LPS elevation through gut microbiota modulation [18].

**Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce LPS-Induced Endotoxemia**

Physical exercise, quercetin, curcumin, sulphorophanes, resveratrol, EPA/DHA omega fatty acids, Bifidobacteria probiotics, and Megaspore probiotic [17].

**Gut Microbiome Diversity**

We need our microbiomes to be functioning at optimum to keep the gut lining intact and reduce the chance LPS will end up in the bloodstream [17]. Eating a variety of fruits and vegetables, especially those that are high in fiber, have been shown to increase gut microbiome diversity [17]. Three ways to increase gut microbiome diversity: (1) Eat more fruits and vegetables (especially high-fiber foods like onions, leeks, garlic, asparagus, artichokes, dandelion greens); (2) Avoid sugar-free sweeteners (which cause microbiome imbalance and glucose intolerance); (3) Drink coffee (shown to improve the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio, associated with better metabolism) [17].

**UPF-Induced Dysbiosis and Disease Links**

**Diabetes:** Higher Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio and lower Akkermansia muciniphila (which improves insulin sensitivity) [16]. **Inflammatory Bowel Disease:** Reduced α-diversity and low anti-inflammatory bacteria (Roseburia hominis, Akkermansia muciniphila) [16]. **Cancer:** Colorectal cancer associated with loss of anti-inflammatory bacteria and increased pathobionts (Bacteroides fragilis, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Parvimonas micra) [16]. **Neurological Disorders:** Gut-brain axis disruption linked to Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and major depressive disorder (characterized by reduced microbial richness and diversity) [16].

### B4. PSYCHOLOGICAL AND BEHAVIORAL FACTORS

**Hedonic Hunger and UPF Consumption**

A study published in Frontiers in Public Health (February 16, 2026) investigated how food and nutrition literacy (FNL) relates to ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption, hedonic hunger, emotional eating, and sleep quality among 1,400 university students in Ankara, Türkiye (522 males, 878 females; mean age 22.1 years; 67.1% normal weight) [51]. Key findings: Females scored significantly higher than males in FNL knowledge and attitude sub-dimensions (p<0.001), but no gender difference was found in the behavior sub-dimension. Females had higher hedonic hunger (PFS scores), higher emotional eating (EEQ scores), and poorer sleep quality (PSQI scores) than males (p<0.05). No significant gender differences were found in UPF consumption. Individuals with lower FNL levels showed higher hedonic hunger, poorer sleep quality, greater UPF consumption, and more pronounced emotional eating (p<0.05). UPF consumption was high overall: 67% of participants were classified as high UPF consumers, and 77.7% had poor sleep quality. The relatively high cost of fresh fruits and vegetables compared with the low price and long shelf life of UPFs may discourage healthier choices among students with limited financial resources [51].

**Impulsivity and Delay Discounting**

A study on hedonic hunger, UPF consumption, and the moderating effects of impulsivity in pregnant individuals with BMI ≥ 25 included 220 participants (mean age 31.6 years, mean pre-pregnancy BMI 32.0) [76]. UPF consumption averaged 62.5% of total energy intake. Hedonic hunger was not significantly associated with UPF consumption (p=.47). Self-report impulsivity did not moderate this association (p=.11), but delay discounting did (p=.01). Among participants with lower delay discounting (less impulsive decision-making), a one-unit increase in hedonic hunger was associated with 7% lower UPF intake (p=.01). Among those with higher delay discounting, the association was not significant (1% higher UPF intake, p=.57). These findings contrast with research in non-pregnant samples, suggesting that lower delay discounting may serve as a protective factor during pregnancy, associated with reduced UPF consumption at higher levels of hedonic hunger [76].

Delay discounting (DD) is a measure used to assess impulsivity, quantifying how people make decisions based on time to receive and amount of reward [78]. Overeating is believed to result when the appetitive motivation to consume palatable food exceeds an individual's capacity for inhibitory control of eating [79].

The pathogenesis of food addiction involves reward dysfunction, impulsivity, and emotion dysregulation as basic mechanisms that trigger both eating dysfunctions and addictive behaviors [67].

**Stress Reactivity and Emotional Eating**

Chronic stress, via glucocorticoids, stimulates appetite for palatable foods and contributes to leptin resistance and insulin resistance [12].

Emotional eating is driven by emotional cues (depression, anxiety, happiness, boredom) rather than hunger. It is regulated by the brain's reward system, which involves motivation (wanting), outcome (liking), memory (learning), and habituation (adapting). Palatable foods (high-sugar, high-fat) act like addictive substances in the reward system [71]. About 3.5% of women and 2% of men in the US are diagnosed with binge eating disorder at some point in their lives [71].

**Mental Well-Being and UPF Consumption**

An analysis of Global Mind Project data from 400,787 adults across 60 countries, published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Bala et al., 2025), found that frequent consumption of UPFs is associated with worse overall mental well-being [54]. The study revealed that 28% of participants showed clinical mental distress levels, while 31% reported consuming UPFs at least once a week. Among those who rarely or never consumed UPFs, 20% were classified as clinically distressed, compared to 54% in the highest UPF consumption group. The main contributors to this link were increased symptoms of depression and challenges with emotional and cognitive control. The mental distress burden linked to UPF consumption in the United States and the core anglosphere was higher than the global average. The study is cross-sectional, meaning causal inferences cannot be drawn—while UPFs may worsen mental well-being, people with poor mental health may also be more likely to consume UPFs due to reduced capacity to prepare nutritious meals [54].

**Psychological Factors in Food Addiction**

At behavioral level, food addiction has high degrees of similarity with other eating disorders, a phenomenon that creates difficulties in finding specific diagnostic criteria [67]. Genetic factors, childhood traumatic experiences (CTEs), attachment insecurity, and emotional dysregulation are risk factors for food addiction [66].

### B5. SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC FACTORS

**Systematic Review of Sociodemographic Determinants**

A systematic review published in Nutrition Research Reviews (Cambridge University Press, October 31, 2023) examined sociodemographic determinants of UPF consumption using nationally representative samples [56]. The review included 55 papers spanning 32 countries and 36 nationally representative surveys. Thirteen sociodemographic variables were identified, all significantly associated with UPF intake in at least one study. Higher UPF intakes were associated with younger age, urbanization, urban residence, and being unmarried, single, separated, or divorced. UPF intake differences of 10-20% of total energy were seen across age, race/ethnicity, rural/urbanization, food insecurity, income, and region. Education, income, and socioeconomic status showed varying associations depending on the country. Household status and gender were generally not associated with UPF intake. In multivariate analyses, associations were independent of other sociodemographic factors [56].

**Country-Specific Results**

**Australia:** UPF = 38.8% of energy; younger age, lower education, and middle income associated with higher intake [56]. **Brazil:** UPF = 20-30% of energy; younger age, higher income, higher education, and urban residence associated with higher intake [56]. **Canada:** UPF ≈ 45-47% of energy; younger age, male gender, lower education, food insecurity, and non-immigrant status associated with higher intake [56]. **Chile:** UPF = 28.6%; younger age, higher income, urban residence associated with higher intake [56]. **Colombia:** UPF = 15.9%; younger age, female gender, higher socioeconomic status, urban residence associated with higher intake [56]. **France:** UPF ≈ 31%; younger age, higher education, urban residence associated with higher intake [56]. **Italy:** UPF = 17.3% in adults; younger age, female gender, urban residence, unmarried status associated with higher intake [56]. **Korea:** UPF = 24.9%; younger age, male gender, higher education, urban residence associated with higher intake [56]. **Mexico:** UPF = 29.8%; younger age, higher education, higher socioeconomic status, urban residence associated with higher intake [56]. **Netherlands:** UPF = 61% of energy; younger age, middle education, urban residence associated with higher intake [56].

The review concludes that significant sociodemographic variation exists in UPF consumption, highlighting public health inequalities and the urgent need for policy action to minimize social injustice-related health inequalities. Risk of bias assessment averaged 5.7/10 on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [56].

**U.S. Disparities in UPF Purchases**

A study from researchers at the Global Food Research Program at UNC-Chapel Hill and The George Institute for Global Health, published in Public Health Nutrition, examined over 33 million packaged food and beverage purchases from 2020 across nearly 60,000 U.S. households [58]. Nearly half of all packaged food purchases and over one-third of beverage purchases were ultra-processed. Specific categories were overwhelmingly ultra-processed — 90% of carbonated soft drinks, 81% of mixed dishes and soups, and 71% of sweets and snacks fell into the UPF category, with these three categories making up 36% of total purchases. Only 12% of purchases were minimally processed items like fruits, vegetables, nuts, and oils. Disparities were observed across socioeconomic groups: lower-income and lower-education households purchased more UPFs, while non-Hispanic White households purchased significantly more UPFs than Black, Hispanic, or other race/ethnic groups. The study underscores the need for policy interventions that address food processing levels, not just nutrient content, noting that current U.S. dietary guidelines do not make recommendations based on food processing levels unlike some other countries [58].

**Acculturation and UPF Consumption**

A study published in Frontiers in Public Health (May 15, 2025) investigated the relationship between acculturation and UPF consumption among foreign-born adults in the United States using data from 3,639 non-US born adults (aged 19-70) from NHANES 2011-2018 [57]. Overall, 43.3% of dietary energy came from UPFs among foreign-born adults. As acculturation increased, UPF consumption rose linearly: each unit increase in AcI score corresponded to a 3% increase in mean UPF consumption (β=0.03, s.e.=0.004, p<0.001). Non-Hispanic White individuals had the highest UPF intake (47.9%), while NH-Asians had the lowest (35.5%). No significant interaction was found between race/ethnicity and acculturation on UPF consumption (p=0.052), meaning the effect of acculturation on UPF intake was similar across all racial/ethnic groups. The authors recommend targeted interventions promoting healthier dietary choices while preserving culturally relevant eating habits, and improved food labeling indicating processing levels [57].

**UK Adolescents**

A study published in 2024 examined UPF consumption among UK adolescents using data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey (NDNS) spanning 2008/09 to 2018/19, analyzing 2,991 adolescents aged 11-18 years [59]. Mean UPF consumption was 861 g/day, accounting for 65.9% of total energy intake (TEI). Between 2008 and 2019, mean UPF consumption decreased from 996 to 776 g/day [−211 (95%CI −302; −120)] and from 67.7% to 62.8% of TEI [−4.8% (95%CI −8.1; −1.5)]. Higher %TEI was consumed by adolescents with lower socioeconomic status, white ethnicity, and living in England North. A higher weight of UPF consumption (g/d) was associated with being male, white, age 18y, having parents with routine or manual occupation, living in England North, and living with obesity. Adolescents from a non-white ethnicity (vs white) reported lower %TEI from UPF [−8.0% (95%CI −9.8; −6.1)] as well as those living in England South (including London) (vs England North) [−3.2% (95%CI −4.9; −1.5)]. The study found significant social and regional patterning of UPF consumption, suggesting inequalities associated with UPF intake and factors beyond individual choice [59].

**Brazilian and International Data**

A Brazilian-led study by researchers from the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation in Rio de Janeiro found a "linear dose-response association" between UPF consumption and premature death [84]. Analyzing data from eight countries, the study found that for countries like the US and UK, as many as 1 in 7 deaths could be attributed to UPF consumption. Nutritional epidemiologist Eduardo Nilson led the study, which examined dietary patterns rather than single nutrients. Latin American countries had the lowest UPF intake and premature death rates, while Anglosphere economies (Australia, Canada, UK, US) had the highest. Nilson attributes durable food cultures (Japan, Italy, France, Mediterranean countries, Brazil) as protective factors [84]. The study recommends systemic improvements including sugar taxes, zero taxes on fresh foods, incentives for farm diversification, and better labeling systems [84].

Nilson et al. (2025) found that each 10% increase in the percentage of UPFs in total energy intake corresponded to a 2.7% increase in all-cause mortality risk, with population attributable fractions ranging from 3.9% (Colombia) to ~14% (UK and US) [1].

**Maternal and Child Health**

The MAHA Report (White House, 2025) notes that over 40% of America's 73 million children (aged 0-17) have at least one chronic health condition. The U.S. ranks last in life expectancy among high-income countries despite spending more than double per capita on healthcare. Over 75% of youth aged 17-24 are ineligible for military service primarily due to obesity, poor fitness, and mental health challenges. Childhood obesity has increased over 270% since the 1970s, with severe obesity up over 500% [89].

In high-income countries, children and adolescents derive 50-60% of daily energy from UPFs (58% in US, 42% in Australia, 25.9% in Italy). In low/middle-income countries, UPFs account for 16-30% of energy intake [86]. High UPF intake is linked to excess weight gain, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular risk, dental caries (71% increased risk), and allergic diseases (atopic dermatitis, asthma) [86]. Childhood obesity rates have risen dramatically (0.7% to 5.6% in boys, 0.9% to 7.8% in girls from 1975-2016) [88].

**Health Outcomes Summary**

A 2024 review of 45 meta-analyses covering nearly 10 million participants found "convincing" evidence that high UPF consumption increases cardiovascular death risk by 50% and anxiety risk by 48%. "Highly suggestive" evidence links UPFs to 66% higher heart disease death risk, 55% higher obesity risk, 40% higher Type 2 diabetes risk, and 21% higher early death risk [2]. UPFs also harm gut health by starving gut microbes and damaging the intestinal barrier [2].

Epidemiological data show UPF consumers have 15% increased all-cause mortality risk (HR=1.15), 11% increased cardiovascular disease risk (HR=1.11), and each 10% increase in UPF intake associates with 10% higher type 2 diabetes risk (RR=1.10) [4]. UPFs have been associated with 32 health impacts including obesity, diabetes, heart disease, cancer, and cognitive decline [84].
